stink of the chemical, your own breath going hot against the little window.

Through the eyepiece, through the smoke, the winding towers.

Half past six. The guns stop.

Beside you on the ladder is {mate}. In the hood his breath goes in and out, in and out, and
you think of the cage at the top of the shaft, the gate going across, the drop.

[if war.stalled]You get your head over the top. The first wave is lying down in rows in the grass, too straight, and in front of them their wire is standing whole.[else]You get your head over the top. The first wave is walking into the smoke towards the pit heaps with their rifles at the port, and nobody's falling yet.[/if]

choices.text: Over the top. Walk with the wave. ({risk_push})
Go up with {mate}. Stay at his shoulder. ({risk_help})
Over, and straight down into the first shell hole. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_loos_pit_trench.title: Loos
b_loos_pit_trench.text:
Their front line, chalk and grey men, and then the village beyond it, and it's a pit village.
Rows of little brick houses, back to back, with their yards and their wash-houses and their
netties at the bottom, the same as Blackhaugh, only smashed. A woman's apron on a line. A
birdcage in a window with no glass. Over a shop door, in blue paint, Épicerie.

The Germans are in the cellars. You go along the rows, house by house, and the bombs go down the
cellar steps, and the cellars cough smoke and plaster dust, and sometimes men, hands up, calling Kamerad.

[if war.stalled]A machine gun in the end house opens up straight down the row, and the bombers go flat in the yards, and don't get up, and the row is theirs again.[else]The sergeant's lost his hood and half his ear. "Down the row! Clear the cellars! Go on, go on!"[/if]

choices.text: Down the row after the bombers. ({risk_push})
Stay with {mate}. Watch his back at the doors. ({risk_help})
Get down in a yard behind the wash-house wall. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_loos_pit_hold.title: Loos
b_loos_pit_hold.text:
By the afternoon you're dug in at the foot of a slag heap, a crassier on the
officers' maps, and the rain's come on. The heap's
been burning inside for years, the way they do, and where the shells have opened it the smoke
comes out yellow and stinking of sulphur, the smell of the pit heap at home on a wet night, so
strong you could cry.

Nobody's brought water. The gas has left a taste like sucking a penny.

They're on the top of the heap. They've been there all along. And now they're coming down it.

choices.text: Stand up and fire up the heap at them. ({risk_push})
Keep {mate} fed with clips. Stay low beside him. ({risk_help})
Get down in the slag and fire from cover. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

l_pit_1915.title: Home on leave
l_pit_1915.text:
The last train up the branch line, and the dark, and the pit heap glowing red on the skyline
where it's been burning since your grandfather's time, and then the smell of it through the
carriage window, sulphur and smoke, and you have to put your face against the glass.

The rows are dark. The pit buzzer goes for the night shift while you're walking up from the station,
and you stop dead in the street, because you haven't heard it in seven months, and it sounds
like a coal box coming over.

Your mother has the set-pot boiling before you're through the door. She doesn't say anything.
She puts the tin bath in front of the fire, the way she has for your father every day of his
life, and you get in it, and she washes your back, which she's not done since you were small,
and the water goes grey with France. [if flag.pit_wrote_home]Your letter's on the mantel behind the tea caddy, with your father's pay notes.[/if][if flag.pit_postcard]The field postcard is on the mantel. "Quite well," your father says, from his chair, and coughs, and says it again. "Quite well."[/if][if !flag.pit_letter]"You might have written," she says, to the set-pot.[/if]

Your father coughs half the night through the wall. He's still on the fore shift.

[if war.mate1]On the Saturday old Mr Robson takes you down to his cree at the end of the rows and shows you the young birds, one at a time, and asks after Tommy. You tell him Tommy's well.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.pit_saw_loft] You tell him what Tommy said about the army's birds. The old man laughs out loud, the first time anybody can remember. "Nowt special," he says. "Nowt special. That's my lad."[/if][if !war.mate1]The Robsons' blinds are down. Old Mr Robson's birds are still flying. He lets them out every morning and stands in the yard and watches them go round, and doesn't clock them in.[/if][if !war.mate1 && flag.pit_wrote_robson] He's had your letter. He doesn't say anything about it. He gives you a bird to take back, a blue hen, in a basket, and you can't tell him they'd never let you.[/if]

[if war.mate2 && flag.stood_with_bell]At the Miners' Hall on the Sunday, Bell's father, who's on the lodge committee, shakes your hand in front of everybody. "Our Jim says you stood up for him," he says. "In a beer vat." The whole hall laughs.[/if][if war.mate2 && flag.told_bell_shut]At the Miners' Hall, Bell's father asks after Jim, and you tell him Jim's well, still talking. "Aye," he says. "He would be. Somebody has to."[/if][if !war.mate2]Bell's father is on the lodge committee. He gets up at the Miners' Hall on the Sunday and starts to say something about his lad, and can't, and sits down.[/if][if !war.mate2 && flag.pit_wrote_bell] He keeps your letter in his jacket. He reads bits of it to men in the club who never asked.[/if]

[if war.mate3 && flag.pit_helped_charlton]Mrs Charlton has had a letter from George. He's with the horses. She reads it to you on the step, all of it, and it's all horses, a page and a half about a mule called Jerusalem, and nothing at all about the war, and she's never been so happy.[/if][if war.mate3 && !flag.pit_helped_charlton]Mrs Charlton asks if George is eating. You tell her he gives his crusts to the mules. She laughs, and says that's him, that's him.[/if][if war.mate3 && flag.pit_kept_charlton] You told him the section needed him more than the horses did. You don't tell her that.[/if][if !war.mate3]Down at the pit stables, the old horse-keeper tells you Captain's not been right since George went. He doesn't know about George yet. You don't tell him.[/if][if !war.mate3 && flag.pit_wrote_charlton] Mrs Charlton has your letter. She's put it in the Bible.[/if]

[if flag.pit_dug_out]At the club a man from the next row stands you a pint and won't say why. Later somebody tells you: his cousin was the one you dug out of the crater, and wrote home about it.[/if][if flag.pit_held_lip]In the club they've heard about the mine. Everybody wants to know about the mine, and they're pitmen, and they all know what a fall is, so you don't have to tell them much.[/if]

[if flag.pit_spoke_at_roll]On the Sunday a woman from the far end of the rows stops you on the chapel steps. "You were the one who said about our Ned," she says. "They wrote that he never knew." She holds your hand in both of hers. You don't remember if he knew. You say he didn't.[/if][if flag.pit_silent_at_roll]In the Store a woman is saying that her lad's only missing, that missing means taken, he'll turn up. You saw. You buy your father's baccy and go out without your change.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_truth]On her afternoon off Lizzie Milburn walks out along the waggonway with you towards the sea, and her sister doesn't come. She's read your letters till they've gone soft, and she asks after the rats by name. At the dunes, with the wind full of sand and the smoke of the sea-coal fires on the beach, she takes your hand and puts it in her coat pocket with hers.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_cheer]Lizzie Milburn walks the waggonway with you on her afternoon off, and at the first gate she turns round and says, "Football," and you're having a row before you know it: the lists in the Journal, the Blackhaugh lads, the letters full of eggs. She cries, cross, into her glove, and you stand there with the wind off the sea in your face. Coming back she takes your arm, tight, as if you might get away.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_little]Lizzie Milburn is coming out of the Store as you go in. She stops. "I had your card," she says. "Quite well." She looks at you a minute. "I'm glad you're quite well." She goes up the rows with her basket and doesn't look back, and then, at the top, she does.[/if]

At night you lie in your own bed and listen for the roof.

w_tunnel_pit.title: The tunnellers
w_tunnel_pit.text:
A Royal Engineers officer comes to the billet in the new year with a list. He's not like the
infantry officers. He's got clay on his boots up to the ankle and he talks like a mining
engineer, because that's what he was, and he wants colliers.

Six shillings a day, against your shilling. Work you know: picks, timber, pumps, air,
listening. The tunnellers don't go over the top. They go under it.

[if flag.pit_reported]"Somebody in this company heard them digging last summer," he says, "and told his officer, and we had that bay down to two sentries before it went." He looks round the barn. You keep quiet.[/if][if flag.pit_mine && !flag.pit_reported]"You'll have seen what a mine does," he says. "Last summer, four bays along. Eight men. That's what we're for."[/if]

[if war.mate1]Robson listens to all of it with his arms folded. "It's the face," he says to you after. "Only the face, with Fritz at the far end of it." He doesn't put his name down. "I'm stopping with the lads," he says. "Somebody has to."[/if][if war.mate2] Bell says he came out to fight the Alleyman, not to dig for him, and he's not leaving the section.[/if]

choices.text: Go to the tunnellers. You'll leave the section.
Stay with the men from home.

v16c_holland.title: F. Holland
v16c_holland.text:
A letter from Miss Holland, the fourth since Christmas. They come every fortnight now, on the
firm's paper, which she says she's not supposed to use, and she uses it anyway.

The F is for Florence. She's learned the Marine ledgers and Mr Gedge has stopped checking her
sums. She went to the Coliseum with her sister and saw a sketch about a Tommy on leave that
made her laugh and then made her cry, and she doesn't know why she's telling you that.

At the bottom, after her name, small, squeezed in: Do you think you might call me Florence, when you
write? Only if you'd like to.

choices.text: Write back. Dear Florence.
choices.text_after:
Dear Florence. You write it, and look at it, and it looks like somebody else's letter. You
tell her about the farm women and the oxen, and the nightingale, and that you'd like to go to
the Coliseum, after. You write "after" and look at that too.

choices.text: Write back as before. Dear Miss Holland.
choices.text_after:
Dear Miss Holland. You can't, yet. It feels like tempting something. You tell her about the
weather and the food and sign it with your initial, and she writes back just the same, and
doesn't mention it again.

v16c_notebook.title: The second notebook
v16c_notebook.text:
Webb's filled his first notebook. Every shell, the minnies in a column of their own, every tour, every man killed in the company with
the date and the place and how. The totals at the bottom of every page, in a column, carried
forward.

He shows you the last page by a candle. The total for 1915, for the company. It's a number. It's
only a number, in his neat office hand, and you look at it a long time.

Now he's started a second. And the new company officer has said that the next man found with a
diary will be on a charge.

choices.text: Keep the first notebook for him, sewn into your pack lining.
choices.text_after:
You sew it in that night with your housewife needle, flat against the canvas, where nobody
will look. It's there every time you put your pack on. You can feel the corners of it.

choices.text: Tell him to post it home to his mother, sealed.
choices.text_after:
He does, in a parcel with a pair of socks to darn, so the censor won't look inside. Two weeks
later his mother writes that she's had the socks. She doesn't say anything about the book.
He's not sure what that means. Neither are you.

v16c_fenton_ball.title: A new ball
v16c_fenton_ball.text:
A parcel for Fenton from his father: a new football, leather, laced, the best you can buy at
Gamages, and painted on it in white, in his father's careful sign-writer's hand: LOOS, 1915.
And under it, smaller: AND NEXT TIME.

Fenton turns it round and round in his hands. The Loos ball is out there somewhere on the
Double Crassier, gone flat in the rain.

"He's proud," he says. "He's put it up in the shop window, the newspaper bit about the football.
Everybody comes in to look." He holds the new ball against his chest. "There's going to be a big
push this summer, they're saying. I'm going to kick this one across too."

choices.text: Tell him you'll go after it with him.
choices.text_after: "Right half," he says, and grins, and you shake on it like a contract at the office.

choices.text: Tell him to leave it. Once was enough.
choices.text_after:
He looks at you, and at the ball, and puts it back in its paper. "You're right," he says.
Then, after a minute: "It's not for them, you know. The Germans. It's for us. So we're not
just walking."

v16c_marsh_school.title: The Sunday school
v16c_marsh_school.text:
Marsh has a parcel from the Sunday school at the chapel in Leyton: letters from the children,
a dozen of them, in pencil, with drawings. A soldier with a rifle bigger than he is. A ship. A
German with horns. Teacher, are you brave. Teacher, have you killed a German. Teacher, when are
you coming home.

He reads every one twice, with his steel spectacles pushed up on his forehead and the letter
held close. Then he sits with a pencil and the back of a field postcard, trying to answer.

"What do I tell them?" he says. "Have you killed a German. What do I tell them?"

choices.text: Tell him to tell them the truth, gently.
choices.text_after:
He writes it the way he'd teach a Bible story: that soldiers are frightened, and that's all
right, and that the Germans are men like their fathers, and that he hopes none of them ever
has to come here. It takes him all night. In the morning he reads it to you and asks if it's
too much. It isn't.

choices.text: Tell him to tell them about the birds and the poppies.
choices.text_after:
He writes them about the larks over the trenches, and the poppies, and the French farm dog
that kills rats. He draws a rat. They'll love the rat. He doesn't answer the question, and
neither do you.

v16c_gommecourt.title: The new trench
v16c_gommecourt.text:
June, and the whole division has dug a new trench out in no man's land, at night, four hundred yards nearer the Germans, in three nights. Clerks with picks. Three thousand of you out in the open in the dark, digging, with the moon behind cloud and the Germans watching, and for some reason
they didn't fire.

Now there's a week of bombardment, and the rumour that runs along the trench is that you're not
the real attack. You're the feint. The real push is down south, and the Londoners at Gommecourt
are here to make the Germans look the wrong way. Behind you in Funky Villas, which is all the battalion can make of
Foncquevillers, the last wall of the estaminet still says Vins et bières. The smoke candles are stacked in the bays.

Nobody knows if it's true. It doesn't help either way.

choices.text: Write a letter and leave it in your pay book.
choices.text_after:
Shorter than the one before Loos. The firm will see Mother right. My bat to the boys' club.
[if flag.c16_florence]A line to Florence that you write and cross out and write again.[/if] Love to all. You fold it small.

choices.text: Count the smoke candles. Work out whose bay they're for.
choices.text_after:
You count them like stock in a warehouse. Forty to a bay. Enough to hide a company for ten
minutes, if the wind holds. You don't know what the wind's going to do. Neither does anybody.

v16c_after.title: The lists
v16c_after.text:
The London papers come up a week late with the lists. Columns of them. The London Scottish, the
Rangers, the Queen Victoria's, the Kensingtons, the London Rifle Brigade, the whole of the division, and
under each name the regiment and the parish. Your own battalion goes on for half a page.

It was the feint. It was true. The real push was down south, and they needed the Germans to look
at Gommecourt, and they looked.

A letter comes from the manager at the Gresham and Lombard. The Roll of Honour in the front hall
is to have a second panel. They've ordered it from the same gilder.

choices.text: Read every name in the lists.
choices.text_after:
Clerks from Lloyd's, from the Pru, from the banks in Lombard Street. Men you passed in the
street at dinner time. A man you sat next to at evening classes in book-keeping. You read
them all and fold the paper and put it in your pack, and you don't know why you keep it.

choices.text: Don't. You were there.
choices.text_after:
You give the paper away to a man from Hull who wants it to light the brazier. "Napoo kindling," he says. You watch the
names go brown and curl and go.

v16c_cuffley.title: A letter from home
v16c_cuffley.text:
"Dear Son, you will have read about the airship. Your father woke me at two in the morning and
we went out in the street in our coats, the whole street did, and there it was over to the north,
caught in the searchlights, and then a little light underneath it, and then it was all on fire,
the whole length of it, red, and it came down slowly, burning, over towards Enfield. And the
whole of London cheered. You could hear it all round, miles of it, people cheering in the streets
in their night things, and the church bells, and the trains blowing their whistles.

I cheered too. Then I thought of the men in it, and I went in and sat in the kitchen. Your father
says I am too soft. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write back. Tell her she's not too soft.
choices.text_after:
You tell her she's not. You tell her that out here the men think of the men in the other
trench the same, some nights, and that nobody would ever say it in a pub at home. You don't
know if that's the kind of thing you can write. The censor lets it through.

choices.text: Keep it with the others.
choices.text_after:
It goes in your breast pocket. You read the bit about the whole of London cheering again, and
try to imagine the sound of it, and can't, and can imagine the kitchen exactly.

b_somme_city_1.title: The first of July
b_somme_city_1.text:
The first of July comes up hot, mist in the hollows, and at twenty past seven the smoke goes
over: the candles lit all down the line, thick white smoke rolling out across no man's land,
tasting of sulphur and paraffin, hiding everything.[if flag.c16_counted_smoke] Forty to a bay. You counted.[/if]

Half past seven. The whistles. You go up out of the new trench into the smoke.

[if war.path == rifleman]{mate} is beside you in the smoke, a shape, then a man, then a shape again.[/if][if war.path == nco]Seven men behind you, and in the smoke you can't see any of them.[/if][if war.path == lewis]You go in the second line with the Lewis gun on your shoulder and your No. 2 behind with the drums of cartridges.[/if][if war.path == signals]You go with the company officer, the telephone wire paying out behind you into the smoke.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You go with the bombers, a bucket of Mills bombs in each hand.[/if][if war.path == snipe]You go behind the second line with the scoped rifle, and in the smoke it's no use at all.[/if][if war.path == bearer]You go out behind the first wave with the stretcher, into the smoke, a red cross on your arm and no rifle.[/if][if war.mate2 && flag.c16_after_the_ball] Somewhere to your left, in the smoke, you hear the thump of a boot on a ball, and Fenton shouting.[/if]

[if war.stalled]The smoke thins too early. Out of it, their wire, standing, and the machine guns open up from the park at Gommecourt behind it, and men are going down all along the line before they're halfway.[else]Out of the smoke, their wire, cut, and their front trench, and nobody in it yet, because Fritz is still down his dugouts. You're in.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == lewis]Get the gun up into their trench.[/if][if war.path == signals]Keep going, paying out the wire.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Run for their trench with the buckets.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Get into their trench and find a loophole.[/if][if war.path == nco]Take the section in at a run.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]Run for their trench.[/if][if war.path == bearer]Go forward into the smoke to the men going down.[/if] ({risk_push})

[if war.path == nco]Get your wounded into a shell hole first.[/if][if war.path == lewis]Get the drums forward to the men who need them.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]Drag {mate} into a shell hole. He's hit in the leg.[/if][if war.path == signals]Stay with the officer. He's down.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Get a wounded bomber back to the new trench.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Spot for the Lewis gun beside you.[/if][if war.path == bearer]Carry the nearest man back to the new trench.[/if] ({risk_help})
Get down in the smoke. Wait for it to clear. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

l_city_1916.title: Home on leave
l_city_1916.text:
Victoria again, in your mud, at night. London's darker than last year. The lamps are painted
blue on top and there are women conductors on the buses, and girls on the Underground in
trousers from the munitions, and everybody looks tired.

Your mother's at the door. Your father shakes your hand and says, "Well, then," and goes to put
the kettle on himself, which he has never done in his life.[if flag.c16_wrote_mother] "You told her she wasn't soft," he says, from the scullery, when she's gone up. "Thank you for that."[/if]

[if flag.c16_read_lists]You know which houses in the street. You read the lists. There are three with a card in the front window now, a printed card with a name and a regiment, and a little flag.[/if][if !flag.c16_read_lists]There are three houses in the street with a card in the front window now, a name and a regiment, and a little flag. You didn't read the lists. You read them now, on the way up the street.[/if]

On the Monday, the office. The Roll of Honour has its second panel. [if flag.c16_florence]Florence meets you on the steps at one o'clock, because she said she would, and you go to the Lyons on the corner, and she has a poached egg and you have a pork pie, and you sit there in your uniform with the steam on the windows and the waitresses going past, and talk for an hour about nothing at all, and it's the best hour of the war.[/if][if flag.city_wrote_holland && !flag.c16_florence]Miss Holland is at your desk. She stands up and shakes your hand, and calls you by your surname, and so do you.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_wed16]You and Ivy are married at St Mary's on the Wednesday, by licence, with the girls from the exchange whispering in the front pews. She's in a costume her sister altered for her, with violets off a barrow. The wedding breakfast's in your mother's front room: ham, and a cake her mother saved the sugar for since the summer. You have two nights at Southend, out of season, the pier empty and the wind coming off the estuary, and the mud going out for miles under the moon.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after]On the Saturday you take Ivy to the Hollow Ponds, and by the boathouse you give her the ring from the jeweller's in the High Road. She puts it on herself before you can. "After," she says. "You said after. I'll hold you to it."[/if][if flag.ro_sw_let_go]Ivy Lambert sings the alto in the anthem at St Mary's and shakes your hand in the porch after, kind, the way she would any of the boys home.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_silent]Ivy Lambert says good evening on the church steps the way she'd say Number please.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_florence && flag.ro_sw_blessed]Ivy Lambert is in the choir at St Mary's. In the porch after she says, "Mind you don't catch a crab," and smiles, and goes off with her sister.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_florence && !flag.ro_sw_blessed]Ivy Lambert is in the choir at St Mary's. She nods to you in the porch and goes off with her sister, arm in arm.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_first && !flag.ro_sw_16 && !flag.ro_sw_ended]You take Ivy to the Forest on the Saturday, and talk about the exchange and the Zeppelins and nothing at all, and neither of you says the thing. At her gate she says, "Well," and goes in.[/if]

[if flag.ro_fr_met]Your mother wants to know what the French eat. "Oofs," you say, before you think. Eggs. Egg and chips, and she doesn't believe a word of it.[/if]

[if war.mate1 && flag.c16_kept_notebook]Mrs Webb asks if Arthur's still writing in that book. You say he is. You don't tell her the first one is in your pack, sewn into the lining.[/if][if war.mate1 && !flag.c16_kept_notebook]Mrs Webb has had a parcel of socks from Arthur, to darn, with something else inside. She hasn't opened it. She asks you if she ought.[/if][if !war.mate1]The Webbs have Arthur's card in the window.[/if][if !war.mate1 && flag.c16_kept_notebook] His first notebook is still sewn in your pack. You take it round, and put it in his mother's hands, and she holds it the way you'd hold a bird.[/if]

[if war.mate2]Fenton's father has the newspaper cutting about the football at Loos in his shop window, and a new one beside it, about the first of July, though it was a different football and a different battalion.[/if][if !war.mate2]Fenton's father has taken the football out of the shop window. The cutting's still there, gone yellow.[/if]

[if war.mate3 && flag.c16_marsh_truth]At chapel the Sunday school children have pinned Marsh's letter on the wall. The superintendent read it out to them, and some of the parents complained, and he left it up.[/if][if war.mate3 && !flag.c16_marsh_truth]At chapel the children have drawn a hundred rats, after Mr Marsh's letter.[/if][if !war.mate3]At chapel the Sunday school has a new teacher, and Leonard Marsh's spectacles case on the windowsill, which nobody will move.[/if]

{money_line}

{offers_line}

Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

v16f_tribunal.title: The tribunal
v16f_tribunal.text:
February, and the papers from home are full of the new Act. Conscription. Every single man of
military age, unless the tribunal lets him off.

And the tribunals are letting farmers' sons off. A letter from your mother: the Vellacotts' two
boys at Higher Barton went before the tribunal at South Molton, and their father stood up and
said they were needed for the harvest, and the magistrate, who hunts with Mr Vellacott, gave
them both exemption. Two great lads, twenty and twenty-two, cushy at home on the farm. And you out
here, with the Dunsworthy lads.

[if war.mate2]Pearce reads it over your shoulder. "Vellacotts," he says. "I'd have their pheasants, when I get home. Every one." He means it as a comfort, and it is, a bit.[/if]

choices.text: Write home and say what you think of the Vellacotts.
choices.text_after:
You write it in one go and post it before you can change your mind. Your mother will read it
to your father in the kitchen. Your father will say nothing, and agree with every word, and
go on buying his seed from Vellacott at market.

choices.text: Let it be. Somebody has to get the harvest in.
choices.text_after:
Somebody has to. You know it. You think of the Long Field, and your father on his own with
the old mare, and you wish, for a minute, that you'd had a magistrate who hunted.

v16f_new_officer.title: Mr Rudd
v16f_new_officer.text:
[if war.servant == 2]You've been Mr Rudd's servant since Loos.[else]Mr Rudd has had the platoon since Loos.[/if] He's from Birmingham, who was a clerk in a brass foundry and
went to the grammar school on a scholarship. Temporary gentlemen, the old officers call them,
behind their backs. He's twenty, a one-pip wonder, and he talks too much and he doesn't know a ewe from a wether.

The men from Dunsworthy don't take to him. He isn't Mr Venn. He doesn't know their mothers.[if war.mate1] He calls Will Cottle "Cottle" in the voice Mr Venn used for his dogs.[/if]

[if war.servant == 2]Now he wants to learn the ground, and he asks you, because you're his servant and the only man in the platoon who'll tell him the truth.[else]He asks the sergeant who knows the ground, and the sergeant points at you.[/if]

choices.text: Help him. He's trying, and he's as frightened as you were.
choices.text_after:
You show him where to stand, and when not to talk, and that a man from Exmoor will do
anything for an officer who says please. He learns. By May the Dunsworthy men have stopped
calling him the brass button behind his back. Mostly.

choices.text: Do your duty. Nothing more.
choices.text_after:
You do your duty, nothing more. He notices. He doesn't say anything. You see him alone in the
dugout at night writing letters, a lot of them, and you don't know who to.

v16f_dog.title: The dog
v16f_dog.text:
A dog turns up in the support line, a black and white French farm dog, thin as a rake, from
some farm that isn't there any more. She goes from man to man along the trench, sniffing, not
begging, the way a working dog looks for its master.

She stops at Cottle. Of course she does. He puts his hand down without looking and she puts her
nose in it, and that's that.

"She'm a sheepdog," he says. "Look at her eye. She's been working ewes." He gives a whistle, low,
two notes, the one he uses for Fly at home, and the dog drops flat in the mud as if she'd been
shot, and looks at him, waiting.

choices.text: Help him keep her. Share your rations.
choices.text_after:
She stays. She sleeps on Cottle's feet in the dugout and kills rats, a dozen a night, quick
and clean, a shake and a drop, and the whole platoon feeds her, and the officer pretends he
hasn't seen her. Cottle calls her Fly, the same as the dog at home, because he says he can't
be doing with learning a new name.

choices.text: Tell him she'll be shot as a stray. Send her back.
choices.text_after:
He knows. He takes her back down the communication trench himself, and the next morning she's
there again, at his feet. In the end the transport sergeant takes her for the horse lines.
Cottle goes down to see her every time you're at rest.

v16f_bert_peal.title: A quarter peal
v16f_bert_peal.text:
Bert has a letter from the tower captain at Dunsworthy, old Mr Squance, who taught him to ring
when he was twelve. Bert reads it out, because he can't keep it in.

The ringers are short, with the young men gone, so the old men and two of the girls from the
school have learned, and on Easter Sunday they rang a quarter peal of Grandsire Doubles for the
Dunsworthy men at the front. Twelve hundred and sixty changes. The first the girls ever rang.
They put all your names in the peal book.

Bert folds the letter up, and turns away, and his shoulders are going.

choices.text: Sit with him. Don't say anything.
choices.text_after:
You sit with him on the firestep. After a while he starts to say the changes under his breath,
the order of the bells, one, two, three, four, five, the way he learned them, and you can
hear the tower at home in it.

choices.text: Ask him to read out the names in the peal book.
choices.text_after: He reads them out: who rang, and who it was rung for. Your name's there. He reads it twice.

v16f_mametz.title: The model
v16f_mametz.text:
A week of bombardment, our guns day and night, and the company up in a little wood the maps call
Mansel Copse, looking out across a dip at the village of Mametz on the far slope.

An officer in the next company has made a model of the ground, in clay, on a table in a dugout,
every fold of it, and he shows it to anybody who'll look. There's a crucifix on the road by
Mametz, a shrine, and he puts his finger on it. "There's a machine gun there," he says. "And it
can see the whole of this slope. When we go over, it'll have us."

Everybody's been told the wire's cut and Fritz is dead in his dugouts. Everybody
looks at the clay.

choices.text: Write a letter and leave it in your pay book.
choices.text_after:
Shorter than the one before Loos. Tell Father to rest the mare. Tell Mother I'm not to be
fretted over. My best boots to whoever needs them. Love to all. You fold it small.

choices.text: Look at the model a long time. Learn the ground.
choices.text_after:
You learn it the way you'd learn a new farm: where the dip is, where the bank is, which side
of the copse has cover and which hasn't. When you go back to the trench and look over, the
ground fits the clay exactly, and the crucifix is just where he said.

v16f_held.title: The Devonshires
v16f_held.text:
Three days after, the Devons bury their dead from the slope below Mansel Copse, and the Dunsworthy men are laid with them, side by side. There are so
many that they don't carry them back. They put them in our old front-line trench, where they
went over from, side by side, a hundred and sixty of them, and fill it in.

Somebody makes a board for the end of it, and paints it, and nails it to a post:
THE DEVONSHIRES HELD THIS TRENCH. THE DEVONSHIRES HOLD IT STILL.

The padre reads the service. The guns are still going, further off. Larks over the slope.

choices.text: Take a shovel. Fill it in with the burial party.
choices.text_after:
It's work you know: earth, a shovel, a rhythm. You fill it in the way you'd close a drain, and
you know some of the faces before the earth goes over them, and you keep the rhythm. Your
back aches like harvest. Afterwards you can't eat.

choices.text: Stand by the board. Read it till you have it by heart.
choices.text_after: You don't need to read it twice. You'll have it by heart the rest of your life.

v16f_letter.title: A letter from home
v16f_letter.text:
"Dear Son, the harvest is in, and I do not know how. Your father and old Tucker and me and two
schoolboys from the village and the Squance girl that rings the bells. Your father was in the
field from four in the morning to dark every day for three weeks and he is not the man he was.

The blinds were down all along the street in July. Mrs Venn came down from the big house and
went in every house that had a letter and sat in the kitchen. She sat in ours an hour, in case,
she said, and drank her tea out of the cracked cup and did not seem to mind.

Keep your feet dry. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write to your father. Tell him to rest.
choices.text_after:
He won't rest. You know it. But you tell him anyway, and you tell him about the French farms,
and the stooks you saw standing out in no man's land, never carted, gone black in the rain,
because he'll understand that better than anything.

choices.text: Keep it with the others.
choices.text_after:
It goes in your breast pocket. You read the bit about Mrs Venn and the cracked cup again, by
the brazier, and can see her, in your mother's kitchen, with her gloves in her lap.

b_somme_farm_1.title: The first of July
b_somme_farm_1.text:
The first of July comes up hot, mist in the dip, burning off, and by seven the sun's on your
neck and the tin hat's hot to the hand. Larks going up over the slope. You're in the trench at the edge of Mansel Copse, sixty
pounds on your back.

Half past seven. The guns stop. The whistles.

[if war.path == rifleman]You go up the ladder with {mate} on the rung below you, and out of the trees into the open.[/if][if war.path == nco]Seven men behind you on the ladder, watching your back.[/if][if war.path == lewis]You go in the second line with the Lewis gun on your shoulder and your No. 2 behind with the drums.[/if][if war.path == signals]You go with the company officer, a reel of wire paying out behind you.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You go with the bombers, a bucket of Mills bombs in each hand.[/if][if war.path == snipe]You go behind the second line with the telescope-sighted rifle, looking for the shrine.[/if][if war.path == bearer]You go out of the copse behind the first wave with the stretcher, and the slope fills with your work before you're ten yards out.[/if][if flag.f16_learned_ground] You know the ground. You know where the bank is.[/if]

The machine gun by the crucifix opens up before the first wave is twenty yards out of the copse.
It's exactly where the officer said. It sweeps the slope like a man scything, left to right, and
the line goes down in front of it the way the corn goes down.

[if war.stalled]Nobody gets past the dip. The slope's full of men lying down, and the gun goes on.[else]Some of them get up and go on. Down into the dip, where it can't reach.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == lewis]Get the gun into a shell hole and fire on the shrine.[/if][if war.path == signals]Keep going, paying out the wire.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Run for the dip with the buckets.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Find a fire position and hunt the gun at the shrine.[/if][if war.path == nco]Take the section on at a run for the dip.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]Run for the dip.[/if][if war.path == bearer]Go down the slope to the men the gun has had.[/if] ({risk_push})

[if war.path == nco]Get your wounded back into the copse.[/if][if war.path == lewis]Get the drums forward to the men who need them.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]Drag {mate} into a shell hole. He's hit in the leg.[/if][if war.path == signals]Stay with the officer. He's down.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Get a wounded bomber back into the trees.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Spot for the Lewis gun beside you.[/if][if war.path == bearer]Carry the nearest man back into the copse.[/if] ({risk_help})
Get down. Wait for the gun to turn away. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_somme_farm_3.title: Mametz
b_somme_farm_3.text:
In the afternoon, Mametz. What's left of it: a village of rubble and cellars on the slope, brick
dust and the smell of old cider from a smashed press, and Germans in every cellar.

It goes on all afternoon. Cellar by cellar. A bomb down the steps, wait, then down after it. A
German officer comes up out of one with his hands up and his hat on straight, says "Kamerad" once, and asks for a
receipt for his men. Out of the next one comes a machine gun.

[if war.stalled]The village won't go. Every time the bombers get to a cellar, the next one opens up.[else]By evening the village is ours, or what's left of it is.[/if]

choices.text: Down the cellar steps after the bombs. ({risk_push})
Get the prisoners and the wounded out into the street. ({risk_help})
Get behind a wall and cover the cellar doors. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_somme_farm_4.title: The slope
b_somme_farm_4.text:
Night. Back down the slope below the copse, where the gun at the shrine caught the first wave,
to bring in the wounded.

It's full of men. They're lying in rows where they went down, the way a field lies after the
binder. Some of them are calling. You know the voices. That's the worst of it, at Dunsworthy you
knew everybody's voice from across a field, and you still do.

choices.text: Run for the copse with a man on your back. ({risk_push})
Crawl to the voices you know and bring them in. ({risk_help})
Crawl, shell hole to shell hole, as slow as it takes. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

l_farm_1916.title: Home on leave
l_farm_1916.text:
December, and the lane up from the carrier's cart is ice in the ruts. The farm's there. The
smoke's going up straight from the chimney. Your father's in the yard with a lantern, though it's
not milking time, because your mother told him which train.

He's smaller. He shakes your hand, and then he doesn't let go of it.[if flag.f16_wrote_father] "I had your letter," he says. "About the stooks in no man's land." He shakes his head. "Black in the rain. Never carted." It's the thing that's stayed with him, out of the whole war.[/if]

The street has its blinds down in a row. Every third house. [if flag.f16_buried]You helped fill in the trench below Mansel Copse. You know which houses before anybody tells you.[/if]

[if war.mate1 && flag.f16_kept_dog]Old Mr Cottle has had a letter from Will about a French dog called Fly. He reads it out to the real Fly, on the hearth, and she bangs her tail on the stones.[/if][if war.mate1 && !flag.f16_kept_dog]Old Mr Cottle asks after Will, and you tell him he's well.[/if][if !war.mate1]Up at Cottle's they've stopped drawing the blinds. Fly's still at the gate. She'll be there till she dies, everybody says.[/if]

[if war.mate2]Pearce's mother asks if it's true Dan's a sniper now, and whether that means he's poaching for the King, and laughs at her own joke till she has to sit down.[/if][if !war.mate2]The keeper at the big house has let the rabbits go. Nobody to set against them, he says.[/if]

[if war.mate3 && flag.f16_bert_peal]On Sunday the ringers ring for your leave. The two girls from the school are on the treble and the second, and old Mr Squance on the tenor, Bert's bell. You stand in the tower and listen, and it's like being let out of something.[/if][if war.mate3 && !flag.f16_bert_peal]On Sunday the bells ring, short-handed, for the men home on leave. They keep the tenor rope looped up for Bert.[/if][if !war.mate3]The tenor's rung half-muffled on Sundays now, for the Dunsworthy dead, and the girl who rings it was taught by Bert's old tower captain.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_wed16]You and Rose are married at Dunsworthy church on the Wednesday, the banns read three Sundays while you were still in France. The ringers ring what bells they have. She's in her mother's dress let out, with a sprig of holly because there's nothing else in December, and her father gives her away with flour on his good black coat. The wedding breakfast's at the mill: ham, cider, and a cake her mother saved the sugar for since Michaelmas. One night at the inn in South Molton, with the market under the window at five in the morning, cattle and dogs and men shouting prices, and Rose laughing into the pillow.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after]On the Sunday you walk Rose down to the mill, and on the footbridge, with the river going under brown and loud, you give her the ring from the jeweller's in Barnstaple. She puts it on herself before you can. "After," she says. "You said after. I'll hold you to it."[/if][if flag.ro_sw_let_go]Rose Huxtable is three pews ahead in church. At the lych-gate she shakes your hand and asks after your feet, kind, the way she'd ask any of the boys home.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_silent]Rose Huxtable says good morning at market the way she'd say it to the corn merchant.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_first && !flag.ro_sw_16 && !flag.ro_sw_ended]Rose walks the lane to the mill with you on the Sunday, and back, and you talk about the hoist and the tribunal and nothing at all, and neither of you says the thing. At the mill door she says, "Well," and goes in.[/if]

[if flag.ro_fr_met]Your mother wants to know what the French eat. Oofs and chips, you tell her, eggs, and she doesn't believe a word of it.[/if]

[if flag.f16_wrote_vellacott]At market your father sells two heifers to Mr Vellacott and doesn't speak to him, and Mr Vellacott doesn't look at you.[/if][if flag.f16_helped_rudd && !flag.sv_second_killed] A letter comes for you at the farm from Mr Rudd, in Birmingham on leave too, to wish you a happy Christmas. Your mother puts it on the dresser with the others.[/if]

{money_line}

{offers_line}

choices.text: Go back on the tenth day. The battalion promotes the men who return.
Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

v16_tin_hats.title: Tin hats
v16_tin_hats.text:
February, and the ground's iron. Your breath freezes on the blanket round your face and in the
morning you crack it off like the skin on cold gravy.

The tin hats come up with the rations, a whole limber of them. They're heavier than they look
and they sit on your head like a basin, and the leather lining smells of somebody else's sweat
already. The sergeant says they'll stop a splinter off a whizz-bang but not a bullet, so don't go getting ideas.

[if war.mate2]Duckworth wears his on the back of his head and calls it his Sunday best.[/if] A draft comes up the same week: Derby men, attested
last autumn, some of them older than your father, one with a cough you can hear three bays off.
They look at the old hands the way you looked at the old hands, last May.

choices.text: Show the new men how to stand on a firestep.

v16_edith.title: Edith
v16_edith.text:
Shaw has a photograph in his pay book now, between the pages where he keeps his next-of-kin.
A girl in a white blouse in front of a painted garden at the studio on Market Street, trying
not to laugh.

"Edith," he says. "Edith Holt. From the card room." He keeps it out of the wet in an oilskin
tobacco pouch. "We're getting wed. Next leave, if they give me one before Whitsun."

He's red to the ears. He keeps turning the pouch over in his fingers like a shuttle.

"Will you stand up with me? Best man. You're the one who wrote her the letters, near enough."

choices.text: Say yes. Shake his hand on it.
choices.text_after:
His grip's like a vice. "Right," he says. "Right, then." And then, because he can't think
of anything else: "She does a lovely meat-and-potato pie." It's the most words in a row
you've had out of him since France.

choices.text: Tell him to ask you after the war, when it's done.
choices.text_after:
"After the war," he says, as if he's trying the words for size. He puts the photograph back
in the pouch, and the pouch back in the pay book, carefully, and buttons the pocket.

v16_pilling_papers.title: Papers
v16_pilling_papers.text:
March, and it's Pilling's birthday, and his mam's sent a cake in a tin with SEVENTEEN TODAY
piped on it in white. Everybody in the bay reads it. Nobody says owt.

By the next morning there's a paper for him at the orderly room. His mother's written to the
War Office, and to the MP, and the War Office has finally written to the battalion. He's to go
down the line to the base, until he's old enough.

He comes and finds you behind the cook-house with the paper folded small in his fist.

"I'm not going," he says. "I'm not leaving you lot. They'll put me in a bloody bakery at Eat Apples with the base wallahs, and
you'll all be up here." His voice cracks on bloody, and he's furious about it.

choices.text: Tell him to go. Get on the lorry and don't look back.
choices.text_after:
He goes to the orderly room. He comes back an hour later without the paper. "They've lost
it," he says. He doesn't look sorry. He doesn't look at you either.

choices.text: Tell him it's his choice to make, not yours.
choices.text_after:
He tears the paper up small and puts the bits in the brazier, one at a time, and
watches each one catch. Then he cuts the cake with his bayonet, eight ways.

v16_eve_somme.title: The bombardment
v16_eve_somme.text:
A week of it. Seven days and nights of our guns, so many of them that the noise stops being
noise and turns into the ground you stand on. You feel it in your back teeth. You feel it in
your water. They say nothing can live under it. They say the wire will be cut.

At night the sky over their line flickers like the cinema on Bury Road with the reel slipping.
You can't sleep and then you sleep standing up.

The colonel comes round. Walking pace, he says. Keep your dressing. The guns will have done
it for you; you'll be in their third line by dinner time.

[if flag.last_letter]Your letter from Loos is still in your pay book, gone soft as cloth.[/if] The company sergeant major is round with the pay books again.

choices.text: Write a letter for the pay book. A new one.
choices.text_after:
It comes out different this time. Shorter. You tell them you're not frightened, which they
won't believe, and that if it comes to it, it'll have been quick, which nobody can promise.
You tell your father he was right about the trade.

choices.text: Leave the pay book as it is.
choices.text_after:
You lie on the firestep with your eyes shut and count the guns till you lose count, and
then you start again.

v16_after.title: July
v16_after.text:
For weeks after, the men who were caught on the wire are still on it. Nobody can get out to
them in daylight and at night their snipers watch the wire. July is hot. When the wind comes
from no man's land you breathe through your mouth and it doesn't help, because then you can
taste it.

The battalion that walked out on the first of July was eight hundred men and some. The one that
answered the roll the next day you could have got in the chapel. Napoo, the old hands say, and that's all they say.

One night they ask for men to go out and bring in identity discs. Just the discs. So the
mothers will know.

choices.text: Go out for the discs.
choices.text_after:
Two hours on your belly in the dark, with a pair of scissors and a sandbag. You cut the
cords by feel. Some of the faces you know by feel too. You bring back nineteen. Your hands
stink for a week however you scrub them, and you scrub them till they bleed.

choices.text: Stay in. You haven't got it in you tonight.
choices.text_after:
You lie in the dugout and listen to the others go out, and come in, one at a time, quiet.
Nobody says anything to you about it, then or after.

v16_tank.title: The tank
v16_tank.text:
September. Behind the lines one evening there's a noise like the engine house at the mill when
the big flywheel's going, and something comes down the road at walking pace that you have no
word for. An iron box the size of a tram, with a gun sticking out of each side and a tail of
two wheels dragging behind it, and it stinks of hot oil and petrol and men.

The crew climb out at the end of the road, and they're grey in the face and being sick in the
ditch, and one of them's got blood running out of his ear.

[if war.mate2]"It's a loom," says Duckworth, staring. "It's a bloody loom on legs. Me dad'd have it running in a week."[else]Somebody says it's a water carrier. Somebody says it'll end the war by Christmas. The crew don't say anything at all.[/if]

choices.text: Walk round it once. Put your hand on the iron.

v16_word_from_crater.title: A letter from the old line
v16_word_from_crater.text:
A letter comes from a man you knew at the depot, who went to the other battalion. They're in
your old line now, by the crater. He writes that it's cushy, nothing doing. He writes that they've had three
men killed in a month, all in the same bay, all through the head, all in the morning.

"The lads call him Fritz-at-the-crater," he writes, as if you wouldn't know. "Somebody says he
was there before your lot came. Somebody says he's been there since 1914."

You fold the letter up and put it with the others. You can see the bay. You can see the sack
over the low place.

choices.text: Write back. Tell him where the low places are.

b_somme_1.title: The first of July
b_somme_1.text:
The first of July comes up hot. Mist in the valley, burning off, and by seven the sun's on your
neck. You're carrying sixty-odd pounds: rifle, two hundred rounds, a pick, rations, two
sandbags, a groundsheet, a tin triangle sewn to your pack so the gunners can see how far you've
got. It's like a sack of flour on your shoulders, and the sack has to walk.

At twenty past seven, away to the south, a mine goes up under their line. The ground lifts
under your boots like the weaving shed floor when the engine starts. Then our guns stop, all of them,
and in the quiet you can hear a man three bays down being sick, and a bird, and your heart.

Half past seven. Whistles.

[if war.path == rifleman]You go up the ladder behind your corporal with {mate} on the next rung down.[/if][if war.path == nco]The section's yours now. Seven men on the ladder behind you, looking at your back to see when to go.[/if][if war.path == lewis]You go in the second line with the Lewis gun on your shoulder and your No. 2 behind you with the drums. Twenty-eight pounds of gun on top of the sixty.[/if][if war.path == signals]You go with the company officer, a reel of cable paying out behind you and the telephone banging on your hip. Battalion will want to know where the company is. The line has to get there with you.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You're with the bombers, a bucket of Mills bombs in each hand. Their trench is your job, if anybody gets there.[/if][if war.path == snipe]You go behind the second line with the scoped rifle wrapped in sacking. Their machine gunners are your job, if you can find them.[/if][if war.path == bearer]You go over behind the first wave with a stretcher, a red cross on your arm and no rifle, and the whole of no man's land in front of you is going to be your work.[/if]

[if war.stalled]By the time you're up, the first line is lying down in rows forty yards out, and the noise from the ridge has started: their machine guns, the whole length of the ridge at once, like every loom in the shed starting together. Their wire is standing. Nobody cut it. It's thick as a hedge, and there are men hung up on it like washing.[else]The first line is walking, rifles at the port, and the noise from the ridge has started: their machine guns, the whole length of the ridge at once, like every loom in the shed starting together. Men go down in rows, neatly, the way washing comes off the line in a wind. Some get up again.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == lewis]Get the gun into a shell hole and fire on their guns.[/if][if war.path == signals]Keep going, paying out the wire.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Run for their wire with the buckets.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Find a fire position and hunt their gunners.[/if][if war.path == nco]Take the section on at a walk.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]Walk on into it.[/if][if war.path == bearer]Go forward with the wave to the men going down.[/if] ({risk_push})

[if war.path == nco]Get your wounded into cover first.[/if][if war.path == lewis]Get the drums forward to the men who need them.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]Drag {mate} into a shell hole. He's hit in the leg.[/if][if war.path == signals]Stay with the officer. He's down.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Get a wounded bomber back to the sap.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Spot for the Lewis gun beside you.[/if][if war.path == bearer]Carry the nearest man back to the trench.[/if] ({risk_help})
Get down. Wait for the fire to slacken. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_somme_2.title: The first of July
b_somme_2.text:
You don't remember crossing. You remember the wire: a gap a shell had blown, men crowding to it,
and the machine gun that knew about the gap. Then you're down in their trench, and it's quiet,
and it's deep, deeper than ours, with steps cut down into the chalk. At the bottom of the steps
there's electric light. Wooden walls. Bunks with blankets. A picture postcard of a woman pinned
over a bunk, and a coffee pot, and the coffee's still warm.

Then the bombs start coming over the traverse from the next bay.

[if war.path == lewis]The gun's choked with chalk. You strip the cocking handle with your fingers shaking and it goes on the parapet, facing the wrong way, and your No. 2 is gone and you don't know when.[/if][if war.path == nco]You count your men. Four. You don't know where the others are and there isn't time to know.[/if][if war.path == signals]The wire's cut somewhere behind you. You've two pigeons in a wicker basket on your back, and one of them is dead.[/if][if war.path == bomb]This is your work. A bay at a time: pin, throw, count, round the traverse after it.[/if][if war.path == snipe]In a trench the scoped rifle's a club. You leave it in the dugout and pick up a dead man's rifle with a bayonet on.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]You've lost your corporal. {mate} is with you, white as paper, his rifle shaking.[/if][if war.path == bearer]You've a man on the stretcher already, a lad with his foot gone, and nowhere to take him but forward into their trench.[/if]

[if war.stalled]There are eleven of you. You can't see anyone else from the battalion, left or right. Behind you no man's land is a field of men lying down.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == bomb]Round the traverse with the bombs.[/if][if war.path == lewis]Clear the gun and hose the next bay.[/if][if war.path == nco]Lead the four of them round the traverse.[/if][if war.path == rifleman || war.path == signals || war.path == snipe]Round the traverse after the bombers.[/if][if war.path == bearer]Get round the traverse to the wounded there.[/if] ({risk_push})
Keep the wounded together at the dugout steps. ({risk_help})
Get down into the dugout entrance and stay there. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_somme_3.title: The first of July
b_somme_3.text:
The afternoon goes on and on. The sun comes round and the trench fills with heat and flies.
You've drunk your water. You've drunk the water of the dead man by the steps. Your lips have
split and your tongue's a strip of leather.

Nobody's coming. Every time anyone puts his head over the back, towards our line, the machine
guns open up on no man's land again, and no man's land is full of men who aren't moving, and
some who are.

[if war.path == lewis]You're on your last drum. You've been counting rounds in your head the way you'd [if start == mill]count picks on a loom[/if][if start == city]add a column of figures[/if][if start == farm]count sheep through a gate[/if].[/if][if war.path == nco]You've four men, and a lance corporal who won't stop talking about his allotment.[/if][if war.path == signals]You let the live pigeon go with a message on its leg: cut off, need bombs and water. It goes round twice and then off the right way, and you watch it till it's gone.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You've six bombs left, and their bombers have the whole of their own trench to fetch more from.[/if][if war.path == snipe || war.path == rifleman]You've ninety rounds and a bayonet and your own two hands.[/if][if war.path == bearer]You've used every field dressing you had and three you took off the dead. The wounded lie along the bottom of their trench, and there's no carrying them back across that.[/if]

They come at you from both ends of the trench at once, about four o'clock. Bombs first.

choices.text: Up on the firestep. Meet them. ({risk_push})
Pass up bombs and clips. Keep the others fighting. ({risk_help})
Stay under the parapet. Throw blind. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_somme_4.title: The first of July
b_somme_4.text:
Dark at last. Somebody says go, and you go, back over the parapet into no man's land.

It isn't empty. It's full. Men lying everywhere in the long grass, and the ones who are alive are
calling out. Water. Stretcher-bearer. Mother. A name, over and over, a girl's name. One of them
gets hold of your ankle as you go past and doesn't let go.

A flare goes up and everybody freezes and the machine guns sweep the field low, just over the
grass, and stop. The calling starts again.

choices.text: Get up and run for our wire. ({risk_push})
Bring in the man who has your ankle. ({risk_help})
Crawl, shell hole to shell hole, as slow as it takes. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_somme_autumn_1.title: The Somme, October
b_somme_autumn_1.text:
It's rained for a week. The ground between here and the next ridge isn't ground any more, it's
porridge with things in it. Your puttees are clay to the knee and the clay weighs more than
your boots.

On the right one of the new tanks is going forward, slow as a cart, rocking like a boat. It
noses down into a shell hole, and stops, and sits there tilted with its tail in the air,
smoking. Nobody climbs out.

[if war.path == lewis]The gun's wrapped in a groundsheet against the wet and it'll jam the moment it comes out.[/if][if war.path == signals]Nobody has even tried to run a wire across this. It's runners or nothing.[/if][if war.path == nco]Your section is three old hands and four lads from the last draft, who've never been over.[/if][if war.path == bomb]The bombs are wet. Half of them won't go.[/if][if war.path == snipe]You can't see fifty yards in this rain.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]{mate} goes in to the waist in the first ten yards and you haul him out by his webbing.[/if][if war.path == bearer]Four of you to a stretcher in this, and it isn't enough: the mud takes you to the knee at every step, and the man on it cries out at every jolt.[/if]

[if war.stalled]The first wave's stuck in the mud forty yards out, going nowhere, and they're being shot where they stand.[else]Whistles. Up and over, and the mud takes your boot off on the first step.[/if]

choices.text: Keep going. Get across before you sink. ({risk_push})
Haul out the men who are stuck. ({risk_help})
Get down in a shell hole, water or not. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_somme_autumn_2.title: The Somme, October
b_somme_autumn_2.text:
Their trench, when you get to it, is mostly water, with duckboards floating in it and a dead man
floating face down among the duckboards. The Germans in it are as wet and as filthy as you are.
Some of them want to surrender and some of them don't, and you can't tell which from their faces.

Somebody's bombing up the trench towards you, steady, a bay at a time.

choices.text: Go to meet them round the traverse. ({risk_push})
Get the prisoners down and the wounded out of the water. ({risk_help})
Get down behind the traverse and hold it. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_somme_autumn_3.title: The Somme, October
b_somme_autumn_3.text:
Night, and the rain again, and they come back at you out of it. You only see them by the flashes:
a helmet, a face, a man with his mouth open, gone. You fire at where the last flash was. Your
hands are so cold you can't feel the bolt.

choices.text: Stand up in the water and fire. ({risk_push})
Keep the new lads firing. Load for them. ({risk_help})
Stay down in the water and fire over the top. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

l_mill_1916.title: Home on leave
l_mill_1916.text:
December again, the second one. The town's quieter than you remember, and it takes you till the
end of the station road to work out why. There are women everywhere: on the trams, in the
railway yard in men's caps, coming off shift at the mill with their hair tied up in scarves.
And every third house has its blinds down.

July came here too. It came in August, mostly, in buff envelopes, a street at a time. Your
mother says Mrs Ormerod had two in one week.

[if war.mate1 && flag.best_man]Shaw and Edith were wed in October on his leave. You weren't there. He had his cousin stand up with him instead. Edith shows you the photograph and says, "He kept your place," and you don't know what to say to that.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.after_the_war]Edith Holt stops you on Market Street. "Has he said anything?" she says. "About after?" You tell her he has. You don't tell her he's waiting till it's over.[/if][if !war.mate1]Edith Holt is in black, though they weren't wed. Nobody tells her she can't be.[/if]

[if war.mate3]Mrs Pilling has a new hat. [if flag.urged_pilling_go]"They lost the papers," she says, "can you credit it," and looks at you as if she knows exactly who didn't lose them.[/if][if flag.let_pilling_stay]"He wrote me," she says. "He says he's needed." She says it with her mouth tight, proud and furious at once.[/if][/if][if !war.mate3]The Pillings have taken in a lodger, a Belgian. Mrs Pilling doesn't go out.[/if]

[if flag.brought_discs]Somewhere in this town a mother has a disc on a cord that you cut by feel in the dark. You'll never know which one. You look at every woman in black at chapel and wonder.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_wed16]You and Nellie are wed at chapel on the Wednesday, by licence, because there's no time for anything else. She's in a borrowed costume, blue, with a spray of wax flowers from the market, and her brothers stand at the back in their Sunday collars like bailiffs. The Sunday school does the tea: ham, and a cake her mother saved the sugar for since Whitsun. You have two nights in a boarding house at Blackpool, out of season, the wind off the sea rattling the sash and the landlady's clock on the landing striking every quarter. You hear every one.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after]On the second night you walk Nellie up to the tower in the frost and give her the ring from the jeweller's on Market Street. She puts it on herself before you can, and holds her hand up against the lights of the town below to see it. "After," she says. "You said after. I'm holding you to it."[/if][if flag.ro_sw_let_go]Nellie Whittaker is across the aisle at chapel with her mother. At the door she nods to you, kind, the way she'd nod to any lad home on leave. You go home the long way.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_silent]Nellie Whittaker crosses Bury Road when she sees you coming. You let her.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_first && !flag.ro_sw_16 && !flag.ro_sw_ended]Nellie walks up to the tower with you on the Sunday, and back, and you talk about the shed and the girls at the munitions and nothing at all, and neither of you says the thing. At her door she says, "Well," and goes in.[/if]

[if flag.ro_fr_met]Your mother wants to know what the French eat. Egg and chips, you tell her, and she doesn't believe a word of it.[/if]

Your mother took your father to see the Somme film at the Hippodrome in the summer. She tells you
about it at tea: the guns, the men going over, the wounded smiling at the camera. She wants to
know if it's like that. You say yes.

In September a Zeppelin came over in the night and bombed Bolton. Your father went up on the
roof to watch. You can hear the pride in his voice, telling it.

{money_line}

{offers_line}

choices.text: Go back on the tenth day. The battalion promotes the men who return.
Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

v16p_gone_under.title: The ones who went under
v16p_gone_under.text:
February, and eleven men from the company have gone to the tunnellers. Six shillings a day.
You see them sometimes, coming up out of a hole behind the support line at the end of a shift,
grey-white with chalk from head to foot, blinking at the daylight the way you used to at bank.
They walk different already. They walk like men going home.

The infantry don't like them. The infantry say it's a cushy job, six times the pay to stay out
of the rain. Then one night a camouflet goes up under the next company's sap, and in the morning
the tunnellers carry out four of their own, wrapped in groundsheets, and nobody says it again.

[if war.mate1]Robson watches them go down every evening. "I could have," he says.[/if]

choices.text: Stand with Robson and watch the shift go down.
choices.text_after:
Neither of you says anything. The last man down turns on the ladder, a pitman from the
next row at home, and lifts a hand to you, the way you would at the shaft top.

choices.text: Go back to the dugout. You made your choice.
choices.text_after:
You made it. You stay with it. That night, on sentry, you listen to the ground under your
boots, and it's the tunnellers you hear now, and you can't
tell if that's worse or better.

v16p_bell_brother.title: Matty Bell
v16p_bell_brother.text:
Bell's had a letter, and he's not said a word about it for two days, which is the longest
he's been quiet since the Miners' Hall.

It comes out on sentry. His brother Matty, the young one, who's not down the pit because he
was bad with his chest as a bairn and works in the Store. He's had his calling-up papers under the new Act,
and he's gone before the tribunal and said he won't. Won't fight, won't wear the uniform, won't
carry a stretcher. Conscience. The tribunal gave him nothing. He's in the guardroom at Newcastle,
and they say he'll go to prison.

"Our Matty," Bell says. "Wouldn't hurt a fly. Used to cry at the killing of the pig." He's
looking out at the wire. "Half the company'd shoot him. I don't know if I would."

[if war.mate1]Robson, on the next step, says nothing at all.[/if]

choices.text: Tell Bell his brother has more nerve than most of the company.
choices.text_after:
Bell looks at you a long time in the dark. "Aye," he says. "Aye. He has." And then, because
he's Bell: "Daft little beggar." He laughs, and it cracks in the middle.

choices.text: Say nowt. It's not a thing you can say anything to.
choices.text_after:
You stand the rest of the watch together and don't talk. Near dawn he hands you his tin of
tobacco without being asked, which is Bell's way of saying he knows.

v16p_birds.title: The basket
v16p_birds.text:
For the big push every company is to carry pigeons, two birds in a wicker basket, with little
aluminium tubes for messages, because the telephone wires won't last. The company officer
asks who knows birds.

Twenty men look at Robson.

He takes the basket like it's a bairn somebody's handed him. That night in the dugout he has
the lid open and the birds out, one in each hand, turning them over, looking at their eyes and
their feathers, talking to them low. "This one's a good 'un," he says. "This one wants feeding
up." He saves bits of his biscuit for them, soaked in his tea.

choices.text: [if war.path == signals]Help him look after them. Show him the message tubes.[else]Help him look after them. Learn the message tubes.[/if]
choices.text_after:
[if war.path == signals]You show him how to roll the flimsy and slide it into the tube, and he shows you how to
hold a bird so it doesn't panic:[else]He shows you how to roll the flimsy and slide it into the tube, and how to hold a bird so
it doesn't panic:[/if] firm round the wings, its feet between your fingers. It's warm, and its
heart goes like a watch. "If I'm down," Robson says, "you take the basket." It's the most
he's said about the first of July.

choices.text: Leave him to it. They're his.
choices.text_after:
He doesn't mind. He sits up with them by the candle long after the dugout's asleep, and in
the morning the basket smells of tea.

v16p_bombardment.title: The bombardment
v16p_bombardment.text:
A week of it. Our guns, all of them, day and night, and the noise goes on so long you stop
hearing it, the way you stop hearing the screens at bank, and then you only hear it when it
stops for a minute and the quiet hits you like cold water.

The lads are cheerful. Fritz is napoo, they say. Nothing can live under that. We'll walk over, the officers say. Take a
walking stick.

In front of you, across the valley, the German line goes up past the village on a little rise,
and just to the right of the village is the place they call the Glory Hole, where the lines
are so close you can hear them cough. Everybody knows by now. Under the Glory Hole the
tunnellers have put a mine. The biggest ever, they say. It goes up two minutes before zero.

[if war.mate3]Charlton's been taking mules up with ammunition every night. He says there are more guns behind you than there are lamps in the lamp cabin, wheel to wheel, all down the valley.[/if]

choices.text: Write a letter and leave it in your pay book.
choices.text_after:
It's shorter than the one before Loos. Look after Father. Make him go to the doctor. The
pit boots to whoever needs them. Love to all. You fold it small and it sits against your
chest.

choices.text: Try to sleep. You'll need it.
choices.text_after:
You lie on the firestep with your tin hat over your face and the guns going and you
sleep, an hour, two, and dream you're at the face with your father, and the roof's talking,
and he says it's all right, it's only the roof.

v16p_july.title: July
v16p_july.text:
For days after, they're still coming in from no man's land, the ones who can crawl. Then the
ones who can't are brought in by the burial parties.

The crater's a mark on everything. You can see it from anywhere: a white hole in the chalk a
hundred yards across, deep as a shaft, and men from both sides still in the bottom of it. The
smell of it comes over on the wind in the evenings, chalk and lime and the other thing.

The battalion's a third of what it was. They bring the company out to a field and sort out who's
left into new sections, and the sergeant major reads names off a list, and men from Blackhaugh
are put with men from places they've never heard of, and stand there not looking at each other.

The papers from home come up a week late. The whole of the North East is in them. Column after
column. Every village.

choices.text: Read the lists. Every name.
choices.text_after:
It takes you an hour, in small print, by the light from the dugout door. Men you went to
school with. Men you stood beside at the face. Two from your own row. You read every name
and you put the paper down, and then you pick it up and read them again.

choices.text: Don't. You were there.
choices.text_after:
You use the paper to light the brazier. It catches slowly, the lists curling and going
brown and then black, and you hold your hands over it till the warmth comes.

v16p_mule.title: The mule
v16p_mule.text:
September, and the rain's come, and the tracks behind the line have gone to porridge. You're on
a carrying party, coming back empty, and you come on Charlton's limber stuck to the axles, and
one of his mules gone off the track into a shell hole full of water. It's in up to the neck. Its
eyes are rolling. It's making a noise you didn't know a mule could make.

Charlton's in the water with it, holding its head up, talking to it, the way he used to talk
to the ponies when the roof was working. A corporal from the transport is standing on the edge
with his rifle.

"Can't get her out," the corporal says. "I've seen 'em go like this. She's finished."

"She's not," Charlton says. "She's not. Give us a rope."

choices.text: Get the party on a rope. Pull.
choices.text_after:
Eight of you on the rope, up to your knees in the porridge, heaving, and Charlton in the
water pushing from behind, and she comes out of it at last with a great sucking noise,
shaking and steaming, and stands on the track with her legs spread. Charlton puts his face
against her neck. Nobody says anything about the time.

choices.text: Tell Charlton the corporal's right. Get him out of the water.
choices.text_after:
You get him out. He comes, in the end, because he knows. He turns his back while the
corporal does it, and you stand with him on the track, and he's shaking, and it isn't the
cold. "I'll not forget her," he says. "Her name was Bella."

v16p_first_shift.title: Under
v16p_first_shift.text:
The shaft goes down from a dugout behind the support line, forty feet on a ladder, and at the
bottom it's chalk. Not coal. White chalk, wet, that glows in the candlelight and takes the print
of your hand.

You work it with a bayonet, not a pick. A pick rings. You work in your socks, on sandbags laid
along the floor, and nobody talks above a whisper, because somewhere the other side of the
chalk the Germans are working too, and listening. You prise out a lump, catch it before it
falls, pass it back hand to hand to the man with the sandbags. Hour after hour. The air's thick
