and warm and stinks of candle smoke and sweat and wet chalk, and after an hour your head aches
with it, the way it does when the air's going in an old working.

There's a canary in a cage at the face. You know what it's for. Every man here knows what it's
for. You look at it more than you look at anything.

It's the face. It's only the face. You'd forgotten how much you'd missed it, and how much you
hated it.

choices.text: Get your head down and work.

v16p_crew.title: The crew
v16p_crew.text:
There are four of you on a shift, and you live together, eat together, sleep in the same hole
in the chalk, and you know them by their breathing in the dark.

Evans is from the Rhondda, a hewer, short and wide, with a voice that fills a gallery when he
forgets to whisper. He came out on strike with the rest of South Wales last July. "They called us
traitors," he says, "and then they sent for us to dig." Pascoe's a tin miner from Camborne, old,
forty if he's a day, who's dug in Cornwall and South Africa and Montana and never once raised his
voice. And Mott, the kicker, a little Londoner who dug the tunnels for the Underground railway
lying on his back on a wooden cross, kicking out the clay with a spade on his feet. He talks
about the Tube as if it's a cathedral.

Four trades, four ways of talking. Underground none of it matters. You can all hear the same
thing.

choices.text: Tell Evans about Jim Bell in the beer vat.
choices.text_after:
Evans laughs so loud Pascoe has to put a hand over his mouth. "Your Bell," he says, in a
whisper, delighted. "I'd buy your Bell a pint. I'd buy him a barrel."

choices.text: Listen to them. Say little.
choices.text_after:
You say little. It's a pitman's way, and they're all pitmen of some sort, and they don't
mind. By the end of the month Pascoe calls you "my 'andsome" and Mott calls you "Geordie"
and Evans calls you "boyo", and you answer to all three.

v16p_charge.title: The charge
v16p_charge.text:
June, and the guns going day and night overhead so the chalk trembles, and down here it's
quiet as chapel. You're carrying the charge in.

Ammonal, in tins like syrup tins, fifty pound a time, passed hand to hand along the gallery,
man to man, in silence, from the shaft to the chamber at the end, a thousand feet away under
their line. Then sandbags to tamp it, hundreds of them, packed tight behind the charge so the
blast goes up and not back. Then the leads, paid out carefully all the way back.

It takes days. When it's done, the chamber at the end of the gallery has more explosive in it
than you thought was in the world. The men in the trench above it are Germans. You've heard
them, through the chalk, through the geophone, talking, coughing, a gramophone once.

The last tin goes in. Somebody's chalked something on it.

choices.text: Chalk your own name on a tin, and the date.
choices.text_after:
Your name, and BLACKHAUGH, and 28.6.16, in chalk on the lid, by the light of a candle. Evans
writes CYMRU on the next one. You don't know why you did it. It's like signing your name
to something before you know what it is.

choices.text: Leave it. Just get it done.
choices.text_after:
You pass the last tin on and wipe your hands on your trousers and don't look back down the
gallery. Mott, behind you, whistles under his breath, low, a music-hall tune, the
same three bars over and over, until Pascoe tells him to stop.

v16p_listening.title: The geophone
v16p_listening.text:
A listening post at the end of a gallery, alone, on your stomach in the chalk, with the two
discs of the geophone pressed to the floor and the earpieces in your ears like a doctor's. It's
so quiet you can hear your own blood.

Then you hear them. Picks, faint as a clock in the next house. A pause. Voices. Germans, talking, not whispering, the
way men talk at the face when they think nobody's near. Somebody laughs. Somebody starts singing,
a slow song, a hymn maybe, and the others join in, and it comes through the chalk thin and
far away, like the chapel choir heard from the end of the rows on a summer night.

They're close. Ten feet. Less. If they're laying a charge, it'll be under the gallery Evans and
Pascoe are working in.

The rule's simple. You report it, and the officer decides, and he'll blow a camouflet, and
the singing will stop.

choices.text: Go back and report it. Now.
choices.text_after:
The officer listens himself, then nods. The charge goes in that night, a small one, tamped
hard, meant to crush their gallery without breaking the surface. When it goes, the ground
thumps under you like a door slamming in an empty house. Next shift you listen at the same
place, a long time. Nothing. Only the chalk.

choices.text: Wait. Let them finish their song.
choices.text_after:
You lie there till they finish. It's a long song. Then you go back and report it, and the
officer blows a camouflet that night, and it's the same in the end, and it isn't. You find
yourself humming the tune for weeks, and you never learn what it was.

v16p_visit.title: The battalion
v16p_visit.text:
The battalion's out at rest in a village four miles back, and you walk over on your afternoon
off to find the lads. You try the estaminet first, Vins et Bières over the door. It takes you an
hour to find anybody you know.

It's a third of what it was. There are new faces everywhere, lads from Sunderland and Hull and
places you've never heard of, in Blackhaugh's company.

[if war.mate1]Robson's there, sat on an upturned bucket cleaning his rifle. He looks up, and nods, as if you'd been gone ten minutes. "All right," he says. "All right, Tommy," you say.[/if][if !war.mate1]Robson's not there. Somebody tells you, as if you knew.[/if][if war.mate2] Bell's there, and talks for an hour without stopping, about July, about the generals, about the wire that was never cut, and his voice goes on and on and you let it.[/if][if !war.mate2] Bell's not there either.[/if][if war.mate3] Charlton's down at the horse lines. He walks you back to the road with his hand on a mule's neck.[/if][if !war.mate3] Nobody's at the horse lines that you know.[/if]

choices.text: Stay till dark. Share what you've got.
choices.text_after:
You've a tin of pineapple chunks and twenty cigarettes, six shillings a day buys a lot,
and they go round. When you leave in the dark, walking back to your hole in the chalk, you
feel like a man who's been to a funeral and a wedding on the same day.

choices.text: Go back early. You're not one of them now.
choices.text_after:
You go before the light goes. On the road back you meet a sapper from your own company and
walk with him, and talk about timbering, and it's easier.

v16p_letter.title: A letter from home
v16p_letter.text:
"Dear Son, I hope this finds you well as it leaves us at present. Your father has had to come
off the face. His chest got too bad. They have put him on at bank on the screens with the old
men and the lads, picking stone out of the coal, and he comes home and sits in the chair and
does not say anything. He says it is like being a bairn again.

They have took boys on underground at thirteen now, they are that short. Mrs Armstrong's
youngest went down Monday. [if war.transferred]Your money came. I have bought a new mangle and put the rest in the Store, and your father says six shillings a day is more than he ever made and he does not know whether to be proud or ashamed.[/if][if !war.transferred]The whole village had the blinds down in July. There is not a row without one.[/if]

Keep your feet dry. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write to your father. Just to him.
choices.text_after:
It's the first letter you've ever written him. You don't know what to say, so you tell him
about the face, [if war.transferred]the chalk and the socks and the canary, the timbering,[/if][if !war.transferred]the timbering in the German dugouts, the depth of them,[/if] the things he'd want to know.
At the end you put: I wish you were here to see it. You don't know if that's true, but it's
what you'd say to him at the face.

choices.text: Keep it with the others.
choices.text_after:
It goes in your breast pocket. You read the bit about the screens again, by the brazier, and
you can see him, bent over the belt with the old men, picking stone, coughing.

b_somme_pit_1.title: The first of July
b_somme_pit_1.text:
The first of July comes up hot, mist in the valley burning off, and by seven the sun's on your
neck.

[if war.path == tunnel]You're at the firing point, a dugout at the head of the gallery, with the leads coming up out of the dark and the exploder on a ration box. The officer looks at his watch every half a minute. Down there, at the end of a thousand feet of chalk, is every tin you carried.[else]You're in the assembly trench at the head of the valley, sixty pounds on your back, and to your right, on the rise, is the Glory Hole. Under it is the mine. Everybody's watching it. Nobody's watching anything else.[/if]

Twenty-eight minutes past seven.[if war.path == tunnel] The officer pushes the handle down.[/if]

The ground doesn't shake. It lifts, like the floor of the cage when the brake comes off. Then
the noise, and a column of earth and chalk goes up out of the German line, higher than the pit
heap, higher than the church, higher than anything, and hangs there, and comes down. For two
minutes it rains chalk: lumps the size of a man's head, then stones, then dust, white over
everything, in your mouth, tasting of chalk and burnt ammonal.

Half past seven. Whistles. Somewhere on the left, bagpipes.

[if war.path == rifleman]You go up the ladder with {mate} on the next rung, chalk dust coming down on you both like flour.[/if][if war.path == nco]Seven men on the ladder behind you, watching your back to see when to go.[/if][if war.path == lewis]You go in the second line with the gun on your shoulder and your No. 2 behind you with the drums.[/if][if war.path == signals]You go with the company officer, a reel of wire paying out behind you.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You go with the bombers, a bucket of Mills bombs in each hand, for the crater.[/if][if war.path == snipe]You go behind the second line with the scoped rifle wrapped in sacking, looking for their machine guns.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]You go over in the second wave with a party of sappers, for the crater, to blow in any dugout that still has Germans in it.[/if][if war.path == bearer]You go over in the second wave with the stretcher, into the chalk dust, a red cross on your arm and no rifle.[/if]

[if war.stalled]The mine didn't touch the village. The machine guns in it open up straight down the valley, all of them at once, like the coal-cutter starting at the face, only it doesn't stop. The first line goes down before it's twenty yards out, in rows.[else]The first line goes forward into the white dust. The machine guns in the village open up, and men go down in rows, and some get up, and the rest go on.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == lewis]Get the gun into a shell hole and fire on the village.[/if][if war.path == signals]Keep going, paying out the wire.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Run for the crater with the buckets.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Find a fire position and hunt the guns in the village.[/if][if war.path == nco]Take the section on at a walk.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]Walk on into it.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]Go for the crater with the sappers.[/if][if war.path == bearer]Go forward into the valley to the men going down.[/if] ({risk_push})

[if war.path == nco]Get your wounded into cover first.[/if][if war.path == lewis]Get the drums forward to the men who need them.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]Drag {mate} into a shell hole. He's hit in the leg.[/if][if war.path == signals]Stay with the officer. He's down.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Get a wounded bomber back to the sap.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Spot for the Lewis gun beside you.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]Carry a wounded sapper back to the trench.[/if][if war.path == bearer]Carry the nearest man back to the trench.[/if] ({risk_help})
Get down. Wait for the fire to slacken. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_somme_pit_2.title: The crater
b_somme_pit_2.text:
The crater. You've never seen a hole like it, not at any pit, not anywhere. A hundred yards
across and deep as a shaft, white chalk sides still smoking, and men sliding down into it for
cover, ours and theirs, and at the bottom water and broken timber and things you don't look at.
[if war.path == tunnel]You made it. You carried it in, tin by tin.[/if][if war.path == tunnel && flag.p16_chalked_tin] Somewhere down in the bottom of it, in a thousand pieces, is your name.[/if]

On the far lip, what's left of their trench. Their dugouts go down thirty feet into the chalk,
timbered better than any pit you ever worked, and there are Germans in them still, and the
potato mashers start coming over the lip at you.

[if war.path == bomb]This is your work. Pin, throw, count, along the lip.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]A dugout entrance, smoke coming out of it. You've a charge in your haversack and a fuse.[/if][if war.path == nco]You count your men. Four.[/if][if war.path == lewis]The gun's choked with chalk. You strip it with your fingers shaking.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]{mate} is beside you on the lip, white with chalk, like a man come up from the screens.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == tunnel]Blow the dugout entrance.[/if][if war.path != tunnel]Go round the lip for their trench.[/if] ({risk_push})
Get the wounded down into the crater out of the fire. ({risk_help})
Get down on the crater's inside slope and stay there. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_somme_pit_3.title: The crater
b_somme_pit_3.text:
The afternoon in the crater. Hot. No water. The chalk throws the sun back at you so your eyes
run, and the flies come, thousands of them, and the shells come in on the lip and every one
brings the sides down in a slide of chalk and stones.

Nobody knows where anybody is. Battalion doesn't know where you are. The wire's long gone.

[if war.mate1 && flag.p16_birds]Robson has the basket. He writes the message out on his knee, the officer's words, slow and careful, and rolls it and slides it into the tube on the bird's leg, and holds her up in both his big hands, and lets her go. She goes up out of the crater, round once, round twice over the chalk, the way his da's birds go round over the rows, and then straight west, and Robson watches her till she's gone.[/if][if !war.mate1 && flag.p16_birds]You have the basket. Robson said you'd take it if he was down. You write the message, and roll it, and hold the bird the way he showed you, firm round the wings, and let her go. She goes round once over the crater and then west, and you watch her all the way.[/if]

Late in the afternoon they come out of the village to take the crater back.

choices.text: Up on the lip and fire into them. ({risk_push})
Pass up ammunition from the dead. ({risk_help})
Keep down inside the crater. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_somme_pit_4.title: Night
b_somme_pit_4.text:
Night, and quiet, or nearly. Out in the valley, all across it, the wounded are calling. Hundreds
of them. Water, and stretcher-bearer, and names, and mam. Some of them in Blackhaugh voices. You
know some of the voices.

You know what you'd do if a man was trapped at the face. Everybody would go. Nobody would wait to
be asked.

But this isn't the face, and the flares are going up, and their machine guns swing across the valley
every few minutes, slow, like a man sweeping a yard.

choices.text: Go back across for water and bring it out. ({risk_push})
Crawl out to the nearest voice and bring him in. ({risk_help})
Stay in the crater till you're relieved. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_butte_1.title: The Butte
b_butte_1.text:
October. The rain hasn't stopped in a fortnight and the ground's gone to a paste that takes your
boots off. In front of you, across a mile of it, there's a hill, if you can call it a hill: a
great white mound of chalk, bare, with nothing growing on it, like the pit heap at home if the
pit heap were made of bone. They call it the Butte. Fritz has tunnelled it through and
through, and it's full of machine guns.

[if war.path == tunnel]You're up with the infantry to dig them in on whatever they take, and to find the tunnels in the Butte if anybody gets there.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]{mate} goes over the bag beside you and sinks to his knees in the first yard.[/if][if war.path == nco]Your section goes over the bags behind you, slow, the mud holding every step.[/if][if war.path == lewis]The gun's caked. The drums are caked. You've wrapped the gun in a sandbag and you'll unwrap it when you get there.[/if][if war.path == signals]No wire across this. Runners. You're the runner.[/if][if war.path == bomb]The bombs are in a sandbag on your back, wrapped against the wet.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Your rifle's wrapped in sacking. You're looking for the slits in the chalk.[/if][if war.path == bearer]The stretcher's no use in this mud. You'll carry them on your back, one at a time, if you can carry them at all.[/if]

[if war.stalled]The barrage gets away from you in five minutes. Nobody can walk fast in this. The Butte opens up, and men stand stuck in the mud and are shot standing.[else]The barrage goes over, and you go after it, slow, a yard at a time, like wading the burn in flood.[/if]

choices.text: Keep up with the barrage, whatever the mud does. ({risk_push})
Pull men out of the mud as you go. ({risk_help})
Get into a shell hole and wait for the fire to slacken. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_butte_2.title: The Butte
b_butte_2.text:
A trench at the foot of the Butte, or what was one, half full of water, and Germans in it with
their hands up, and Germans in it fighting, and you can't tell which from ten yards in the
rain.

Above you, in the white side of the Butte, the slits. Every one of them a gun.

choices.text: Bomb up the slope at the nearest slit. ({risk_push})
Get the prisoners and the wounded down into the trench. ({risk_help})
Get down in the water and fire at the slits. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_butte_3.title: The Butte
b_butte_3.text:
Night, and rain, and the Butte still theirs above you, and the trench you've got is a ditch with
the dead in the water. Your hands are so cold you can't feel the bolt. Somebody passes along a
tin of rum and it's the only warm thing in France.

Before dawn they come down the Butte at you, out of the tunnels, out of the chalk, like men
coming up out of a drift mine.

choices.text: Stand up in the ditch and fire into them. ({risk_push})
Keep the next man's rifle working. ({risk_help})
Keep down below the lip of the ditch. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

l_pit_1916.title: Home on leave
l_pit_1916.text:
December, and the village is quiet the way it's never quiet. The buzzer still goes, the cage
still winds, the heap still burns red on the skyline, but the rows are full of drawn blinds and
black armbands, and the women stand in their doorways in the cold and watch you come up the
street, and you know every one of them is looking at your face to see if it's somebody else's.

Your father's in his chair by the fire. He's thinner. He doesn't get up. He holds his hand out
and you take it, and it's an old man's hand, soft from the screens, the calluses gone.[if flag.p16_wrote_father] "I got your letter," he says. He's got it in his waistcoat pocket. He doesn't say anything else about it. He doesn't need to.[/if]

[if war.transferred]Your mother's got a new mangle in the wash-house, and she shows it to you twice. "Six shillings a day," your father says, and coughs. "Down a hole. In France." He laughs till the coughing stops him. "I could have told you that was where you'd end."[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p16_chalked_tin] You don't tell anybody about the tins, and your name on the last one.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p16_blew_camouflet] Some nights in your own bed you feel the ground thump under you, like a door slamming in an empty house, and you're awake before you know why.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p16_visited] You carry the lads' messages round the rows, from the afternoon you walked over to the battalion, and the mothers make you say them twice.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p16_heard_the_song] At chapel on Sunday they sing a hymn you don't know, and for a moment, in the second verse, you think it's the one. It isn't.[/if]

[if !war.transferred && flag.p16_read_lists]You know every house with the blinds down. You read them all, in France, in small print. You go round them, one a day, and sit in their kitchens, and tell the mothers what you can.[/if][if !war.transferred && !flag.p16_read_lists]You didn't read the lists. You learn them now, walking up the rows, a blind at a time.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_wed16]You and Lizzie are wed at the chapel on the Wednesday, by licence, in a week. She's in a borrowed costume with her tram cap on top, because the girls from the depot dared her and she never could refuse a dare, and the back pews are full of conductresses. The tea's in the schoolroom: ham, pease pudding, a cake her mother saved the sugar for since October. You have one night at Whitley Bay in a boarding house that smells of mothballs and the sea, and walk the empty promenade in the morning with the waves coming up grey over the rocks.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after]On the Sunday you walk Lizzie to the end of the waggonway, where it looks over the sea, and give her the ring from the jeweller's in Grainger Street. She puts it on herself before you can. "After," she says. "You said after. I'll hold you to it, mind."[/if][if flag.ro_sw_let_go]Lizzie Milburn is in chapel with your mother, the way she said she'd be every Sunday. At the door she shakes your hand, kind, and asks after your feet.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_silent]Lizzie Milburn passes you in the rows and says good morning, the way she'd say it to the insurance man.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_first && !flag.ro_sw_16 && !flag.ro_sw_ended]Lizzie walks the waggonway with you on the Sunday, and you talk about the trams and the pit and nothing at all, and neither of you says the thing. At her mother's gate she says, "Well, then," and goes in.[/if]

[if flag.ro_fr_met]Your mother wants to know what the French eat. Egg and chips, you tell her; oofs, the lads call them. She doesn't believe a word of it.[/if]

[if war.mate2 && flag.p16_backed_matty]Mrs Bell takes you aside at the Store. Matty's in prison, in Durham. Jim wrote that you stuck up for him. She doesn't say thank you. She gives you a quarter of black bullets and goes.[/if][if !war.mate2]Bell's father doesn't come to the Miners' Hall any more. Matty's in prison. Jim's in France, under it.[/if]

[if war.mate1]Old Mr Robson's out at the cree. [if flag.p16_birds]Tommy wrote him about the basket on the first of July. He wants to know everything: which way she went, how long she circled, whether she came in. You tell him she came in. You don't know. He nods as if he knew she would.[/if][if !flag.p16_birds]He asks after Tommy, and you tell him Tommy's well, still saying nothing.[/if][/if][if !war.mate1]Old Mr Robson's given up the birds. The cree's empty, the door open, banging in the wind.[/if]

[if war.mate3 && flag.p16_saved_mule]Mrs Charlton has a letter from George, all about a mule called Bella who fell in a shell hole and came out again. "You were there," she says. "He says you were on the rope."[/if][if war.mate3 && flag.p16_shot_mule]Mrs Charlton says George's letters have gone short. She doesn't know why. You do, and don't tell her.[/if][if !war.mate3]In the pit stables, the old horse-keeper has put George's photograph up on a nail by Captain's stall.[/if]

{money_line}

{offers_line}

choices.text: Go back on the tenth day. [if war.corps == air]The squadron[else][if war.transferred]Your company[else]The battalion[/if][/if] promotes the men who return.
Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

v17c_orderly_room.title: The orderly room
v17c_orderly_room.text:
The adjutant wants a clerk. The orderly-room sergeant has gone sick and battalion headquarters
is drowning in returns: so many men to ration, so many casualties, indents for boots, the whole army
run on paper, and nobody in the battalion who can keep a ledger straight.

Somebody's told him about Webb.

It's a dugout three hundred yards behind the front line, with a table and a lamp and a typewriter.
It's still the line. But it's not a firestep. Cushy, the section would call it. Webb looks at you. He's asking.

choices.text: Tell him to take it. Somebody should keep the real books.
choices.text_after:
He takes it. You see him after in the orderly-room dugout with his sleeves rolled and his pen
going, and the returns in neat piles, and the battalion's losses in red in the casualty column.
"It's the same as my notebook," he says. "Only now it's official." It doesn't seem to help.

choices.text: Tell him the section needs him. It does.
choices.text_after:
He stays. He tells the adjutant he'd rather stop with the men from the office. The adjutant
looks at him as if he were mad. Webb goes back to the firestep and gets out his notebook.

v17c_caves.title: Under Arras
v17c_caves.text:
The night before Arras, under the town, in the old chalk quarries, with electric light strung
along the walls and thousands of men waiting. It's like the Underground on a Bank Holiday: the
same damp, the same press of bodies, the same smell of wet wool and pipe smoke and too many
people breathing.

Somebody in the next cave has a copy of Pickwick, and he's reading it aloud, the bit about the
cricket match, doing all the voices, and a whole chamber of men is listening and laughing in the
wrong places and the right ones.

choices.text: Sit and listen to Pickwick.
choices.text_after:
You sit on your tin hat with your back against a sandbag and listen to Mr Pickwick and Mr Jingle
and Dingley Dell, and for an hour there isn't a war. When the reader's voice gives out, a man
from Bermondsey takes the book and carries on, worse, and nobody minds.

choices.text: Write a letter for the pay book.
choices.text_after: The third. The firm will see Mother right. My bat to the boys' club. [if flag.c16_florence]A line to Florence, crossed out, written again, left in.[/if] You fold it small.

v17c_waac.title: Florence
v17c_waac.text:
A letter from Florence, and it isn't on the firm's paper. It's on Army paper.

She's joined the Women's Army Auxiliary Corps. They want women for clerks in France, to free the
base wallahs for the line, and she can do a ledger as well as any man in Cornhill,
and better than some. She's at a base camp on the coast. She doesn't say where; she can't. She has a khaki coat-frock to her ankles and a little cap and she shares a hut with eleven girls from
Glasgow.

"So I am in France too," she writes. "Fifty miles from you, perhaps less. It is a funny thing to
be so close and no nearer."

choices.text: Write back and tell her you're proud of her.
choices.text_after:
You tell her. You tell her you're proud, and that the base offices are lucky, and that if
they ever send you down the line wounded you'll ask at every office on the coast for a girl
who knows the Marine ledgers. You don't know if that's a proper thing to write. You post it.

choices.text: Write back and ask her to be careful.
choices.text_after:
You ask her to be careful. She writes back that she's three days' march behind the line at a
base full of clerks and cooks, and the worst danger she's met is a sergeant from Leith, and
that you are to be careful, and that she means it.

v17c_marsh.title: Signals
v17c_marsh.text:
[if war.path == signals]Marsh has been to the signals course, and they've sent him to you: the newest man in your
signal section, with crossed flags on his sleeve so new they're still bright, a buzzer he holds
like a hymn book, and two pigeons in a basket.[else]Marsh has been to the signals course. He came back with crossed flags on his sleeve and a head
full of Morse, and now he's the company's signaller, with a buzzer and a field telephone and a
reel of wire and two pigeons in a basket.[/if]

He's good at it. Better than good. It turns out a man who learned the eye chart by heart in a
night can learn anything by heart. He taps out Morse on his knee in his sleep. "It's like the
books of the Bible," he says. "You learn the order, and then it's yours."

But signallers go out to mend the wire when it's cut, and it's always cut.[if war.path == signals] And now you're
the one who sends them.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == signals]Take him out on the line yourself till he knows it.[else]Learn the Morse with him. You might be needed.[/if]
choices.text_after:
[if war.path == signals]You take him out on the line at night, the two of you, the wire running through your
fingers, and show him where the breaks come and how to find them by feel. In a week he splices
in the dark faster than you do. "Like the books of the Bible," he says.[else]He teaches you on sentry, tapping on your arm in the dark, letter by letter, the whole
alphabet in a week. By the end you can send your name and HELP and WATER and ALL WELL. "That's
all anybody ever needs to send," Marsh says.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == signals]Let him learn the line the way you did.[else]Leave him to it.[/if]
choices.text_after:
[if war.path == signals]You let him find it for himself, the way you had to. On bad nights you send him out, and
lie in the signals dugout listening to the buzzer, short, long, short, until his test call
comes through.[else]You leave him to it. On bad nights you hear the buzzer going in the signals dugout, short,
long, short, and you know it's him, and you lie and try to read it, and can't.[/if]

v17c_gothas.title: A letter from home
v17c_gothas.text:
"Dear Son, you will have read that they came in the day this time. Aeroplanes, not airships. A
whole flight of them at twenty to twelve in the morning, in the sun, and everybody in the street
stood looking up, they looked like silver birds, and then the bombs came down on the City and the
East End. Liverpool Street station. And a school in Poplar, a council school, the infants'
class. Eighteen of them, the paper says. Little ones.

Your father was at work and I did not know till three o'clock if he was all right. Now when the warning goes we go down in the crypt at St Mary's. I have been twice. It is like a Sunday school treat that has gone wrong.

[if war.mate2]Mr Fenton's shop window has gone again. He has put the football cutting back up behind a board with a hole cut in it.[/if]

Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write back. Tell her to go down the Underground every time.
choices.text_after:
You tell her to go down every time, whatever your father says, and to take the good blanket. You
don't tell her that out here it's the same, the warning and the going down, only underground
is a dugout and the blankets are wet.

choices.text: Keep it with the others.
choices.text_after:
It goes in your breast pocket. You read the bit about the infants' class again, and put it away,
and stand your sentry looking at Jerry's line, and don't think anything at all for two hours.

v17c_fenton.title: The battalion cup
v17c_fenton.text:
At rest, in July, before Wipers, the brigade has a football cup. Twelve teams, a pitch marked
out in a field with lime from the sanitary men, a real cup that the brigadier bought in
Amiens.

Fenton's captain of the battalion side. He picks a team from every company: two pitmen in the
defence, a farm lad from Exmoor in goal who can't kick but won't let anything past him, a weaver
from Lancashire on the left wing. Half the battalion's on the touchline.

choices.text: Ask Fenton for a place. Right half, the way you played before.
choices.text_after:
You play. You lose in the semi-final to a Welsh battalion, three goals to one, and Fenton
scores the one and says san fairy ann, there's next year, and the whole battalion sings on the way back to the billets, all the towns
together, pitmen and weavers and farm lads and clerks, the same songs. For a night you're one
thing.

choices.text: Cheer from the touchline.
choices.text_after:
You shout yourself hoarse. They lose in the semi-final to a Welsh battalion, three goals to one, and Fenton scores
the one, and the battalion sings all the way back to the billets, every town together, the
same songs.

v17c_mud.title: The totals
v17c_mud.text:
October in Flanders. Rain, and mud, and the duckboard tracks going out across it to nowhere.

[if war.mate1]Webb's done the totals for Passchendaele. He shows you in the candlelight, the column, carried forward. He doesn't say anything. He doesn't need to. He closes the notebook and puts it away and sits with his hands round his mug and doesn't drink it.[/if][if !war.mate1]You find yourself doing what Webb did: counting. The shells, the men, the days. You don't write it down. You can't stop counting.[/if]

choices.text: Go back up the line.

l_city_1917.title: Home on leave
l_city_1917.text:
Victoria again. London's grey and tired and hungry. There are queues outside every grocer's in
Leyton for margarine and tea and sugar, women standing two hours in the cold with their baskets,
and the bread's grey and tastes of potato.

[if war.corps == tank]They rang the bells in London for Cambrai, your father says, and he stood in the street to listen; and a fortnight later the papers went quiet and the ground was gone again. At the office the whole of the third floor wants to know what it's like inside one, and the chief clerk takes you to lunch to ask, and pays. Hot, you tell him, and loud, and you can't hear yourself think, and he writes it down. There's a tank coming to Leyton town hall in the new year for the War Bonds, a real one, and your mother means to buy a certificate off it with her savings.[if flag.tk17_told_mother] She's shown your letter to half the street. The picture's still pinned up in the scullery.[/if][if flag.tk17_kept_quiet] She had you in the motor transport, till your father showed her the picture in the scullery and the badge in your photograph. She doesn't mention your letter.[/if][/if][if war.corps == air]In Leyton nobody thinks aeroplanes are wonderful, not since the German ones came over in the summer. The boys in the street still want to know if you've seen Richthofen, and how many you've got, until their mothers call them in. Your father wants to know the pay. He works out the flying pay on the back of an envelope in pounds a year, like a clerk, and tells you how much you could put by if you were careful, and then he puts the envelope in the fire. Your mother has heard the fliers get sent home after a while, to teach. She asks if it's true. You say sometimes. A boy from two doors down asks why you don't learn to fly them yourself, and you say it'd mean months at a school in England, and your mother says she'll write to the King.[/if]

Your mother's thinner. She's given you her sugar for a week without saying. Your father's grown
a moustache and it's gone white.

When the warning goes, on your third night, the whole street goes down into the crypt at St Mary's
with their blankets and their Thermos flasks and their children, and you go with them, and sleep on
the flagstones among the tombs with your head on your kitbag, and it's the first time you've slept
underground with nobody shooting.[if flag.c17_wrote_gothas] Your mother takes the good blanket.[/if]

[if flag.c17_florence_waac && flag.c17_proud_of_florence]Florence isn't here. She's in France, at the base, in her khaki and her little cap. At the office there's a new girl at your desk, and on the desk, in a frame, a postcard from Florence of the sea at Boulogne, addressed to you, care of the Gresham and Lombard.[/if][if flag.c17_florence_waac && !flag.c17_proud_of_florence]Florence isn't at the office. She's in France. You go to the Lyons on the corner on your own and sit where she sat.[/if][if flag.c16_florence && !flag.c17_florence_waac]Florence meets you at the Lyons on the corner again. She's thinking of joining the women's army, she says, they want clerks in France. You don't know what to say. You say she'd be good at it.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_wed16]Ivy and the baby are at your mother's, in your old room, and the house smells of drying napkins and the baby's noise goes up and down the stairs. [if flag.ro_sw_named]She has the name you wrote. Your father says it's a name for a duchess, and says it at breakfast every day.[else]She's called after Ivy's mother, and you find you don't mind.[/if] At night you lie and listen to her breathe in the drawer they've made a bed of, the way you used to listen for the next shell.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_wed17]You and Ivy are married at St Mary's on the Thursday, by licence, the girls from the exchange in the front pews. There's no icing on the cake; there's no sugar in London for icing. One night at her aunt's in Walthamstow, and the guns going in the parks for a raid that doesn't come.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_wed17]Ivy wears the ring on a ribbon at the exchange, under her blouse, and on her finger on Sundays. You walk to the Hollow Ponds in sleet. [if flag.ro_sw_wait2]"After," she says. "You said it again." She laughs, and it isn't much of a laugh.[else]She doesn't ask you anything, and you could kiss her for that, and do.[/if][/if][if flag.ro_sw_jilted]You see Ivy Lambert on the High Road with Mr Pratt from the exchange, in his thick spectacles, and she sees you see her. She comes over on her own. "I'm sorry," she says. "I am." [if flag.ro_sw_blessed]"I kept your letter." You tell her he looks a good sort, and he does.[else]You tell her it doesn't matter, and she knows it does, and lets you say it.[/if][/if][if flag.ro_sw_let_go]Ivy Lambert is walking out with a clerk from the Prudential, your mother says, and seems happy.[/if]

[if flag.ro_fr_writes]In your pack there are three letters from Ternecourt, in French, that you can read about half of. You don't take them out in this house.[/if]

[if flag.c17_pickwick]You find a copy of Pickwick at the second-hand stall in Leyton market and buy it for fourpence, and read the cricket match on the tram, and laugh out loud, and the woman opposite moves seats.[/if]

[if war.mate1 && flag.c17_webb_clerk]Mrs Webb says Arthur writes that he's in an office now, at the front, doing the returns. "An office," she says. "In the trenches. Is that safe?" You tell her it's safer.[/if][if war.mate1 && !flag.c17_webb_clerk]Mrs Webb asks if Arthur's still writing in his book. You say he is.[/if][if !war.mate1]Mrs Webb gives you Arthur's pen, the one from the office, with his initials. "He'd want it used," she says.[/if]

[if war.mate2 && flag.c17_cup_played]Mr Fenton wants to hear about the brigade cup, every kick, and the Welsh, and the one goal. He has it written up on a card in the shop window by the end of the week.[/if][if war.mate2 && !flag.c17_cup_played]Mr Fenton wants to hear about Percy, every bit of him, and you tell him what you can, and leave out what you can't.[/if][if !war.mate2]Mr Fenton has given Percy's football to the boys' club. They play with it on the marshes every Saturday.[/if]

[if war.mate3 && flag.c17_learned_morse]At chapel the Sunday school children have learned Morse from Mr Marsh's letters, and tap ALL WELL to you on the pew in front.[/if][if war.mate3 && !flag.c17_learned_morse]Mrs Marsh says Leonard is a signaller now, and asks what that means, and you tell her it means he's the cleverest man in the company.[/if][if !war.mate3]At the chapel there's a brass plate for Leonard Marsh by the Sunday school door.[/if]

v17f_horses.title: The horse lines
v17f_horses.text:
April, and snow, and the whole army waiting in and under Arras. On the road out of the town the
cavalry are waiting too, a whole division of them in the fields, the horses standing in the snow
under their rugs with their heads down and their backs white, steaming, stamping, waiting for a
gap that the brass hats say the infantry will make in the morning.

You go down to look. You can't help it. It's the smell: horse and hay and wet leather, the
stable on a winter morning before your father lights the lantern. A big bay hunter turns its
head and looks at you over the rope, the way old Blossom does over the door.

The trooper who has him is a farm lad from Lincolnshire. He's been in France two years and never
once been in a charge. "Tomorrow," he says. "They keep saying tomorrow."

choices.text: Give the hunter your bread ration. Stand with him a bit.
choices.text_after:
He takes it off your palm with his lips, soft as anything, and then pushes his nose into your
chest for more, and you stand there with your face against his neck in the snow, breathing
him in, for longer than you'd like anybody to know about.

choices.text: Go back and write a letter for the pay book.
choices.text_after:
The third one. Shorter again. Rest the mare. Don't fret. Love to all. You write it in the
caves by the electric light, with the smell of the horses still on your hands.

v17f_land_girl.title: A letter from home
v17f_land_girl.text:
"Dear Son, we have a land girl. The War Agricultural Committee sent her. Her name is Miss
Pugsley and she is from Exeter and she wears breeches, in the yard, in front of everybody, and
your father did not know where to look the first week. She cannot milk. She can drive the
tractor the committee lent us, which your father cannot, and will not learn, and they argue
about it across the yard all day like an old married couple.

And there are German prisoners working on the Vellacotts' land. Six of them, with a guard. They are quiet and polite as chapel and one of them was a farmer and knows sheep, and Mr Vellacott says he
is the best shepherd he ever had and will not hear a word against him.

Keep your feet dry. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write back. Tell your father to learn the tractor.
choices.text_after:
You tell him to learn the tractor, and that you've seen what they can do out here, and that
the horse is finished whether he likes it or not. You know he won't like it. You put it gently.

choices.text: Keep it. Read the bit about the prisoners again.
choices.text_after:
A German prisoner shepherding on Vellacott's land, up on the hill with the ewes, and the moor behind him.
You read it three times. You don't know what you feel about it. You look over the parapet at
Jerry's line, a field away, and think of him.

v17f_fly.title: Fly
v17f_fly.text:
The signals officer has been watching Cottle's dog. Fly, the French one, who sleeps on his feet
and kills rats and comes to two notes of a whistle from anywhere in the line.

They're trying dogs for messages, he says. Running back with a tube on the collar when the wires
are cut and the runners are dead. He's seen her. He'd like to try her.

Cottle looks at the dog. The dog looks at Cottle.

choices.text: Tell Cottle to let her. She'll save lives.
choices.text_after:
Cottle trains her himself, behind the line, every rest day: he walks her up to the front line
and gives her to a stranger and goes back to battalion headquarters, a mile, and whistles, and
she comes. Every time, through anything. By the summer she's running messages in the line, through shellfire, with a tube on her collar.

choices.text: Tell him to keep her. She's all he's got.
choices.text_after:
He tells the officer she's too much of a pet, she'd only come to him. It's a lie and the
officer knows it. He lets it go. Cottle puts his hand on her head and leaves it there.

v17f_pearce.title: Gone
v17f_pearce.text:
Pearce is missing at morning stand-to. Rifle gone, cap gone, nobody saw him go. The sergeant's
face goes still. If he's not back by dark, he's a deserter, and you know what they do to those.

You know where he is. He's out there. He said last night there was a German sniper in the
ruined farm across the way who'd killed two men in a week, and nobody was doing anything about
it, and he'd had about enough.

choices.text: Cover for him. Tell the sergeant he's on a carrying party.
choices.text_after:
You lie. The sergeant looks at you and lets you. Pearce comes back at dusk, over the parapet,
filthy, grinning, with a German sniper's rifle with a telescope on it and a hare by the
back legs. "Carrying party," the sergeant says, loud enough for the whole bay, looking at the hare. "Was it."
The hare goes in the pot. Nobody's shot in that bay again.

choices.text: Tell the sergeant where he's gone. Before it's desertion.
choices.text_after:
The sergeant sends an officer's patrol out after dark. They meet Pearce coming back with a
German sniper's rifle and a hare. He gets seven days' pay stopped and a mention in the
colonel's report in the same week. He doesn't speak to you for a fortnight. Then he gives you
half the hare.

v17f_bert.title: Stretcher-bearer
v17f_bert.text:
Bert's asked to go to the stretcher-bearers. He's been to the sergeant major. He says he can't
keep shooting at men. He's not a conchie, he says, he'll go anywhere, he'll go in front of
everybody, only let him carry instead of shoot. The bearers have lost so many at Arras they'll
take anybody.

"I rang the bells for the funerals at home," he says. "Every one. I can carry them out of here."

choices.text: Tell him you think he's right.
choices.text_after:
He goes to the bearers the next week, with a red cross on his arm and no rifle. You see him in
the line after, at the end of every bad night, with his hands and his sleeves black, carrying,
and he looks more like himself than he has since the boat.

choices.text: Tell him the bearers die faster than anyone.
choices.text_after:
"I know," he says. "I've counted." He goes anyway. You see him on every bad night after, at the
end of a stretcher, and you can't look at him without your stomach turning over.

v17f_plough.title: The plough
v17f_plough.text:
May, behind the line, and a French farmer's ploughing the field next to the billet, right up to
the edge of the shell holes, with a cow in the shafts because his horses went to the army the
same as yours. An old man. The cow won't go straight and the furrows wander like a drunk going
home.

The farm lads stand at the hedge and watch him. You can feel every one of them wanting to go and
take the handles.

choices.text: Go and ask him for the handles. Show him a straight furrow.
choices.text_after:
He doesn't understand a word you say, and he understands everything. He gives you the
handles. The cow's a cow, but you talk to her, low, the way you'd talk to Blossom, and the
furrow goes straight to the hedge. The old man walks it and kicks the soil and nods. "C'est droit," he says: it's straight. Then he
takes the handles back, and does the next one straight himself.

choices.text: Watch from the hedge. It's his field.
choices.text_after:
It's his field and his cow and his crooked furrows. By evening the field's turned, and the
smell of it comes in through the billet window all night, turned earth, and you sleep like
you haven't since the boat.

v17f_mud.title: The gateway
v17f_mud.text:
October in Flanders, out beyond Wipers. You know this mud. It's the mud in the gateway to the Long Field in
February, where the cattle have trodden it to soup, the mud that takes your boot and keeps it.
Only here it's every field, and it goes on to the sky, and there are horses in it.

Pack animals, carrying shells up the plank roads, and when one slips off the planks it goes in to
the girth and can't get out, and the drivers shoot it where it stands and push it aside, and the
next one comes on. Along the plank road they lie every few yards, half under.

[if flag.f17_fed_the_bay]You think of the big bay hunter at Arras, in the snow, taking bread off your hand.[/if]

choices.text: Keep your eyes on the planks.

l_farm_1917.title: Home on leave
l_farm_1917.text:
December. The carrier's cart from South Molton, and the lane, and the farm in the dusk. There's a
noise in the yard you don't know, an engine, a clattering, and it's a tractor, a grey American thing, with a girl in breeches on it and your father walking beside it shouting.

[if war.corps == tank]They rang the bells at Dunsworthy for Cambrai, a whole afternoon of it; then the paper came on the carrier's cart with the ground all lost again, and the ringers felt foolish. Your father wants to know if it's like a traction engine. You tell him it's a traction engine with the threshing drum built on top and eight men shut inside the drum, and he thinks about that, and says he wouldn't. In the Royal Oak everybody wants to know what it's like inside. There's a tank coming round the big towns for the War Bonds, and Barnstaple's to have it after Christmas, they say, and the schoolmistress means to take the children on the train.[if flag.tk17_told_mother] Your mother's told the whole parish. The vicar shakes your hand at the porch as if you'd built it.[/if][if flag.tk17_kept_quiet] Your mother had you in the motor transport till the carrier told her different. She doesn't mention the letter.[/if][/if][if war.corps == air]The whole of Dunsworthy knows you fly. The schoolmaster had the children write you a letter in their best copperplate, and the vicar's prayed for the airmen two Sundays running. The land girl, Miss Pugsley, wants to know if you've seen Richthofen, and she's put out that you haven't. Your father wants to know what they pay you for it, and when you tell him he whistles, and says it's more than a horseman's wage, and then he stands in the yard looking up at the sky over the Long Field, as if he's working out how far up two miles is. Your mother asks if it's true they send the airmen home after a while, to teach the young ones. You say sometimes. Nobody asks why you don't learn to fly it yourself, and you don't say that you could put in for that too, and be months in England at a school.[/if]

[if flag.f17_tractor]"Your letter," your father says, before he's even said hello. "You and your tractor." But he's learned it. He shows you, the next morning, grim as a funeral, and drives it into the gatepost.[else]Your father won't touch it. Miss Pugsley drives it, and he follows behind on foot telling her she's doing it wrong, and she's not.[/if]

The prisoners on Vellacott's land wave to you from the hill. One of them's got Vellacott's dog at
his heel.

[if flag.f17_ploughed]You tell your father about the French farmer and his cow and the straight furrow. He laughs till he coughs. "A cow," he says. "In the shafts. Well, I've seen it all now." He tells it to everybody at market.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_wed16]Rose is living in at the farm with the baby, the way you settled it, and your mother's given her the best room and the warming pan. [if flag.ro_sw_named]The baby has the name you wrote. Your father says it's a name for the big house, and says it to the cows.[else]She's called after Rose's mother, and you find you don't mind.[/if] At night you lie and listen to her breathing in the drawer by the bed, the way you used to listen for the next shell.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_wed17]You and Rose are married at Dunsworthy church on the Thursday, the banns read while you were in France. There's no icing on the cake; there's no sugar for icing in the whole of Devon. The girls ring the trebles, and you have one night at the inn in South Molton, with the market under the window at five.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_wed17]Rose wears the ring on a string at the mill, for the machinery, and on her finger on Sundays. You walk down to the footbridge in sleet. [if flag.ro_sw_wait2]"After," she says. "You said it again." She laughs, and it isn't much of a laugh.[else]She doesn't ask you anything, and you could kiss her for that, and do.[/if][/if][if flag.ro_sw_jilted]You see Rose Huxtable at market with Harry Moule, the carrier's son, and she sees you see her. She comes across on her own. "I'm sorry," she says. "I am." [if flag.ro_sw_blessed]"I kept your letter." You tell her Harry's a good sort, and he is.[else]You tell her it doesn't matter, and she knows it does, and lets you say it.[/if][/if][if flag.ro_sw_let_go]Rose Huxtable is walking out with the young carter at Vellacott's, your mother says, and seems happy.[/if]

[if flag.ro_fr_writes]In your pack there are three letters from Ternecourt, in French, that you can read about half of. You don't take them out in this house.[/if]

[if war.mate1 && flag.f17_fly_runs]Old Mr Cottle has heard about the French Fly running messages. He sits at the fire with Will's letter, and the real Fly at his feet, and reads it to her, and she listens.[/if][if war.mate1 && !flag.f17_fly_runs && flag.f16_kept_dog]Old Mr Cottle asks after Will and the French dog, and laughs that there's two of them called Fly now.[/if][if war.mate1 && !flag.f16_kept_dog]Old Mr Cottle asks after Will, and you tell him he's well.[/if][if !war.mate1]Old Mr Cottle has stopped going to market. The sheep go on. Fly still goes to the gate.[/if]

[if war.mate2 && flag.f17_covered_pearce]Mrs Pearce has heard about the German sniper and the hare. Everybody has. Dan wrote to the keeper at the big house about it, of all people, and the keeper's had it read out in the Royal Oak.[/if][if war.mate2 && !flag.f17_covered_pearce]Mrs Pearce asks if Dan's in trouble again. You say no. She doesn't believe you.[/if][if !war.mate2]At the Royal Oak they've stopped telling the stories about Dan Pearce. Nobody can tell them right.[/if]

[if war.mate3 && flag.f17_bert_bearer]Mrs Yeo has heard Bert's a stretcher-bearer now. She's proud and frightened in equal parts and can't say which. The ringers rang for the bearers on All Souls' Day.[/if][if war.mate3 && !flag.f17_bert_bearer]Mrs Yeo asks you to look after Bert. You say you will. You don't know how.[/if][if !war.mate3]The tenor bell is rung half-muffled every Sunday now.[/if]

v17_pilling_eighteen.title: Eighteen
v17_pilling_eighteen.text:
In March Pilling turned eighteen, and nobody sent a cake. He's old enough now, in the eyes of the
War Office. He's been old enough in everybody else's for a year.

He's not the lad who cried for his mam on the boat. He volunteers for everything, raids,
patrols, wiring, as if he's owed something and means to collect it. He's got a German officer's
watch on his wrist that he won't talk about. When the new draft comes up he looks at them the
way the old sweats looked at you.

"Eighteen," he says, and laughs, and it isn't his laugh. "Me mam said I could join up at
eighteen."

choices.text: Tell him to ease off. Nobody's counting.
choices.text_after:
"Somebody is," he says. He doesn't say who. That night he's out with the wiring party,
and he comes back with his hands cut to ribbons, singing.

choices.text: Leave him be. He's a man now; it's his war.
choices.text_after:
You share your rum with him, without saying it's a birthday present, and he knows, and
doesn't say thank you, and drinks it.

v17_caves.title: The caves
v17_caves.text:
Under Arras there are caves, old chalk quarries from hundreds of years back, and the tunnellers
have joined them up into a town under the town. Thousands of you are down here, waiting. There's
electric light strung along the walls, and a light railway, and water dripping everywhere, and
the air is thick with the breath of a whole brigade and the smell of wet chalk and paraffin and
feet.

Somebody's carved his name in the chalk, and a date, and a girl's name. Somebody else has
carved a picture of a woman that the sergeant major makes them chip off.

The attack's tomorrow. Up the steps and out into the morning. You can't sleep. Nobody can.

choices.text: Write a letter for the pay book.
choices.text_after:
You write it on your knee by the electric light. It's the third one now. They get shorter
each time. This one says: Look after Mother. Tell Jack he's not to join up, whatever they
say at the drill hall.

choices.text: Carve your own name in the chalk.
choices.text_after:
You do it with your bayonet, slowly, in capitals, and the town after it, and the date. The
chalk comes away soft as cheese. It'll be there, you think, after.

v17_airman.title: Aeroplanes
v17_airman.text:
Since Arras the sky has been full of aeroplanes, Jerry's and ours, and every afternoon there's a
fight up there, Archie bursting black all round it, that you watch with your neck cricked back, like a football crowd. Ours keep
falling. The lads call it Bloody April, and they mean the Flying Corps.

One comes down near your bay in the evening, on fire, slowly, turning over and over, and you
can see a man in it. It hits beyond the support line with a sound like a dropped tray.

choices.text: Run to the wreck with the others.
choices.text_after:
There's nothing to do when you get there. The smell of the burning dope on the wings is
sweet and chemical, like pear drops, and under it the other smell. One of the lads takes
the pilot's goggles, which are lying in the grass without a mark on them. You don't stop him.

choices.text: Stay where you are. Turn away.
choices.text_after: You turn your back on it and clean your rifle, every part of it, twice, until it's dark.

v17_crater_hunt.title: The crater again
v17_crater_hunt.text:
After Arras they send the battalion north, to rest, they say, and it turns out to mean the old
line. The crater. The same bay, the same low place, the sandbags rotted and patched and rotted
again.

He's still there. Two men from the battalion you relieved were shot through the head in that bay
last month, both in the morning, both looking at the sunrise.

The sniping officer, a long thin man from Fleetwood who used to shoot rabbits for a living, is
going to have him. He wants a man who knows the ground. [if war.path == snipe]He wants you. It's your work, now.[else]He looks at you.[/if]

choices.text: Go with him. Find the man at the crater.
choices.text_after:
Three days in a hide in the old crater lip, lying in the stink of it, watching a heap of
bricks through a telescope until your eye waters. On the third morning, the flash. The
officer fires once. Nothing more comes from the bricks, that day or any day after.

Nobody ever sees him. Nobody ever knows for sure. But after that week no one is shot in that
bay again, and the men stand up in it to stretch, and after a while they forget they ever
didn't.

choices.text: Let somebody else go. You've had enough of that bay.
choices.text_after:
The officer goes with somebody else. Three days later there's a single shot from the old
crater lip, early, and then nothing, and nobody tells you anything, and you never find out
whose shot it was.

v17_shaw_father.title: A letter for Shaw
v17_shaw_father.text:
Shaw gets a letter and reads it standing up, by the ration dump, and then sits down on a box
of bombs, which you're not supposed to do, and reads it again.

"A lad," he says. "Seven pound four. Born Tuesday." He looks up at you and his face is wet and
he doesn't seem to know it. "She's calling him Albert. I told her not to. She's calling him
Albert anyway."

choices.text: Wet the baby's head with the section's rum.
choices.text_after:
The corporal looks the other way. The rum goes round the section in a mess tin lid, each man
saying something, to the lad, to Albert, to Edith, to home. Somebody sings. Shaw keeps the
letter inside his shirt against his skin.

choices.text: Take his turn on sentry so he can write back.
choices.text_after:
You stand his two hours on the firestep in the cold. Behind you in the dugout you can hear
him writing, the pencil going slow and careful, the way you taught him or the way he taught
himself.

v17_shaw_edith_writes.title: A letter for Shaw
v17_shaw_edith_writes.text:
Shaw gets a letter and reads it once and folds it small and puts it in his pocket and
goes back to cleaning his rifle.

It's two days before he says anything, and then it's in the dark, on sentry. "She's walking
out with a lad from the gasworks," he says. "Exempt. Reserved occupation." He says it as if he's
reading it off a notice. "Said she couldn't wait for after. Said after might not come."

He's quiet a long while. "She's not wrong," he says.

choices.text: Stay on the firestep with him till his turn's done.
choices.text_after:
Neither of you says anything else. Towards dawn he gives you half his cigarette without
being asked, and you smoke it, and the sky gets light over the German wire.

choices.text: Leave him be. He'll want to be on his own.
choices.text_after:
You leave him be. In the morning he's the same as always. "San fairy ann," he says, when the corporal asks about the letter, and nobody mentions Edith Holt
again, ever.

v17_mustard.title: Mustard
v17_mustard.text:
A new gas, in Flanders. The shells come over with a soft plop, not a bang, and you think
they're duds. It doesn't smell of much: mustard, some say, or garlic, or horseradish. It hangs
in the shell holes and the low places and soaks into everything.

Hours later the men who were in it start to blister, under the arms, between the legs, wherever
they were sweating. Then their eyes go. They come down the communication trench in a line, each
man with his hand on the shoulder of the man in front, bandages over their eyes, shuffling, like
a Sunday school treat going home.

choices.text: Lead the line of blinded men down to the aid post.
choices.text_after:
The first man's hand is on your shoulder all the way, light, trusting, and he keeps asking
whether it's dark yet, because he can't tell.

choices.text: Stay at your post. Somebody has to.
choices.text_after:
You watch them go past you, one hand on each shoulder, and the line goes round the traverse,
and the last man's hand is reaching for a shoulder that's already gone round the corner.

v17_mother_letter.title: A letter from home
v17_mother_letter.text:
"Dear Son, just a few lines. We are all right but the queues are something cruel, I stood two
hours for margarine Saturday and they run out before me. Sugar is a scandal. Your father says
the Germans are trying to starve us out with their submarines and they will not manage it
because Lancashire folk can live on fresh air and spite.

You will have heard about the explosion at Ashton in June. We heard it here, it rattled every
window in the street. Forty-odd killed, they say, women and children some of them.

[if !war.mate1]Mrs Shaw asked after you. She asks every week.[/if][if war.mate1]Mrs Shaw says to tell Albert his dad's chest is bad again.[/if] Look after yourself. Do not volunteer for anything. I know you. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Keep it in your breast pocket with the others.
choices.text_after:
It goes in with the rest, a fat damp wad of them now, held with a bootlace. You've never
thrown one away.

b_arras_1.title: Arras
b_arras_1.text:
Up the steps out of the caves at half past five, into sleet. After a night underground the cold
takes your breath. The guns open all at once behind you, more guns than you knew there were in
the world, and the barrage starts walking, a wall of bursts a hundred yards in front, moving
forward a bit at a time like a man pacing out an allotment.

"Lean on it," the officers keep saying. "Keep close to the barrage. Lean on it."

[if war.path == rifleman]{mate} is beside you, snow on his helmet.[/if][if war.path == nco]Your section's behind you in a line, and the new men are watching the old ones to see what to do.[/if][if war.path == lewis]The gun's on your shoulder, wet, the drums in their panniers clanking behind you.[/if][if war.path == signals]You go with the company officer and the wire goes out behind you, and for once, the first hour, it holds.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Their first trench is yours if it's still got men in it.[/if][if war.path == snipe]You go behind the first wave, looking for the machine guns the barrage missed.[/if][if war.path == bearer]You go up the steps with the stretcher folded on your shoulder, behind the first wave, into the sleet.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]You were at the end of an exit gallery with the charge set and the leads in your hand. At zero you blew the last few feet, and the daylight came down on you with the chalk, and the infantry came up past you out of the ground.[if flag.p17_exits] Your props held, every one.[/if] Now you go up after them, with a bag of charges, for their dugouts.[/if][if flag.p17_kiwi && war.path != tunnel] Keep your head down coming out the top, the New Zealander said. You keep it down.[/if]

[if war.stalled]On the left the barrage has got away from the men. It's two hundred yards ahead and their machine guns are up and firing into the gap.[else]Their front line comes up out of the sleet, smashed flat, the wire in heaps, and grey figures climbing out of it with their hands up.[/if]

choices.text: Lean on the barrage. Keep right up to it. ({risk_push})
Keep the line together. Bring up the stragglers. ({risk_help})
Get down and let the barrage go on ahead. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_arras_2.title: Arras
b_arras_2.text:
It's working. For the first time in two years, it's working. You're through their first line
and their second and there are prisoners going back past you in dozens, some of them carrying
our wounded without being asked.

Then, unbelievably, cavalry. A whole squadron of them, coming up behind you at a trot through
the snow, lances up, the horses steaming. The lads cheer them. Ten minutes later you see some of
the horses coming back with no riders.

Then a pocket of them in a sunken road that the barrage missed, firing.

choices.text: Go for the sunken road. ({risk_push})
Get the wounded and the prisoners down into cover. ({risk_help})
Get down in their trench and fire on the road. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_arras_3.title: Arras
b_arras_3.text:
By evening it's snowing properly, big wet flakes that settle on the dead. The guns can't get
forward over the broken ground and you're out on your own on the far slope, in shell holes, with
no wire, no water and no hot food. Your feet have gone.

In the dusk they come back at you, out of the village on the hill, in long grey lines.

choices.text: Stand up and fire. Stop them coming. ({risk_push})
Go along the shell holes, keep the men firing. ({risk_help})
Keep down in the shell hole. Fire from cover. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_pass_1.title: Flanders
b_pass_1.text:
In front of Wipers, and it hasn't stopped raining since the end of July. The ground here was always low and wet, and
the shelling has smashed the ditches that used to drain it, and now it's not ground. It's a sea
of mud and water with shell holes in it, rim to rim, each one full to the brim with green water
and some of them with men in.

You go up to the start line in the dark on the duckboard track, single file, a pace apart. Step
off the boards and the mud takes you to the thigh. A man two ahead slips off and goes in to his
chest and they can't get him out, and the column can't stop, and you go past him.

[if war.path == lewis]The gun's twenty-eight pounds and the mud's on it like porridge.[/if][if war.path == signals]No wire across this. Runners and pigeons, and the pigeons won't fly in the rain.[/if][if war.path == nco]You've counted your men onto the duckboards and you count them off.[/if][if war.path == bomb]The bombs are in a sandbag on your back, wrapped in your groundsheet against the wet.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Your rifle's wrapped in sacking, and so is the sight.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]You're with the tunnellers, sent up behind the infantry to turn whatever pillboxes they take into shelters, with a bag of tools and no idea where the line will be.[/if][if war.path == rifleman]{mate} has his hand on your pack strap so as not to lose you in the dark.[/if][if war.path == bearer]Six men to a stretcher on this ground, and you're one of the six.[/if]

[if war.stalled]At zero the barrage goes over and the first wave goes out after it, and the barrage gets away from them in ten minutes because nobody can walk fast in this.[else]At zero the barrage goes over, and you go out after it, slow, from shell-hole rim to shell-hole rim, like walking on a pudding.[/if]

choices.text: Keep up with the barrage, whatever the mud does. ({risk_push})
Pull men out of the shell holes as you go. ({risk_help})
Go to ground on the nearest rim. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_pass_2.title: Flanders
b_pass_2.text:
A pillbox. You've heard about them: concrete, three feet thick, half sunk in the mud, with a
machine gun firing out of a slit at the level of your knees. Our shells bounce off them. This one
sits on a little rise and fires across everything.

The bombers are working round it from the side, in the mud, a yard at a time. Somebody has to
keep its slit busy while they do.

choices.text: Work round to the back of it and bomb the door. ({risk_push})
Fire at the slit to keep their heads down. ({risk_help})
Get down behind the rim and wait for it to be over. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_pass_3.title: Flanders
b_pass_3.text:
There's no trench to hold. There's a line of shell holes with men in them, up to their waists in
water, a few yards apart, and that's the new front line. The rain keeps coming. Your rifle's so
caked with mud the bolt won't move, and you open it with the heel of your hand, and it jams again.

Their counter-attack comes in the afternoon, through the rain.

choices.text: Climb out of the water and fire standing. ({risk_push})
Keep the next hole's men supplied and firing. ({risk_help})
Stay down in the water. Fire over the rim. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_pass_4.title: Flanders
b_pass_4.text:
Night, and the relieving battalion comes up. Getting out is worse than getting in. It takes six men to carry one
stretcher across this, and they have to put it down every fifty yards, and there are more
stretchers than there are men.

Around you in the dark, in the shell holes, the wounded who can't be got to are calling. Some of
them are sliding down, slowly, into the water, and calling all the way.

choices.text: Get yourself out. Keep to the boards. ({risk_push})
Take a corner of a stretcher. ({risk_help})
Wait in the hole for the shelling to stop. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

l_mill_1917.title: Home on leave
l_mill_1917.text:
The third December. Your mother looks smaller. She's had her hair cut short, for the mill, and
she touches the back of her neck all the time as if she's forgotten.

[if war.corps == tank]The bells rang for Cambrai, your mother says, every church in the town, and folk stood in Bury Road to hear them; and a fortnight after, the paper said the ground was lost again, and nobody rang anything. Everybody wants to know what it's like inside one. At the Co-op the manager asks is it right there's a gramophone in them. In the mill yard at dinner time the weavers crowd round, and you tell them it's hot and loud and you can't hear yourself speak, and they laugh, because that's the weaving shed. There's a tank coming to the town hall after Christmas, a real one, for the War Bonds, and your mother wants you to go down and stand by it in your uniform.[if flag.tk17_told_mother] She's told the whole street you're in one. The name's written on a card behind the clock.[/if][if flag.tk17_kept_quiet] She had you in the motor transport. She looks at you a long while over the teapot, and doesn't say anything about the letter.[/if][/if][if war.corps == air]The whole street knows you fly. Our Jack's told everybody. He's got aeroplanes cut out of the papers pinned all round his bed, and he wants to know if you've seen Richthofen, and how many you've brought down, and whether you carry a revolver. You tell him you've seen a lot of sky. He asks why you don't learn to fly them yourself, and you say it'd mean months at a school in England, and your mother, at the sink, says "Well, then," and doesn't turn round. Your father wants to know what the flying pay comes to, to the penny, and writes it on the back of the rent book, and looks at it, and says it's more than a tackler gets, and doesn't sound pleased. Somebody at the mill has told your mother the airmen get sent home after a while, to teach. She asks you if it's true. You say sometimes.[/if]

There's no sugar in the tea and the bread's grey, war bread, with potato in it. She's saved
the butter ration for a week so you can have it on your first morning, and she watches you eat
it and won't have any.

[if war.mate1 && flag.best_man]Edith brings the baby round. He grabs your finger and won't let go, and Edith laughs and says he's got his father's grip, and you look at the little fist and think of Shaw's hand on the rung of the ladder at Loos.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.best_man && flag.wet_babys_head] "Albert wrote that the whole section drank his health," she says. "In rum. I hope you all had headaches."[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.best_man && flag.stood_shaws_watch] "His long letter came," she says. "Six pages. He said a pal stood his watch for him." She looks at you.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.after_the_war]Edith Holt is married, to the lad from the gasworks. You see her in the Co-op queue. She looks at you and away.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.after_the_war && flag.sat_with_shaw] You think of the firestep, and the half cigarette, and you look away first.[/if][if !war.mate1 && flag.best_man]Edith brings the baby round. She's in black. The baby grabs your finger and won't let go. "He's got his dad's grip," she says, and then she has to go outside.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_wed16]Nellie's at your mother's when you come in, with the baby in a shawl tied round the both of them, the Lancashire way, and you stand in the kitchen in your greatcoat not knowing how to hold her. [if flag.ro_sw_named]She has the name you wrote. Your mother says it's a name for a duchess, and says it all day.[else]She's called after Nellie's mother, and you find you don't mind.[/if] At night you lie awake listening to her breathe in the drawer they've made a bed of, the way you used to listen for shells.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_wed17]You and Nellie are wed at chapel on the Thursday, by licence, with the girls from her loom alley at the back in their shawls. There's no icing on the cake; there's no sugar for icing in the town. Her brothers shake your hand like men pulling on a rope. You have one night at her aunt's in Rochdale, in a back bedroom, with the goods trains going by.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_wed17]Nellie wears the ring on a ribbon round her neck at the looms, for the shuttles, and on her finger on Sundays. You walk up to the tower in sleet. [if flag.ro_sw_wait2]"After," she says at the top. "You said it again." She laughs, and it isn't much of a laugh.[else]She doesn't ask you anything, and you could kiss her for that, and do.[/if][/if][if flag.ro_sw_jilted]You see Nellie on Bury Road with Jack Kenyon, his stiff arm through hers, and she sees you see her.
