She comes over on her own. "I'm sorry," she says. "I am." [if flag.ro_sw_blessed]"I kept your letter." You tell her he looks a decent sort, and he does.[else]You say it doesn't matter, and she knows that's a lie, and lets you have it.[/if][/if][if flag.ro_sw_let_go]Nellie Whittaker is walking out with a lad from the card room, your mother says, and seems happy.[/if]

[if flag.ro_fr_writes]In your pack there are three letters from Ternecourt, in French, that you can read about half of. You don't take them out in this house.[/if]

[if war.mate3]Mrs Pilling asks if he's eating. He's eighteen and he's killed men, and he's still not eating, and you tell her he is.[/if][if !war.mate3 && flag.wrote_to_mrs_pilling]Mrs Pilling has your letter in a frame, next to his photograph.[/if]

[if flag.went_to_airman]Your mother's bought pear drops for you from the Co-op, a quarter in a paper twist, as a treat. You can't eat them. You can't say why.[/if][if flag.led_the_gassed] At chapel on Sunday the minister reads about the blind leading the blind, and you get up in the middle of it and go out.[/if]

[if flag.left_fritz]Some nights you wake to a single shot from a crater lip, and lie there not knowing whose it was.[/if]

[if flag.hunted_fritz]You don't tell anyone about the crater. There's nothing to tell, and too much.[/if][if flag.carved_name]Somewhere under Arras your name's carved in the chalk, and the town, and the date. Nobody here will ever see it.[/if]

[if war.commission]A letter has come for you, buff, official: you're to go before a board for a commission. An officer. You. Your mother reads it four times and puts it behind the clock with the rent book, and then she takes it out and reads it again.[/if]

{money_line}

{offers_line}

choices.text: Go back on the tenth day. [if war.corps == air]The squadron[else][if war.transferred]Your company[else]The battalion[/if][/if] promotes the men who return.
Go before the board. Come back an officer, a temporary gentleman.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

v17p_frost.title: Frost
v17p_frost.text:
The hardest winter anybody can remember. The ground's iron a foot down, and the bread comes up
frozen, and the tea freezes in the dixie between the cookhouse and the line. Men lose toes.
The latrine buckets freeze solid and have to be chipped.

And the battalion wants a new trench dug. In this.

The officers look at the ground and then they look at the Blackhaugh company, because
everybody knows pitmen can dig anything.

[if war.mate2]Bell's on his feet before the sergeant's finished. "Rum first," he says. "Before, not after. That's the rate for hard ground at any pit in the county." The sergeant stares at him. The officer, who's from Gateshead, starts to laugh.[else]Somebody from the back says rum first, before, not after, that's the rate for hard ground at any pit in the county. The officer, who's from Gateshead, starts to laugh.[/if]

choices.text: Get stuck in. Show them how it's done.
choices.text_after:
You get the rum first. Then you dig, all night, in shifts, the way you'd work a hard seam,
short and steady, nobody racing, the picks ringing on the frozen clay like on stone. By
dawn there's a trench where there wasn't, and the company from Hull that was meant to help
is stood watching with their hands in their armpits.

choices.text: Dig at the pit's pace. No faster than you're paid for.
choices.text_after:
Steady, and not a stroke more. The officer comes by at two in the morning and watches you
a while and says nothing, because it's the right pace, and he can see it is.

v17p_caves.title: Under Arras
v17p_caves.text:
Under Arras there are old chalk quarries, hundreds of years old, and somebody's joined them up
with tunnels into a town under the town. Thousands of you are down here waiting, under electric
light, with water dripping and the air thick with the breath of a brigade.

You can't stop looking at the workings. Galleries cut square, timbered right, the props set
true, drainage in the floor. Whoever did this knew the job. The tunnels have names painted up
at the junctions: Wellington, Auckland, Christchurch. New Zealanders, a sapper tells you. Gold
miners and navvies from the other side of the world.

The attack's in the morning. Up the steps and out.

choices.text: Find a New Zealander and ask about the timbering.
choices.text_after:
He's a big quiet man from a place called Waihi, a gold miner, and he talks timber with you
for an hour in the electric light like two men at the pit gates on a Sunday. When you go
he shakes your hand. "Good luck in the morning, mate," he says. "Keep your head down when
you come out the top. That's where Fritz'll be looking."

choices.text: Write a letter for the pay book.
choices.text_after:
The third one now. They get shorter. This one says: Look after Father. Make him rest. Tell
him the timbering here is the best I ever saw, he'd like it.

v17p_russia.title: News
v17p_russia.text:
The news comes up the line in old newspapers, and it comes all at once. The Tsar of Russia's
gone. Thrown out, by his own soldiers and his own workmen. And the Americans have come in.

Bell reads it out in the dugout by a candle, every word, twice, and then he puts the paper down
and he's grinning like a lad.

"Soldiers and workmen," he says. "Did you hear that? His own soldiers and his own workmen. Ten
million men, and they just said no more." He looks round at all of you. "Imagine that."

A corporal from another company tells him to watch his mouth. Bell doesn't hear him.

choices.text: Drink to it with him, in tea.
choices.text_after:
Two mess tins of cold tea, clinked. "To the soldiers and the workmen," Bell says, and drinks.
You drink. You don't know what you're drinking to, quite. Neither does he.

choices.text: Tell him to be careful who hears him.
choices.text_after:
"I know," he says. "I know." He folds the paper small and puts it in his breast pocket,
over his heart, and pats it. "But it happened. They can't make it not have happened."

v17p_blue_hen.title: The blue hen
v17p_blue_hen.text:
Robson has a letter from his da, and he reads it standing up, and then he sits on the firestep
with it on his knee.

The army's asking the fanciers at home for birds. His da's given them his best. The blue hen
that took first at Bedlington, and the two cocks he's been breeding off her for four years.
They've gone in a basket on the train to the army loft.

"Me da," Robson says. "He'd not sell her for ten pound. He turned down ten pound." He looks at
the letter. "He's given her to the army."

choices.text: Tell him his da's done a fine thing.
choices.text_after:
"Aye," Robson says. "Aye, he has." After a while: "Might be her carries the next one out of
a crater. Might be she knows the way better than the army's birds." He nearly smiles.

choices.text: Say nothing. Sit with him.
choices.text_after:
You sit with him. He folds the letter up small, and smaller. Then he unfolds it and reads it again,
and you know he's reading the bit about the hen.

v17p_horses.title: The horse lines
v17p_horses.text:
Flanders, and Jerry shells the horse lines at night the way he shells everything. In the morning there are horses dead in their rows, still tied, and mules lying
in the mud with their legs out stiff, and a smell of singed hair and blood and dung.

[if flag.pit_helped_charlton]Charlton's been up all night with them. He's sat in the mud with a horse's head in his lap, a big grey that can't get up, and he's stroking its face and talking to it, and he won't let the farrier near it yet.[else]Charlton went down to the horse lines as soon as he heard. He's sat in the mud with a big grey's head in his lap, a horse that can't get up, stroking its face, talking to it, and won't let the farrier near.[/if]

choices.text: Sit in the mud with him till the farrier comes.
choices.text_after:
You sit with him. The grey's breath comes slower, warm on your hands. When the farrier
comes Charlton nods, and stands, and turns his back, and you turn with him.

choices.text: Get the farrier. It's kinder.
choices.text_after:
You fetch the farrier and Charlton lets him. He doesn't look at you for two days. On the
third he gives you half his bread without a word, and that's that.

v17p_subways.title: The subways
v17p_subways.text:
They've sent the company to Arras, to help join up the old quarries under the town with
subways out to the front line, so a whole army can wait underground and come up at the
moment. New Zealanders did most of it: gold miners, navvies, men from the other side of the
world, who name their galleries after home. Wellington. Auckland. Christchurch.

Your job's the exits. Short galleries running up from the subways to just under the front-line
trench, stopped a few feet short of the air. On the morning, you'll blow the last few feet, and
the infantry will come up out of the ground.

[if war.mate1 || war.mate2 || war.mate3]Somewhere in these galleries, on the night, the Blackhaugh company will be waiting with the rest. You think of them coming up past you into the daylight.[/if]

choices.text: Do the job right. Every exit true.
choices.text_after:
You set the props in your exit as if your father were coming up through it. Evans laughs at
you for it. Then he goes back and redoes his own.

choices.text: Get it done. There's no time for the fine work.
choices.text_after:
You get it done. It's a good enough job. Pascoe goes along after you, without a word, and
knocks in two more wedges you'd missed.

v17p_gas.title: The canary
v17p_gas.text:
After a mine is blown, the gallery fills with the fumes, and the fumes don't smell of anything, and that's
what kills you. You know that. Every pitman knows that. It's afterdamp. It's the thing that
killed the men at every disaster your father ever told you about.

Pascoe went in too soon to look at the face. Now he's not answering. The canary in the cage at
the gallery mouth is on its back on the floor of the cage.

There's a Proto set hanging in the shaft dugout, the breathing apparatus, the same as the rescue
brigade's at Blackhaugh, that you trained on once on a Sunday in the Miners' Hall. The rescue
men are coming. They're ten minutes away.

choices.text: Get the Proto on and go in for him.
choices.text_after:
The mask, the nose clip, the bag on your chest, oxygen hissing, and the gallery in the light
of your lamp, quiet, and Pascoe on his face at the end of it like a man asleep. You get him
under the arms and drag him the whole way. He comes round on the shaft floor, grey and
sick, and spends a week coughing, and lives. "My 'andsome," he says, when he can talk. It's
all he says about it.

choices.text: Wait for the rescue men. That's the rule.
choices.text_after:
That's the rule, because men who go in without the training die beside the men they went
for. You know it. You wait the ten minutes. They bring him out on a stretcher, and the
officer kneels by him, and shakes his head. Pascoe, from Camborne, who dug in Cornwall and
Africa and Montana and never once raised his voice.

v17p_clay.title: Blue clay
v17p_clay.text:
After Arras they send the company north, to Flanders, to the galleries under the Messines
ridge. These galleries are older than your time in France. Some were started in 1915. A
hundred feet down, under the wet sand, there's a blue clay, smooth and stiff as cold suet,
and it holds without timber, and it makes no noise when you work it.

It's Mott's clay. London clay, he says, it's the same as the Tube. He lies on his back on his
cross, a plank set at a slant against the face, with a spade on his feet, and kicks out the
clay, a lump at a time, silent, and passes it back, all shift, without a word, as happy as
you've ever seen a man.

The galleries run out under the German ridge. At the ends of them, the charges have been in
place a long time, waiting. Your work is keeping the water out, and listening.

choices.text: Get Mott to teach you to kick.
choices.text_after:
It takes a week, and your back aches in places it never ached at the face. "Like riding a
bike," Mott says. "Backwards. Lying down. Underground." By the end of the week you can do
it, slow. Mott's as proud of you as if he'd taught you to read.

choices.text: Stay on the pumps. You know pumps.
choices.text_after:
The pumps go day and night, and you nurse them like the engine-man at Blackhaugh nursed his,
by the sound. When one starts to labour you hear it before anyone, and that's worth
something here, where water will drown a gallery in a night.

v17p_messines.title: Messines
v17p_messines.text:
Ten past three in the morning, the seventh of June. You're in a dugout at the top of a shaft,
with the crew, waiting. Nobody's talking. Evans has his hand flat on the timber of the dugout
wall, the way you'd feel a roof.

Nineteen of them. Nineteen mines, under the whole length of the ridge, some of them two years
in the making. Every gallery you've kept dry since May is under that ridge, full to the end.

Then they go.

It isn't a noise. It's the ground being taken out from under you and given back. The dugout
lifts and drops and lifts. Dust comes out of every crack in the timber. Up above, through the
shaft, a light, red, then white, all along the ridge, as if the sun's come up wrong. And then
the noise arrives, after, rolling, like every pit heap in Northumberland falling at once.

They'll say later that they heard it in England.

choices.text: Go up the shaft and look.
choices.text_after:
You climb out into the dawn. The ridge is gone, and where it was there's smoke and dust going
up into the sky, and the guns have started behind you, all of them. Evans comes up beside you
and stands there with his mouth open, and says something in Welsh, and you'll never know
what, and you don't need to.

choices.text: Stay below. You don't want to see it.
choices.text_after:
You stay in the dugout with your back against the timber, feeling it shake as the guns open
up, and you think of the Germans in their galleries, the ones you've heard through the clay
for a month, laughing, coughing, singing. You don't go up. Mott brings you down a tin of tea.

v17p_evans.title: Singing
v17p_evans.text:
Autumn, and the rain, and the company building deep dugouts behind the line at Wipers, forty
feet down in the clay, for red tabs who will move in when they're done and never say thank
you.

At the end of a shift, in the dugout, Evans starts to sing. Not loud. In Welsh, a hymn, slow,
and the dugout goes quiet. His voice fills the timbered dark the way it fills a gallery when he
forgets to whisper, and the drips from the roof keep time.

[if flag.p17_lost_pascoe]Pascoe used to hum along. Nobody does now.[/if][if flag.p17_saved_pascoe]Pascoe, on his bunk, still coughing, hums along under his breath.[/if]

choices.text: Join in. You know the tune from chapel, if not the words.
choices.text_after:
You know the tune. Half of Blackhaugh chapel sings it in English. You come in on the second
verse in English, and Evans doesn't stop, and the two languages go on together in the dark
and it sounds right.

choices.text: Lie on your bunk and listen.
choices.text_after:
You lie and listen with your eyes shut. When he stops, nobody says anything, and Mott, who
has never been to chapel in his life, says "Again," and Evans sings it again.

v17p_father.title: A letter from home
v17p_father.text:
It's in your mother's hand, but the pencil's gone soft and wandering, as if she wrote it on her
knee.

"Dear Son, I do not know how to put this so I will just put it. Your father passed away on
Thursday night. It was his chest. He was in his chair and he said he was tired and he would go
up, and I went up after and he had gone. He did not suffer the doctor says.

The lodge sent the banner and the band and they walked him up to the chapel, the whole row came
out. The manager sent a wreath. Your father would have had something to say about that.

I am all right. Mary is with me. Do not worry about me. Keep yourself safe, that is all I want
now. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Ask for compassionate leave.
choices.text_after: [if war.transferred]Your officer hears you out, and he's sorry, and he means it. There's no leave. There's no leave for anybody this summer.[else]The company officer hears you out in his dugout, and he's sorry, and he means it. There's no leave. Not this summer. Not for anybody.[/if] You knew. You had to ask.

choices.text: Write to your mother tonight.
choices.text_after:
You write it three times. In the end you put that you're proud of him, and that he was the
best man at the face in Blackhaugh, and that you'll be home at Christmas, and you'll go up
to the chapel with her. You don't know if that last part is true. You put it anyway.

l_pit_1917.title: Home on leave
l_pit_1917.text:
[if flag.p17_father_letter]The chair's still by the fire. Nobody sits in it. Your mother's put his pipe on the mantel and his cap on the hook by the door, where they always were, and she doesn't move them.[else]Nobody wrote it to you. Your mother couldn't, and the letter she tried went somewhere in France and never found you. She tells you on the step, before you've put your kit down. Your father's dead since the summer. His chest. The chair's still by the fire.[/if]

[if war.corps == tank]They rang the church bells in the town for Cambrai, your mother says, and chapel folk walked over to hear them though they weren't their bells; and then the ground was lost again, and nobody said much. At the club the old men want to know about the engine. How many horse. A hundred and five, you tell them, a Daimler, and eight men shut in with it, and they whistle, and want to know about the ventilation, and you laugh till you have to stop. There's a fan, you tell them, and all it does is pull the fumes past your face on their way out. There's a tank coming to the town hall in the new year, for the War Bonds, and the lodge is getting up a trip to see it.[if flag.tk17_told_mother] Your mother has told everybody at the Store you're in one, and the name of it.[/if][if flag.tk17_kept_quiet] She had you in the motor transport. She found out at the Store, from somebody's letter, and she hasn't forgiven you, and she's glad.[/if][/if][if war.corps == air]Mary heard you were in the Flying Corps from the girls at the works before your letter came, and she's been proud of it in front of them for a month. She wants to know if you've seen Richthofen, and if he's as handsome as they say. At the club the old men want to know what the flying pay is, and when you tell them, one of them says your father would have had something to say about a man getting paid extra to sit down. They laugh, and then they stop, and buy you a half. Mary asks why you don't learn to fly the thing yourself; it'd mean months at a school in England, you tell her, and your mother looks up from the fire. She's heard the airmen get sent home after a while, to teach. She asks if it's true. You say sometimes.[/if]

You go up to the chapel on the Sunday, the way you said you would[if !flag.p17_father_letter], though you never said it[/if], and stand at the grave with her. It's raw yet. The lodge has put a stone, plain, with his name and the pit and the years. Your mother holds your arm and doesn't cry, and you know she's done her crying, and that she's done it alone.

[if flag.p17_asked_leave]The company officer wrote to her himself, in the summer, to say he was sorry he couldn't send you home. She's kept it with your father's papers.[/if]

The heap's still burning on the skyline. The buzzer still goes. Your sister Mary's at the munitions works in Newcastle now, and comes home yellow, from the powder, and laughs about it.

[if !war.transferred && flag.p17_dug_frost]At the club they've heard, from somebody's letter, that the Blackhaugh lads dug a trench through frozen ground in one night that the Hull company couldn't have dug in a week. By the time it reaches you it's a mile long.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p17_learned_kick] Some nights you're on Mott's cross again, kicking the clay, and you wake with your legs going.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p17_saw_messines]You tell nobody about Messines. Then in the club an old pitman reads out of the paper that they heard a bang in London in June, the Prime Minister himself, from France, and everybody laughs at the papers, and you have to go outside.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p17_saved_pascoe] A letter's come for you from Camborne, from Pascoe's wife. You don't open it till you're on the train.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p17_lost_pascoe] You write to Camborne, to Pascoe's wife, from your mother's kitchen table. It takes all evening.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_wed16]Lizzie's living at your mother's now with the baby, in your old room, and the house is full of washing and the baby's noise, and your mother's never been so tired or so pleased. [if flag.ro_sw_named]The bairn has the name you wrote. Your mother says it's a name for the gentry, and says it a hundred times a day.[else]She's called after Lizzie's mother, and you find you don't mind.[/if] At night you lie and listen to her breathing in the drawer they've made a bed of, the way you used to listen for the roof.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_wed17]You and Lizzie are wed at chapel on the Thursday, by licence, with the girls from the tram depot at the back in their caps. There's no icing on the cake; there's no sugar in the county for icing. One night at her aunt's in Morpeth, and the train back in the dark.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_wed17]Lizzie wears the ring on a string under her blouse on the trams, and on her finger on Sundays. You walk the waggonway to the sea in sleet. [if flag.ro_sw_wait2]"After," she says. "You said it again." She laughs, and it's not much of a laugh.[else]She doesn't ask you anything, and you could kiss her for that, and do.[/if][/if][if flag.ro_sw_jilted]You see Lizzie Milburn at the Store with Ned Forster, the deputy's lad, still black from the shift, and she sees you see her. She comes over on her own. "I'm sorry," she says. "I am, mind." [if flag.ro_sw_blessed]"I kept your letter." You tell her Ned's a good lad, and he is.[else]You tell her it doesn't matter, and she knows it does, and lets you say it.[/if][/if][if flag.ro_sw_let_go]Lizzie Milburn is walking out with a tram driver from Byker, your mother says, and still comes round of a Sunday, less often.[/if]

[if flag.ro_fr_writes]In your pack there are three letters from Ternecourt, in French, that you can read about half of. You don't take them out in this house.[/if]

[if war.mate1 && flag.p17_blue_hen]Old Mr Robson's had a letter from the army loft. The blue hen's been flying messages. He keeps the letter in the cree, pinned up over the nesting boxes.[/if][if !war.mate1]The Robsons' cree is empty and the door's off. Somebody's had it for firewood.[/if]

[if war.mate2 && flag.p17_toasted_russia]Bell's father asks if Jim's still talking about Russia. You tell him he's never stopped. "Good," the old man says. "Good lad."[/if][if !war.mate2]On the board for the lodge's dead at the Miners' Hall, Jim Bell's name is spelt right and his age is wrong, and nobody's put it straight. He'd have had something to say.[/if]

[if war.mate3 && flag.p17_sat_with_charlton]Mrs Charlton says George wrote about a grey horse. Just that, a page about a grey horse. She doesn't understand why he'd write a whole page about a horse, and you don't explain.[/if][if !war.mate3]Down at the pit stables somebody's tied a black ribbon on Captain's stall, and nobody's taken it off.[/if]

{money_line}

{offers_line}

choices.text: Go back on the tenth day. [if war.corps == air]The squadron[else][if war.transferred]Your company[else]The battalion[/if][/if] promotes the men who return.
Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

v18c_posts.title: Posts
v18c_posts.text:
January, south, in the old French line, with the poilus' names still cut in the chalk. The brass hats' new idea is posts, little islands of men a hundred
yards apart in the chalk, with wire round them, and the redoubts behind. On the map they look
tidy as a ledger. On the ground they look like what they are: a few men, alone, in the frost.

The officer wants the post deepened.

choices.text: Dig it deep. Twenty steps.
choices.text_after:
Three weeks with a pick. Clerks' hands, four years hard now, but still clerks' hands, and the
blisters come up and break and come up. By February there's a dugout twenty steps down, and
you're prouder of it than of anything you ever did at the office.

choices.text: Dig to the book and no more.
choices.text_after:
To the book. You finish early and spend the evening playing whist on an ammunition box with a
candle in a vin blank bottle, and win fourpence.

v18c_waiting.title: The returns
v18c_waiting.text:
February. Jerry's coming. Everybody knows it.

[if war.mate1 && flag.c17_webb_clerk]Webb, in the orderly room, has seen the intelligence summaries, the returns from brigade. He can't tell you what's in them. He tells you anyway, in the dark, in a whisper, the way he'd tell you a figure that didn't balance. "Forty divisions," he says. "Opposite us. They've moved forty divisions." He's not writing it in his notebook. That frightens you more than the number.[/if][if war.mate1 && !flag.c17_webb_clerk]Webb has the numbers anyway. The prisoners, the deserters, the airmen, every rumour, entered in his notebook with the date and the source, and added up. "It's coming," he says. "It doesn't balance any other way."[/if][if !war.mate1]You find yourself counting, the way Webb used to: the carts at night, the guns registering, the deserters. It doesn't balance any other way. It's coming.[/if]

choices.text: Write home. Tell them not to worry.
choices.text_after:
You tell them not to worry. You tell them it's quiet. It is quiet. It's the quietest it's ever
been, and that's the thing you don't tell them.

choices.text: Sleep while you can.
choices.text_after: You sleep in your boots, every night, with your rifle across your knees. Everybody does.

v18c_abbeville.title: The camp
v18c_abbeville.text:
The news comes round the battalion the way bad news does, from a man who heard it from a man. The
German aeroplanes have bombed a camp at the base, on the coast, at night. A women's camp. The
WAACs. Some of them killed, in their huts, in their beds.

It's four days before a letter comes. Her hand. Shaky, but her hand.

"I am all right. I was in the trench. They made us dig trenches by the huts after the first raid
and we laughed about it and I am not laughing now. Two of the girls from my hut. One of them was
from Glasgow and was teaching me to dance the Gay Gordons.

I am all right. Please write and tell me you are."

choices.text: Write back and ask her to marry you, when it's over.
choices.text_after:
You write it four times. In the end it's two lines, in your best office hand, the way you'd
write a cheque you meant: Dear Florence. When it is over, will you marry me. You post it before
you can do it a fifth time. Her answer comes in nine days. It's one word, and a blot where she
pressed too hard.

choices.text: Write back that you're all right. That's what she asked.
choices.text_after:
You tell her you're all right. You tell her to keep digging trenches by the huts, and to get in
them. You tell her you'll dance the Gay Gordons with her, after, badly. She writes back that she
will hold you to that.

v18c_marsh.title: The lamp
v18c_marsh.text:
Open country now, after the summer. No trenches, no wire to lay, the line moving every day.
Marsh signals with a lamp now, at night, from a hilltop, a box with a shutter, flashing Morse to
another hill a mile back where somebody's watching for him.

You lie beside him in the dark and watch him work: the shutter clicking, the light going out
across the fields, dots and dashes, and far off the answering light, small as a match.

"I used to think nobody was listening," he says, between messages. "At chapel. When I prayed. And
now look." He nods at the far light. "Somebody always is."

choices.text: Read the far light for him. You know the Morse.
choices.text_after:
You read it off for him as it comes, letter by letter, and he writes it down. R-E-C-E-I-V-E-D.
A-L-L W-E-L-L. "That's all anybody ever needs to send," you say, and he laughs, and sends the
next one.

choices.text: Lie and watch the lights.
choices.text_after:
You lie and watch the two lights talking across the dark, like two people in windows across a
street, and you think of Leyton at night, all the lit windows, before the war.

v18c_gommecourt.title: The new trench
v18c_gommecourt.text:
The end of August, going forward, and the road goes through Funky Villas and past Gommecourt. The park with its broken
trees. The German wire, still there, rusted brown.

And out in front of where our line was, a ditch running across the grass, fallen in, grown over.
The new trench. The one the whole division dug in no man's land in three nights in 1916, three thousand
clerks with picks, at night, under the moon. You can follow it with your eye the whole way across.

[if flag.c16_counted_smoke]You counted the smoke candles in that trench. Forty to a bay.[/if]

choices.text: Walk along it a little way.
choices.text_after:
A few yards. It's shallow now, a dip in the grass with poppies in it. You find a rusted
entrenching tool in it, the blade gone thin as paper. You leave it where it is.
[if war.mate1]Webb stands at the end of it and doesn't say anything, and then takes out his notebook and writes something, the first time in months.[/if]

choices.text: Keep marching.
choices.text_after:
You keep marching. You can feel it there on your left, the whole way past, the way you'd feel
your old desk in the office if you walked through the long room with your eyes shut.

v18c_flu.title: A letter from home
v18c_flu.text:
"Dear Son, the influenza is cruel bad in London. They say it is in every street. The schools in the borough are shut, and the man next door to the Webbs died on Tuesday and was well on the Sunday. Your father wears a
mask to the office, a bit of gauze, and looks a fool, and says he does not care.

I am keeping in. Do not worry. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write back. Tell her to keep in.
choices.text_after:
You tell her to keep in, and your father to keep the mask on, and not to go to the crypt or the
Underground or anywhere there's a crowd. You read your own letter back and laugh at it, a man
in France telling his mother to keep out of danger, and then you don't laugh.

choices.text: Keep it with the others.
choices.text_after:
It goes in your breast pocket. The man next door to the Webbs. You knew him. He used to give you
a ha'penny for running his betting slips.

e_armistice_city.title: The Armistice
e_armistice_city.text:
{ending_line}

[if war.mate3 && flag.c18_read_the_lamp]Marsh takes it down. At ten to seven in the morning, on the buzzer, in the signals dugout: Hostilities will cease at 1100 hours today. He reads it twice, and takes his spectacles off, and cleans them, and reads it again, and then he puts his head out of the dugout and says it to you, quite quietly, like a man reading out a hymn number.[/if][if !war.mate3 || !flag.c18_read_the_lamp]It comes up in the morning on a message form. Hostilities will cease at 1100 hours today. Nobody believes it, and then everybody does.[/if]

The guns go on to the last minute. Then eleven, and the quiet, so sudden you can hear your own
watch. "La guerre est finie?" an old woman asks from a doorway, and somebody says, "Oui, madame.
Napoo," and she cries into her apron.

[if war.mate1]Webb gets out his notebook, and writes the time and the date, and rules a double line under it, in pencil, with the edge of his pay book, and writes Closed. Then he closes the book and puts it away and doesn't take it out again.[/if][if !war.mate1]You think of Webb, who would have ruled the line.[/if][if war.mate2] Fenton's found a football somewhere, a French one, half flat, and he kicks it high up into the quiet, and nobody shoots at it.[/if][if !war.mate2] Somewhere on the Double Crassier there's a football, gone to leather and grass.[/if][if !war.mate3] You think of Marsh, who learned the eye chart by heart.[/if]

In London, they tell you after, the maroons went off at eleven, the warning guns, and everybody
ran for shelter, and then understood, and came out again, and the whole City came out of its
offices into the street. The clerks threw their ledgers out of the windows. Big Ben rang for the first time in years. And then the influenza took thousands of them in the next few weeks, and nobody threw anything.

You don't get home till the spring. Victoria, and this time you're clean.[if flag.c18_wrote_dont_worry] Your mother has your letter from February in the tea caddy, the one that said it was quiet. "You liar," she says, and holds on to you.[/if][if flag.c18_wrote_flu] Your father kept the mask on, the way you told him. He shows it you, the bit of gauze, folded in his waistcoat pocket.[/if][if flag.c18_walked_trench] Some nights you're back in the shallow trench at Gommecourt, among the poppies, following it across.[/if]

[if flag.c18_proposed]Florence is on the platform. She's in her WAAC coat still, demobbed the week before, and she doesn't wave, she just stands there, and you walk down the whole length of the train to her, and it's the longest walk in the war.[/if][if !flag.c18_proposed && flag.c16_florence]Florence is at the office, at your old desk, back from France. She stands up when you come in. Neither of you says anything for a long while, and then she says, "The Gay Gordons," and you say, "Badly," and that's that settled.[/if][if !flag.c16_florence]There's a girl at your old desk, typing, who looks up at you and doesn't know who you are, and you find you don't mind.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_wed16]Ivy is on the platform at Victoria with the baby on her hip, walking now, in a knitted bonnet, who looks at you hard and then hides in Ivy's collar. It's a week before she'll come to you.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_wed17]Ivy is on the platform at Victoria, with the ring on the outside of her glove so you'll see it from the carriage.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_told18] She has your letter from the spring in her handbag. She knows. You don't have to tell it again.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married && !flag.ro_sw_ended && !flag.ro_fr_promise]Ivy is on the platform at Victoria with the ring on, and you're married at St Mary's in May, and the choir sings for nothing.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married && !flag.ro_sw_ended && flag.ro_fr_promise]Before anybody else, you write to Ivy, about Ternecourt. It's the hardest letter of the war. She answers it, which you don't deserve: four lines, and the ring, wrapped in an exchange message slip.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_jilted]Ivy is married and lives off the High Road. You see her in the market with a pram, and lift your hat, and she smiles at you[if flag.ro_sw_blessed] and says you look well, the way her mother would[/if].[/if][if flag.ro_sw_let_go]Ivy Lambert married her clerk from the Prudential, your mother wrote, and has a little boy. You're glad. You find you are.[/if]

[if flag.ro_fr_promise]In the summer you go back to France on your own money, Folkestone and Boulogne and a slow train that stops at every halt, and walk the last miles from Albert with a cardboard suitcase, on roads where the shell holes are filled with broken brick. The estaminet has its roof on. Marthe is in the door before you've reached the pond.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_let_go]A card comes from Ternecourt at Easter, the church with its tower in scaffolding. Marthe and Gaston are married, and there's to be a child in the autumn, and the eggs are good again.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_writes && !flag.ro_fr_promise && !flag.ro_fr_let_go]Letters come from Ternecourt for a year, in French, and then only at Christmas, and then not.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_address && !flag.ro_fr_writes && !flag.ro_fr_promise && !flag.ro_fr_let_go]A letter comes to your mother's house with a French stamp, from Amiens, in a schoolmistress's hand, to say the Delattres are alive and going home. You answer it. You don't hear again.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_parted && !flag.ro_fr_address && !flag.ro_fr_promise && !flag.ro_fr_let_go]Sometimes, frying an egg, you think of Ternecourt, the steam on the windows and a girl making you say oeufs till you could.[/if]

The Roll of Honour in the front hall at the Gresham and Lombard has four panels now. You stand in front of it on your first morning back and read every name, and then you go up to the third floor, and sit down at a desk, and look out at the fog on the river.

[if war.servant >= 1]Mr Carew's mother has you to tea in Kensington, with the cake on a stand and a maid to pass it, and thanks you for bringing him home. He walks you to the Underground after, and shakes your hand on the steps.[/if][if flag.sv_second_killed]Mrs Carew writes from Surrey on black-edged paper, to thank you for the cap. She'd forgotten he had it.[/if][if flag.sv_first_killed && war.servant == 0 && !flag.sv_second_killed]Mr Pryor's name is on the first panel. His uncle has you up to the board room that morning, and shakes your hand, and says the firm won't forget, and you go back down to the Fire ledgers a grade up, at Mr Pryor's old desk.[/if]

You are {age} years old and {rank_a}.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

v18f_posts.title: Hard ground
v18f_posts.text:
January, south, in a quiet stretch the French have handed over. The new idea is posts, little
islands of men in the chalk with nothing between them but frost. The ground's iron. Your
father would say it's no use to man or beast till March.

The officer wants the post deepened, frost or no frost.

[if war.mate1 && flag.f16_kept_dog]Cottle's French Fly lies on the parapet with her nose on her paws, looking out at the wire the way she'd watch a gate for a fox.[/if]

choices.text: Get the pick into it. Dig it deep.
choices.text_after:
Three weeks, in shifts, the pick ringing on the frost like on a flint. By February there's a
dugout under the post, twenty steps down. It's the deepest hole you've ever dug, and you've
dug wells.

choices.text: Dig to the book and no more. Save your back.
choices.text_after:
You dig it to the book. Your back thanks you. At night you sit round the stove the poilus left
behind and roast potatoes you've found in a field clamp, and they taste of home.

v18f_rooks.title: The rooks
v18f_rooks.text:
February. They're coming. Everybody knows it.

There was a rookery in the wood behind the German line, the last trees standing for miles, and
the rooks have gone. All of them, in a week. Nobody else has noticed. You've noticed. At home the
rooks leave a wood before it's felled; they know before the men come with the saws.

[if war.mate2]Pearce has noticed too. "Rooks've gone," he says, low, at stand-to, not looking at you. "Jerry's bringing something up through that wood. Guns, I'd say."[/if]

choices.text: Tell the officer about the rooks.
choices.text_after:
He listens. He doesn't laugh, which surprises you. "My father kept a rookery," he says. He
writes it in his notebook: rooks gone from wood at map reference so-and-so. "It'll go to
brigade," he says, "and they'll laugh. But it's going."

choices.text: Keep it. Who'd listen to a farm lad about rooks?
choices.text_after:
You keep it. Every morning at stand-to you look at the wood, empty, quiet, and know what it
means, and can't say.

v18f_bert.title: Carrying
v18f_bert.text:
April, after the retreat. The battalion's a third of what it was, and the rest is boys from the
depot.

[if flag.f17_bert_bearer]Bert carried for eleven days without sleeping, they say. Back across the whole of the old Somme ground with the wounded, while the Germans came on behind, and never left a man he could lift. They've put him in for a medal. He doesn't want it. He says the man who should have it is the one who carried the other end.[else]Bert carried in the retreat, though he's not a bearer. Picked up a wounded boy from the depot on the second day and carried him on his back for nine miles. He won't talk about it.[/if]

choices.text: Tell him you're proud of him.
choices.text_after:
He goes red, the way he did as a boy at the harvest supper when Mr Venn's mother gave him a
sixpence for the bells. "I just kept going," he says. "You do."

choices.text: Say nothing. He doesn't want it said.
choices.text_after:
You say nothing. You sit with him on the step in the sun, and he falls asleep sitting up, and
you let him.

v18f_pearce.title: After
v18f_pearce.text:
A warm evening behind the line, and Pearce lying in the grass with his hands behind his head,
chewing a stalk.

"When it's over," he says, "I'm going to ask the squire for the keeper's job."

You laugh. He doesn't. "I mean it. Old Dawe's past it. And who knows the poachers better than me?
I know every wire on Exmoor. I set most of them." He turns the stalk round. "Mrs Venn'd give it
me. She's not the squire, but she runs him now, since Mr Venn."

choices.text: Tell him he'd be the best keeper Exmoor ever had.
choices.text_after:
"I would," he says. "Every poacher in three parishes'll curse the day." He's grinning at the
sky. "Write and tell your mother. Get it round the village. Then it's half done."

choices.text: Tell him he'd last a week before he was poaching his own birds.
choices.text_after:
"A week," he says. "I'd give it a fortnight." And he laughs, and you laugh, and a lark goes up
out of the grass by your feet, and you both lie and watch it go.

v18f_letter.title: A letter from home
v18f_letter.text:
"Dear Son, the wheat on the Long Field is the best your father ever grew. The government pays a
fixed price now and wants every acre ploughed, even the old pasture on the hill that has not seen a
plough since your grandfather, and your father has ploughed it, with the tractor and Miss Pugsley,
and says nothing about it at all, which means he is pleased.

Mrs Venn has started a committee for a memorial, a cross on the green, with the names. She came
to ask me about the spelling of some of them. I said I would ask you, as you would know the men.

Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write back with the names, and the right spellings.
choices.text_after:
You write them out, every Dunsworthy man you know is dead, with his full name and his age and
where. It takes a whole evening and two pages. You check them twice. You stop at the end and
look at the space under the last one, and fold the letter.

choices.text: Keep it. You can't write the names yet.
choices.text_after:
You can't, yet. You put it in your breast pocket. The names go round in your head on sentry
instead, in order, like the changes Bert says under his breath.

v18f_trench.title: Mansel Copse
v18f_trench.text:
The end of August, going forward, and the road goes up past Mametz. Past Mansel Copse, what's
left of it, and the slope where the gun at the shrine had the first wave.

And the trench. Our old front line, where you went over from, filled in. The board's still
there, weathered grey, the paint faded but you can read it. THE DEVONSHIRES HELD THIS TRENCH.
THE DEVONSHIRES HOLD IT STILL. Somebody has put a little wooden cross at each end, and there are
poppies all along the top of it, the length of the trench, as if they'd been sown.

[if flag.f16_buried]You filled it in. You know where every man in it lies.[/if]

choices.text: Fall out for a minute. Stand by the board.
choices.text_after: The sergeant lets you. [if war.mate1]Cottle stands with you, and takes his cap off, and doesn't say anything.[/if][if war.mate3] Bert says the names he knows, under his breath, like changes.[/if] Then you go after the column, up the road, past the shrine, which is still standing, with the crucifix on it and not a mark.

choices.text: Keep marching. They'd want you to keep going.
choices.text_after:
You keep marching. You can feel it there on your right all the way past, the way you can feel
a gateway in the dark without seeing it.

v18f_fly.title: Home
v18f_fly.text:
Going forward through villages the Germans have held for four years, with old women at the
doors saying "Les Boches sont partis," the Boche are gone, and in one of them the French Fly
stops dead in the street, and whines, and runs.

Down a lane, into a farmyard, a burnt-out farm with the walls standing. Cottle goes after her. She's
sitting in the yard by the ruin of the dairy, looking at the door. It's where she came from. You
know it the minute you see it. It's her home, and there's nobody in it.

choices.text: Help Cottle coax her on. She's coming with you.
choices.text_after:
It takes Cottle half an hour, sitting in the yard with her, talking low. In the end she comes,
with her head down, and walks at his heel out of the yard, and looks back once from the lane,
and doesn't look back again.

choices.text: Tell him to leave her. She's home.
choices.text_after:
He knows. He sits with her a while and then stands up, and she doesn't follow him, and he
doesn't call. Two days later, an old woman comes back to that farm from wherever she's been for
four years, and finds a black and white dog waiting at the dairy door. You never know that. But
it's what happens.

e_armistice_farm.title: The Armistice
e_armistice_farm.text:
{ending_line}

It comes up in the morning on a message form. Hostilities will cease at 1100 hours today.
"Guerre napoo," somebody says. Nobody believes it, and then everybody does.

The guns go on to the last minute. Then eleven. And the quiet comes down like snow on the moor,
so you can hear a long way: a dog, a cart, a cockerel in a farm behind the line that doesn't know
anything has happened.

[if war.mate1 && flag.f18_fly_stays]Cottle sits down on the bank and whistles, the two low notes, and the French Fly comes and lies across his feet.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.f16_kept_dog && !flag.f18_fly_stays]Cottle sits down on the bank and whistles, the two low notes, and nothing comes, and he whistles again anyway.[/if][if war.mate1 && !flag.f16_kept_dog]Cottle sits down on the bank and whistles the two low notes for Fly at home, out of habit, and laughs at himself.[/if][if !war.mate1]Somewhere at home a black and white dog is lying by a gate, looking up a lane.[/if][if war.mate2] Pearce takes off his cap and throws it in the air and catches it.[/if][if war.mate2 && flag.f18_pearce_keeper] "Keeper," he says. "You watch."[/if][if !war.mate2] Dan Pearce would have been out in no man's land by now, looking for hares.[/if][if war.mate3] Bert stands with his hands curled, the way they curl round the sally, and his lips are moving, and you know it's the changes.[/if][if !war.mate3] You think of Bert, who was going to ring the whole peal, after.[/if]

[if war.mate3 && flag.f18_proud_of_bert]Bert's medal comes through in the new year. He keeps it in a drawer and won't wear it to church.[/if][if flag.f18_stood_at_trench] Some nights you're back by the board on the Devonshires' trench, reading it.[/if][if flag.f18_fly_home] Somewhere in France an old woman has a black and white dog at her dairy door.[/if]

They let the farm men go early, for the spring ploughing, and you're home in February. The hedges are bare, and the lane's
deep in mud, and the smoke goes up straight from the chimney.

They rang the bells at Dunsworthy on the day, your mother says. The old men and the schoolgirls,
all afternoon, every bell they had, till the ropes were wet with their hands. [if war.mate3]On your first Sunday home, Bert rings the tenor, in the whole peal, the way he said he would. You stand in the churchyard among the graves and listen to it go out over the fields, and it's the end of the war.[/if][if !war.mate3]On your first Sunday home they ring the tenor half-muffled, once, for Bert, and then the peal open, for the rest of you.[/if]

[if flag.f18_names]Mrs Venn's cross is on the green, with the names you sent, spelt right.[/if][if !flag.f18_names]Mrs Venn's cross is on the green, with the names. Two of them are spelt wrong. You go and look every day for a week.[/if][if war.mate2 && flag.f18_pearce_keeper] Dan Pearce is the keeper at the big house by Lady Day. Every poacher on Exmoor curses the day.[/if]

[if flag.farm_servant]Mrs Venn sends the groom down the week you're home. When a farm on the estate falls vacant, she says, it's yours, at your father's rent. "He'd have wanted it," she says, and you don't know if he would, and you tell her you'll ask your father.[/if][if war.servant >= 1] Mr Rudd writes from Birmingham at Christmas, from his old stool at the foundry.[if flag.f16_helped_rudd] He says please all the way through.[/if][/if][if flag.sv_second_killed] Mr Rudd's mother writes from Small Heath at Christmas, to thank you for his things, and for the letter.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_wed16]Rose is at the bottom of the lane when the carrier's cart comes, with the baby on her hip, walking now, in a knitted bonnet, who looks at you hard and hides in Rose's neck. It's a week before she'll come to you.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_wed17]Rose is at the bottom of the lane when the carrier's cart comes, with the ring on the outside of her glove so you'll see it from the road.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_told18] She has your letter from the spring in her apron pocket. She knows. You don't have to tell it again.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married && !flag.ro_sw_ended && !flag.ro_fr_promise]Rose is at the bottom of the lane with the ring on, and the banns are read the next three Sundays, and the ringers ring the whole peal for it.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married && !flag.ro_sw_ended && flag.ro_fr_promise]Before anybody else, you write to Rose, about Ternecourt. It's the hardest letter of the war. She answers it, which you don't deserve: four lines, and the ring, folded in a twist of paper with flour in it.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_jilted]Rose is married and lives over at Brendon. You see her at market with a pram, and lift your cap, and she smiles at you[if flag.ro_sw_blessed] and says you look well, the way her mother would[/if].[/if][if flag.ro_sw_let_go]Rose Huxtable married her carter, your mother wrote, and has a little boy. You're glad. You find you are.[/if]

[if flag.ro_fr_promise]In the summer you go back to France on your own money, Folkestone and Boulogne and a slow train that stops at every halt, and walk the last miles from Albert with a cardboard suitcase, on roads where the shell holes are filled with broken brick. The estaminet has its roof on. Marthe is in the door before you've reached the pond.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_let_go]A card comes from Ternecourt at Easter, the church with its tower in scaffolding. Marthe and Gaston are married, and there's to be a child in the autumn, and the eggs are good again.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_writes && !flag.ro_fr_promise && !flag.ro_fr_let_go]Letters come from Ternecourt for a year, in French, and then only at Christmas, and then not.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_address && !flag.ro_fr_writes && !flag.ro_fr_promise && !flag.ro_fr_let_go]A letter comes to your mother's house with a French stamp, from Amiens, in a schoolmistress's hand, to say the Delattres are alive and going home. You answer it. You don't hear again.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_parted && !flag.ro_fr_address && !flag.ro_fr_promise && !flag.ro_fr_let_go]Sometimes, frying an egg, you think of Ternecourt, the steam on the windows and a girl making you say oeufs till you could.[/if]

Your father walks you round the farm the first morning: the Long Field, the hill pasture ploughed
for the first time in eighty years, the stable with the tractor in it where Prince and Duke used
to stand. At the gate he stops, and puts his hand on your shoulder, and leaves it there.

You are {age} years old and {rank_a}.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

v18_french_line.title: The French line
v18_french_line.text:
January, and they've moved you south, a long way south, to take over a stretch of line from
the French. The poilus have left it the way the French leave things: a stove in every dugout,
empty vin blank bottles in the sump, a cat that won't come out from under the duckboards, and a
picture of a woman in stockings pasted on the dugout wall. Nobody chips her off this time.

It's quiet. The old hands say it's too quiet, and then laugh at themselves for saying it. On a
still night you can hear a cart on the German side, miles off, with a wheel that wants grease.

And there's no line, not as you'd know it. The new idea is posts: little islands of men in the
chalk, a hundred yards apart, with wire round them, and the big redoubts further back. Between
the posts there's nothing but frost.

The ground's frozen a foot down. The pick rings on it like on a flagstone and jars you to the
teeth.

choices.text: Dig the post deeper while there's time.
choices.text_after:
Three weeks of it, in shifts, through the frost and then the thaw. Chalk under your nails,
chalk in your tea, chalk in the cracks of your hands till they look like your gran's. By
February there's a dugout under the post, twenty steps down, timbered with planks you
stole from the French.

choices.text: Get the French stove going. Make the post fit to live in.
choices.text_after:
It roars like the boiler house and you sit round it in your shirtsleeves for the first time
since October, toasting bread on bayonets, the cat on somebody's knee.[if war.mate2]
Duckworth teaches the cat to sit up for bacon rind and calls it Joffre.[/if]

v18_waiting.title: Waiting
v18_waiting.text:
February. Jerry's coming. Everybody knows it. The prisoners say it, the airmen say it, the
deserters who come over in the night with their hands up say it, and give dates, and the dates
are all different.

You can hear them getting ready. Every night there are carts and lorries on roads you can't
see, and the clink of harness, more of it every week. Their guns register one at a time, a
single shell here, a single shell there, careful, like a man tapping the walls of a house he
means to buy.

At stand-to you look at the grey wire and the grey sky and think about the weaving shed at half past
five on a winter morning, the gas mantles popping on one after another down the long room and
the first looms starting up. You'd give your back teeth for that noise.

[if war.mate2]Duckworth has a sweep going on the date. A franc a go. He's written the days up on a bit of ration box, and men keep coming to look at it as if it'll tell them.[else]A lance-corporal in B Company has a sweep going on the date. A franc a go, the days written up on a bit of ration box, and men keep coming to look at it as if it'll tell them.[/if]

choices.text: Put a franc on the twenty-first.
choices.text_after: [if war.mate2]"The twenty-first," Duckworth says, licking the pencil. "That's a Thursday. Nowt ever happens of a Thursday."[else]He writes your name against the twenty-first. "Thursday," he says. "Nowt ever happens of a Thursday."[/if]

choices.text: Keep your franc. It's asking for it.
choices.text_after:
You keep it. It's a dirty little paper note with a corner torn off, and you fold it into your
pay book, and it's still there months after, gone soft as cloth.

v18_boys.title: Backs to the wall
v18_boys.text:
April. What's left of the battalion is out of the line in a village nobody's heard of, being
made up with drafts. The drafts are boys. After March they've started sending them out at
eighteen and a half, and here they are, boots squeaking, hair cropped by the depot barber,
eating anything they can find.

On parade the colonel reads out an order from the Commander-in-Chief. Every position to be held
to the last man. No retirement. Our backs to the wall. He reads it twice, the second time
slower, because the wind took it the first time.

The boys listen with their mouths open. The old hands look at their boots.

[if war.mate3]Pilling's a corporal now, nineteen, with a face like a shut door. He's been given a lad called Tattersall from Darwen, who follows him round like a dog and stands the way he stands.[/if][if war.mate3 && flag.told_pilling_ease] He's stopped volunteering for everything. He says it's because he's got Tattersall to think about.[/if]

choices.text: Take one of the boys on. Show him how to stay alive.
choices.text_after:
His name's Clegg and he's from Rochdale and he's frightened of everything except what he
ought to be frightened of. You show him how to keep his feet dry, how to tell their shells
from ours by the sound, when to run and when to lie still. He writes it down in a notebook
with a pencil he keeps behind his ear.[if war.mate3] Across the billet Pilling's telling
Tattersall the same things in the same order, in the words you used to him in 1915, and
doesn't know you can hear.[/if]

choices.text: Keep away from the boys. Don't learn their names.
choices.text_after:
You don't learn their names. You learn them anyway, the way you learn the looms in a shed
without meaning to: Clegg, Tattersall, the two Hargreaves who aren't brothers.[if war.mate3]
Pilling sees you not looking at them. "You were like that with me," he says. "At first."[/if]

v18_flu.title: Three-day fever
v18_flu.text:
May, and the weather's turned lovely, and the battalion's going down like skittles.
Three-day fever, the MO calls it. The papers from home call it the Spanish flu. A man goes from
right as rain to shaking in an hour, with a head like a cracked slate and his bones aching from
the inside, and three days later he's up again, wobbly on his legs, and the man next to him is
going down.

You feel it coming on at stand-to: a heat behind the eyes, a cold sweat down the back, the
rifle sling too heavy all at once for your shoulder.

choices.text: Go sick. Lie down before you fall down.
choices.text_after:
Three days in a barn on straw with forty other men, sweating and shivering and coughing in
the dark, an orderly coming round with a bucket of tea and a tin of Number Nines. You dream
about the shed, the racket of it, and wake with your teeth chattering in time to the looms.

choices.text: Stay at duty. Everybody's got it.
choices.text_after:
Nobody's going to say you were swinging the lead. You stand your sentry with your teeth going and the wire swimming in front of you. At dawn
the sergeant takes one look and sends you down anyway, and you cry all the way to the aid
post. It's the fever, you tell yourself. It's only the fever.

v18_yanks.title: Americans
v18_yanks.text:
Americans, at last. A company of them comes up to learn the line, big and well fed, with
cigarettes in packets of twenty with pictures on, and tinned peaches, and they call everybody
buddy, and they want to see a Jerry so badly it hurts to watch.

Duckworth adopts one, a long lad from somewhere called Ohio who has never seen a mill and wants
to hear all about it. So Duckworth tells him. The shed, the noise, the tackler, the weavers
mee-mawing to each other across the looms because you can't hear yourself speak, the knocker-up
rattling the bedroom window at five. The American listens as if it's the Bible.

choices.text: Trade him your spare cap badge for a tin of peaches.
choices.text_after:
He gives you two tins, and a packet of cigarettes, and shakes your hand as if you'd given
him a medal. You and Duckworth eat the peaches in the bottom of the trench off a jack-knife,
turn and turn about, drinking the juice out of the tin, and they're so sweet that neither
of you can talk.

choices.text: Get Duckworth to tell him a tackler's tale.
choices.text_after:
It's the one about the tackler who took his pigeon to the doctor's. It has never once been
funny, not in the shed, not in the drill hall, not at Loos. The American laughs till he has
to sit down on the firestep and wipe his eyes, and Duckworth looks at him like a man who has
found the one person in the world who understands him.

v18_censor.title: The letters
v18_censor.text:
Every night in the dugout, by a candle in a bottle, you read the platoon's letters. It's an
officer's job. You sit with a blue pencil and a pile of envelopes and read their mothers and
their wives and their girls, and strike out the names of places, and pass the rest, and sign
the corner.

You know these men. You know their mothers. You stood in the Co-op queue behind some of them.

[if war.mate1]Shaw's is on top, in the round careful hand he learned out here.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.best_man] "Dear Edith, I am keeping well.[/if][if war.mate1 && !flag.best_man] "Dear Mother, I am keeping well.[/if][if war.mate1] We have a new officer, you know who. He is all right. He still has his tea out of the dixie with us when he thinks nobody is looking."[/if][if war.mate3] Pilling's is half a page of nothing, I am well, hope you are well, and at the bottom, crossed out, but you can read it: Mam I am that tired.[/if][if !war.mate1 && !war.mate3]A boy from Bacup has written to his mother that the new officer is a mill lad himself, and the men don't know yet whether to like it.[/if]

choices.text: Pass them all as they are. Sign the corners.
choices.text_after:
You sign them and seal them and they go down the line in the sack with the rest. You don't
strike a word. Let somebody at home know where we are, you think. Let somebody know.

choices.text: Do it by the book. Strike out the places.
choices.text_after:
Blue pencil through every village and every wood. That's the rule, and men have died for
less than a careless letter.[if war.mate3] You leave Pilling's crossed-out line alone.
It isn't a place.[/if]

v18_moving_up.title: Keep your mouth shut
v18_moving_up.text:
July. They move you at night, only at night, and in the day you lie up in woods and barns out
of sight of the aeroplanes. Somebody has pasted a notice inside the cover of every pay book:
KEEP YOUR MOUTH SHUT. The roads at night are packed with guns, limbers, lorries, and tanks under
tarpaulins, all going one way with no lights, the drivers swearing in whispers. The air's thick
with petrol and horse dung and the dust off the road, and it never settles.

Something big. Nobody says it.

The post comes up with the rations, and there's one from your mother.

"Dear Son, just a few lines. Our Jack has had his papers, he went Tuesday to the camp at Prees
Heath. Your father walked him to the station and came home and went straight down the yard and
stopped there. Jack keeps asking me what it is like out there and I said ask your brother. So
he will be writing to you. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write to Jack and tell him what it's like.
choices.text_after:
You write it in a barn by a candle stuck in a bully tin, and it takes two nights. You can't
tell him the worst of it. You tell him enough. Keep your feet dry. Keep your head down. Don't
volunteer. Don't believe a word they tell you at the depot. Write to Mother every week, even
if it's only a field card, because she stands at the door for the post.

choices.text: Write to Jack that it's not so bad.
choices.text_after:
You tell him the grub's all right and the lads are a good crowd and he'll be fine if he keeps
his nose clean. It's all true, near enough. You write it fast so you won't put anything
else, and seal it before you can read it back.

v18_old_ground.title: The old ground
v18_old_ground.text:
The end of August, and you're going forward. Forward, every day. You come over a rise one
morning and you know it before you know why: the slope of the land, the line of a road, a
stump of a tree. It's the old ground. The first of July.

There's our old front line, the trench you went over from, fallen in and grassed over. The wire
in front of it is still there, rusted the colour of a cart axle, with grass growing up through
it. Out in the middle the craters have gone soft and green, with poppies in them, and there are
little crosses everywhere, leaning, dozens of them, and in the long grass the bits of things: a
water bottle, a boot, a helmet with a hole in it, a tin of something with the label gone.

It smells of hay. You'd forgotten how short a walk it was.

choices.text: Walk out to where you think it was.
choices.text_after: You can't find it. Everything's where it was and nothing is. [if flag.brought_discs]You stand where you think you crawled out for the discs, that night, and there's only grass, and a lark going up.[else]You stand in the long grass where you think it was, and a lark goes up, and keeps going up, singing, till you lose it in the sun.[/if]

choices.text: Keep your eyes on the man in front. Keep walking.
choices.text_after:
You keep walking. The column goes down the road into the next valley and the old ground
falls behind, and you don't look back, and you know exactly where it is behind you all day,
the way you know where the fire is in a dark room.

v18_shaw_photo.title: Walking
v18_shaw_photo.text:
Shaw's had a new photograph from home: the lad, stood up, holding on to a chair, in a little
frock, with his hair done in a curl on top. Albert Shaw, a year old and a bit.

"He's walking," Shaw says. "Edith says he's walking. He was walking in June and I never knew
till now."

He keeps it in the oilskin pouch with the old one of Edith from the studio on Market Street,
and on sentry you see him take it out and hold it up to the light of the flares, and put it
back, and take it out again.

choices.text: Tell him you'll get him home to see it.
choices.text_after:
"You will," Shaw says, flat, as if you'd told him the time. He puts the photograph away. Then,
not looking at you: "You'd better."

choices.text: Ask to see it properly.
choices.text_after:
He hands it over as if it's an egg. The lad's got Shaw's ears, sticking out, and Edith's
mouth. On the back, in pencil, in Edith's hand: For his Dad.[if flag.wet_babys_head] "He's
had his rum ration already," Shaw says. "Off the section. He'll be a sergeant."[/if]

b_spring_1.title: The twenty-first of March
b_spring_1.text:
You wake because the ground is moving. It's a little before five and dark, and the whole of
the east is lit up from underneath, end to end, flickering, like the sky over the foundry on a
casting night. Then the noise reaches you, and it isn't guns any more. There are no gaps in it
to count.

Gas with it. The sneezing kind first, that gets in behind the mask and makes you want to tear
it off, then the other kind. Through the eyepieces everything's green and running, and the
rubber stinks, and your own breath roars in your ears.

When it gets light, it doesn't get light. Fog. Thick as a wet blanket on a line. You can't see
the next post, forty yards off. You can hear it.

[if flag.p18_reported]The officer had you all stood to since four. He'd listened.[/if][if flag.f18_rooks]The officer had you all stood to since four. Brigade laughed at the rooks. He didn't.[/if][if flag.p18_reported && flag.dug_deep] [/if][if flag.f18_rooks && flag.dug_deep] [/if][if flag.dug_deep]The dugout you dug in January holds. The timbers groan and drop chalk down your neck, but they hold.[/if][if flag.french_stove]The French stove goes over in the first minute and you stamp out the coals in the dark with your mask on, and the post fills with the stink of hot iron and scorched wool.[/if][if flag.sweep_21 && war.mate2] Duckworth gets his mouth right up against your ear in the din. "You've won," he shouts. "You jammy beggar. You've won the sweep."[/if]

[if war.path == rifleman]Beside you {mate} is counting the shells under his breath, and gives up.[/if][if war.path == nco]Your section is spread over two posts you can't see from each other. You have to choose which one you're in.[/if][if war.path == lewis]The gun's on the parapet under a groundsheet, the drums stacked in the recess, and there's nothing in the fog to fire at.[/if][if war.path == signals]The buried cable goes in the first ten minutes. A lamp's no use in fog. You've two pigeons in a basket, and a runner, and the runner's gone.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You've two boxes of Mills bombs and a fog you can't see ten yards into.[/if][if war.path == snipe]A sniper in fog is a man with a rifle. You wrap the telescope in a sock and put it in your pack.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]You're with the tunnellers in the battle zone, behind, with charges laid under the bridges and the dumps, and orders to blow them when the infantry are back through.[/if][if war.path == subaltern]Your platoon is in four posts and you can see none of them. The last order from company, an hour old, was to hold the forward zone at all costs. You've a revolver, a whistle and a map of a country you can't see.[/if][if war.path == bearer]You're at the aid post, a dugout behind the post, with the stretchers and the doctor, when it starts.[/if]

Then, somewhere about twenty to ten, the noise changes. The shells go over, further back. Out in
the fog, something is coming.

choices.text: Get up on the firestep, mask on, and face the fog. ({risk_push})
Go along the post getting the masks on the new lads. ({risk_help})
Get down the dugout steps till it lifts. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_spring_2.title: Out of the fog
b_spring_2.text:
They don't come at the front. They come round. The first you see of them is a man on the
parados, behind you, in a coal-scuttle helmet, throwing something. Then they're everywhere,
little groups of them, quick, with light machine guns and flame-throwers, slipping between
the posts in the fog and leaving the posts for the men behind them.

The post on your left goes quiet. Then the one past it. You hear them go out, one at a time, by
the sound: the rifles, a bomb, shouting, then nothing.

Down the trench a whole platoon comes up out of a deep dugout with their hands up, one man at a
time, blinking in the fog, because a German at the top of the steps has a bomb in his hand and
there's only one way out.[if flag.dug_deep] Twenty steps. You dug every one.[/if]

[if war.path == lewis]The gun fires at shapes. You change drums by feel.[/if][if war.path == subaltern]A runner gets through to you with an order from company to fall back on the redoubt. He's the third they sent.[/if][if war.path == nco]You count your men. You keep getting a different number.[/if][if war.path == bearer]The aid post is full, and the walking wounded are coming in out of the fog with the Germans behind them.[/if]

choices.text: Fire at the shapes, front and back. ({risk_push})
Get the post back to the redoubt together, wounded and all. ({risk_help})
Stay down in the bottom of the trench and let it go over. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_spring_3.title: Back
b_spring_3.text:
After that it's back. Five days, six, you lose count. March by night, dig in by day, and they're
on you again by the afternoon. Men go to sleep walking and walk into the man in front. A
quartermaster pours a whole dump of rum into a ditch so the Germans won't get it, and men lie
down in the ditch to drink it.

Behind you the dumps burn. Bully beef, biscuits, a canteen store with tins of pineapple bursting
in the fire, so the whole night smells of burnt sugar and petrol.

And the names on the signposts. You know the names. You're going back over the old Somme ground,
the ground that took a summer and a half to win, and you're giving it up in a day.[if start == pit] Somewhere out there on your left is the great crater at La Boisselle.[/if][if start == farm] Somewhere out there is Mansel Copse, and the trench the Devonshires hold.[/if][if start == city] Somewhere out there to the north is Gommecourt, and the trench you dug in no man's land.[/if][if flag.brought_discs]
Somewhere out there is where you crawled for the discs.[/if]

[if war.path == tunnel]Your charge is under a bridge over a canal. You wait in the reeds for the last of the infantry, counting them over. Behind them, the first grey helmets.[/if][if war.path == signals]No wire, no lamps, no pigeons. You carry messages on foot, and half the time the battalion headquarters has moved before you find it.[/if][if war.path == subaltern]You've nineteen men left of thirty-eight, and a map that ran out yesterday.[/if]

choices.text: Stay with the rearguard on the ridge. ({risk_push})
Carry the wounded lad between you, whatever it slows you. ({risk_help})
Lie up in a cellar and let them go by. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_spring_4.title: The embankment
b_spring_4.text:
The end of March, and a railway embankment in front of a town you've never heard of, and
somebody says that's it, no further. You believe it because you can't walk any further.

They've slowed. The word is they stopped at our dumps, and found the white bread and the jam and
the boots and the whisky, and couldn't believe it, and some of them are drunk in the cellars.
They thought we were starving.

New men come up on your right in slouch hats, Aussies, who look at you as if you're
something the cat brought in, and give you their water.

At dusk the grey lines come up the slope at you one more time.

[if war.path == lewis]You set the gun up on the rails, on its bipod, between two sleepers, and the barrel's still hot from the morning.[/if][if war.path == subaltern]You walk the embankment behind your men, which is where an officer walks, and the bullets go over the rails with a noise like tearing calico.[/if][if war.path == bearer]You've carried for six days. Your shoulders are raw where the poles go.[/if]

choices.text: Get up on the embankment and fire into them. ({risk_push})
Go along the embankment with ammunition. ({risk_help})
Keep under the embankment and let the guns do it. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_amiens_1.title: The eighth of August
b_amiens_1.text:
Twenty past four in the morning, and fog again. This time it's ours.

There's been no bombardment, no days of it the way there was before the Somme, no warning. The
guns open all at once, every gun at once, and the barrage comes down a couple of hundred yards
in front and starts walking. Out of the fog behind you come the tanks, dozens, more than you
knew there were in France, lurching and roaring, and the air's full of hot oil and petrol and
their exhaust.

The ground's green. That's what you can't get over. Standing corn, uncut, up to your waist, and
poppies in it, and the fog lying on it white.

[if war.path == rifleman]Beside you, {mate} wades through the corn with his rifle held up out of it like a man crossing a river.[/if][if war.path == nco]Your section goes forward behind a tank, the way they've practised, in little worms of men, and you've never seen it work before.[/if][if war.path == lewis]You fire from the hip as you go, the way you were never taught, and the corn in front of you jumps.[/if][if war.path == signals]You go behind the company with a reel on your back, and the wire runs out behind you in the wet corn, and holds.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You've bombs in a bucket, and the men you're going for are behind the tanks, not in front of them.[/if][if war.path == snipe]You're out on the flank looking for their machine guns in the edges of the woods.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]You go up behind the infantry to search the dugouts they take for charges set to blow. They've been leaving them, lately, under the stairs.[/if][if war.path == subaltern]You blow your whistle and nobody hears it, and they go anyway, because they know what to do now better than you do.[/if][if war.path == bearer]You go behind the tanks with the stretcher, and the corn's full of men lying down, and some of them are ours.[/if]

[if war.stalled]On the left the fog lifts too soon. A tank's burning by a copse, black smoke rolling off it low over the corn, and a machine gun in the copse has the whole company down.[else]Their front line comes up out of the fog, and it's half empty, and the men in it have their hands up before you get there. Their breakfast is still on the fire.[/if]

choices.text: Keep up with the tanks. ({risk_push})
Keep the section together in the fog. ({risk_help})
Get down in the corn till the fog clears. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_amiens_2.title: The wood
b_amiens_2.text:
A wood, with a road running into it, and machine guns at the edge. The tanks go at it and one
stops with smoke coming out of it, and the crew climb out and lie under it.

Most of them give up. They come out of the dugouts in crowds, with their hands up and their kit
packed, as if they'd been waiting. An officer asks you in English for a receipt for his field
glasses. But the machine-gunners at the edge of the wood are the other sort, the old sort, and
they fight till they're dead.

choices.text: Go in at the guns from the side. ({risk_push})
Get the tank crew back out of the open. ({risk_help})
Get down behind the bank and fire at the wood's edge. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_amiens_3.title: Open country
b_amiens_3.text:
By the afternoon you're further than anybody has been since 1914. Seven miles, somebody says.
There are no trenches here. There are fields and hedges and a farmhouse with the washing still
on the line, and cavalry go past you at a trot, real cavalry, through the oats.

Their field guns are firing over open sights from behind a hedge, at the tanks, and at you.
You dig in at dusk in a field of oats, scraping a hole with your entrenching tool, and the
earth's soft and brown and smells of rain. Like the allotment.

choices.text: Go for the guns behind the hedge. ({risk_push})
