Dig the hole for two. Bring the wounded man in. ({risk_help})
Dig in deep and keep down. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_oct_1.title: The river
b_oct_1.text:
A river, in October, in the dark. The sappers have been out all night putting footbridges over
it, planks on floats, and you go over in single file with the water black and quick under the
boards and the smell of it cold and green, like [if start == pit]the burn below the pit heap[/if][if start == mill]the canal under the mill[/if][if start == farm]the river below the farm in flood[/if][if start == city]the river at Wapping on a winter night[/if] in winter.

Gas in the valley, lying in the low places. Fog over it.

[if war.path == rifleman]Behind you, {mate} has hold of your pack strap. On the bridge his boot goes through between two planks and you haul him up by the collar.[/if][if war.path == nco]You count your section onto the bridge, and off.[/if][if war.path == lewis]The gun's on your shoulder. If you go in, you'll go straight to the bottom with it.[/if][if war.path == signals]The wire goes over the river with you, pegged to the floats.[/if][if war.path == bomb]You go over with the bombs in a sandbag held up against your chest.[/if][if war.path == snipe]On the far bank, the railway embankment. You know they're on it. You look for the glint.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]You're on the bridges themselves, up to your waist in it, lashing the floats while they cross.[/if][if war.path == subaltern]Your platoon's first over. You go first on the bridge, which is what they pay you for.[/if][if war.path == bearer]You're on the bridge with a stretcher, and the bridge is two planks wide.[/if]

[if war.stalled]The far bank opens up before half of you are over. A bridge goes, men and all, and the river takes them.[else]On the far bank there's an embankment, and a hedge, and the barrage coming down on both.[/if]

choices.text: Get over and up the embankment. ({risk_push})
Stop on the bank and pull men out of the water. ({risk_help})
Get down under the near bank. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_oct_2.title: The village
b_oct_2.text:
A village, still standing, with roofs on, and people in it. The German board, Kommandantur, is still nailed over the door of the Mairie.

They come up out of the cellars when the firing's moved on: old men, women, children with faces
the colour of candles. Four years they've been behind the German lines. An old woman in a black
shawl kisses you on both cheeks and smells of onions and cellars. "Enfin," she keeps saying, "enfin, les Anglais," at last, at last, and she pushes a cup into your
hands. It's coffee made of roasted barley, and it's the best thing you've ever tasted.

There's a machine gun in the church tower. It's firing down the street.

choices.text: Go for the church through the gardens. ({risk_push})
Get the people back down into the cellars. ({risk_help})
Get into a doorway and fire at the tower. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

b_oct_3.title: The last of it
b_oct_3.text:
They come back once more, at evening, out of an orchard, and it's half-hearted, and it's still
enough to kill men. Apples on the ground everywhere, gone soft, and wasps in them, and the smell
of cider in the dusk.

After that, quiet. Just the guns, further off every day.

There's a rumour, the way there's always a rumour. Only this time the officers are saying it too.

choices.text: Go out into the orchard after them. ({risk_push})
Get the wounded in out of the orchard. ({risk_help})
Keep down behind the wall. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

e_armistice_mill.title: The Armistice
e_armistice_mill.text:
{ending_line}

It comes up in the morning with the rations, on a message form, in the adjutant's hand.
Hostilities will cease at 1100 hours today. Nobody believes it. Then everybody does, all at
once, and nobody knows what to do with their hands.

The guns go on to the last minute. A battery behind you fires off everything it has, as if it's
somebody's birthday, and at a minute to eleven a German machine gun across the valley fires a
whole belt into the sky. Then a man stands up beside it, takes his helmet off, bows, and walks
away.

Then eleven. It goes so quiet you can hear a wood pigeon, and a cart a long way off, and the man
next to you breathing.

[if war.mate1 && flag.best_man]Shaw sits down in the road and gets the photograph out, and doesn't put it away again all day.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.promised_shaw] "Well," he says. "You got me home, then." It isn't true yet. You let him have it.[/if][if !war.mate1 && flag.promised_shaw]You told Shaw you'd get him home to see the lad walk. You think of Edith, and the little fist round your finger.[/if][if war.mate2] Duckworth starts to tell a joke and can't get to the end of it.[/if][if war.mate2 && flag.tackler_tale] "There's a lad in Ohio," he says, "telling the one about the pigeon. That's what I did in the war."[/if][if !war.mate2 && flag.gave_fags] You light a Woodbine and think of Duckworth, who owed you one, and paid up.[/if][if war.mate3] Pilling stands in the road and doesn't know what to do, and in the end he takes his tin hat off and throws it as far as he can into a field of turnips.[/if][if !war.mate3] You think of Walter Pilling, sixteen at Loos, who'd have been twenty in March.[/if]

You don't get back to Blighty till the spring. The letters come. The influenza's in the street, the bad
sort this time; Mrs Ormerod's two girls; the schools shut. On the day, your mother says, every
mill buzzer in the town went off at eleven, all at once, and the chapel bells after, and your
father stood in the yard and wouldn't come in for an hour.[if flag.had_the_flu] You've had it,
out here, and got up again. You read that part twice.[/if]

[if flag.told_jack_truth]Our Jack never went out. He was at Prees Heath when it finished. He writes that he read your letter till it fell to bits, and he's glad, and he's sorry, and he doesn't know which.[/if][if flag.told_jack_easy]Our Jack never went out. He was at Prees Heath when it finished, and he writes that he's fed up, he's missed it, it isn't fair. You put the letter in the stove.[/if][if !flag.told_jack_truth && !flag.told_jack_easy]Our Jack never went out. He was at the camp when it finished. Your mother says it three times in one letter, as if she's counting.[/if][if flag.walked_old_ground] Some nights you're back in the long grass on the old ground, looking for the place.[/if][if flag.peaches] You can't look at a tin of peaches.[/if][if flag.took_a_lad] Clegg writes from Rochdale, once, to say he's back at the dye works and thank you.[/if]

[if war.servant >= 1]Mr Kershaw's staying in. The army's all he knows, he says, and he'll not go back to Bolton to be called sir by men he was at school with. His wife writes to your mother at Christmas, to thank her for the loan of you.[/if][if flag.sv_second_killed]Mrs Kershaw writes from Bolton at Christmas, four lines in a hand that presses through the paper, to thank you for his things and your letter. She's taken in washing.[/if][if flag.sv_first_killed && war.servant == 0 && !flag.sv_second_killed]In the spring the master stops you at the mill gate and shakes your hand in front of the whole shed coming in. Mrs Ainsworth kept your letter, he says. There's a tackler's job for you when you want it.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_wed16]Nellie meets the train with the baby on her hip, walking now, in a knitted bonnet, and the baby looks at you hard and then hides in Nellie's neck. It's a week before she'll come to you.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_wed17]Nellie meets the train in the blue costume she was married in, with the ring on the outside of her glove so you'll see it from the carriage.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_told18] She has your letter from the spring in her apron pocket. She knows. You don't have to tell it again.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married && !flag.ro_sw_ended && !flag.ro_fr_promise]Nellie's on the platform with the ring on her finger, on a weekday, in front of everybody, and you're wed at chapel in May, and the whole alley comes, and her brothers dance.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married && !flag.ro_sw_ended && flag.ro_fr_promise]Before you write to anybody else, you write to Nellie, about Ternecourt. It's the hardest letter of the war, and you post it before you can stop yourself. She answers it, which you don't deserve: four lines, no blots, and the ring, wrapped in a bit of cotton waste from the shed.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_jilted]Nellie's married and lives up by the cemetery. You see her in the market with a pram, and lift your cap, and she smiles at you[if flag.ro_sw_blessed] the way she used to across the alley, and mouths something you can still read: you look well[/if].[/if][if flag.ro_sw_let_go]Nellie Whittaker married her lad from the card room, your mother wrote, and has a little boy. You're glad. You find you are.[/if]

[if flag.ro_fr_promise]In the summer you go back to France on your own money, Folkestone and Boulogne and a slow train that stops at every halt, and walk the last miles from Albert with a cardboard suitcase, on roads where the shell holes are filled with broken brick. The estaminet has its roof on. Marthe is in the door before you've reached the pond.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_let_go]A card comes from Ternecourt at Easter, the church with its tower in scaffolding. Marthe and Gaston are married, and there's to be a child in the autumn, and the eggs are good again.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_writes && !flag.ro_fr_promise && !flag.ro_fr_let_go]Letters come from Ternecourt for a year, in French, and then only at Christmas, and then not.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_address && !flag.ro_fr_writes && !flag.ro_fr_promise && !flag.ro_fr_let_go]A letter comes to your mother's house with a French stamp, from Amiens, in a schoolmistress's hand, to say the Delattres are alive and going home. You answer it. You don't hear again.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_parted && !flag.ro_fr_address && !flag.ro_fr_promise && !flag.ro_fr_let_go]Sometimes, frying an egg, you think of Ternecourt, the steam on the windows and a girl making you say oeufs till you could.[/if]

You are {age} years old and {rank_a}, and you went out of the shed a boy.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

v18p_ashington.title: The new posts
v18p_ashington.text:
January, and the battalion's moved south into a quiet stretch the French have handed over,
the poilus' wine bottles still in the dugouts.
The new idea is posts, little islands of men in the chalk a hundred yards apart, with
nothing between them but frost.

And new men. A Tyneside battalion has been broken up, there aren't enough men to go round any
more, and sixty of them come into the company in one night. Pitmen, most of them, from
Ashington and Bedlington and Choppington, with the same blue coal scars on their foreheads as you,
and they stand in the snow with their kit at their feet and won't look at anybody, because
their battalion's gone, and their pals with it.

The ground in the posts is frozen. The officer wants them deepened.

choices.text: Get the Ashington men on the picks with you. Dig the post deep.
choices.text_after:
You put them on the picks beside the Blackhaugh lads and by the end of the first shift
they're talking, about seams, about managers, about whose pit has the worst roof. By
February there's a dugout under the post, twenty steps down, timbered the way you'd timber
at home, and the Ashington men did half of it.

choices.text: Leave them be. Let them grieve their own battalion.
choices.text_after:
You leave them be. They keep to themselves in the next post, and sing at night, low, their
own songs, and after a week one of them comes over for a light and stays an hour.

v18p_bell_corporal.title: Lance-Corporal Bell
v18p_bell_corporal.text:
They've given Bell a stripe. Jim Bell, who argued with every sergeant in France, who read the
Herald in the beer vat, who drank to the Russians. A lance jack.

"They've run out of men," he says. "That's all it is. They've run clean out." But he's sewn it
on straight, you notice, and he's the first up at stand-to now, and he goes round the new lads
at night making sure their feet are dry, and he gives them his own socks when theirs are wet.

"Somebody has to look after them," he says, when he sees you watching. "God knows nobody else
will."

choices.text: Call him Corporal, and salute.
choices.text_after:
He tells you exactly where to put your salute, in words the Herald wouldn't print. Then he
laughs, properly, the first time since the spring. "Corporal," he says, trying it. "Me da'll
never live it down."

choices.text: Help him with the new lads. Say nothing about the stripe.
choices.text_after:
You do the feet with him, the two of you going along the posts in the dark with a tin of
whale oil and a sack of dry socks. He talks the whole time, about the war, about the owners,
about after. You let him. Somebody has to listen.

v18p_combout.title: The comb-out
v18p_combout.text:
April, and after March the battalion is half new faces. Some of the faces you know. The army's
combed out the pits for men, the young starred men they kept back as war work, and here they
are in a draft from the depot: lads you went to school with, who stayed at the face when you
went, in khaki now, with new boots.

Joe Todd from the bottom row, who was a shot-firer, comes up to you at the cookhouse. He went
down the pit the same week as you. He stayed. He looks at you the way you'd look at a man who'd
come up out of a fall.

"They said you'd be here," he says. "I didn't think you would be. Still."

choices.text: Show him the ropes. All of it.
choices.text_after:
You show him where to stand, when to duck, how to keep his feet, the sound of the shells
that matter, the whizz-bang and the five-nine. He listens the way he'd listen to a deputy. At the end of it he says, "You've
changed." You don't know what to say to that, so you say nowt.

choices.text: Leave him to the sergeant. He stayed home.
choices.text_after:
You leave him to it. It isn't fair, and you know it isn't. He didn't choose to be starred any
more than you chose to be eighteen. But you can't make yourself, not yet.

v18p_robson.title: After
v18p_robson.text:
A warm evening behind the line, the two of you sat on a bank with your backs to a hedge,
and swallows going over. Robson's quiet, the way he always is. Then he says the longest thing
you've ever heard him say.

"I'm not going back down. After. If there's an after. I've been under the ground in France
four year one way and another, and I've been under it at home since I was twelve, and I'm not
going back down." He's pulling at the grass. "Me da's got the birds. I'll get a bit of a
smallholding. Hens. Birds. I'll work in the light."

He looks at you. "What about you?"

choices.text: Tell him you're not going back down either.
choices.text_after:
"Good," Robson says. "Good." He goes back to pulling at the grass. After a while: "You'll
have to come and help with the hens, then. You're no use for owt else." It's the nearest
he's ever come to a joke.

choices.text: Tell him you'll go back. It's what you know.
choices.text_after:
He nods. He doesn't argue. "Aye," he says. "Your da did." After a while he says, "I'll keep
you a pair of birds. You can fly them from the pit gates," and that's the end of it.

v18p_charlton.title: The farmer
v18p_charlton.text:
Going forward through villages the Germans have held since 1914, and in one of them an old
farmer standing in his yard with nothing in it. No cow. No pig. No horse. The Germans took the
lot. "Les Boches," he says. "Il n'y en a plus." Napoo, the lads make of that: all gone. He's
stood looking at the empty stalls.

Charlton's with the transport, coming up the road behind the battalion, and he sees the old
man, and stops. He's got a spare mule, lame in the off fore, that the transport officer's
marked down to be shot.

choices.text: Help Charlton leave the mule in the old man's yard.
choices.text_after:
Charlton leads her in and ties her in an empty stall and shows the old man the bad foot,
in signs, and how to poultice it, and the old man takes hold of Charlton's face in both his
hands and kisses him on the forehead. The transport officer is told she died. Charlton
whistles all the way to the next village.

choices.text: Tell him he'll be on a charge. Keep going.
choices.text_after:
Charlton keeps going. He looks back once at the old man in his empty yard, and the mule
limps along behind the limber, and that night the farrier shoots her, and Charlton doesn't
eat.

v18p_dugouts.title: Dugouts
v18p_dugouts.text:
January, and the mining war's over, near enough. Nobody's digging under anybody's line now.
The company's put to dugouts for headquarters, and subways, and bridges, and once, for a
week, a bath-house for a brass hat.

[if !flag.p17_lost_pascoe]Pascoe says it's the first time in thirty year he's dug a hole that nobody wanted to blow up.[/if][if flag.p17_lost_pascoe]Evans says it's a waste of good miners. He says it every day, the way Pascoe used to say his prayers.[/if] Mott says san fairy ann, a hole's a hole, but he'd sooner have the Tube.

And the officer wants the dugout under the forward post sunk deep, in case they come in the
spring.

choices.text: Sink it deep. Twenty steps at least.
choices.text_after:
Twenty steps, timbered like a shaft, the way your father taught you to set a prop. You put
the last frame in on the first of February and stand at the bottom looking up at the square
of grey sky, and think, that'll hold anything.

choices.text: Dig it to the book and no more.
choices.text_after:
To the book, and the book's not bad. You finish a week early and get three days in a barn
with straw and a stove, and Mott teaches the crew a card game from the docks that nobody
else in France has heard of.

v18p_mott.title: Mott
v18p_mott.text:
A shell on the dump at the shaft head, and Mott's in the way of it. Not bad. His leg, below the
knee, a clean one. A Blighty one. He's sat on the duckboards grinning white while you put the
dressing on.

"Blighty," he says. "Blighty, Geordie. I'll be on the Tube by Sunday." Then he stops grinning
and grips your sleeve. "You look after Evans. He's soft, under all that singing."

choices.text: Carry him down to the aid post yourself.
choices.text_after:
Two miles on your back, him talking the whole way, about the Tube, about his mum's pie shop
in Bermondsey, about a girl. At the aid post he shakes your hand like a man at a station.
"Come and see the Tube," he says. "I'll show you every yard of it."

choices.text: Get him onto a stretcher and get back to the shaft.
choices.text_after:
The bearers take him. He waves from the stretcher like a lad on a charabanc. You go back
down, and Evans is at the face on his own, not singing, and you take Mott's place beside
him.

v18p_traps.title: Traps
v18p_traps.text:
Going forward, and Jerry has left his dugouts full of presents. A helmet on a table
with a wire under it. A loose duckboard on the stairs. A stove that will go up when it's lit.
And worse: charges buried under crossroads and bridges with clocks on them, acid eating
through a copper wire, set to go days after the last German has gone.

The infantry won't go into a dugout now till the tunnellers have been through it. So you go
first. Down the steps with a candle, slow, looking at everything, the way you'd go into an old
working that's been shut up for years, feeling for the wire before you see it.

At the bottom of this one there's a gramophone on a box, and a record on it, and the handle
wound.

choices.text: Leave it. Trace the wire first, however long it takes.
choices.text_after:
An hour on your knees with the candle. There's a wire, fine as cotton, from under the
gramophone down into the floor, to enough explosive to bring down the dugout and everybody
in it. You cut it. Then, because nobody's looking, you play the record. It's a waltz, and
it's scratched, and it goes round and round in the dugout under the ground.

choices.text: Get out and call up the officer. It's his decision.
choices.text_after:
The officer comes, and looks, and has the whole dugout blown in with a charge from the top,
gramophone and all. Probably the right thing. You hear the record in your head for a week,
a tune you never heard.

v18p_waiting.title: The ground
v18p_waiting.text:
February. Jerry's coming. Everybody knows it. The deserters say it, the airmen say it.

[if war.transferred]Down in your dugout you lie with your ear to the floor at night, the way you'd listen to a roof, and the ground's alive with it. Not picks: wheels, thousands of them, and hooves, and the deep thud of guns being dug in, miles off, coming through the chalk like through a drum.[/if][if !war.transferred && war.mate1]Robson's on his knees on the floor of the post with his ear to the chalk, the way he was the first night in 1915. He stays there a long time. "Wheels," he says. "Thousands. And guns, being dug in. It's coming through the ground like a drum."[/if][if !war.transferred && !war.mate1]You put your ear to the floor of the post at night, the way Robson did the first night in 1915. Wheels, thousands of them, and the thud of guns being dug in, miles off, coming through the chalk like through a drum.[/if]

choices.text: Tell the officer what the ground's saying.
choices.text_after:
He listens. He writes it down. "Everybody's hearing it," he says. "Everybody knows." He looks
at you. "Still. Thank you. [if flag.pit_reported]You're the one who heard them in 1915, aren't you? Somebody told me.[/if][if !flag.pit_reported]Pitmen hear things.[/if]"

choices.text: Lie and listen. There's nothing anybody can do.
choices.text_after:
You lie and listen till you can't tell it from your own heart. Then you sleep, and dream of
the cage going down, and the roof talking, and your father saying it's only the roof.

v18p_letter.title: A letter from home
v18p_letter.text:
"Dear Son, just a few lines. I am keeping well. Mary is still at the works in Newcastle and
comes home yellow and says the girls call each other canaries and laugh about it. I do not
think it is funny.

They have combed the pit again and took the young starred men. The manager has took women on
at bank, on the screens, where your father was. I went to look. I could not stop.

[if war.transferred]Your money still comes. I have put most of it in the Store. You will want something when you come home, for a start, whatever you do.[/if][if !war.transferred]Mrs Todd says her Joe is with you now, and she is glad of it, she says it is the only thing that lets her sleep.[/if]

I sit in your father's chair now of a night. I could not, at first. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write back. Tell her about after.
choices.text_after: You tell her about after: [if flag.p18_not_going_down]that you'll not go back down, that you'll find something in the light, that Tommy Robson's going to keep hens and you'll help[/if][if flag.p18_going_down]that you'll go back down, to the face, your father's seam[/if][if !flag.p18_not_going_down && !flag.p18_going_down]that you don't know yet, that you'll know when you're home, that there'll be time[/if]. You tell her to keep sitting in the chair.

choices.text: Keep it with the others.
choices.text_after:
It goes in your breast pocket with the rest. Your father's letter's in there too, the one
he never wrote, the one you keep expecting.

v18p_crater.title: The Glory Hole
v18p_crater.text:
The end of August, going forward, and the road goes past La Boisselle. Past the crater.

It's grassed over at the edges now. Poppies on the lip. A hundred yards across, and the white
chalk still showing on the steep sides where nothing will grow, and at the bottom a pool of
green water. There are crosses round the rim, little wooden ones, and some have names you know.

[if war.transferred]You made it. Two years ago, with Evans and Pascoe and Mott, tin by tin, in your socks, in the dark.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p16_chalked_tin] Somewhere in all this, your name in chalk on a syrup tin.[/if][if !war.transferred]You stood there that morning and watched it go up, higher than the pit heap, higher than anything. You were in it all that afternoon.[/if][if !war.transferred && flag.p16_birds] It's where the bird went up from, round once, round twice, and west.[/if]

choices.text: Fall out for a minute. Walk round the rim.
choices.text_after: The sergeant lets you. You walk round the lip slowly, reading the crosses. [if !war.mate1]You look for Robson's name, and don't know if you want to find it.[/if][if war.mate1]Robson walks round with you, and doesn't say anything, and stops at one cross, and stays there till the sergeant shouts.[/if] At the far side there's a lark going up, and you stand and listen to it, and then you go after the column.

choices.text: Keep marching. Don't look.
choices.text_after:
You keep your eyes on the pack in front. You can feel it there on your left all the way
past, the way you can feel a pit shaft in the dark without seeing it.

e_armistice_pit.title: The Armistice
e_armistice_pit.text:
{ending_line}

It comes up in the morning on a message form. Hostilities will cease at 1100 hours today.
Nobody believes it, and then everybody does.

The guns go on to the last minute. Then eleven. And then a quiet like the quiet at the face
when the cutter stops and the dust settles, a quiet you can hear, and in it, somebody's
laughing, and somebody's crying, and a wood pigeon.

[if war.transferred]Evans sings, in Welsh, and this time nobody tells him to whisper.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p18_carried_mott] Mott's on the Tube by now. He wrote you twice, from Bermondsey, on pie-shop paper.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p17_saved_pascoe] Pascoe's somewhere behind the line, coughing. He'll go home to Camborne.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p17_lost_pascoe] You think of Pascoe, who never raised his voice.[/if]

[if war.mate1]Robson sits down at the roadside and takes off his helmet and lifts his face to the sky, and keeps it there.[/if][if war.mate1 && flag.p18_not_going_down] "Hens," he says, to nobody. "Birds. In the light."[/if][if !war.mate1]Robson isn't here to hear it. He'd have had his ear to the ground.[/if][if war.mate2] Lance-Corporal Bell gets the section in a ring and makes a speech, about the soldiers and the workmen, about after, about the owners, and for once nobody tells him to shut his mouth.[/if][if war.mate2 && flag.p18_ribbed_bell] He still won't let you salute him.[/if][if war.mate2 && flag.p18_helped_bell] After, he tells you he'd never have managed the feet on his own, and it's the only time he ever thanks anybody for anything.[/if][if !war.mate2] Jim Bell would have had something to say about it, and it would have taken all afternoon.[/if][if war.mate3] Charlton's down with the transport, and you find him in the horse lines with his face against a mule's neck.[/if][if war.mate3 && flag.p18_gave_mule] "There's a mule in a French farmer's yard," he says, "that's never going to hear a gun again."[/if][if !war.mate3] Somewhere at home there's a black ribbon on a pony's stall.[/if]

[if !war.transferred && flag.p18_showed_todd]Joe Todd from the bottom row finds you in the road and shakes your hand, and doesn't say why, and doesn't need to.[/if][if war.transferred && flag.p18_traced_wire]Some nights for years you'll hear a scratched waltz going round under the ground.[/if][if flag.p18_walked_crater] Some nights you're on the rim of the crater again, reading the crosses.[/if]

They let the miners go first, for the coal, and you're home by the new year. The heap's still burning on the skyline, and at
eleven on the day, your mother says, the pit buzzer went and didn't stop, five minutes of it, and
the whole village came out into the rows, and nobody knew what to do, so they went to chapel.

[if war.servant >= 1]Mr Hindmarsh is back at his school by the spring. He writes to ask if you'll come and tell the top class what it was like, and you go, and stand by the stove with forty bairns looking at you, and tell them about the mules.[/if][if flag.sv_second_killed]Mrs Hindmarsh writes from Morpeth. She has his little book with the bairns' names in it, and she's sending every family the page with theirs.[/if][if flag.sv_first_killed && war.servant == 0 && !flag.sv_second_killed]The manager sends for you the week you're home. Mrs Straker sits in the window with your letter in her lap and doesn't speak, and the manager says there's a place for you at Blackhaugh as long as there's a pit, at bank or below, whichever you want.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_wed16]Lizzie meets the train with the bairn on her hip, walking now, in a knitted bonnet, who looks at you hard and then hides in Lizzie's neck. It's a week before she'll come to you.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_wed17]Lizzie meets the train in her tram coat, with the ring on the outside of her glove so you'll see it from the carriage.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_told18] She has your letter from the spring in her pocket. She knows. You don't have to tell it twice.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married && !flag.ro_sw_ended && !flag.ro_fr_promise]Lizzie's at the station with the ring on, in the cold, and you're wed at chapel before the snow's off the heap, and the whole row comes.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married && !flag.ro_sw_ended && flag.ro_fr_promise]Before anybody else, you write to Lizzie, about Ternecourt. It's the hardest letter of the war. She answers it, which you don't deserve: four lines, and the ring, wrapped in a tram ticket.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_jilted]Lizzie's married and lives at the bottom of the rows. You see her at the Store with a pram, and lift your cap, and she smiles at you[if flag.ro_sw_blessed] and says, "You look well, hinny," the way her mother would[/if].[/if][if flag.ro_sw_let_go]Lizzie Milburn married her tram driver, your mother wrote, and has a little lad. You're glad. You find you are.[/if]

[if flag.ro_fr_promise]In the summer you go back to France on your own money, Folkestone and Boulogne and a slow train that stops at every halt, and walk the last miles from Albert with a cardboard suitcase, on roads where the shell holes are filled with broken brick. The estaminet has its roof on. Marthe is in the door before you've reached the pond.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_let_go]A card comes from Ternecourt at Easter, the church with its tower in scaffolding. Marthe and Gaston are married, and there's to be a child in the autumn, and the eggs are good again.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_writes && !flag.ro_fr_promise && !flag.ro_fr_let_go]Letters come from Ternecourt for a year, in French, and then only at Christmas, and then not.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_address && !flag.ro_fr_writes && !flag.ro_fr_promise && !flag.ro_fr_let_go]A letter comes to your mother's house with a French stamp, from Amiens, in a schoolmistress's hand, to say the Delattres are alive and going home. You answer it. You don't hear again.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_parted && !flag.ro_fr_address && !flag.ro_fr_promise && !flag.ro_fr_let_go]Sometimes, frying an egg, you think of Ternecourt, the steam on the windows and a girl making you say oeufs till you could.[/if]

Your father's chair is by the fire. Your mother sits in it now.[if flag.p18_wrote_after] Your letter about after is on the mantel, behind the tea caddy, where his pay notes used to go.[/if]

[if flag.p18_not_going_down]You don't go back down. You told Robson you wouldn't, and you don't. You stand at the pit gates on the first Monday, and watch the cage go, and walk away up the road in the light.[/if][if flag.p18_going_down]On the first Monday you go back down, to your father's seam. The cage drops and the dark comes up round you, still dark, the dark that doesn't move, and you're surprised how glad you are of it.[/if][if !flag.p18_not_going_down && !flag.p18_going_down]On the first Monday you walk to the pit gates and stand there. The cage is winding. You don't know yet. You stand there a long time.[/if]

You are {age} years old and {rank_a}.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

a_firing.title: The firing party
a_firing.text:
The sergeant major takes you aside behind the cookhouse, where nobody else can hear, and doesn't
look at you while he says it.

A man from another battalion of the brigade has been court-martialled. Desertion. He walked away
from the line in the spring and was picked up at a railway station forty miles back, asleep on a
bench, and the sentence has been confirmed. It's to be carried out at first light tomorrow, in a
quarry behind the village, and the party is to be found from this battalion. Twelve men.

"You've been picked," the sergeant major says. "It's not a punishment. It's a duty." He's
looking at the cookhouse chimney. "One rifle will have a blank in it. Nobody knows which. That's
so every man can think it was his."

[if war.rank >= 5]As the officer, you would command it. You'd give the orders. And if it isn't clean, the rule says the officer finishes it, with his revolver.[/if]

choices.text: Do it. It's a duty, and somebody has to.
choices.text_after:
First light, in a chalk quarry, cold, with a mist on the ground. A post, and a man brought out
tied to it, with a white square of cloth pinned over his heart, and a hood. He's smaller than you
thought. He's shaking so hard the post moves. The order. Twelve rifles, one sound. You don't
know if yours had the blank. You'll never know. You walk back to the billets and nobody in the
party speaks, and at breakfast you can't hold the mug.

choices.text: Ask to be excused. Say you can't.
choices.text_after:
The sergeant major looks at you then, properly, for a long moment. "Right," he says. "Right." He
finds another man. He doesn't say anything else to you about it, and he doesn't need to: it's in
how he says your name for the rest of the month. At first light you hear it from the billet, far
off, one sound, and you lie there.

a_escort.title: Prisoners
a_escort.text:
Thirty German prisoners from the last show, to be marched back to the prisoners' cage at the railhead, eight
miles, and you're one of the four escorts.

They're sat in a field in their grey, filthy, some of them bandaged, some of them boys and some of
them older than your father, and they're eating the bully beef somebody's given them as if they
hadn't eaten in a week, which they haven't. One of them has a photograph out, a woman and two
children in front of a painted garden, and he's showing it to the man next to him.

It's eight miles out of the line, along roads the German guns still reach now and then.

choices.text: Take them back to the cage.
choices.text_after:
Eight miles in the sun. They march better than you do. Halfway, at a crossroads, one of them
asks for water in careful English and you give him your bottle and he gives it back half full,
which you didn't expect. At the cage a corporal counts them in like sheep through a gate, and
you walk back alone with an empty road and your rifle on your shoulder and feel, for an hour,
like a man going home from work.

choices.text: Get somebody else to go. You're needed here.
choices.text_after:
The corporal finds someone. You watch them go off down the road, thirty grey and four khaki,
getting smaller, the photograph man still talking to his neighbour, and you go back to cleaning
your rifle.

a_guide.title: The relief
a_guide.text:
A battalion fresh out from England is taking over the line tonight, and they don't know it. Every
company needs a guide to bring them in: up the communication trench in the dark, through the
junctions where the boards are gone and the trench is blown in, to the right bays, without losing
anybody.

You know this line the way you know your own street at home. The sergeant knows you know it.

choices.text: Go back down and bring them in.
choices.text_after:
They're green as grass. They clank, they talk, they light matches. You bring them up a hundred
men in single file, whispering back over your shoulder at every junction: mind the hole, keep
left, duck here, he's got a gun on this bit. One of their officers, younger than you, thanks you
at the end as if you'd shown him round a cathedral. Then you go back down the trench alone
in the dark, and it's your line no more.

choices.text: Tell the sergeant somebody else knows it better.
choices.text_after:
He sends somebody else. In the morning the word is that one of the new companies lost its way at
the junction by the old mine shaft and walked along the top in the dark for twenty minutes. Nobody
was hit. Nobody says anything to you about it. You think about it anyway.

a_burial.title: Burial party
a_burial.text:
After the battle there are the dead. Theirs and ours, out on the ground they fought over, where
they've lain for days now in the sun or the rain, and the smell comes in over the parapet when the
wind's that way.

A burial party is wanted, tonight and every night this week. Picks and shovels, sandbags, a
sergeant with a notebook for the identity discs and the pay books, and a padre who'll come out to
say the words if it's quiet.

choices.text: Take a shovel and go out with them.
choices.text_after:
Four nights. You learn to work with your mouth shut and breathe through your teeth. You learn
to take a disc off a cord without looking at the face, and then you look at the face anyway.
You put them in shell holes, mostly, two or three together, and a rifle upside down for a
marker, and the sergeant writes it in his book. One of them, on the third night, you knew.
You don't tell anybody which.

choices.text: Get out of it. You've seen enough of the dead.

a_instructor.title: The school
a_instructor.text:
A letter from brigade: a man is wanted as an instructor at the divisional school, behind the
lines, for a fortnight. Teaching drafts the work you know, on a range, in a field, with a hut and a
stove and a bed with sheets.

The company officer says your name's been sent up. It's a fortnight out of the line. Nobody would
blame you.

choices.text: Go to the school.
choices.text_after:
Two weeks of it. A bed. Oofs and chips in the village of an evening. Lads straight off the boat, keen and stupid and frightened, and
you tell them what you wish somebody had told you, and some of them listen. At night you lie in
the sheets and can't sleep for the quiet, and think about the section in the line without you,
and what's happening to them while you're eating eggs.

choices.text: Turn it down. Stay with the section.
choices.text_after:
The company officer looks at you as if you'd turned down a fortune, which you have. Somebody from
another company takes it. You stay, and the section doesn't say anything, and that night your
share of the rum is a bit more than your share.

a_concert.title: The concert party
a_concert.text:
The division has a concert party: a barn behind the lines with a stage made of ammunition boxes,
a piano with half the keys gone, and a curtain made of sandbags sewn together. They've heard you
sing. Somebody always hears you sing.

They want you for a turn on Saturday night. A song. In front of five hundred men.

choices.text: Go up and sing.
choices.text_after:
You sing what your mother used to sing at the copper on washdays, and five hundred men go so
quiet you can hear the lamps hiss. Then the second verse, and they're singing it with you, the
whole barn, low, and some of them aren't singing at all, just sitting with their caps in their
hands. You walk back to the billet in the dark with it still going round your head.

choices.text: Not this time. You don't feel like singing.
choices.text_after:
You don't go. On Saturday night you can hear the barn from the billet, the piano, the laughing,
a man singing a comic song about a sergeant major, and the cheers, and you lie on the straw and
listen to it through the wall.

x_battle_after.title: After {after_name}
x_battle_after.text:
[if war.after == loos]Loos, 25 September 1915: the first great British attack of the war, behind a cloud of gas. The first German line was taken that morning. The second never was. The reserves came up a day late and walked into the machine guns.[/if][if war.after == somme_1_july]The first of July 1916. A week of bombardment had not cut the wire or reached the deep dugouts, and the British Army lost more men that day than on any day before or since: nearly sixty thousand, about twenty thousand of them killed.[/if][if war.after == somme_autumn]The Somme went on into November, a few hundred yards at a time, until the rain and the mud stopped it. In four and a half months the line moved about six miles.[/if][if war.after == arras]Arras, from 9 April 1917. The first day was the best the British Army had yet had: over three miles in places, and the Canadians took Vimy Ridge. Then the German reserves came up, and for the rest of April it cost more men a day than any British battle of the war.[/if][if war.after == passchendaele]Third Ypres, from 31 July 1917. The rain came in the first days of August and hardly stopped. The Canadians took what was left of Passchendaele village on 6 November, about five miles from where it began.[/if][if war.after == cambrai]Cambrai, 20 November 1917. The tanks went through the Hindenburg Line on the first morning, and the church bells rang in England. On 30 November the Germans counter-attacked and took most of it back.[/if][if war.after == spring_offensive]The German offensive, from 21 March 1918, out of the fog behind the heaviest bombardment of the war. In a fortnight the line went back as much as forty miles. It bent. It did not break.[/if][if war.after == hundred_days_august]Amiens, 8 August 1918, in fog, with hundreds of tanks. Seven miles in a day. Ludendorff called it the black day of the German Army.[/if][if war.after == hundred_days_october]October 1918. The Hindenburg Line is behind you, and the advance goes on village by village, into towns the fighting passed over in 1914, where the people come out to meet you.[/if]

[if war.after_fought && war.after_hit == none]You came through it on your feet.[/if][if war.after_hit == light]You were hit, lightly, and walked back to the aid post with your field dressing on.[/if][if war.after_hit == severe]You were hit badly, and carried back, and most of it you only know from what you were told.[/if][if !war.after_fought && war.after_why == course]You missed it. You were away on a course when the battalion went over, and you heard it from the men who came back, the ones who would talk.[/if][if !war.after_fought && war.after_why == wound]You missed it. You were in hospital with your wound, and read about it in the paper, and then in a letter, and the letter was worse.[/if]

[if war.after != cambrai && war.after_lost == 0]Of the men from home, none was killed in it.[/if][if war.after_lost == 1]Of the men from home, {after_lost_names} was killed in it.[/if][if war.after_lost >= 2]Of the men from home, {after_lost_names} were killed in it.[/if] [if war.after != cambrai]{section_line}[/if]

[if war.after_award]Your name is in orders: {after_award_name}.[/if][if war.after_near]Your name went in for a medal. Nothing came of it. Most recommendations come to nothing, the company commander says, and he says he put it in anyway.[/if][if war.after_promoted] There's a stripe in it too: you're {rank_a} now.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.after_lost >= 1]Write their names down.[else]Go on.[/if]

x_fallen_webb.title: Arthur Webb
x_fallen_webb.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Webb's beside you, and then he's sitting in the bottom of the trench with his back against the wall, upright, the way he sat at his desk, and his hand goes to his inside pocket, to the notebook, and stays there.

"Put it down," he says. "The time. Somebody put the time down." And then he doesn't say anything else.[else][if war.transferred]Word comes over from the battalion, a week late. Arthur Webb. Killed {fallen_where}.[else]You hear it at the ration dump, in the dark. Arthur Webb. Killed {fallen_where}.

You sat next to him for three years. You knew the sound of his pen. You'd know it anywhere.[/if][/if][if flag.city_diary_warned] You told him diaries were forbidden. You hope somebody of ours finds the notebook first.[/if][if flag.city_diary_kept] Somewhere there's a little black notebook with every shell in it, and the totals.[/if]

choices.text: Write to Mrs Webb yourself, tonight.
choices.text_after:
You write it in your best office hand. You put that he didn't suffer, which you don't know.
You put that he kept the books to the end, which is true.

choices.text: Leave it to the officer's letter. You can't.

x_fallen_fenton.title: Percy Fenton
x_fallen_fenton.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Fenton's running, the way he always runs, as if there's a ball in front of him, and then he goes down, sliding, the way a centre-forward goes down in a tackle on a wet pitch, and lies there, and you wait for him to get up, because he always gets up.

He doesn't get up.[else][if war.transferred]Word comes over from the battalion, a week late. Percy Fenton. Killed {fallen_where}.[else]Somebody tells you at the water cart. "Fenton's gone west." Percy Fenton. Killed {fallen_where}.

You think of him on the wing at Walthamstow on a Saturday, in the mud, with the whole office shouting.[/if][/if][if flag.city_played] You played behind him once, against the pitmen, in a stubble field in France.[/if]

choices.text: Write to his father. Tell him about the match.
choices.text_after:
You tell him about the stubble field and the rifles for goalposts, and both goals. He never
missed a Saturday. He'll want every kick.

choices.text: Leave it. You'd never get him right.

x_fallen_marsh.title: Leonard Marsh
x_fallen_marsh.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Marsh goes down on his hands and knees, and his spectacles come off, and he feels about in the mud for them, quite calm, the way he'd feel for them on the bedside table in the morning.

You find them and put them in his hand. He holds them. He doesn't put them on. "It's all right," he says. "I can see."[else][if war.transferred]Word comes over from the battalion, a week late. Leonard Marsh. Killed {fallen_where}.[else]You hear it from a stretcher-bearer who knew him from chapel. Leonard Marsh. Killed {fallen_where}.

He learned the eye chart by heart, the night before the recruiting office, the whole thing, so they'd let him come.[/if][/if]

choices.text: Write to Mrs Marsh yourself.
choices.text_after:
You tell her he taught the section the books of the Bible, in order, on sentry, to keep awake.
You tell her he was never frightened of anything except being sent home.

choices.text: Leave it. She'll have the official letter.

c_close.title: In front of you
c_close.text:
[if war.close_battle == loos && war.close_phase == 1]The smoke and the gas have got mixed out here, and you're walking blind in it, in the flannel gas helmet, your own breath roaring in your ears. A shell hole opens at your feet. There's a German in it. He's got a wet rag tied over his mouth and nose and his eyes are streaming, and he's coughing, a dry bark you can hear through the flannel. A grey moustache. He's old enough to be your father. His rifle's across his knees, and he looks up at you through the gas, waiting to see what you are.[/if]

[if war.close_battle == loos && war.close_phase == 2]Over their parapet, and you drop, and the chalk floor of the trench jars your teeth. A yard away a man is pressed flat against the trench wall. White dust all down him, in his eyebrows, in the creases of his neck, like a baker at the end of a shift. His hands are half up. There's a gold ring on one of them. His rifle's leaning on the wall where he could have it in a second. Along the trench somebody is screaming in German, and he's breathing through his mouth, fast, the same as you.[/if]

[if war.close_battle == somme_1_july && war.close_phase == 1]A place where a shell has thinned their wire, and you're through it on your knees with the barbs in your sleeve. Twenty yards on, their parapet. A man is kneeling up on it with the sky behind him, reloading, and his fingers won't do it. He drops the clip in the chalk and gets another out of his pouch, and his lips are moving. The machine guns are going on both sides of you, and the air tastes of hot oil and cordite. He hasn't seen you. Then he has.[/if]

[if war.close_battle == somme_1_july && war.close_phase == 2]At the head of a dugout stair a man comes up into the daylight and stops on the top step, blinking. Shirt sleeves, braces down, half a sausage in his fist. He was eating it down there when our guns stopped. His cap is pushed through his belt, with a little round badge on it, black and red. Behind him the stair goes down thirty feet into the chalk, and up it comes a smell of coffee and tobacco and men asleep. He looks at you. He's still chewing.[/if]

[if war.close_battle == somme_autumn && war.close_phase == 1]Halfway over, the mud has you to the knees, and a yard to your left it has a German to the thighs. He must have been out in a shell-hole post all night. He's trying to get one leg free with both hands locked round his knee, grunting, the way you'd pull a stake out of wet ground. His helmet's slid to the back of his head, the coal-scuttle shape of theirs, and the face under it is grey with stubble and cold. The rain's running off the pair of you. His rifle's in the mud beside him. He looks at it, and then at you.[/if]

[if war.close_battle == somme_autumn && war.close_phase == 2]Their trench is a ditch of brown water. You slide down into it to the waist, and the cold stops your breath, and there's a man in it with you, three yards off, at the bend of the bay. Somebody has tied a field dressing round his head and it's slipped down over one eye. His teeth are chattering so hard you can hear them over the bombing. He's holding his rifle up out of the water with both hands. So are you.[/if]

[if war.close_battle == arras && war.close_phase == 1]Five yards ahead, in the sleet, a man climbs up out of a shell hole in front of their wire. He's been out there all night, by the look of him, in a hole with a groundsheet over it. There's snow on his helmet and on his shoulders, and the face under the helmet is a boy's, with fluff on the lip. He's stiff with the cold and his legs won't work. He's trying to get his rifle up. The barrage is going over the both of you with a noise like a train in a cutting, and you can smell the wet wool of his greatcoat.[/if]

[if war.close_battle == arras && war.close_phase == 2]Their second line. Round a traverse there's a German kneeling in the snow beside one of ours, a lad from the first wave with his leg smashed. He's tying a field dressing on it, one he's torn out of the lad's own tunic, and he's doing it properly, the knot and all. His rifle's on the fire step behind him. He looks up at you with the end of the bandage in his teeth and sleet on his eyelashes. The lad on the ground is saying something, but the guns are too loud to hear it.[/if]

[if war.close_battle == passchendaele && war.close_phase == 1]There's no line out here, only holes, and some of the holes have Germans in. You come over the rim of one and there's a man in it up to his chest in green water, holding his rifle up out of it. He's got a rag tied round the bolt to keep the mud out, the same as you have. A beard coming, red-brown. His lips are blue. The water has a skin on it, and the smell coming off it is gas and rot. The barrage is walking away from the pair of you.[/if]

[if war.close_battle == passchendaele && war.close_phase == 2]The back of a pillbox, where the door is. The door's open. A man comes out of it bent double, his hands up to his shoulders and no higher, and stops in the mud a few yards off. Grey hair cropped short. Spectacles, mended at the hinge with cotton. Behind him in the dark of the doorway something moves, and out of it comes a smell of candle grease and wet concrete and men shut in too long. He's saying something over and over, low.[/if]

[if war.close_battle == hundred_days_august && war.close_phase == 1]Three yards off, a German stands up out of the corn. He must have been lying in it since the barrage came down. The fog's on him the way breath goes on a window, and his uniform is too big for him: the cuffs turned back twice, the collar standing off his neck. He's younger than the lads in the last draft. His bayonet's fixed. The tanks are roaring somewhere in the fog behind you and you can't hear what he shouts. The corn round your legs smells green and crushed.[/if]

[if war.close_battle == hundred_days_august && war.close_phase == 2]At the edge of the wood, behind a fallen trunk, there's a machine gun with one man still on it. The others are gone, or they're lying beside him. He's feeding in a new belt, quick and calm, the way a man is at a job he knows. There's a wedding ring on the hand that's feeding it. You came round the side through the bracken, and you're closer than he knows: you can smell the hot oil on the gun and hear the belt clack home.[/if]

[if war.close_battle == hundred_days_october && war.close_phase == 1]A hedge, and a German in a rifle pit behind it, eating an apple. There are apples all over the grass on his side, windfalls, wet, from the orchard at his back. His rifle's resting on the bank and the apple has one bite out of it. He's looking the wrong way, along the hedge. You come up through the long grass with the sweet rotten smell of the windfalls all round you, and you hear him bite, and he turns his head.[/if]

[if war.close_battle == hundred_days_october && war.close_phase == 2]In a farmyard off the street, at the pump, a German is filling water bottles. He has a dozen of them hung round his neck on their straps, so he clanks when he moves, and he's working the handle with one hand and holding a bottle under the spout with the other. Forty if he's a day, with a moustache and a bald patch. The pump squeaks. He looks round at you with the water running over his hand and on to his boots.[/if]

[if war.close_key == raid && war.stake == 0]Halfway across, a shell hole you didn't know was there, and a listening post in it: one man, under a groundsheet, twenty yards out from their wire. He's awake. Greatcoat, a scarf wound round and round his neck, his rifle on the rim beside him. He's eating something out of a tin with his fingers, slowly, making it last. You're on the rim above him. You can smell what he's eating: fish, and oil. He looks up.[/if]

[if war.close_key == raid && war.stake == 1]A flare goes up and you roll into the nearest shell hole, and there's a man already in it. One of theirs, out on patrol or out to listen. He's lying on his back against the slope with his rifle across his chest, as flat as you are, and his face is a foot from yours. The flare comes down slowly, hissing, and in the light of it you see him: thin, unshaven, ears sticking out from under his cap like a lad's. He smells of coffee and wet cloth. He's as frightened as you. Neither of you moves. The flare goes out.[/if]

[if war.close_key == bomb && war.stake == 0]Over their parapet and down, as quietly as you can, which isn't quietly. You land on the fire step of a bay with a sentry in it, and he has his back to you. He's looking out over the parapet, the wrong way, at the dark you've just come out of. A greatcoat, a scarf, a pipe gone out in his teeth, and you can smell the old tobacco in it. He's humming. Then he isn't. He's heard the gravel shift under your boots.[/if]

[if war.close_key == bomb && war.stake == 1]Down into their trench, and the first thing in front of you is a dugout entrance with a blanket across it. The blanket goes back. A man comes up the steps in his shirt and socks with a candle in his hand, yawning. He was asleep. His hair is stuck up at the back the way a lad's is in the morning. The candle lights his face and yours, a yard apart, and up past him comes the fug of the dugout, sweat and coke fumes and sour bread. His mouth is still open from the yawn.[/if]

[if war.close_where == battle][if war.path == lewis]The gun's in your hands, hot, half a drum left on it.[elif war.path == snipe]You've the scoped rifle. This close you don't need the scope.[elif war.path == signals]Your rifle's slung behind the reel of wire, and getting it round takes a second.[elif war.path == bomb]There's a bomb in your hand with the pin already straightened.[elif war.path == nco]Two of your section are a yard behind you, waiting to see what you do.[elif war.path == subaltern]The revolver's in your hand on its lanyard. Your platoon sergeant is at your shoulder, and he's watching you, not the German.[elif war.path == rifleman]Your bayonet's been fixed since the start line.[/if][/if][if war.close_where == sortie][if war.path == subaltern]You're the officer. The others are behind you, waiting on what you do.[elif war.path == nco]You've the stripes. The men behind you will do what you do.[/if][/if]

[if war.killed == 0]You've fired at flashes and grey shapes and loopholes. You've never killed a man whose face you could see.[elif war.killed == 1 && flag.cl_close_kill]Once before, close. Your arms remember it before you do.[elif war.killed == 1]Once before, at a distance. You saw him drop, and you never saw his face.[else]There've been others. You don't let yourself count them, and the number's there all the same, like the numbers on the hymn board.[/if][if flag.cl_let_go] Another time, you let one go. You've told nobody.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.close_where == sortie && war.path == subaltern]Shoot him with the revolver.[elif war.close_where == sortie]Shoot him, and never mind the noise.[elif war.path == lewis]Give him a burst from the gun.[elif war.path == snipe]Shoot him from the shoulder, no sight.[elif war.path == subaltern]Shoot him with the revolver from where you stand.[else]Shoot him from where you are.[/if] ({risk_close_shoot})
choices.text_after: [if war.sortie == raid || war.result_key == raid && war.result != none]The shot is the loudest thing you have ever heard. He slides down the side of the hole and lies still, and the rest of you lie still with him, listening.[elif war.sortie == bomb]You fire from the hip. In the flash you see his face, surprised, and then you don't.[elif war.path == lewis]A short burst from the hip. He folds over in the middle of it, and the empty cases spill hot over your boots.[elif war.path == snipe]You don't use the sight. You fire the way any man would, and he drops, and the brass case jumps out bright and lands by your hand.[elif war.path == subaltern]The revolver kicks up. You fire again because you can't tell, and then you can.[else]You fire. He sits down as if somebody had pulled a chair out from under him, and coughs once, surprised, and doesn't get up.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.close_key == bomb && war.stake == 1]Shove him back down the steps and a bomb after him.[elif war.close_key == bomb]The cosh, before he turns round.[elif war.close_where == sortie && war.path == subaltern]The revolver, at arm's length.[elif war.close_where == sortie]The cosh. Now, before he moves.[elif war.path == subaltern || war.path == lewis]Go in close with the revolver.[elif war.path == snipe]Go in with the rifle butt.[elif war.path == bomb && war.close_battle == arras && war.close_phase == 2]Go in with the bayonet.[elif war.path == bomb]Get back a pace, pull the pin, and throw.[else]Go in with the bayonet.[/if] ({risk_close_bayonet})
choices.text_after: [if war.path == subaltern]Arm's length. You fire twice, because after the first you can't tell, and his hand takes hold of your sleeve and holds on.[elif war.sortie == raid || war.result_key == raid && war.result != none]You hit him, and again, the way you were taught, and he goes still. Out there the only sound is your own breath.[elif war.sortie == bomb || war.result_key == bomb && war.result != none]It's quick. You're shaking after, and your mouth tastes of the smoke, like a penny held on the tongue.[elif war.path == lewis]Arm's length. You fire twice, because after the first you can't tell, and his hand takes hold of your sleeve and holds on.[elif war.path == snipe]The butt. It's harder than you thought, and it takes longer, and he says something at the end, one word.[elif war.path == bomb && war.battle != arras || war.path == bomb && war.phase != 2]You throw and get down, and the bang comes up through the ground into your chest. When you look again he's lying where he was, smaller.[else]It goes in easier than the sacks on the training ground, and comes out harder. His hand closes on the barrel of your rifle, holding it, and then it doesn't.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.close_key == raid]Get hold of him and keep him quiet. He's what you came for.[elif war.close_key == bomb]Take him. Get his hands up and send him back.[else]Shout at him to put his hands up.[/if] ({risk_close_prisoner})
choices.text_after: [if war.sortie == raid || war.result_key == raid && war.result != none]He doesn't fight. He's shaking so hard you can feel it through his coat, and he keeps hold of your sleeve all the way to the man who'll take him back.[elif war.sortie == bomb || war.result_key == bomb && war.result != none]His hands go up so high his shirt comes out of his belt. You push him at the parapet, towards our lines, with a man behind him, and he goes without looking back.[else]His hands go up. He keeps saying the same thing, over and over, and you never find out what it was. When you point back the way you came, he nods, as if you'd given him directions in the street.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.close_where == sortie]Keep still. Let him go.[elif war.close_phase == 2]Look the other way. Let him go.[else]Go on past him. Let him be.[/if] ({risk_close_spare})
choices.text_after: [if war.sortie == raid || war.result_key == raid && war.result != none]You keep still, and he goes, on his elbows, into the dark the way he came. You can hear him for a while after you can't see him.[elif war.sortie == bomb || war.result_key == bomb && war.result != none]You let him be. He backs away from you into the dark, slowly, the way you'd back away from a strange dog.[else]You look past him, and he understands, and goes. The last you see of him is the soles of his boots, the nails worn bright at the toes.[/if]

w_corps_air.title: The Flying Corps
w_corps_air.text:
May, and the battalion's out at rest after Arras, in a village with the blossom just going over.
A Flying Corps officer comes round the billets in a motor car, with a list. He's young, younger
than you, with wings on his tunic and a cough he turns away to finish.

Everybody knows what April cost the Flying Corps. You watched it, every afternoon, from the
trench. Now the squadrons want gunners. Not officers: men from the ranks, to fly in the back
seat of a two-seater with a Lewis gun on a ring. Lewis gunners first. A man who can clear a
stoppage by feel, he says, with gloves on, two miles up, in the cold.

"Better pay," he says. "Flying pay, on top of your own. A bed with sheets, miles behind the
line. Hot food. No trenches." He looks along the row of you. "I won't tell you it's safe. It
isn't. We've no parachutes. Men are killed every week, and you'd be up every week." He coughs.
"And it's for good. You'll not come back to this battalion."

[if flag.went_to_airman]You think of the goggles lying in the grass without a mark on them.[/if]

[if start == mill]In the barn after, the mill lads have it out over the stew.[if war.mate2] Duckworth says it's like being made a tackler: more money, and everybody hates you.[/if][if war.mate1] Shaw says your mother'll have a fit, and then he says he would, in your place, and then he says he wouldn't.[/if][/if][if start == pit]In the billet after, the Blackhaugh lads have it out.[if war.mate2] Bell says flying's for the gentry, and you'd be the gentry's servant, cleaning their gun for them.[/if][if war.mate1] Robson says he'd sooner be at the face than up there with nowt under him but air.[/if][/if][if start == farm]In the barn after, the Dunsworthy lads have it out.[if war.mate2] Pearce says if they'd give him a gun up there he'd have every pheasant in Picardy.[/if][if war.mate1] Cottle looks up at the sky over the orchard as if he's pricing it at market.[/if][/if][if start == city]In the billet after, the City lads have it out.[if war.mate1] Webb works out the flying pay on the back of a field postcard and shows you the sum, and under it, in pencil, he's put down how many airmen the paper said were lost in April.[/if][if war.mate2] Fenton says it's like being sold to another club in the middle of the season.[/if][/if]

You'd leave them. All of them, the whole section from home, and not come back.

choices.text: Put your name down for the Flying Corps. Leave the section for good.
Stay with the men from home.

bt_air.title: {battle_name}
bt_air.text:
{phase_count}

[if war.battle == passchendaele && war.phase == 1]The thirty-first of July. Up at four, in the dark, to a sky like a wet slate. You're the contact patrol for the attack: under the cloud, below a thousand feet, over the battalion, to find out where the front line's got to so the guns and the generals know. Beneath you the barrage is a strip of flashes as far as you can see, and the machine jumps and drops in the air the shells push up, and the smoke comes up past you smelling of cordite. Ferrier sounds the Klaxon over the place where the battalion should be, a short blare and a long one, the Morse for A: where are you? You lean out over the side with the map on your knee, the wind tearing at it, and look for the flares.[if war.section >= 1] Somewhere down there are the men from home.[/if][/if][if war.battle == passchendaele && war.phase == 2]Days of rain, and the machines in the hangars. When the cloud lifts you go up to find the pillboxes for the guns: grey lumps of concrete in the brown, and round them the shell holes full of water that flash like tin when the sun gets on them. One of them is holding up the battalion's front. The heavies fire at it one round at a time, slow, and each burst throws up a brown fountain, and the correction goes down in Morse, and you watch the sky behind the tail and the burst both, with your neck aching from turning.[/if][if war.battle == passchendaele && war.phase == 3]From the air you see it before the battalion can. Grey men in the low ground behind the German line, a few at a time, running from shell hole to shell hole, gathering behind a farm that's only a heap of bricks now. A counter-attack, forming, and the men in the water-filled holes in front of it can't see a thing. If the guns know in time, it never starts. Ferrier puts the nose down to make sure, and something from the bricks starts firing up at you, and holes walk across the lower wing.[/if][if war.battle == passchendaele && war.phase == 4]Evening, and rain coming in from the west in grey curtains. You fly over the relief, the battalion coming out: lines of little figures on the duckboard tracks, all going one way, slow, bent, and the stretcher parties, six to a stretcher, putting it down and picking it up. You can see from up here what they can't. How far it is. How many tracks are broken. The petrol smell of the engine and the wet in your face, and down there, men you might know, walking out of it.[/if][if war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase == 1]The twenty-first of March. You wake to the guns, before five, a noise from the east like the whole sky being shaken out, and the hut window rattling in its frame. Fog on the aerodrome, thick as wet flannel. Nobody can fly. You stand by the hangars with [if !flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_ferrier_killed]Ferrier[/if][if flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_hollis_killed || flag.af18_ferrier_killed && !flag.af18_hollis_killed]Hollis[/if][if flag.af18_hollis_killed]Lyle[/if] and Sallis, listening, and nobody says what everybody's thinking about the battalions in the forward posts. When it thins, near noon, you go up, and the line isn't where it was. There's smoke, and on the roads behind it, columns. Grey ones, coming.[/if][if war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase == 2]The aerodrome's moved back. Twice in three days: the hangars struck by lamplight and folded onto lorries, the machines flown off at dawn, Sallis riding on the tailboard of a Crossley tender with his toolbox on his knees. Now you fly from a field with cows still in it, and the farmer at the gate every morning saying "Pas bon, pas bon" over the wheel ruts. Every machine's out over the roads, low, after the columns: men marching, wagons, a gun team, packed between the poplars. You can see their faces turn up when you come over. You can see them run for the ditches.[/if][if war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase == 3]Under you the old Somme ground, the ground the battalion took a summer and a half to win, going back to them in days. From here the old trenches of 1916 are still there in the grass, pale lines like old scars, with the new war running over the top of them. Dumps burning, black smoke lying along the valleys. Somewhere in it the battalion's falling back, and you can't tell which of the little khaki groups on the roads is them.[/if][if war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase == 4]The end of March, and a railway embankment in front of a town, and the line's there, the word is, and holding. Contact patrol at dusk. [if !flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_ferrier_killed]Ferrier[/if][if flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_hollis_killed || flag.af18_ferrier_killed && !flag.af18_hollis_killed]Hollis[/if][if flag.af18_hollis_killed]Lyle[/if] sounds the Klaxon over the embankment, and this time the flares come up, a string of them along the rails, sputtering, and you mark them on the map with frozen fingers, and below you a man in a shell hole is waving his tin hat.[/if][if war.battle == hundred_days_august && war.phase == 1]The eighth of August. Fog again at dawn, but this time it's ours. You take off into it, and come up into sunlight, and when it thins you see the tanks, dozens of them, grinding through the standing corn, and behind them the infantry in little worms of men. Contact patrol over the battalion. [if !flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_ferrier_killed]Ferrier[/if][if flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_hollis_killed || flag.af18_ferrier_killed && !flag.af18_hollis_killed]Hollis[/if][if flag.af18_hollis_killed]Lyle[/if] takes you down to five hundred feet, and the corn's so green it hurts, and the smoke from a burning tank lies across it flat and black.[/if][if war.battle == hundred_days_august && war.phase == 2]The bridges. The order is to break the bridges over the Somme, so their men can't get away and their help can't get across, and the bombers and the scouts go for them low, all day. Your job's the German guns on the far bank, for our batteries. Over the river at five hundred feet, with every gun on the far bank firing up and the water flashing under you, and the stink of the river and the hot engine. A scout ahead of you, going down on a bridge, goes straight into the water and doesn't come up. [if !flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_ferrier_killed]Ferrier[/if][if flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_hollis_killed || flag.af18_ferrier_killed && !flag.af18_hollis_killed]Hollis[/if][if flag.af18_hollis_killed]Lyle[/if] doesn't turn his head.[/if][if war.battle == hundred_days_august && war.phase == 3]Open country, the third day. Low over the advance: cavalry going through the oats at a trot, real cavalry, and their guns behind a hedge firing over open sights at the tanks. From up here the hedge is a green line with flashes along it. The battalion's in the field in front of it, lying down. If the guns behind them knew where that hedge was, they'd be up and on in an hour.[/if][if war.battle == hundred_days_october && war.phase == 1]A river in October, with fog lying on it. You fly the contact patrol at first light along the bank, and the footbridges are black threads on the water with men on them, single file, and one of the threads breaks while you watch. [if !flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_ferrier_killed]Ferrier[/if][if flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_hollis_killed || flag.af18_ferrier_killed && !flag.af18_hollis_killed]Hollis[/if][if flag.af18_hollis_killed]Lyle[/if] sounds the Klaxon, and you look for the flares on the far bank, and the gas in the low places is lying yellow in the fog.[/if][if war.battle == hundred_days_october && war.phase == 2]A village with roofs on, and people in it. They come up out of the cellars when you go over low, and wave anything white at you, sheets, shirts, a tablecloth, a baby's napkin on a stick. And from the church tower a machine gun fires up at you, and down the street at the battalion.[/if][if war.battle == hundred_days_october && war.phase == 3]The last of it. Every road east is full of their columns going back, slow, guns and carts and men walking, and a few still turn and fight in the orchards, enough to kill. The battalion's down there in the apples. From the air you can see where the next machine gun is, behind a wall, before they walk onto it.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.battle == passchendaele]Go down low and find the battalion's flares. Their line is what the guns need.[/if][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go down on the columns coming at the battalion.[/if][if war.battle == hundred_days_august]Stay low over the battalion and mark what's holding them up.[/if][if war.battle == hundred_days_october]Go down low over the men from home and find what's stopping them.[/if] ({risk_push})
Watch the pilot's tail. Keep the scouts off the machine. ({risk_help})
Stay high. Tap his shoulder and point for home. ({risk_ground})

s_air_1.title: Over the line
s_air_1.text:
[if war.stake == 0]An artillery shoot. You climb over the aerodrome in wide circles to get your height, and the cold
comes up through the floor of the cockpit into your boots, and the wind finds the gap between
your helmet and your scarf. Whale oil on your face against the frost; you can smell it over the
hot oil and the exhaust. Then the line, a brown smear across the green, and the first Archie: a
black puff ahead, a cough you hear over the engine, another, closer, and the machine lifting
under you like a cart going over a stone. For the shoot the pilot has to fly the same beat up
and down, straight and level, for an hour. The German gunners know it as well as you.[/if][if war.stake == 1]A photographic job, the line opposite the corps, in strips. The camera's a box as big as a bread
bin, fixed to the fuselage by your cockpit, looking straight down, and the pilot has to fly dead straight over the line so the
photographic plates join up, and dead straight is what the Archie gunners want. The cold at five thousand
feet goes through the leather coat and the jersey and the shirt as if they were wet paper. Your
breath is ice on your scarf. Out to the east there's sun on the cloud, bright enough to hurt,
and that's where they'll come from, if they come.[/if]

choices.text: Stand up in the ring and watch everything, the whole sky. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You stand with the wind trying to tear you out of the cockpit, turning, turning, and your eyes stream behind the goggles.

choices.text: Watch your own quarter of the sky, and the sun. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: The tail and the sun, the tail and the sun, the way you'd watch a loophole. Nothing yet.

choices.text: Keep down out of the wind, and look out over the side. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You crouch behind the edge of the cockpit with your face in your scarf and look out when you can bear it.

s_air_2.title: Over the line
s_air_2.text:
[if war.stake == 0]The battery's strips are out on the grass behind their guns, white cloth laid in a shape that
means ready. The call goes down in Morse, and far below a gun flashes, and you count,
and the burst comes up near the German battery in the wood, short and left. The clock code: the
target's the middle of a clock face, twelve is north, and the rings round it have letters. The
burst goes down in the code, and the strips change, and the next one comes. Then the engine coughs, and
picks up, and coughs again. And out of the sun, high, you see a speck that wasn't there.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Halfway along the line, and the speck comes out of the sun the way they always do: a German
scout, fast, coming down on your tail. You swing the Lewis round on the Scarff ring, and the ring
is stiff with cold, and the drum is the big one, ninety-seven rounds, twice what you carried in
the battalion. You fire, and after a dozen rounds the gun stops. A stoppage. Your fingers have
gone dead in the gauntlets. You know this gun. You learned it in a barn behind the line with your
eyes shut.[if flag.af17_bare_hands] The two fingers you skinned in July ache before you've touched it.[/if] The engine's missing, too: you can feel it in the floor.[/if]

choices.text: Clear it bare-handed and give him the rest of the drum. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You pull the gauntlet off with your teeth. The metal takes the skin off two fingers. The cocking handle goes back, and the gun's firing before you've thought about it.

choices.text: Short bursts. Make him keep his distance. Let the pilot finish. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Short bursts, the way you'd fire across a wire gap, and he sheers off and circles, and the pilot holds his line.

choices.text: Bang on the pilot's shoulder. Get down low, out of his way. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: The pilot puts the nose down hard and your stomach stays behind, and the ground comes up brown and broken.

choices.text: The engine's missing. Point him home, now. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: He nods, and turns west, the engine coughing all the way, and you watch the speck behind you until it gives up.

s_air_3.title: Over the line
s_air_3.text:
[if war.stake == 0]The job's done, or done enough, and you turn for home, and the scout comes down on you out of
