the sun with his guns going. You hear him before you see him: a dry rattle, and the wires
singing, and splinters off the edge of the cockpit. Then he's there, behind the tail, where the
pilot can't see him and you can, close enough to see his goggles and the paint on his cowling.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Home across the line, low, with the plates in the box and the engine running rough, and the
Archie has your height again. Black bursts in front, in a row, walking towards you. The
machine's shot about: a wire hanging loose and flapping, a long tear in the fabric of the
upper wing that opens and shuts in the wind like a mouth. The aerodrome's twenty miles off.
The pilot looks round at you, and you look at him.[/if]

choices.text: Swing the gun round on him and hold it on. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You hold it on him, and the tracer goes into him, or near him, and the gun bucks and the empty cases rattle round your feet.

choices.text: Keep watching. Let the pilot fly it home. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You keep your eyes on the sky and your hands on the gun and let him fly, and the miles go by under you slow as a Sunday.

choices.text: Get down in the cockpit and hold on. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You get down on the floor of the cockpit with your arms round the gun post, and the sky goes round and round over the top of you.

x_air_done.title: Down again
x_air_done.text:
[if war.result == ok]The wheels touch, and bounce, and touch, and the noise of the engine stops, and you can hear a lark. Sallis is at the edge of the field with his cap pushed back, counting the machines in. He walks round yours and puts his finger in the holes, one after the other, and says the pilot can thank him for the wires. In the hut there's tea with sugar in it, and in the evening the battery's officer telephones to say the shoot was the best they've had, or the photographs come out of the dark room joined up like a map.[/if][if war.result == failed]It went wrong. The shoot was called off half done, or the plates came out fogged, or the scout drove you off it, and the job will have to be flown again by somebody, maybe you. The pilot climbs down without a word and walks off to the office. Sallis counts the holes, and doesn't say a thing about the wires.[/if][if war.result == turned]You came home with the job not done. Sallis takes the cowling off before the propeller's stopped and puts his ear to the engine, and you stand on the grass in your coat waiting to hear him say it was all right after all. He doesn't say anything. He gets his spanners out.[/if]

{result_note}

choices.text: Get out of your coat. Go and get warm.

v17air_aerodrome.title: The aerodrome
v17air_aerodrome.text:
The aerodrome's a big field of grass with a wood at one end and a row of canvas hangars along
the road, their sides flapping, like a fair that's put up in the wrong town. The first thing is
the smell: petrol, hot oil, and the dope they paint on the wings, sweet as pear drops, that gets
into your clothes and your bread. Across the field a squadron of scouts is running up its
engines, and the wind brings the castor oil off them thick enough to taste.

You've a bed. An iron bed, in a hut, with a mattress and two sheets and a pillow with a slip on
it. You stand and look at it with your kit still on your back. Nobody here is lousy. Your boots
are the only muddy thing in the hut, and the corporal looks at them.

The machine is an RE8, a big khaki two-seater the men call the Harry Tate, with a ring in the back
cockpit for the gun. Its fitter is Air Mechanic Sallis, a Coventry man with grey in his moustache
who built bicycles before the war. He wipes his hand on a rag before he shakes yours.

The pilot comes over in the evening: Lieutenant Ferrier, a Canadian, twenty, with big red hands
and a sunburnt neck. "You're my gunner," he says. "Good. Do you know what a binder is?" You don't.
"It cuts the wheat and ties it," he says. "I drove one at eleven, back home in Manitoba. This is
the same, only it goes up." He shakes your hand. Officers don't.

choices.text: Go out to the hangar with Sallis and look her over.
choices.text_after:
He shows you the machine by the light of a hurricane lamp, every wire, every turnbuckle,
the way a man shows you round his allotment. "She's sound," he says. "I see to that. You see
to the gun. Then we both get our tea." He's got a little book where he writes down every
machine that goes out and every one that comes back.

choices.text: Lie down on the bed and sleep.
choices.text_after:
You mean to take your boots off first. You wake at six with them on, and the sheets
haven't a mark on them, because you never got under them.

v17air_photographs.title: From above
v17air_photographs.text:
July. A photographic job over the battalion's own sector; the officer in the flight office
says the map square, and you know the name. In the evening the photographic sergeant pins the
prints up to dry on a line in his hut, like washing, and the place smells of vinegar and wet
paper.

You find it. You know it by the shape: the bend where the communication trench goes in, the
sap, the wood that's only stumps. From two miles up it's thin and grey, a crooked line across
the fields like a scar on a man's arm. Every shell hole's a little white ring. The wire's a
grey fuzz, like mould on a crust. You can't see a single man in it. You know there are
hundreds, and that some of them are men from your street.

choices.text: Ask the sergeant for a spoiled print, to keep.
choices.text_after:
He gives you one with a fogged corner. You can't send it home; the censor would have you.
You keep it folded in your pay book, and some nights you take it out and look for your own bay of the trench.

choices.text: Leave it. Go and get your tea.
choices.text_after:
You go and get your tea. On the way you look north, to where the line is, and there's
nothing to see but a lark going up, and the heat shaking over the grass.

v17air_jam.title: Six thousand feet
v17air_jam.text:
July, and at six thousand feet it's winter. Your fingers have gone inside two pairs of gloves.
The wind has its hand flat on your face and pushes.

A Hun two-seater comes up behind the tail, and you get half a drum into it, and the gun stops.
You can't feel the cocking handle. You can't feel anything. Ferrier's turning to give you a shot,
and the German's gunner is firing, and you can hear the bullets going through the fabric behind
you like somebody tearing a sheet.

It was a barn behind the line, the Lewis course, with a sergeant who made you strip the gun
blindfold and timed you on his watch. You remember his voice better than his face.

choices.text: Take the glove off and clear it by feel, like on the course.
choices.text_after:
The metal burns like a stove lid. You find the handle, and pull it back, and feel the round
that's stuck, and get it out with your nail, and the gun's going again. The German goes away
east, low, with smoke coming off him or not; you can't tell. That night Sallis puts goose
grease on your fingers and tells you about a man at Coventry who lost three to a lathe.

choices.text: Change the drum and pray it was the drum.
choices.text_after:
It wasn't the drum. By the time you've got it cleared the German's gone and Ferrier's put
the machine into a dive for home. On the ground he looks at the gun, and at you, and goes off to the office.

v17air_archie.title: Archie
v17air_archie.text:
September. The men call the German anti-aircraft fire Archie, and nobody can tell you why. Black
puffs, all round, and a cough you hear over the engine, and the machine jumping. Bits come
through the wings and leave little ragged holes that Sallis will patch tonight with dope and
linen, whistling.[if flag.af17_sallis_engine] You'll hold the lamp for him, the way you did the first night.[/if]

On the way home you see one of ours go down. It's a mile off and far below, a two-seater from
another squadron, and it's burning. Not fast. A little flame at the engine and a long thread of
smoke, and it goes down in big slow turns, like a leaf off a sycamore. A man climbs out of the
back cockpit onto the wing.

There are no parachutes for the aeroplanes. The balloon men have them; you've seen them come
down under silk when a balloon goes, swinging, slow. Not for you.

choices.text: Watch it all the way down.
choices.text_after:
You watch till it's a smudge of smoke on the ground. The talk in the hut that night is of
revolvers, who carries one and who doesn't. You don't ask what for.

choices.text: Turn your back on it. Watch your own sky.
choices.text_after:
You watch your bit of sky, the bit behind the tail that nobody else is watching, all the way
home. Ferrier lands, and sits in the cockpit after the engine's stopped, a good minute, before
he climbs down.

v17air_letters.title: Letters
v17air_letters.text:
October, and the weather closes in, and there are days on end when nothing flies. The post
comes up. Ferrier gets a fat letter from Manitoba every week, from his mother, with a wheat ear
in it, or a pressed flower that falls out in bits, and he reads them out to you in the back of
the hangar where nobody can see an officer reading his letters to a ranker. A major has told him
he's too familiar with his gunner. He tells you so himself, laughing, then not laughing.

[if start == pit]There's nothing for you. There's been nothing from home since you left the battalion. The post's lost you somewhere between the two.[else]Your own is from your mother, in pencil.

"Dear Son, just a few lines hoping this finds you well as it leaves us. We had your letter about the Flying Corps. I have read about the airmen in the paper and I am more frightened than I was before, they put their photographs in, young lads, and how many Germans they have brought down, and then a week after, there they are again in the column with the others.[if start == mill] Our Jack has cut an aeroplane out of the paper and pinned it over his bed, I have told him it is not a game.[/if][if start == farm] Your father says it is no place for a farm lad, up in the air where nothing grows.[/if][if start == city] After the German aeroplanes and the poor children at Poplar I cannot look up at one of ours without feeling sick.[/if] Do not do anything daring. Your loving Mother."[/if]

choices.text: Tell Ferrier you'll come and see the farm, after.
choices.text_after:
"You'll come at harvest," he says. "I'll put you on the binder." He writes the address on
the back of a cigarette packet, the post office, and under it a township and a section
number to find the farm by, and you put it in your pay book.

choices.text: Write home tonight. Tell them about the bed with sheets.
choices.text_after: [if start == pit]You write to your mother about the bed and the sheets and the hot dinners, and at the end you ask why nobody's written. You lick the envelope. It tastes of dope.[else]You write about the bed and the sheets and the hot dinners, and that you're miles behind the line. You don't write the rest. You lick the envelope, and it tastes of dope.[/if]

v18air_hollis.title: A sergeant pilot
v18air_hollis.text:
[if war.month <= 2]Snow on the aerodrome, and the oil like treacle in the mornings; the mechanics warm it before they'll start an engine. [/if]A new pilot comes to the flight: Sergeant Hollis. He was a fitter in the Flying Corps, a
mechanic, and he put in to learn to fly, and they let him. He's thirty, short, with oil worked
so far into the lines of his hands that no soap will shift it.

He walks round every machine on the line before he'll look at you twice. He listens to the
engines with his head on one side, like a thrush on a lawn, and tells Sallis that one of
his cylinders is firing late. Sallis says it isn't. It is.

"The officers fly," Hollis says, in the hut, filling his pipe. "I just drive the thing. Anybody
can drive it. It's knowing why it stops."

choices.text: Help him and Sallis take the engine down.
choices.text_after:
All afternoon in the cold hangar with your hands in the paraffin, passing spanners, Hollis
and Sallis arguing over it the way two old men argue over a pigeon. When it runs, it runs
sweeter. They both say it was their idea.

choices.text: Keep your distance. You've a pilot.
choices.text_after:
You leave him to the engines. He doesn't seem to notice. Some evenings, though, you hear him
out on the field after dark, running one up, listening, and you find you're listening with him.

v18air_ferrier.title: Ferrier's hands
v18air_ferrier.text:
[if war.month == 2]February. [/if]Ferrier's been flying since the spring, and it's got into his hands. He
can't light a cigarette. He holds the match in one hand and the box in the other and they won't
meet, and you light it for him, and neither of you mentions it.

He doesn't sleep. You hear him at night on the cinder path by the officers' huts, walking.
Last week he landed and sat in the cockpit with the engine still running, looking at the dials,
till Sallis climbed up on the wing and switched it off for him.

"Don't tell them," he says to you on the field, in the morning, not looking at you. "They'll
mark me NYD and send me home. I've a few months more to do and I'll do them."

The flight commander has been asking. He's asked Sallis. He'll ask you.

choices.text: Tell the flight commander. He needs to go home.
choices.text_after:
You stand to attention in the flight office and say his hands shake, and that's all you
say, and it's enough. Ferrier is posted to Home Establishment at the end of the month: England, and
teaching young officers to fly. He doesn't look at you for a week. On the last morning he comes to the
hangar with his kit on a tender and shakes your hand, hard, and doesn't let go, and then
he does. You fly with Hollis after that.

choices.text: Keep it to yourself. It's his to tell.
choices.text_after:
When the flight commander asks, you say Mr Ferrier's the best pilot in the flight, which
is true. A packet of cigarettes turns up on your bed that night by way of Sallis[if war.rank < 6], because
an officer can't be seen to[/if]. You go on flying with Ferrier.

v18air_ferrier_down.title: Ferrier
v18air_ferrier_down.text:
[if war.month <= 4]The worst of the retreat's over, and the squadron's on its third field in a fortnight.[else]Summer, and the roads behind their line are busy.[/if]
Every day you're out low over the roads. On a road below a wood something fires up at you, one
burst, and the machine gives a jerk as if somebody's kicked it.

Ferrier doesn't turn round. He flies it home, low, all the way, slow and level and careful, the
way you'd drive a binder down a hill, across our line and over a field of beet, and he puts it
down on the rows, and it runs, and stops.

You climb out and go round to him. He's sat up straight with his hands still on the controls.
The bullet came up through the floor. The doctor says after that he should have been dead a
mile before the line.

Hollis is your pilot from the next morning. He walks round the machine twice before he gets in.

choices.text: Write to his mother in Manitoba yourself.
choices.text_after:
You write it in the hut by the stove with Sallis reading over your shoulder for the
spelling. You put that he got you home. You put about the binder.[if flag.af17_ferrier_farm] The address is on the back of the cigarette packet in your pay book, a post office and a township and a section number, and it takes you three goes to copy it out.[/if]

choices.text: Leave it to the squadron. An officer's mother gets an officer's letter.
choices.text_after:
The major writes it. You see the envelope on the office table, addressed to Manitoba in a
neat hand, and it looks a long way to go for a letter like that.

v18air_raf.title: The Air Force
v18air_raf.text:
On the first of April the Flying Corps stopped being the army's. It's the Royal Air Force now,
a new service, its own thing, and there's talk of a uniform of its own that nobody here has
seen. The sergeant major says he'll believe in it when he's issued it.

Nothing changes. Same machine, same field, same khaki on your back and the same mud on the
wheels, and Jerry over the line doesn't seem to have heard. Sallis paints nothing out and
nothing in. "They can call me what they like," he says, "so long as they pay me Friday."

choices.text: Drink the new service's health in cocoa.
choices.text_after:
A tin of cocoa round the hut, sweet and scalding, and somebody does a speech in a voice like
the major's, and everybody laughs, and in the morning you fly.

choices.text: Get on with it. The machine wants seeing to.
choices.text_after:
You spend the afternoon on the gun and the ring, cleaning and oiling, till the ring goes
round under your hand without a sound. Sallis watches you from the wing root and nods.

v18air_gunner.title: The other gunner
v18air_gunner.text:
On a line patrol, coming out of a cloud, a German two-seater, close, closer than you've
ever been to one. You can see the gunner in the back
cockpit plain as a man in the street.

He's got a scarf on, striped, knitted, the ends flying. He's got goggles pushed up on his
forehead and a face that needs a shave. He's got his gun on you, the way you've got yours on
him. He's watching his pilot's tail. He's doing his job.

Neither of you fires. The two machines slide past each other in the wet grey.

choices.text: Fire. It's what you're for.
choices.text_after:
You fire a burst, and he fires one, and both of you miss, and then the cloud has him. [if !flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_ferrier_killed]Ferrier[/if][if flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_hollis_killed || flag.af18_ferrier_killed && !flag.af18_hollis_killed]Hollis[/if][if flag.af18_hollis_killed]Lyle[/if]
looks round, and you shake your head. You can smell his exhaust in the cloud, after, sour,
different from ours.

choices.text: Hold your fire. See what he does.
choices.text_after:
He doesn't fire either. Then he lifts one hand off his gun, a small lift, the way one
carter lifts his whip to another on a narrow lane. Then the cloud.

v18air_mess.title: The sergeants' mess
v18air_mess.text:
You've a sergeant's stripes now, and you eat in the sergeants' mess: a hut with a piano that one man can
play, and a cloth on the table on Sundays, and pilots and gunners at the same table, and
nobody asking how you got your stripes. [if flag.af18_hollis && !flag.af18_hollis_killed]Hollis sits at the end with his pipe and talks engines to anyone who'll stand it.[/if]

In orders there's a new medal, for flying men in the ranks: the Distinguished Flying Medal.
The man who reads it out says it's about time. Somebody says it'll be in the post with the
blue uniforms.

It's July, and warm, and through the open door you can see Sallis on his own on the field,
going round the machines on the line with a lamp.

choices.text: Stand your round and sing with them.
choices.text_after:
The piano man plays everything he knows, which is five songs, three times each. You know
all the words by the third time. You walk back to the hut under the stars, and you're happy,
and it frightens you.

choices.text: Go out and sit on the field with Sallis.
choices.text_after:
Sallis doesn't drink. He has a can of cocoa and two mugs, as if he knew. He tells you about
Coventry, the cycle works, the smell of the enamel ovens, his wife, who keeps chickens in the
yard and names them after the foremen. You sit on an upturned petrol tin till the lamp goes out.

v18air_wireless.title: Word from the battalion
v18air_wireless.text:
The battery the squadron shoots for has a wireless operator called Platt, a little man with a
cold that never goes, and his cousin is in your old battalion. He comes up to the aerodrome with
the battery officer to talk about the strips, and finds you behind the hangar, and gives you
what he's got, which is a cousin's letter, read twice and remembered.

{section_line}[if war.mate1] {mate1} is all right, last he heard.[/if][if !war.mate1] He's heard about {mate1}. You tell him you know.[/if][if war.mate2] {mate2} is all right.[/if][if war.mate3] {mate3} is all right.[/if] The battalion's out of the line, then in again, the same as ever. He doesn't know more than that. He doesn't know any of them, only the names.

choices.text: Give him a note to take back for the lads.
choices.text_after:
You write it on a page out of your notebook, leaning on the hangar wall: you're well, the
grub's good, keep your heads down, look up when you hear the Klaxon. You don't know if it
will ever get there.

choices.text: Ask him what the line's like now.
choices.text_after:
"Same," he says. "Wet. Not cushy, like this." He wipes his nose on his sleeve. "They say your lot always know
your machine. They look up and say, there's our gunner." You don't know if he's made it up.

v18air_bridges.title: The bridges
v18air_bridges.text:
Since the eighth it's been the river crossings, day after day: the bombers and the scouts after
the bridges, and you over the far bank finding the German guns for ours, and the squadrons
losing machines over the water faster than new ones come up.

One morning a burst from the far bank goes through the engine. Oil comes back over the
windscreen in a black sheet, and over Hollis, and over you, hot, so you can taste it, and the
engine starts to knock, and then to scream.[if flag.af18_engine] You know every part of it that's screaming; you passed him the spanners for them in the winter.[/if]

Hollis gets it home. He flies it with his goggles pushed up and oil running off his chin, low,
nursing it, talking to it, and it lasts to the aerodrome, and he puts it down, and the
propeller stops before the wheels do.

choices.text: Count the holes with Sallis.
choices.text_after:
Forty-one, not counting the engine. Sallis writes it in his little book. Hollis is under
the cowling before you've finished, oil to the elbows, saying a word he learned at the works.

choices.text: Walk off across the field on your own.
choices.text_after:
You walk to the far hedge and stand there with your back to the hangars, and your legs won't
stop. When you come back Hollis has a mug of tea for you and doesn't ask.

v18air_hollis_down.title: Hollis
v18air_hollis_down.text:
Since the eighth it's been the river crossings, day after day: the bombers and the scouts after
the bridges, and you over the far bank finding the German guns for ours, and the squadrons
losing machines over the water faster than new ones come up.

One morning a burst comes up from the far bank, and Hollis jerks in his seat, once. He
gets the machine back over the river. He gets it over our line. He puts it down in a field of
stubble with a bounce you feel in your teeth, and switches off, and then he leans forward on the
edge of the cockpit as if he's tired.

He's alive at the dressing station, for an hour. He talks about the engine. He says it was
running sweet, right to the end, and you're to tell Sallis so.

choices.text: Go back and tell Sallis what he said.
choices.text_after:
Sallis listens with his cap in his hands, and nods, and goes out to the lorry that's
brought the machine back, and starts taking the engine out of it, on his own, in the dark.
A new pilot comes to the flight the next week, Mr Lyle, nineteen, from Kent, who says please to the mechanics.

choices.text: Stay at the dressing station till they bury him.
choices.text_after:
They bury him in the morning in a row with the others, infantry mostly. The padre gets his
rank wrong, and you tell him, and he puts it right. A new pilot comes to the flight the next
week, Mr Lyle, nineteen, from Kent, who says please to the mechanics.

v18air_counting.title: Counting
v18air_counting.text:
September. Every evening, when the machines come in, Sallis is at the hangar door with his cap
pushed back and his little book, counting. He counts them in over the trees while they're still
specks. He counts them on the grass. He counts them again on the line.

This evening the count's one short. One of the flight's, the other crew, a young officer and a
gunner from Bootle you played cards with on Sunday.[if flag.af18_hollis_killed] He counted Hollis home too, in the end, on the back of a lorry.[/if][if flag.af18_told_sallis] Hollis's engine is on a trestle in the hangar behind him, built up again, and he runs it every Sunday for no reason anybody can see.[/if]

The light goes. The other mechanics go in. Sallis stays out on the field, looking east.

choices.text: Stand out on the field with him till it's dark.
choices.text_after:
You stand with him. The field smells of cut grass and petrol. At ten he shuts his book,
and you walk back together, and at the hangar door he stops, and turns round, and counts
again.

choices.text: Go in. Counting won't bring them.
choices.text_after:
You go in. Through the hut window you can see him, a dark shape by the hangar door, until
you can't, and then you can still see his pipe.

v18air_roads.title: The roads
v18air_roads.text:
October. Low, over country the fighting hasn't touched since 1914: villages with roofs on, cows in the
fields, a woman at a pump who flaps a tea towel at you. And every road east is full of Germans
going back. Guns, carts, a field kitchen with its chimney smoking, and men walking, grey, slow,
a column a mile long.

The order is to go down on them.

choices.text: Go down on the column. It's the order.
choices.text_after:
The gun bucks against your shoulder. Horses go down in the shafts. Men run for the ditches
and some don't reach them. [if !flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_ferrier_killed]Ferrier[/if][if flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_hollis_killed || flag.af18_ferrier_killed && !flag.af18_hollis_killed]Hollis[/if][if flag.af18_hollis_killed]Lyle[/if] pulls up and goes round and comes back, and you fire again, and again, until the drum's empty and the road's still.

choices.text: Save the drum for the guns at the crossroads.
choices.text_after:
You fire on the guns limbering up at the crossroads, and the teams bolt, and you let the
walking men go by under you. One of them looks up. He's carrying a clock under his arm,
a kitchen clock, as if he means to have it on his own wall at home.

e_armistice_air.title: The Armistice
e_armistice_air.text:
{ending_line}

It comes to the aerodrome by telephone at breakfast, and the adjutant reads it out from the
steps of the office with a piece of toast in his other hand. Hostilities will cease at 1100
hours today. Nothing is to fly.

At eleven the whole squadron is out on the field, officers and men together for once, and
somebody fires a Very light into the grey morning, a green one. Then everybody with a pistol
fires everything they've got, red and green and white, till the sky over the hangars is full of
slow coloured stars coming down, and the smoke of them drifts across the grass smelling of
bonfire night. The cows in the next field run to the far hedge and stand there staring.

[if flag.af18_hollis && !flag.af18_hollis_killed]Hollis fires his last cartridge and goes into the hangar, and you find him there ten minutes later with his head inside an engine, listening to it not running.[/if][if flag.af18_hollis_killed]You think of Hollis, who'd have gone to look at an engine.[/if] Sallis stands at the hangar door the way he does every evening, with his cap pushed back, and counts the machines on the line. They're all there. He counts them again.[if flag.af18_stood_with_sallis] Then he shuts his little book and gives it to you to keep.[/if][if flag.af18_sat_sallis] That night he brings out the cocoa can and the two mugs.[/if]

[if flag.af18_ferrier_home]At Christmas there's a letter from Ferrier, from a school in England where he's still teaching boys to fly. He's going home to Manitoba in the spring.[if flag.af17_ferrier_farm] "You're still coming at harvest," he writes. "I've not forgotten. The binder hasn't either."[/if][/if][if flag.af18_ferrier_killed]You think of Ferrier, sat up straight in a field of beet.[if flag.af18_wrote_manitoba] His mother wrote back to you in the summer, a page and a half, with a wheat ear in it.[/if][if flag.af17_ferrier_farm] The cigarette packet's still in your pay book, a township and a section number in Manitoba.[/if][/if]

Somewhere east, under the place the coloured lights are coming down, the battalion's in a field.[if war.mate1] {mate1_first} {mate1} is in it, alive.[/if][if war.mate2] {mate2_first} {mate2} is in it.[/if][if war.mate3] {mate3_first} {mate3} is in it.[/if][if !war.mate1 && !war.mate2 && !war.mate3] None of the three you grew up with is in it.[/if] You'd give a good deal to be in that field too, just for the morning, and you couldn't say why.[if flag.af18_note_home] You never found out if your note got there.[/if][if flag.af18_strafed_column] Some nights, for years, you're back over the road in October with the horses going down in the shafts.[/if][if flag.af18_spared_column] Some nights you think of a German with a kitchen clock under his arm, and hope he got it home.[/if]

[if start == mill]At home, your mother writes, every mill buzzer in the town went off at eleven, all at once, and the weavers came out into the street in their clogs and their aprons and didn't know what to do, so they stood there.[/if][if start == pit]At home, your mother writes, the pit buzzer went at eleven and didn't stop, and the whole village came out into the rows, and in the end they went to chapel because nobody could think of anywhere else.[/if][if start == farm]At home, your mother writes, they rang the bells at Dunsworthy all afternoon, the old men and the schoolgirls, every bell they had, till the ropes were wet from their hands.[/if][if start == city]At home, your father writes, the City came out of its offices at eleven and the clerks threw paper from the windows, ledgers and all, so it came down into the street like snow, and he stood in it in his good coat and let it.[/if]

You are {age} years old and {rank_a}.

[if flag.ro_sw_first][if flag.ro_sw_ended || flag.ro_sw_jilted]{sweetheart} is married to somebody else. You see her at the war memorial when they unveil it, and she squeezes your hand once, and lets go.[else][if flag.ro_sw_married]{sweetheart} is at the station.[if flag.ro_sw_named] So is the baby, who isn't a baby now, and looks at you as if you were a stranger, which you are.[/if][else][if flag.ro_sw_wed16 || flag.ro_sw_wed17]You marry {sweetheart} in the spring of 1919, the bells ringing properly now, every one.[else][if flag.ro_sw_after || flag.ro_sw_wait2]{sweetheart} waited till it was over. You're married in the spring of 1919.[else]You walk out with {sweetheart} on Sundays, the way you did before, and neither of you says much, and that's all right.[/if][/if][/if][/if][/if][if flag.ro_fr_promise || flag.ro_fr_address] In the summer of 1919 a letter comes from France, from Marthe, and you go to the station and ask how much a ticket is.[/if]

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_captured_air.title: Taken
e_captured_air.text:
{ending_line}

You come down on the wrong side of the line, in a field of turnips, too fast. The wheels dig
in and the machine goes over onto its back, and you're hanging upside down in your straps with
petrol running into your hair, and the quiet afterwards is the loudest thing you've ever heard.[if flag.af17_watched_burn] You think of a little flame going down in slow turns, and you get your straps undone faster than you've ever done anything.[/if]

[if war.take == 0][if !flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_ferrier_killed]Ferrier[/if][if flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_hollis_killed || flag.af18_ferrier_killed && !flag.af18_hollis_killed]Hollis[/if][if flag.af18_hollis_killed]Mr Lyle[/if] is alive. He gets you down, and you sit together on the turnips, both of you shaking, and wait for them to come across the field. They come at a run, with rifles, and stop when they see you're not going anywhere.[/if][if war.take == 1][if !flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_ferrier_killed]Ferrier[/if][if flag.af18_ferrier_home && !flag.af18_hollis_killed || flag.af18_ferrier_killed && !flag.af18_hollis_killed]Hollis[/if][if flag.af18_hollis_killed]Mr Lyle[/if] is dead. You get him out and lay him on the turnips, and you're sitting by him when they come across the field with rifles, and one of them takes his cap off.[/if]

They take you to their aerodrome. They're curious, more than anything. Their [if war.rank >= 6]officers[else]sergeants[/if] give you a meal in their own mess, black bread and sausage and coffee made of something that isn't coffee, and a glass of schnapps, and they look at your boots and your coat, and one of them, who speaks a little English, asks how many of them you've shot down. You say you don't know.[if flag.af18_held_fire] You look along the table for a striped scarf. You don't see one.[/if][if flag.af18_fired_gunner] You think of a striped scarf in a cloud, and keep your eyes on your plate.[/if][if flag.af17_kept_print] An officer goes through your pay book and finds the fogged photograph of the battalion's old line, and looks at it a long while, and puts it in his own pocket.[/if]

Then you're a prisoner like any other. Walking east with a column of infantry taken in the
line, then a cattle truck, then a camp behind wire: black bread, turnip soup, letters that
take months. Your mother gets a card in your handwriting from a camp with a name she can't say,
and she takes it round to every house in the street.

[if flag.ro_sw_first][if flag.ro_sw_ended || flag.ro_sw_jilted]{sweetheart} hears from your mother that you are missing, and then that you are a prisoner.[else][if flag.ro_sw_married]{sweetheart} is told you are missing, and for weeks she doesn't know if she's a wife or a widow. Then the card comes through the Red Cross, in your hand, and she sends a parcel every week after that.[else][if flag.ro_sw_wed16 || flag.ro_sw_wed17]{sweetheart} waits for the card through the Red Cross like everyone else, and then writes to the camp every week.[else][if flag.ro_sw_after || flag.ro_sw_wait2]{sweetheart} writes to the camp every week. She is still waiting, she says.[else]{sweetheart} writes to the camp now and then.[/if][/if][/if][/if][/if]

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

w_corps_tank.title: The Heavy Branch
w_corps_tank.text:
January, and a frost that has got into everything, the bread, the boots, the water in the
bottles. An officer you've never seen comes round the billets with the adjutant: a captain with
a cough, a list, and the crossed guns of the Machine Gun Corps on his cap. He wants men for the Heavy Branch of the
Machine Gun Corps. He doesn't say tanks. He doesn't have to.

[if start == mill]He's been told the battalion's full of mill lads who can strip a loom and put it back with their eyes shut, and he wants to know if it's true. Engines are only looms that move, he says.[/if][if start == pit]He's been told there are pitmen in the battalion who've worked the winding engines and the pumps, and it's engine men he wants.[/if][if start == farm]He's been told there are farm lads in the battalion who've kept a threshing engine going through a wet harvest, and he wants men who aren't frightened of an engine.[/if][if start == city]He's been told there are clerks in the battalion who took to the Lewis gun as if it were a ledger, and he wants gunners who can keep count under fire.[/if][if war.path == lewis] He's had your name from the Lewis gun officer. Gunners, he says, are what he's shortest of.[/if]

Everybody's heard about the tanks on the Somme. Half the stories are about the ones that never
got to the start, or got stuck in a shell hole with their tails in the air and burned. In the
billet that night somebody calls them tin coffins, and somebody else says you'd want your head
looking at.

If you go, you go for good. A new corps, a crew of strangers, a camp in Dorset. The section
from home stays here, and goes on without you.

choices.text: Give him your name. Leave the section for good.
Stay with the men from home.

bt_tank.title: {battle_name}
bt_tank.text:
{phase_count}

[if war.battle == arras && war.phase == 1]Half past five, and sleet. You've been inside her since three, eight of you packed round the engine, hot on one side and frozen on the other, and Mr Lacey has been sick twice into a bucket. Then the guns open behind you, all at once, and the steel round you rings with it like a struck pan. Pring lets in the clutch. She lurches, and goes, at a walk, the tracks squealing.

Through the slit, in the grey, the infantry come past on either side of her, bent into the sleet. It's the battalion. You'd know the walk anywhere.[if war.mate1 || war.mate2 || war.mate3] A face turns to look at her, close enough to touch, and it's {mate}. He sees the name on her nose and grins, and is gone into the snow.[if flag.tk17_found_section] He's keeping behind her, the way you told him.[/if][/if]

[if war.stalled]On the left the barrage has got away from them. A machine gun has opened up from the wire and the battalion's down in the snow, and the bullets are hitting her front plates like gravel thrown at a window. Splash comes in round the edges of the slits, little hot flecks of lead that sting your face.[else]Their front line comes up out of the sleet, smashed, the wire in heaps. She goes over the wire as if it were a hedge, and the infantry come through behind her in the gap she's made.[/if][/if][if war.battle == arras && war.phase == 2]Their trench. Pring swings her along it with one track on the parados, and she lies over at a tilt so that your gun looks straight down into it, along its length. Grey figures run along the bottom and round the traverses, and some come up with their hands up, shouting Kamerad, and you have to stop firing for them.

The battalion's bombers are working along behind her a bay at a time.[if war.mate1 || war.mate2 || war.mate3] Through the slit you see {mate} go round a traverse with a bomb in his hand. He doesn't look up at her this time.[/if] [if flag.tk17_stayed_with_her] The guns you stripped twice in the night haven't jammed once.[/if] Then a dugout entrance, and a machine gun firing up out of it at the bombers, and they're down.[/if][if war.battle == arras && war.phase == 3]By the afternoon she's finished. She's in a shell hole on the far slope with a track off and the snow settling on her, and the guns can't get forward over the broken ground. You get the guns out of her and lie with the battalion in the shell holes, in the snow, with no wire and no water. Mr Lacey is with you, and he isn't sick now.

In the dusk they come back at you out of the village on the hill, in long grey lines.[/if][if war.battle == passchendaele && war.phase == 1]It has rained since the end of July, and it's raining now. The ground was always low here, and the shelling has smashed every ditch that used to drain it, and now it isn't ground. You bring her up the last mile in the dark behind a guide who keeps going in to his knees. At zero the barrage goes over and she goes forward into it, and the mud comes up over the tracks at once, thick as porridge, and the whole of her shudders as the engine labours.

[if war.stalled]Ten minutes out, she's slowing. The tracks are turning and she isn't moving with them. The infantry go past her into the rain and leave her behind.[else]She's moving. Slower than a man walks, but moving, and the infantry keep close behind her in a little crowd, as if she were a wall.[/if][/if][if war.battle == passchendaele && war.phase == 2]A pillbox, half sunk in the mud on a little rise: concrete, with a slit at the height of your knees and a machine gun firing out of it across everything. The infantry are flat in the shell holes in front of it, and the water's over their backs.

Pring turns her nose towards it. The bullets come off her plates in sheets and the splash comes in at every crack, and Kearney has one hand over his eyes and is firing with the other.[if war.stalled] Halfway there she slews in the mud and sticks, broadside on, thirty yards short, and the slit in the concrete turns towards her.[/if][/if][if war.battle == passchendaele && war.phase == 3]She's stopped. She's gone down in the mud to her sponsons, and the tracks go round and throw up mud and do nothing else, and the engine screams. Tonks and Murray climb out and chain the unditching beam to the tracks[if flag.tk17_gears], and you take Tonks's levers while he's gone[/if], and it goes under the mud, and she sinks a little more.

Mr Lacey gives the order. You get the guns out of her and climb into the rain and lie in a shell hole with the infantry, up to your waist in water, while their counter-attack comes on across the mud.[/if][if war.battle == passchendaele && war.phase == 4]Night, and you walk back. Four miles of it, carrying the guns, twenty-eight pounds of Lewis gun on your shoulder and a pannier of drums on the other, along a duckboard track that's been shelled into pieces. Behind you she's sitting out there in the dark with her nose up and the water coming in at her doors.

Every shell hole has somebody in it. Some of them are calling.[/if][if war.battle == cambrai && war.phase == 1]Twenty past six, the twentieth of November, in a mist. Hundreds of tanks in a line across downland that hasn't been shelled to mud, grass and stubble, and in front the German wire in belts so deep you can't see the end of them.

They issued the masks for this, steel eye plates and a chain-mail veil. Kearney wore his last night to deal cards in, to make Murray laugh, and then packed it with the spare kit like everybody else.[if flag.tk17_cards] You lost two francs to him in it.[/if]

Then the guns, a thousand of them at once, and she goes forward at a walk with a great bundle of brushwood chained on her roof, and the wire goes down under her like standing corn.

[if war.stalled]On the left a tank has stopped in the wire, smoking, and the infantry behind it are bunched in the gap, and a machine gun has found them.[else]Behind you the infantry come through in files along the lanes she's crushed, and nobody in their front line is shooting any more.[/if][/if][if war.battle == cambrai && war.phase == 2]The Hindenburg Line: a trench so wide no tank can cross it. Pring brings her to the lip and the fascine, the great bundle, goes off her roof into it with a crash, and she goes down on to it nose first and claws up the far side, the whole crew thrown forward on to the engine in a heap, and on.

[if war.stalled]Beyond it the next tank has dropped its bundle in the wrong place and is stuck across the trench like a bridge with its tail in the air, and the infantry can't get round it under the guns.[else]They're coming up out of their dugouts with their hands up, more of them than you've ever seen give up at once, and the infantry wave them back without looking at them.[/if][/if][if war.battle == cambrai && war.phase == 3]The ridge at Flesquières. She comes up over the crest into the open, slow, and there are field guns behind the village, and the gunners have been trained for tanks. The tank on your right stops dead and starts to burn. Then the one beyond it.

[if flag.tk17_lacey_praised]Mr Lacey gets out. He gets down on to the grass in front of her to guide Pring on foot, the way he's seen others do it, so the crew can see him do it, and he's walking ahead of her with his stick, pointing, when the guns find her. When you look for him through the smoke there's only the stick, lying in the grass.[else]Then the guns find her. The noise is everything, and the inside of her is full of smoke and flying bits of her own steel, and Mr Lacey is down on the floor plates with his shoulder laid open, and Pring has hold of him.[/if][if flag.tk17_murray_tin] The tin behind the engine goes up. Fire runs along the floor, and over Murray, and you're all out through the doors in a heap, rolling him on the grass, beating at him with your hands, and she's burning behind you.[else] You're all out through the doors in a heap, and Murray's the last, dragging Tonks by the collar.[/if]

You lie in a shell hole on the ridge with the guns you got out of her, and the infantry beside you, and wait for whatever comes over the crest next.[/if][if war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase == 1 && !flag.tk18_whippet]You wake because the hut is shaking. Before five, dark, and the whole of the east lit up from underneath, flickering, and then the noise, with no gaps in it to count. Gas with it. You're out of the hut in your mask and running for the tanks under their nets in the wood, and the fog's down so thick you find her by touch, her side cold and wet under your hand.

[if war.path == subaltern]The crew are looking at you for an order. Nobody has given you one, so you give one.[else]The orders are to go forward and fight her from wherever she can get to. Nobody knows where the line is any more.[/if] Out in the fog the infantry posts are going out, one at a time. You can hear them go.[/if][if war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase == 1 && flag.tk18_whippet]You wake because the hut is shaking. Before five, dark, and the whole of the east lit up from underneath, flickering, and then the noise, with no gaps in it to count, though the line's miles off.

You've been with the Whippets three weeks, at a camp well back, learning her. Three of you in her: Pring, and you, and an officer called Mr Yarrow who used to sell motor cars in Leeds and talks about her as if she were for sale. She's low and long, the engines in front and the cab at the back like a box on a cart, and the guns in the cab are Hotchkisses, and you've fired them on the range and nowhere else.

On the second day the orders come, and the company goes up the road towards the noise, against everything coming down it: lorries, a battery at the trot, walking wounded, an old woman pushing a handcart with a clock and a feather bed on it. "Les Boches," she says to nobody, and points back up the road. On a straight bit Pring opens her up, and the wind comes in at the slits, and he laughs out loud. You've never heard him laugh before.

By dark you're lying up at a crossroads with the engines ticking over, the shells feeling for the road, and the infantry going back past you in the fog. Nobody knows where the line is, and nobody gives you an order.[/if][if war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase == 2 && !flag.tk18_whippet]She runs out of petrol at noon on the second day, at a crossroads, with the Germans coming through the fog behind. There's no more petrol anywhere. "Napoo," Kearney says, and holds the last tin upside down. Pring and Tonks pour the last of the oil over her engine, and Kearney puts a match to it, and you walk away with the Lewis guns on your shoulders and the smoke going up behind you, and nobody looks round.

You're a Lewis-gun team now, like the infantry, in a ditch by a road.[if !flag.tk17_murray_tin] Murray's feeding the drums.[/if] The grey figures come out of the fog in little groups, quick, with light machine guns, slipping round the ends of everything.[/if][if war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase == 2 && flag.tk18_whippet]Late in March they send you in at last. There's a gap in front of a village on a low ridge, and the infantry are coming back through it in twos and threes, and over the open fields beyond them the Germans are coming on in the daylight, a lot of them, as if there were nothing left in front of them.

Mr Yarrow taps Pring on the shoulder, and she goes. She's faster than anything you've been in. She bucks over the furrows, and the cab fills with the hammer of the engines and the stink of hot oil, and you're on your knees going from gun to gun, the brass coming off them hot down your collar. Through the slit the grey figures stop and stare at her. Some go down in the furrows. Some come on, and out on the left somebody has a machine gun up on a sledge, and it's turning your way.[/if][if war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase == 3 && !flag.tk18_whippet]After that it's back. Days of it, and you lose count. March by night, a hedge bank by day, the gun on its bipod and a drum on, firing till they're close, then up and back to the next hedge. You know the names on the signposts. You marched through these villages going up to the Somme in 1916, and you're giving them back in an afternoon.

Behind you the dumps burn, and the tank parks, and the workshops, and the whole night smells of burning rubber and petrol.[/if][if war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase == 3 && flag.tk18_whippet]After that it's days of it, and you lose count. The Whippets go wherever the line's broken: a run at them across the fields with the guns going, then back behind the infantry for petrol out of two-gallon tins, and out again. You sleep in her, sitting up against a gun mounting, and wake with the shape of it printed on your cheek. Pring drives with his eyes half shut and his jaw going. You know the names on the signposts. You marched through these villages going up to the Somme in 1916, and they're being given back in an afternoon.

Behind you the dumps burn, and the tank parks, and the workshops, and the whole night smells of burning rubber and petrol.[/if][if war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase == 4 && !flag.tk18_whippet]The end of March, a railway embankment in front of a town you've never heard of, and somebody says that's it, no further. You believe it because you can't walk any further.

You set the gun up on the rails between two sleepers, and the barrel's still hot from the morning.[if war.path == subaltern] What's left of your crew is along the embankment with the infantry, and you walk behind them, which is where an officer walks.[/if] [if flag.tk17_aussies] Australians come up on your right at dark, and one of them sees your badge and hands you his water bottle without a word.[/if] At dusk the grey lines come up the slope at you one more time.[/if][if war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase == 4 && flag.tk18_whippet]The end of March, a railway embankment in front of a town you've never heard of, and somebody says that's it, no further. Pring ran her dry on the last run. She sits behind the embankment with her engines ticking as they cool, and the petrol lorry isn't coming, and Mr Yarrow says she'll fight from here or not at all.

You take a gun out of her and set it up on the rails between two sleepers, and the barrel's still hot from the morning.[if flag.tk17_aussies] Australians come up on your right at dark, and one of them sees your badge and hands you his water bottle without a word.[/if] At dusk the grey lines come up the slope at you one more time.[/if][if war.battle == hundred_days_august && war.phase == 1]Twenty past four, the eighth of August, and fog, and this time it's on your side. There's been no bombardment, no warning: the guns open all at once, and more than five hundred tanks go forward into the fog together, and you're in one of them. The ground's green. Standing corn, uncut, up to a man's waist, and poppies in it.

[if flag.tk18_whippet]The Whippets wait behind the heavies for the first hour with their engines running. Then Pring takes her through a gap at a pace the heavies can't touch, past the infantry in the corn. It's the battalion. You see them go by under the cab, in little worms of men behind the tanks the way they've practised.[else]The battalion's behind her. You see them through the slit, in little worms of men behind the tanks, the way they've practised, the corn up to their waists.[if flag.tk18_said_no] Somewhere back in the fog Pring is waiting in his Whippet with his engine running.[/if][/if][if war.mate1 || war.mate2 || war.mate3] {mate} is at the front of one, wading, his rifle held up out of the corn.[/if]

[if war.stalled]On the left the fog lifts too soon. A tank's burning by a copse, black smoke rolling off it low over the corn, and a machine gun in the copse has the battalion down.[else]Their front line comes up out of the fog, half empty, and the men in it have their hands up before you get there.[/if][/if][if war.battle == hundred_days_august && war.phase == 2]A wood, with a road running into it, and machine guns at the edge, and behind it a battery of field guns firing over open sights at anything that moves in the corn.

[if flag.tk18_whippet]Pring runs her along the edge of the wood at a gallop, and you go from gun to gun on your knees as she turns[if flag.tk18_whippet_guns], without looking, the way you learned[/if], firing into the trees, and the splash rattles on the cab like hail on a shed roof.[else]She goes at the wood's edge firing, and the infantry come up behind her a rush at a time. The splash comes in at the slits so thick you fire with your eyes shut.[if flag.tk18_murray_rivets] Not one of Murray's rivets gives.[/if][/if][if war.stalled] A tank on the right stops in the open with smoke coming out of her, and her crew climb out and lie under her, and the machine guns at the wood's edge turn on them.[/if][/if][if war.battle == hundred_days_august && war.phase == 3]By the afternoon you've come further in a day than anybody has since 1914. Fields and hedges and no trenches, and a farmhouse with the washing still on the line.

[if flag.tk18_whippet]Pring doesn't stop. Past the infantry, past everything, out on your own, with their transport running in front of you and a camp of tents emptying as you come. Nobody behind you. Nobody in front but them. Your guns are hot and the water's nearly gone and the cab stinks of cordite.[else]You dig in behind her at dusk, in a field of oats.[if flag.tk18_said_no] Far out ahead, beyond everything, a Whippet is running on its own, small as a beetle, firing into a camp of tents. You know whose it is. You watch it till a fold of the ground takes it.[/if] Their field guns are still firing from behind a hedge, at the tanks, and at you.[/if][/if][if war.battle == hundred_days_october && war.phase == 1]October, and a valley in mist, and there are hardly any tanks left. A handful from the whole battalion go in at dawn with the infantry, and the infantry are glad of you, and don't expect much.

[if flag.tk18_whippet && !flag.tk18_pring_hit]Pring has her at a walking pace for once, feeling the ground.[/if][if flag.tk18_whippet && flag.tk18_pring_hit]The new driver has her at a walking pace, feeling the ground, the way Pring showed him.[/if][if !flag.tk18_whippet && !flag.tk_kearney_taken]Kearney sits at his gun with a card stuck in his helmet band for luck, the ace of spades.[/if][if !flag.tk18_whippet && flag.tk_kearney_taken]Kearney's gun has a lad on it from the reserve who flinches every time she lurches.[/if]

[if war.stalled]The mist lifts on the far slope too early, and a field gun in a farmyard has her before she's halfway up.[else]The far slope comes up out of the mist, and the wire on it is thin and old, and she walks through it.[/if][/if][if war.battle == hundred_days_october && war.phase == 2]Their old trench, and the deep dugouts in it, thirty steps down. The infantry go down them slowly now. There are wires across the steps, a helmet left on a table that's tied to something underneath, a stove with a bomb under the grate. A sapper comes up out of one with a box in his arms, carrying it like eggs.

She stands at the trench's edge with her guns on the far side while they search it.[if war.stalled] A machine gun opens up from a dugout entrance further along, and the infantry go flat, and the sapper with the box goes flat with it.[/if][/if][if war.battle == hundred_days_october && war.phase == 3]An orchard at evening, apples on the ground everywhere gone soft, wasps in them, the smell of cider. They come back once more out of the trees, half-hearted, and it's still enough to kill men.

[if !flag.tk18_whippet && !flag.tk18_tonks_told]Tonks hammers the engine cover and she stops, and he grins at you across the engine, because he heard that one.[/if][if !flag.tk18_whippet && flag.tk18_tonks_told]The new gearsman misses a knock and she slews, and you think of Tonks at a bench at Teneur.[/if] There's a rumour, the way there always is. This time the officers are saying it too.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase == 1 && flag.tk18_whippet]Take her forward and find where the line is.[elif war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase <= 3 && flag.tk18_whippet]Tell Pring to go straight at them.[elif war.battle == spring_offensive || war.battle == arras && war.phase == 3 || war.battle == passchendaele && war.phase >= 3 || war.battle == cambrai && war.phase == 3]Up with the guns and go at them.[else]Keep her going forward, ahead of the infantry.[/if] ({risk_push})

[if war.battle == arras || war.battle == hundred_days_august]Stay by the battalion. Cover the section from home.[else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Cover the men falling back beside you.[else]Stay with the infantry. Keep the crew together.[/if][/if] ({risk_help})

[if war.battle == spring_offensive && war.phase <= 3 && flag.tk18_whippet]Pull her back behind the crest and wait.[elif war.battle == spring_offensive || war.battle == arras && war.phase == 3 || war.battle == passchendaele && war.phase >= 3 || war.battle == cambrai && war.phase == 3]Get down in cover and keep down.[else]Pull her into a fold of the ground, out of their sight, and wait.[/if] ({risk_ground})

s_tank_1.title: Bringing her up
s_tank_1.text: [if war.stake == 0]Dusk, and the nets come off. The engine catches with a roar you'd swear Jerry can hear in his own line, and she shakes herself and crawls out of the wood on to the road. The guide's waiting at the crossroads, an officer from the company with a lamp held behind his back so it only shows to you, and he starts to walk, and she follows his lamp at a man's pace along a white tape laid on the ground.[if war.stage == 3] Mr Lacey is leaning out of the door, being sick.[/if] Four miles of this.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Night, and the tape. Somebody laid it this afternoon from the tank park to the start line, a white strip on the grass that shows grey in the dark, and the guide walks it ahead of her with his lamp. A mile on a shell has come down near the tape, and the glow of it hangs there. Inside her the engine's so loud you won't hear the next one coming, only feel it.[/if]

choices.text: Close up on the guide's lamp and keep her moving. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: She goes along the tape at her best pace, which is a fast walk, and the guide has to trot.

choices.text: Keep her to the tape at a walk. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: At a walk, the lamp swinging ahead, every yard of the tape going under her.

choices.text: Get out and walk with the guide, feeling for the ground. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You walk beside the guide with the tape running through your fingers where it's broken, and she comes on behind you like a cow after a bucket.

choices.text: Say she isn't fit tonight. Turn back for the park. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: You turn her in the road with the guide swearing at you, and go back to the wood the way you came, and the nets go back on.

s_tank_2.title: Bringing her up
s_tank_2.text: [if war.stake == 0]Halfway, and the shelling starts. Not at you, you tell yourself: at the road, at the battery behind the hill. Then near. A five-nine throws earth against her side like a spadeful of gravel, and the guide's lamp goes out, and when it shows again it's twenty yards off to the left, and the tape has gone under a new shell hole that's still smoking.[/if][if war.stake == 1]She ditches. An old trench, fallen in, that nobody marked: her nose goes down and her tail comes up and the whole crew's thrown forward on to the engine. The tracks spin. She doesn't move. Outside, the shelling is walking along the road towards you, a burst at a time, and the air inside her is blue with exhaust.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.stake == 0]Drive on through it. Find the tape after.[else]Full throttle. Drive her out of it.[/if] ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: The engine howls and she heaves and goes, and nobody inside can hear anything but her.

choices.text: [if war.stake == 0]Stop, find the tape, then go on.[else][if war.tour <= 26]Get out and pack brushwood under the tracks.[elif flag.tk18_whippet && war.tour >= 33]Get out and dig under her tracks with the shovels.[else]Get out and chain the unditching beam on.[/if][/if] ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You're out in the open with the shells coming, doing it by feel in the dark with your fingers numb, and then it's done.

choices.text: [if war.stake == 0]Pull her off the road and wait for it to lift.[else]Wait for the shelling to pass, then dig her out.[/if] ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You wait, flat against her side, while it goes over. The steel shakes against your back at every burst.

choices.text: Leave her and get the crew back. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: You get the crew out and back along the road, and leave her there with her engine ticking.

s_tank_3.title: Bringing her up
s_tank_3.text: [if war.stake == 0]The last mile. The sky's going grey in the east, and she has to be on the start line and under her net before it's light enough for their observers to see her. The engine's running hot. You can smell it, hot oil and something scorching, and [if flag.tk18_whippet && war.tour >= 33]Pring at the wheel is[else]the gearsmen at the back are[/if] streaming with sweat.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Nearly there. The tape ends at a sunken road, and the infantry are waiting in it, and they turn their faces up at her as she comes, and in the half dark you can see what they think of the noise she's making. Somewhere overhead an aeroplane drones, Jerry's or ours.[/if]

choices.text: Push her the last of it flat out, before the light. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: She roars up the last slope with the infantry flattening themselves against the bank, and slews into place.

choices.text: Bring her in at a walk and get the net on her. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: In at a walk, the engine off, and all of you up on her in the half light dragging the net over, the poles, the pegs.

choices.text: Stop short, out of their sight, and net her there. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You stop her in a hollow two hundred yards short and get the net on her, and she lies there like a haystack.

choices.text: Turn her round. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: You turn her round in the grey light and go back.

x_tank_done.title: First light
x_tank_done.text:
[if war.result == ok]She's on the start line by first light, under her net, the engine ticking as it cools. An infantry officer comes along the sunken road and puts his hand flat on her side as if she were a horse. You sit with your back against the track and eat bully beef out of the tin with your fingers, and your hands shake so you drop half of it.[/if][if war.result == failed]She didn't get there. She's in a shell hole a mile short with a track off, and the fitters will go out to her tonight if the shelling lets them. One of the crew went back on a stretcher with his hand crushed in a track. The show goes on in the morning without her.[/if][if war.result == turned]You turned back. Another crew took theirs up in her place, and in the morning the infantry went over without you, and in the tank park somebody says you got the wind up, and the rest find other things to talk about when you come in.[/if]

{result_note}

choices.text: Get under the net and sleep.

v17tk_wool.title: Wool
v17tk_wool.text:
The train puts you down at Wool in the dark: a little station in the middle of a heath in
Dorset, and a lorry out to the camp through the gorse. Huts, mud, and a wind off the sea that
tastes of salt.

In the morning they march you to a shed with a sentry on the door. Inside there's a tarpaulin
over something the size of a cottage. The sergeant tells you the story they put about at the
start, that these things were water carriers, which is why everybody calls them tanks. Then he
pulls the sheet off.

She's brown all over, and bigger than you thought, and the shape's all wrong: a lozenge, the way a child
would draw a boat, with the tracks running right round her and a steel box built out on each side, a sponson,
with guns poking out of it. She smells of oil and new paint and cold iron.

"Slower than a bus," says the corporal next to you, a big quiet Londoner called Pring, who
drove a General omnibus for fourteen years. He says it as if he's sorry for her.

Behind you a young officer, fair-haired, his boots still shining from the depot, is looking at her with his hand over his
mouth. That's Mr Lacey, twenty, from a motor works in Coventry. You'll learn he's sick every
time she moves. He's sick now, and she hasn't.

choices.text: Climb in through the little door in the side.
choices.text_after:
You go in head first and crack your shin on something. Inside it's dark and low, and it's
all engine: a great block of it in the middle like a boiler in a cellar, and the eight of
you are to fit round it. You can't stand up straight anywhere. Your hand comes away from
the wall black with oil.

choices.text: Walk all the way round her first.
choices.text_after:
You walk round her twice. The tracks are higher than your head. Close to, the plates are
riveted like the side of a ship, and there's rust already in the seams. Mr Lacey walks
round her too, the other way, and you meet at the back, and he says good morning as if
you'd met in the street.

v17tk_erin.title: Erin
v17tk_erin.text:
February, and France again, but not the France you know. Bermicourt is a village with a
chateau full of brass hats and their motor cars, and two miles down the road at Erin
they're putting up a town of sheds to mend the tanks in, aeroplane hangars, with the first
engines already hung on chains and a din like the inside of a boiler.

Here's the crew. Eight to a tank, and four of them you'll come to know best.

Tonks, from Cradley Heath, a foundry man, with forearms like hams and old burns up both of
them from the ladles. He's a gearsman, at the back. Inside her nobody can hear a word once
she's going, so it's all done with a hammer on the engine cover, so many knocks for this and
so many for that, and Tonks makes you learn the knocks till you knock them in your sleep.

Murray, the other gearsman, a riveter from the yards at Govan. He goes along her plates
tapping every rivet with his knuckle, listening, and shakes his head. "Badly riveted," he
says. "Ah'd have been sacked."

Kearney, off the Liverpool docks, a gunner like you, with a pack of cards gone soft as cloth.
He'll play anybody for anything.

At the end of the week Mr Lacey gets her from the workshops, a female, which is a tank with
machine guns and no cannon, and kneels on the track and
paints the name on her nose himself with a little brush. POLARIS. "The star they steer by,"
he says, when Pring asks. "At sea." Pring says she'll want something to steer her.

choices.text: Learn the gears and the knocks with Tonks.
choices.text_after:
By the end of the month you can work the gears blind. Tonks hits the cover once, twice,
and your hand's on the lever before you've thought. "Yow'll do," he says, which is more
than he says to most.

choices.text: Sit in on Kearney's game.
choices.text_after:
Kearney takes eleven francs off you in a night, and gives you two back so you can buy a
drink, and teaches you a game from the docks that nobody else in the company knows the
rules of, so you never win it.

v17tk_battalion.title: The battalion
v17tk_battalion.text:
April, and Polaris is lying up in the ruins on the edge of Arras under a net, with the snow
coming and going. The orders came last night. Mr Lacey read them out by a candle, and you had
to ask him to read one line again.

She's to go in with a battalion of the line. Your battalion. The section from home is under
the town, in the old quarries, waiting for the morning, a mile from where you're sitting on
her track.

choices.text: Walk over in the dark and find the section.
choices.text_after: [if war.mate1 || war.mate2 || war.mate3]It takes you an hour in the dark and the tunnels to find them, under an electric light strung on a wire. {mate} sees you first. He looks at the new badges on your tunic and laughs, and then stops laughing and shakes your hand. "In one of them," he says. "God help you." You tell them to look out for her in the morning, the one with the name on her nose, and to keep behind her and not in front.[else]It takes you an hour in the dark and the tunnels to find the company. There's nobody left in it you know well enough to talk to. A lance-corporal you half remember tells you who's gone west, and who's in Blighty. {section_line} You go back to her before anybody asks what you came for.[/if]

choices.text: Stay with her. Check every gun again.
choices.text_after:
You strip the guns and put them back and strip them again, by a torch under the net, till
Kearney tells you to give over or he'll strip you. Somewhere under the town the battalion
is waiting, and in the morning you'll see it through a slit the width of your hand.

v17tk_bullecourt.title: Bullecourt
v17tk_bullecourt.text:
May, and the company's back in camp, and when you go down to the village of an evening the
Australians won't drink with you.

It was two days after the battalion's attack. Polaris was still on the far slope with her
track off, and the company going in at Bullecourt was short of men, so you and Pring and Tonks
were sent south to make up one of its crews, in a tank you'd never been inside. You went in
front of the Australians at the wire, in the snow, before it was light. Their whole plan hung
on the tanks. She broke down a quarter of a mile short. Pring and Tonks
worked on the engine with the shells coming down round her, and you sat at your gun with
nothing to fire at and watched the Australians go past her into the wire.

You saw them come back in the afternoon, the ones that came back. You saw their faces as they
went by her.

choices.text: Go into the estaminet anyway, and stand your round.
choices.text_after:
Nobody moves up for you at the bar. "Pas de bagarre, messieurs," says Madame, no fighting,
and fills your glass anyway. Then a sergeant with his arm in a sling takes the
glass off you without a word, and drinks it, and puts it down. It wasn't you, he supposes.
It was them that sent you. Then he turns his back.

choices.text: Keep away from them. Drink in the hut.
choices.text_after:
You drink in the hut with the crew, out of mess tins, and Kearney deals, and nobody
mentions the diggers. Every time the door opens you look up.

v17tk_railhead.title: Tin can
v17tk_railhead.text:
A railhead, and a train of flat trucks with the tanks chained on them under sheets, and a
battalion going up past you on the road. The infantry look at the tanks the way you'd look at
a horse that bit you once.

One of them stops. He's from your battalion: you know him by the shoulder title, and then by
his face, a lad you used to see at [if start == mill]the Co-op on a Saturday[/if][if start == pit]the Store on pay Friday[/if][if start == farm]the market at South Molton[/if][if start == city]the tram stop in Leyton every morning[/if].

"Tin can," he says to you, and spits. Then, in the same breath: "Who's got the rum, then? You
lot always have the rum."

choices.text: Give him a drop out of your bottle.
choices.text_after:
He drinks it standing in the road, and tells you the battalion's news while it lasts.
{section_line} He says the names of the ones who aren't, quickly, to get them said, and
hands the bottle back, and runs to catch his platoon.

choices.text: Tell him to find his own.
choices.text_after:
He grins as if that's what he wanted. "San fairy ann," he says, and goes. You're sorry before he's out of sight. You'd
have liked to ask him about home.

v17tk_fumes.title: The heat
v17tk_fumes.text:
High summer, and a practice attack with the infantry, a mile across country in the sun with
the doors shut. Inside her it's past anything you've known. The engine's in the middle of you,
bare, and the heat comes off it like a kitchen range with the oven door open. The air's blue with
petrol and hot oil, and when the guns fire the cordite smoke stays in. Your head starts to
pound in the first ten minutes.

Half an hour in, the gunner across from you, a new lad from Bristol called Hendy, slides off
his seat on to the floor plates and lies there with his eyes open.

In the basket by the door the pigeons you carry for messages are panting with their beaks
open, the same as you.

choices.text: Get the door open and get him out into the air.
choices.text_after:
Pring stops her, and you and Kearney get Hendy out through the side door on to the grass
and lie him there, and he comes round and is sick. An infantry officer comes over to ask
why the tank has stopped in the middle of his attack. Mr Lacey tells him, white to the lips,
and that evening he writes a chit about the air in the tanks, three pages.

choices.text: Prop him by the crack of the door and keep going.
choices.text_after:
You prop him with his face to the crack round the door, where there's a thread of air, and
keep firing. He comes round on his own at the end, grey, and can't remember his own name
for an hour. Nobody else goes down. You all have the same headache for two days.

v17tk_tin.title: The spare tin
v17tk_tin.text:
July. They're getting the tanks ready for Flanders, and you're loading her, and behind the
engine, wedged where an officer won't see it, there's a two-gallon tin of petrol that isn't on
any list.

Murray's. "The feed pipe," he says. "She's badly riveted. The pipe'll shake loose, and then
where are you, in the middle of nowhere, dry." In the yards he always kept the spare where he
could reach it.

Petrol inside her, by the engine, in a fight. You know what the instructor at Wool said about
that, and so does Murray.

choices.text: Make him take it out.
choices.text_after:
He takes it out, swearing, and stows it on the back with the rest of the stores, and
doesn't speak to you for a day. On the second day he brings you a mug of char and says
you're as bad as a foreman.

choices.text: Leave it. He knows his engine.
choices.text_after:
You say nothing about it. Murray pats the tin like a dog and packs a bit of sacking round
it so it won't rattle.

v17tk_letter.title: A letter from home
v17tk_letter.text:
"Dear Son, just a few lines hoping this finds you well as it leaves us.

[if start == mill]Mrs Ormerod says her cousin's lad says you are in one of those tanks. They had one at the pictures, going over a trench as if it was nothing and knocking a tree down. Your father says it is all nonsense and you are in the motor transport. Are you in one of those.[/if][if start == pit]At the Store they are saying you are in one of those tanks, Mrs Dodds had it from somebody's letter. Mary says they are the safest place to be because they are made of iron. Are you in one of those.[/if][if start == farm]Mr Vellacott says you are in one of those tanks, he had it from the carrier. Your father says if it is anything like a traction engine you will be all right, you were always good with the engine. Are you in one of those.[/if][if start == city]Your father has cut a picture of one of those tanks out of the paper and pinned it up in the scullery, and he says that is where you are, because of the badge. Are you in one of those.[/if] If you are I would rather know than not know.

Look after yourself and do not go volunteering. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write and tell her yes.
choices.text_after:
You tell her yes, and that it's safer than the trenches, which you believe on a good day.
You don't tell her about the heat, or the splash, or the noise. You tell her the name.

choices.text: Write that you're in the motor transport. It's near enough.
choices.text_after:
You write that you're on motor transport behind the lines, which is true of most days. You
can see her reading it out at the kitchen table. You seal it quickly.

v17tk_lacey.title: Mr Lacey
v17tk_lacey.text:
September. What's left of the company is out of the salient at Wipers, and Polaris, dragged out of the mud
after the battle, is at Erin with a new engine and the Flanders mud still caked in her tracks.

Mr Lacey has been sick in every action, and before every action, and on the way up to every
action, and the crew have stopped pretending not to see. He doesn't drink and he doesn't play
cards. He writes to his mother in Coventry every night.

One evening he finds you on your own cleaning the guns, and sits down on an ammunition box,
and asks you straight out whether the crew would rather have another officer.

"I'm no good in her," he says. "I can't think when she's moving. Pring knows more than I do.
You all do."

choices.text: Tell him straight. Pring knows more. Listen to him.
choices.text_after:
He hears you out, white. Then he nods. The next time she moves he crouches by Pring and
asks him, and Pring tells him, and you hear him say right, right, good, and the crew look
at each other. He's still sick. It doesn't seem to matter so much now.

choices.text: Tell him he's doing fine. The crew think the world of him.
choices.text_after:
He looks at you as if he wants to believe it, and then he does. "Right," he says, and
stands up, and straightens his tunic. "Right. Thank you." From then on he wants to do
everything himself, and to do it where the crew can see him.

v18tk_after_cambrai.title: After Cambrai
v18tk_after_cambrai.text:
January, and the tankodrome's frozen. The tanks are lined up in the snow being patched and painted for the
spring, and the paint goes thick on the brush in the cold. They say the Mark V is coming, and nobody has seen one.

The old Polaris stayed on the ridge at Flesquières. The new one has the name on her nose in
the same white letters, done by Pring, who copied it off a photograph.

[if flag.tk17_lacey_praised]Mr Lacey is buried behind the ridge with the others the guns got there. You never saw it done.[else]Mr Lacey is in a hospital in England with a hole in his shoulder the size of your fist, and he won't be coming back to tanks. He wrote to the crew, one letter to all of you, and Pring read it out in the hut. It said thank you, and not much else, and it was the right length.[/if]

[if flag.tk17_murray_tin]Murray is in a burns ward at home. His hands, and one side of his face. He's written once, in somebody else's writing: the tin was his own fault, and he knows it, and they're badly riveted, the lot of them.[else]Murray's still here, going over the new tank's rivets with his knuckle and shaking his head.[/if]

[if war.path == subaltern]And the new officer is you. One pip on your cuff, and a crew who knew you when you had none. Pring calls you sir the first morning and can't keep his face straight, and the second morning he can.[else]The new officer is Mr Fane, nineteen, out from school by way of Wool, with a moustache that won't come. He's younger than any man in the crew, and he has the sense to know it.[/if]

choices.text: [if flag.tk17_lacey_praised]Write to Mr Lacey's mother in Coventry.[else]Write to Mr Lacey in hospital.[/if]
choices.text_after: [if flag.tk17_lacey_praised]You write that he was a brave officer, and that he walked in front of his tank, and that the crew thought the world of him. You read it over. Every word of it is true, and you sit with the pen in your hand for an hour before you can sign it.[else]You tell him about the new tank, and Mr Fane's moustache, and that Pring still drives like a bus with the brakes on.
