He writes back in a fortnight. He's going back to the motor works. He says he still dreams about the knocks.[/if]

choices.text: Go to the camp concert and forget it for a night.
choices.text_after:
A sergeant from the workshops sings in a frock and a wig made out of rope, and a Welshman
sings something that stops the hut dead, and Kearney does a card trick with the major's
watch and gives it back, mostly. You laugh till your sides hurt. On the way back through
the snow you're all quiet, the breath going up from you in the frost.

v18tk_whippet.title: The Whippet
v18tk_whippet.text:
February. Pring comes to find you in the hut with his cap in his hand, and he never takes his
cap off.

The Whippets, he says. The new light tanks: three men to a crew, an officer, a driver and a
gunner, in a thing you could almost park in a street. The first of them are in France now, at
a camp behind the line, with more coming every week, and they want drivers who know what
they're doing. He's put in for one.

[if war.path == subaltern]He's asking you, as his officer, to let him go. He'll take whatever gunner they give him.[else]"And I want a gunner I know," he says. "I want you." Three of you, and none of them Kearney or Tonks[if !flag.tk17_murray_tin] or Murray[/if]. Just Pring, and an officer you've never met, and you.[/if]

choices.text: Go with Pring to the Whippets.
choices.text_after:
Pring shakes your hand as if you'd sold him a horse. Kearney says you're both mad, and
deals you out of the game on the spot, and then deals you back in. The orders come inside a
week: the pair of you to a Whippet company at the start of March, your kit on a lorry.

choices.text: [if war.path == subaltern]Let him go.[else]Stay with Polaris and the crew.[/if]
choices.text_after: [if war.path == subaltern]You sign the paper. He thanks you properly, standing up. He'll go to the Whippets in the spring with a quiet lad from the reserve crew called Dobbs.[else]Pring nods as if he'd known. "Fair enough," he says. He gets a gunner from the reserve crew instead, a quiet lad called Dobbs, and when the Whippets come in the spring he'll go to them.[/if]

choices.text: Keep him. Polaris needs her driver.
choices.text_after:
You tell him no. He takes it like a man told the last bus has gone, and goes back to the
hut, and the next morning he's under her with a spanner as if nothing had been said.

v18tk_burned.title: April
v18tk_burned.text:
April, and a camp of tents in a wet field, with no tanks in it.

You burned her yourselves, in March, at a crossroads, on the second day of going back. You've
been a Lewis-gun team since, like plenty of crews that lost their tanks, in the line with the infantry, and for once
the infantry are glad to see you.

Before the match went in, Kearney took Tonks's hammer to the hinge pins of the steel flap on her
nose, the one her name was painted across, and knocked it off. It's lying on your blanket now. New tanks are coming, they say. You're to wait
for them here, in the rain.

[if flag.tk18_said_no]Pring's had his orders for the Whippets. He goes at the end of the month, with Dobbs, and shakes every hand in the tent.[/if]

choices.text: Keep it. Carry it in your pack.
choices.text_after:
It's heavy for what it is, and it rattles against your mess tin when you march, and you
never take it out to look at it.

choices.text: Give it back to Kearney. He took it.
choices.text_after:
Kearney weighs it in his hand and puts it in his kit without a word. A week later you see
him using it to keep his cards flat in the wind.

v18tk_new_tank.title: The new tank
v18tk_new_tank.text:
April. The new tanks come up on the train, clean and brown, the paint still tacky in the seams.
The crew walk round theirs like men at a cattle sale, and nobody has to ask what she's to be
called.

[if war.path == subaltern]You paint the name on her nose yourself, kneeling on the track, the way Mr Lacey did. POLARIS.[else][if flag.tk18_said_no]Kearney paints the name, because Pring's off to the Whippets, and Kearney's letters lean.[else]Pring paints the name on her nose, in the same white letters.[/if][/if]

[if !flag.tk17_murray_tin]Murray goes along her plates with his knuckle, the whole length of her, and comes back shaking his head, and you'd be frightened if he didn't.[else]A letter comes from Murray the same week, in the same stranger's hand. He wants to know if the new ones are any better riveted.[/if]

choices.text: Go round her with Murray, rivet by rivet.
choices.text_after:
It takes all afternoon. He finds eleven he doesn't like and makes the fitters do four of
them again, and they hate him, and he's happier than you've seen him since Govan came up.

choices.text: Write back to Murray about the rivets.
choices.text_after:
You tell him they're worse. It isn't true, but it's what he'd want to hear. The answer
comes in a month, in the stranger's hand: Told you.

choices.text: Leave her to the fitters. A tank's a tank.
choices.text_after:
You sit on the grass in the sun with your back against her track and let the fitters get
on with it, your eyes shut and the steel warm through your shirt.

v18tk_three.title: Three of you
v18tk_three.text:
April, and a camp of tents in a wet field behind the new line, and the Whippet at the end of a
row of them with her plates scarred bright where the bullets hit. There are gaps in the row.
Nobody talks about them.

Word comes down from the heavies with a lorry driver. Polaris is gone. They ran her dry at a
crossroads on the second day and burned her themselves, and before the match went in Kearney
took Tonks's hammer to the steel flap on her nose, the one with her name across it, and
knocked it off, and he carries it in his kit. They're a Lewis-gun team now, in the line with
the infantry, waiting for new tanks.

Pring hears it out with his cap in his hands. Then he goes out to the Whippet in the rain and
starts on her tracks, and Mr Yarrow puts his head into the tent, smelling of wet oilskin, and
says there's a practice ground behind the camp if anybody wants it.

choices.text: Tell Pring to take her out and open her up.
choices.text_after:
He does. The cab bangs and rattles and the practice ground goes past in a blur of wet
grass, and Mr Yarrow holds on to his cap and shouts that she'll do twice that downhill, and
for ten minutes nobody thinks about March.

choices.text: Learn the guns in her till you could work them blind.
choices.text_after:
A week of it, in the cab, with your eyes shut and Pring timing you with his watch. In March
your hands fumbled the belts. By the end of the week you can change a gun and a belt in the
dark with your hands alone.

v18tk_moving_up.title: Moving up
v18tk_moving_up.text:
July, and they move you at night, only at night. The tanks go up the roads in the dark with
their engines throttled right down, so they sound like a threshing engine three fields off and
not like tanks. In the day you lie up in woods under the nets, and nobody's allowed to light a
fire, and the officers walk about looking at the sky.

Something big. Nobody says it.

The post comes up with the rations, and there's one from home.

"Dear Son, just a few lines. [if start == mill]Our Jack has had his papers, he went Tuesday. Your father walked him to the station. Jack says to tell you he wants to go in the tanks like his brother, and your father told him he will go where he is put.[/if][if start == pit]Mary has finished at the munitions, the yellow was getting on her chest. The union is talking about after, they talk about nothing else, and about the men coming home to the pits.[/if][if start == farm]The hay is in. The girls and the prisoners got it in between them and your father says it is the best stack he has seen on the farm, and then he says it is not as good as yours.[/if][if start == city]There were no raids this month and your father has his allotment on the marshes going, the beans are a picture. He takes them round the street in a basket.[/if] Look after yourself. Your loving Mother."

choices.text: Write back tonight, by a torch under the net.
choices.text_after:
You can't say where you are or what's coming. You write about the weather and the food
and Kearney's cards. At the end, after you've signed it, you write: I'll be home. You look
at that a while, and leave it in.

choices.text: Keep it, to read again on the night.
choices.text_after:
You put it inside your shirt. On the night, waiting for zero, you'll read it again by the
light of a torch, and you'll know it by heart already.

v18tk_kearney.title: Kearney
v18tk_kearney.text:
The end of August. You're going forward every day, and every day there are fewer tanks: a
battle every few mornings, a few tanks to each, whatever can still run.

[if flag.tk18_said_no]Pring didn't come back from the eighth. His Whippet was seen in the afternoon far out beyond the line, on its own, firing into a camp, and then it was seen stopped, and burning. A man from his battalion says Pring was killed getting out. Nobody knows anything about Dobbs.[/if]

A tank in the company has its gunner down with the fever, and the show's in the morning,
and the captain wants a man off Polaris to make up her crew. Kearney says he'll go.
"They owe me eleven francs over there," he says. "I'm not having Fritz kill them before they pay."

choices.text: Let him go. He's asked.
choices.text_after:
He goes over with his kit in the dark. In the morning the other tank goes into a sunken
road beyond their line and ditches there, nose down, and doesn't come out. An infantry
officer says he saw the crew climb out with their hands up, all of them, and walk away east
with a German behind them. Kearney's cards are still in your pack. He left them with you
for safe keeping, so nobody could cheat with them.

choices.text: Tell him not to go. Let them find somebody else.
choices.text_after:
Kearney argues, and then he doesn't. The captain sends a lad from the reserve
instead, one whose name you never learn. In the morning the other tank goes into a sunken
road beyond their line and ditches there, and doesn't come out, and the infantry say the
crew walked away east with their hands up. That night Kearney deals hand after hand on the
floor plates and doesn't win one.

v18tk_heavies.title: The heavies
v18tk_heavies.text:
The end of August. The Whippets go forward every day, and the heavies behind, fewer each
morning. At a crossroads you pass Polaris going up, with the name on her nose, and Kearney's
sitting on her roof dealing cards to Tonks, the pack held flat with the strip of steel off her old nose.

Tonks is shouting. He shouts everything now.

choices.text: Get Pring to stop. Go and see them.
choices.text_after:
Kearney deals you in on her roof without asking, and Tonks shouts that you're putting on
weight in that toy, and [if !flag.tk17_murray_tin]Murray puts his head out of the door and tells you the Whippet's badly riveted, and [/if]for ten minutes at the crossroads it's the old crew, till a redcap moves you all on.

choices.text: Wave, and go on.
choices.text_after:
You wave from the cab. Kearney holds up a card, the ace of spades, and Tonks waves his
hammer, and then the dust from the road comes up between you.

v18tk_tonks.title: Tonks
v18tk_tonks.text:
September. Tonks has stopped answering when you speak to him on his left side. He thinks
nobody's noticed. In the drill he watches the driver's hand instead of listening for the
knocks, and twice now he's missed one, and the track's gone on when it should have stopped,
and she's slewed round with the whole crew thrown against the engine.

[if war.path == subaltern]He's your gearsman, and it's for you to say.[else]Mr Fane is nineteen and hasn't noticed. If anybody tells him, it'll be you.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.path == subaltern]Send him down to the workshops at Teneur.[else]Tell Mr Fane. Tonks will go to the workshops.[/if]
choices.text_after:
Tonks goes down the line to Teneur, to work on engines at a bench where nobody shoots at
him. He won't shake your hand. At the lorry he turns round and calls something back, and
you don't catch it, and he grins as if that's the joke.

choices.text: [if war.path == subaltern]Keep him. Put him where he can see the driver's hand.[else]Keep his secret. Stand on his good side and knock twice as hard.[/if]
choices.text_after: [if war.path == subaltern]You move him to where he can see the driver's hand, and tell the driver to knock hard enough to dent the cover. Tonks knows what you're doing. That night a bottle of vin blank turns up on your blanket, and nobody knows where from.[else]You change places with him in the drill so you're on his good side, and you knock hard enough to dent the cover. He knows what you're doing. When you're both off duty he buys the vin blank, and keeps buying it.[/if]

v18tk_pring.title: Pring
v18tk_pring.text:
September, and a village, and the infantry held up at the end of the street by a field gun
behind a garden wall, firing over open sights. The Whippet's in a farmyard round the corner.

Pring wants to go straight down the street at it. "Like Holborn," he says. "In the rush hour.
They'll get out of the way." Mr Yarrow, the Whippet's officer, looks at you. He's asking.

choices.text: Tell him go on, then.
choices.text_after:
Pring puts her at the street like a bus at a hill. The gun fires once, and the shell goes
past the cab so close you feel the wind of it, and then she's on the wall, and the gunners
run. When you climb out after, Pring's sitting on the cobbles with his arm in his lap and
the sleeve all blood. "Splinter," he says. "Off the wall. A Blighty one." They send him home. He shakes
your hand with the left one.

choices.text: Wait for the infantry to work round through the gardens.
choices.text_after:
You wait. It takes an hour, and the infantry do it the slow way, through the back gardens
and over the walls, and Pring sits at the controls with his jaw going, saying nothing. When
the gun's taken he drives down the street at a walk, to look at it.

e_armistice_tank.title: The Armistice
e_armistice_tank.text:
{ending_line}

It comes to the tankodrome on a message form, in the morning, and the sergeant major reads it
out standing on a tank. Hostilities will cease at eleven. Nobody believes it, and then
everybody does.

There's nothing left to drive. The tanks stand in rows behind the huts with their tracks off
and their engines out, waiting for parts that won't come now, and the crews have been playing
football all week with a ball made of rags. At eleven you're standing in the mud by the
workshop sheds. Somewhere east the guns go on to the last minute, and then stop, and a fitter
on a shed roof lets go of his spanner, and you hear it slide all the way down the corrugated
iron and drop.

[if !flag.tk18_whippet && !flag.tk_kearney_taken]Kearney deals a hand on an upturned petrol tin, and nobody wants to play, and he deals it anyway.[if flag.tk18_gave_plate] He keeps the cards flat with her name.[/if][/if][if flag.tk_kearney_taken]Somewhere in Germany Kearney is in a camp, and you'd lay money he's dealing.[/if][if !flag.tk18_whippet && !flag.tk18_tonks_told] Tonks says what, what, when you tell him, and then laughs, and can't stop.[if flag.tk18_tonks_kept] He leans his good ear to you, and you say it again.[/if][/if][if flag.tk18_tonks_told] Tonks is at Teneur, at his bench, hearing it a minute after everybody else.[/if][if !flag.tk18_whippet && !flag.tk17_murray_tin] Murray goes and pats the nearest tank on her plates, and says badly riveted, the lot of them, and walks off with his hands in his pockets.[/if][if flag.tk17_murray_tin] You think of Murray, and his hands.[/if][if flag.tk18_whippet && !flag.tk18_pring_hit] Pring rolls a cigarette and says he'll be back on the buses by Easter, and he'll never go over four miles an hour again as long as he lives.[/if][if flag.tk18_pring_hit] Pring's at home already, driving again, he wrote, with one hand.[/if][if !flag.tk18_whippet && !flag.tk18_said_no] Pring sits on the step of the hut and looks at his hands on his knees, a bus driver's hands, and turns them over.[if flag.tk18_kept_pring] "You did me a good turn in February, sir," he says, and doesn't say what it was.[/if][/if][if flag.tk18_said_no] You think of Pring, out on his own beyond everything, in August.[/if][if flag.tk18_whippet] Polaris's crew are at another tankodrome down the line, and you can see it as if you were there: Kearney dealing, Tonks saying what, what.[/if][if flag.tk17_lacey_praised] And Mr Lacey, who was sick every time she moved, and went up the ridge on foot in front of her.[/if][if flag.tk17_lacey_praised && flag.tk18_wrote_lacey] His mother has written back to you twice, from Coventry.[/if][if !flag.tk17_lacey_praised] Mr Lacey writes from Coventry the week after, a page to every man of the crew.[/if][if flag.tk18_kept_plate] In your pack the strip of steel with her name on it rattles against your mess tin.[/if]

[if war.mate1 || war.mate2 || war.mate3]The battalion's somewhere east, in the line. You think of the men from home who are in it still:[if war.mate1] {mate1_first},[/if][if war.mate2] {mate2_first},[/if][if war.mate3] {mate3_first},[/if] and the rest, hearing the guns stop.[else]You think of the section from home, and how few of them are left to hear the guns stop.[/if]

[if start == mill]At home, your mother writes, every mill buzzer in the town went off at eleven, and the weavers came out into the street in their clogs and shawls and stood there, and then went back in, because the looms were still running and nobody had told them to stop.[/if][if start == pit]At home, your mother writes, the pit buzzer went at eleven and didn't stop, and the fore shift came up early, black as they were, and stood in the rows with the women.[/if][if start == farm]At Dunsworthy, your mother writes, they rang the bells all the afternoon, and your father left the horses in the furrow and stood in the churchyard with his cap in his hand until it was too dark to plough.[/if][if start == city]In the City, they tell you, the clerks threw paper out of every window, ledgers and forms and blotting paper, till Lombard Street was white with it, like snow.[/if][if flag.tk18_wrote_home] Your letter from July, the one that says you'll be home, is behind the clock.[/if]

You are {age} years old and {rank_a}.

[if flag.ro_sw_first][if flag.ro_sw_ended || flag.ro_sw_jilted]{sweetheart} is married to somebody else. You see her at the war memorial when they unveil it, and she squeezes your hand once, and lets go.[else][if flag.ro_sw_married]{sweetheart} is at the station.[if flag.ro_sw_named] So is the baby, who isn't a baby now, and looks at you as if you were a stranger, which you are.[/if][else][if flag.ro_sw_wed16 || flag.ro_sw_wed17]You marry {sweetheart} in the spring of 1919, the bells ringing properly now, every one.[else][if flag.ro_sw_after || flag.ro_sw_wait2]{sweetheart} waited till it was over. You're married in the spring of 1919.[else]You walk out with {sweetheart} on Sundays, the way you did before, and neither of you says much, and that's all right.[/if][/if][/if][/if][/if][if flag.ro_fr_promise || flag.ro_fr_address] In the summer of 1919 a letter comes from France, from Marthe, and you go to the station and ask how much a ticket is.[/if]

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_killed.title: Killed
e_killed.text:
{ending_line}

[if war.corps == air][if war.end_cause == shell]Archie, close. You hear this one: a crack like a slate splitting, right under you, and the machine stands up on one wing.[else]The German comes in behind the tail, and you've half a drum off at him when the bullets come up through the floor.[/if] The ground comes round the side of the sky, and round again. The wind's loud in the wires, and then it isn't.

At the aerodrome the fitters stand out on the field at dusk, counting the machines in, and count one short. They stay till it's dark. Somebody brings a lamp out, and they stay a while after that.[elif war.corps == tank][if war.end_cause == shell]A shell in the tank park, at night. You're asleep under the tarpaulin off her side, with the rain ticking on it. You don't wake.

In the morning the crew carry you to the cemetery by the road, wrapped in the tarpaulin, and stand bareheaded in the drizzle while the padre reads.[else]Something comes through her plate. A white flash inside her, and a noise like a boiler struck with a sledge, and the dark full of fumes.

What's left of the crew get you out of the door in her side, into the mud, and one of them stays with you in the lee of her, out of the bullets, with his hand flat on your chest, till there's no use staying.[/if][elif war.end_cause == underground]It's the timbers you hear first, a crack like a rifle shot in the dark, and then the clay comes down and the candle goes out.

They dig for you all that shift and the next, turn and turn about, the rescue men in their breathing sets and the rest with their hands. They bring you up into the daylight, and bury you in a proper grave behind the line, with a cross.[else][if war.end_cause == shell]You don't hear the one that does it. The man nearest you does, and afterwards he'll say you made a small sound, surprised, as if you'd dropped something.[elif war.end_cause == battle]Something shoves you hard from behind, like a man in the crowd at a match, and you sit down in the grass. The noise goes on over the top of you. You mean to get up in a minute.[elif war.end_cause == sortie]It's one round, from a man you never see. You hear it hit before you feel it, a slap like a wet cloth on a table. Then you don't feel much. The others finish the job, because there's nothing else to do, and bring you in with them after.[elif war.end_cause == assign]Behind the line, on the job that wasn't meant to be the dangerous one. A shell on the road, and the men you were with sat down in the ditch looking at you.[else]A stray one, from nowhere anybody saw. You were halfway through saying something.[/if]

[if war.end_cause == battle]They can't get you in that day, nor the next. A burial party finds you after, and puts up a cross with a strip of tin stamped with your name and number.[else]They carry you down the trench that night under a blanket, and bury you in the morning in the cemetery behind the line, with the padre and four men, and the guns going on.[/if][if war.corps != tank && war.corps != air && war.path != tunnel][if war.mate1] {mate1} hears it that night from a man who says it quickly, to get it said. He sits on the firestep a while. Then he goes and borrows a pencil.[elif war.mate2] {mate2} hears it that night from a man who says it quickly, to get it said. He sits on the firestep a while. Then he goes and borrows a pencil.[elif war.mate3] {mate3} hears it that night from a man who says it quickly, to get it said. He sits on the firestep a while. Then he goes and borrows a pencil.[/if][/if][/if]

[if war.corps == air]At home the form says missing. Missing isn't killed, and your mother says so to everybody who stops her in the street. The squadron's major writes that your machine was seen going down on the far side of the line, and there is every hope you are a prisoner. She writes to the Red Cross. She writes again.

It's months before they answer. The Germans have sent your name through, in a list: killed on the day you went missing, and buried where you came down, by their own people. Your mother reads it in the kitchen with her coat still on.[elif war.commissioned]The telegraph boy comes up the street on his bicycle, and every woman in it watches to see which door he stops at. The words are pasted on the form in strips: deeply regret to inform you, and your rank and your name, and killed in action, and the date. The Army Council express their sympathy. Your mother reads it in the doorway, with the boy waiting in case there's an answer.[else]At home it comes weeks later in a buff envelope, Army Form B.104-82: "It is my painful duty to inform you that a report has been received from the War Office notifying the death of," and then your number and your name, written in by hand. There's a printed slip in with it, with the King's and Queen's sympathy. Your mother reads it on the doorstep with the postman still stood there, because she knew from his face. He keeps his cap in his hands till she shuts the door.[/if]

[if war.corps != air]Then the letter from [if war.commissioned]your commanding officer[elif war.corps == tank]your section commander[elif war.path == tunnel]your section officer[else]your platoon officer[/if], in ink, on paper from a writing case. You were killed instantly, he writes, and cannot have suffered. You were [if war.commissioned]a gallant officer and your men thought the world of you[else]a good soldier and well liked by all ranks[/if], and [if war.end_cause == battle]you have been laid to rest near where you fell, and the place is marked[else]you are buried in a cemetery behind the lines, where the grave will be looked after[/if]. Your mother reads "instantly" and holds on to it, and carries the letter in her apron pocket for a month, till it goes soft at the folds.[/if][if war.corps != tank && war.corps != air && war.path != tunnel][if war.mate1]

{mate1_first} {mate1}'s letter comes the same week, in pencil, two pages. He was near, he says. It was quick. He saw you after, and you looked as if you were asleep. She doesn't know if it's true, and she doesn't ask him, then or ever.[elif war.mate2]

{mate2_first} {mate2}'s letter comes the same week, in pencil, two pages. He was near, he says. It was quick. He saw you after, and you looked as if you were asleep. She doesn't know if it's true, and she doesn't ask him, then or ever.[elif war.mate3]

{mate3_first} {mate3}'s letter comes the same week, in pencil, two pages. He was near, he says. It was quick. He saw you after, and you looked as if you were asleep. She doesn't know if it's true, and she doesn't ask him, then or ever.[/if][/if]

Your things come months later, in a brown paper parcel with a typed list: a razor, a comb, a photograph gone soft at the corners, a pencil stub, a few French coins.[if flag.last_letter && war.corps == air] The letter you left in your pay book doesn't come. It went down with you, over there.[elif flag.last_letter] The letter from your pay book comes with them. She reads it at the kitchen table, and then she reads it again.[/if][if flag.wd_blighty_section] Somebody out there has put in your letter from the hospital, the one about the egg, gone round the dugouts so often it's soft as a dishcloth.[/if] She puts it all in the biscuit tin with your letters.[if flag.wd_light_joke] The one about the scratch and the fortnight's holiday has a jam tin drawn in the margin. She knew from the paper it was more than a scratch. She never said.[elif flag.wd_light_quiet] She found your name in the paper once, in the wounded, the week your letter was all about the weather. She never let on.[elif flag.wd_light_truth] The one from the rest station, where you told her straight, she reads oftenest, because it sounds the most like you talking.[/if][if flag.wd_blighty_home] The long one from the hospital in England, the one no officer read, is at the bottom, folded small.[/if][if flag.wd_blighty_quiet] She asked you once, at the hospital, what it was like out there, and you said, "Oh, you know." She thinks about that more than she'd like.[/if]

After the war a bronze plaque comes in a stiff card wrapper, about the size of a saucer, with your name on it and a lion, and a scroll with it from the King. She stands the plaque on the mantelpiece by the clock and dusts it on Fridays.

[if start == mill]Up and down the street the curtains are drawn. Mrs Shaw from two doors up comes in without knocking, and puts the kettle on, and stays till dark. Your name goes up in the chapel porch on the roll of honour, in gilt, at the bottom, and the man who does the lettering will be back in a few weeks for the next.[elif start == pit]The blinds go down. The men coming off shift see them, and take their caps off going past, black from the pit, and nobody knocks. At the Miners' Hall your name goes on the lodge's roll, under the banner, and the committee stands for it.[elif start == farm]At Dunsworthy they toll the tenor for you, and then one stroke for every year you had, slow, so the whole valley can count. Your father finishes the milking first. Then he walks out to the gate of the Long Field, where nobody can see him from the house, and stands there.[elif start == city]The Gresham and Lombard sends a letter on the firm's paper, signed by the manager, and your name goes on the Roll of Honour in the front hall. Your father goes up to work the next morning, because he doesn't know what else to do, and comes home at six and sits in the front room without lighting the gas.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_first][if flag.ro_sw_ended || flag.ro_sw_jilted]{sweetheart} hears it from your mother, at the gate. She goes to the service and stands at the back, and leaves before the end.[else][if flag.ro_sw_married]{sweetheart} gets her own letter, because she is your wife. The separation allowance stops and a widow's pension starts, a few shillings a week. She keeps your letters in the drawer with her wedding lines.[if flag.ro_sw_named] The baby is too young to remember you. She tells him about you anyway, every night, so that he will.[/if][else][if flag.ro_sw_wed16 || flag.ro_sw_wed17]Nobody writes to {sweetheart}, because she isn't your wife yet. She hears it from your mother. The banns were to be read for your leave. She wears black for a year, as if she had been married, and nobody says a word against it.[else][if flag.ro_sw_after || flag.ro_sw_wait2]Nobody writes to {sweetheart}, because she is only the girl who was waiting. She hears it from your mother at the door. She had said she would wait till it was over, and she does, a long time, for nothing.[else]{sweetheart}'s last letter comes back with your things, opened and read and folded the way she folded it.[/if][/if][/if][/if][/if][if flag.ro_fr_writes || flag.ro_fr_promise] In Ternecourt, Marthe's letters stop being answered.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_promise || flag.ro_fr_address] In the spring a letter comes to your mother in careful schoolroom English, from a girl in France called Marthe, asking if you are well. Your mother has the vicar write back.[/if]

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

x_fallen_cottle.title: Will Cottle
x_fallen_cottle.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Cottle goes down on one knee, slow, the way he'd kneel to look at a ewe's foot, and then he's on his side in the grass.

"Fly," he says. Just that. The dog's name. And then he's looking past you up at the sky, the way he'd look for weather from the top of the moor, and he doesn't stop looking.[else][if war.transferred]Word comes over from the battalion, a week late. Will Cottle. Killed {fallen_where}.[else]You hear it at the ration dump, in the dark. Will Cottle. Killed {fallen_where}.

You stand there with the bread under your arm. You knew him before you could walk. You learned to whistle a dog from his father.[/if][/if]

At home there's a black and white dog lying by a gate, looking up the lane.

choices.text: Write to old Mr Cottle yourself, tonight.
choices.text_after:
You put that he didn't suffer, which you don't know. You put that the last thing he said was
the dog's name. His father will want that.

choices.text: Leave it to the officer's letter. You can't.

x_fallen_pearce.title: Dan Pearce
x_fallen_pearce.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Pearce was always quick. He's quick now: up and then down, all at once, flat in the grass with his face turned to you, surprised, as if somebody had come on him with a gun when he'd thought the keeper was miles off.

"Well," he says. "They've had me, then." And that's Dan Pearce.[else][if war.transferred]Word comes over from the battalion, a week late. Dan Pearce. Killed {fallen_where}.[else]Somebody tells you at the water cart. "Pearce has copped it." Dan Pearce. Killed {fallen_where}.

You think of him going through the long grass the first night like water. Nobody ever caught Dan Pearce. Fifteen years the keeper tried.[/if][/if][if flag.farm_shared_pearce] Fourteen days on the wheel together, side by side, and he never once stopped talking.[/if]

choices.text: Write to his mother. Tell her about the hare in the wire.
choices.text_after:
You tell her about the hare in the wire the first night, and the partridges, and the wheel.
You tell her he was the best man in the battalion at being where he wasn't supposed to be.
She'll laugh. Then she won't.

choices.text: Leave it. You'd never get him right.

x_fallen_yeo.title: Bert Yeo
x_fallen_yeo.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Bert's beside you, and then he's sat down, and he's holding his hands in front of him, curled, the way they curled round the sally of the tenor bell, as if he's waiting for the rope to come down to him.

You hold on to him. He says something you can't hear for the noise. You think it might be a hymn.[else][if war.transferred]Word comes over from the battalion, a week late. Bert Yeo. Killed {fallen_where}.[else]You hear it from a stretcher-bearer who knew him. Bert Yeo. Killed {fallen_where}.

He was eighteen. He'd rung the tenor at Dunsworthy since he was twelve.[/if][/if][if flag.farm_bert_stopped] He was going to ring the whole peal, after. When you got home.[/if][if flag.farm_bert_rang] He rang one bell in France, once, and you took the blame for it.[/if]

choices.text: Write to Mrs Yeo. Tell her about the bell.
choices.text_after:
You tell her about the French church with half a roof, and Bert with the rope in his hands.
You don't know if it's the right thing to tell a mother. It's the true thing.

choices.text: Leave it. She'll have the official letter.

x_fallen_shaw.title: Albert Shaw
x_fallen_shaw.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}, three yards from you. Shaw sits down the way a man sits on a step at the end of a shift, and puts his hand flat on his chest, and looks at it.

"Oh, hell," he says. "Oh, me mam."

You get to him. You get your field dressing out with your teeth. There's nowhere to put it that would be any use. He's looking past you at something, and then he isn't looking at anything.

Somebody pulls you off him. You've got him to the elbows and it's going cold already, sticky, and it smells like the back of the butcher's on Bury Road.[else][if war.transferred]Word comes over from the battalion, a week late. Shaw. Killed {fallen_where}.[else]You hear it at the ration dump, in the dark. Shaw. Killed {fallen_where}. The man who tells you says it quickly, to get it said, and goes.

You sit on the firestep with the bread under your arm.[/if][if flag.wrote_for_shaw] His mother's last letter from him was in your handwriting. The next one will be in an officer's, and she'll know the difference.[/if][/if]

His mother lives two doors up from yours.

choices.text: Write to Mrs Shaw yourself, tonight.
choices.text_after:
It takes you till stand-to. You put that he didn't suffer, which you don't know. You put
that he talked about her, which is true.

choices.text: Leave it to the officer's letter. You can't.

x_fallen_duckworth.title: Harry Duckworth
x_fallen_duckworth.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Duckworth's halfway through a joke, the one about the tackler and the parson's wife, and then he isn't. There's no sound to it that you can pick out from all the other noise. He's just down, face first, with his rifle under him, and when you turn him over the joke's still on his face.

You stay with him longer than you should. Somebody has to kick your boot.[else][if war.transferred]Word comes over from the battalion, a week late. Duckworth. Killed {fallen_where}.[else]Somebody tells you at the water cart. Duckworth's gone west. Killed {fallen_where}.

"He wouldn't have known a thing," they say. You hope it's true. You hope it hard, like a prayer, standing there with the water tins.[/if][/if]

choices.text: Write to his mam and dad yourself.
choices.text_after:
You tell them about the Woodbines on the first night, and the jokes, all of them, even the
one about the parson's wife, because his dad will laugh at that one and his mam will pretend
she didn't hear.

choices.text: Leave it. You wouldn't know what to put.

x_fallen_pilling.title: Walter Pilling
x_fallen_pilling.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Pilling's next to you and then he's in the bottom of the trench, curled up small, calling for his mam in a voice you've not heard out of him since he was nine and fell off the canal wall.

You hold his hand. It's all there is. His grip goes tight, tighter, like a child's at the fair when the crowd closes in, and then it doesn't.[else][if war.transferred]A letter comes from your mother, a fortnight late. Walter Pilling was killed {fallen_where}. Mrs Pilling has had the telegram, and asked your mother if you were with him. You weren't.[else]The post comes up and there's a letter for Pilling, from his mam, in her careful round hand. The corporal gives it to you because you're from the same street. Pilling was killed {fallen_where} two days since.

You don't open it. You put it inside your tunic, and you can feel it there all night, square and stiff against your chest.[/if][/if]

[if war.stage == 1]He was sixteen. He'd have been seventeen in March.[else]He was eighteen. He'd been telling everybody since March.[/if][if flag.told_on_pilling] You tried, you tell yourself. You tried.[/if][if flag.told_pilling_ease] You told him to ease off. He told you somebody was counting.[/if]

choices.text: Write to Mrs Pilling. Tell her about the birthday cakes.
Leave it. She'll have the official letter.

x_sent.title: The man you sent
x_sent.text: [if war.sent_friend && !war.sent_killed]{sent_first} goes. He comes back at first light, mud to the eyebrows, and drops into the trench beside you and says nothing about it. He doesn't have to. You sent him because he'd do it right, and he did.[/if][if war.sent_friend && war.sent_killed]You sent {sent_name} on {sent_duty}. He didn't come back. The sergeant finds you on the firestep at stand-to and stands there a minute. "You'll have to live with it," he says. "That's what the stripe's for."[/if][if !war.sent_friend && !war.sent_killed]The new man goes, white as paper, and comes back at dawn and can't stop talking. The men from home look at you, and then away. Nobody says anything.[/if][if !war.sent_friend && war.sent_killed]The new man doesn't come back. You never learned his first name. The men from home don't say anything about it, and they don't have to.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.sent_killed]Write it in the section roll.[else]Go on.[/if]

x_wound_light.title: Hit
x_wound_light.text:
Hit {wound_where}.

[if war.corps == air][if war.wound_cause == shell]Archie, right under the tail. A black puff, a bang you feel through the seat, and the machine hops like a cart going over a stone. Something stings your calf through your flying boot, like a wasp got into your sock.[else]A German comes in behind the tail and you're both firing, and something knocks your hand off the gun. There's a neat slit in the leather of your sleeve, and blood coming out at the cuff, and it's so cold up here you hardly feel it.[/if]

Your pilot turns for home. He shouts something back over the engine that you don't catch, and you put your thumb up, and he puts his up.

He puts her down on the aerodrome and taxis right up to the hangars, and the fitters lift you out over the side like a sack of meal. The squadron's medical officer sees to you in the office, among the maps and the telephone, in a smell of oil and cigarettes. Iodine. A needle against lockjaw. A dressing, and a label on your tunic button for the clearing station down the road. They keep you three days there. Then a fortnight on the ground, walking out every morning to watch the machines go, and the fitters bringing you tea, till the medical officer passes you to fly.[elif war.corps == tank][if war.wound_cause == shell]A shell in the tank park, at night. You're asleep under the tarpaulin rigged off her side when it comes, and the next you know you're sat up in the mud with your ears singing, a hot splinter in the meat of your thigh, and the sergeant shouting names.

The orderly at the aid post in the farm picks it out with tweezers by a hurricane lamp.[else]Splash. Bullets rattle on her plates like hail on a tin roof, and the inside of the plate spits back at you, flakes of hot steel no bigger than fish scales. One finds your cheek, under the edge of your mask. Your hand comes away from your face red, and the engine roars on, and there's a gun to work, so you work it.

You stay in her till the rallying point, because there's nowhere else to go. Then the section officer looks at your face by the light of her open door and sends you back along her tracks on foot, to the first infantry aid post you can find, with petrol and cordite still in your nose.[/if] Iodine, a needle against lockjaw, a dressing, a label tied to your button. A fortnight at the rest station, sleeping. Then a lorry back to the company, and the smell of hot oil, and your place in the crew kept for you.[else][if war.wound_cause == battle]It's like a cricket bat across the shoulder, hard, and you're sat down in the muck before you know why. Then the heat comes, and the wet. There's a hole in your sleeve you could put your thumb in.[elif war.wound_cause == shell]A shell comes over and you're down before you know you've heard it. The earth slaps you flat. When you sit up there's a hot sting low in your back, and your hand comes away red. A splinter, no bigger than your fingernail.[elif war.wound_cause == sortie][if war.result_key == bearer]You're bent under the front handles of a stretcher, with a man on it who won't stop asking for water, when something goes through the meat of your forearm like a hot needle through cloth. You don't drop him. You get him in first.[elif war.result_key == signals]You're running with the message, bent double, when something plucks at your thigh like a hand at your trousers. You get the message through. Then you look.[elif war.result_key == snipe]A round comes in at your loophole and hits the plate. The plate holds, and spits splinters of itself into your face and the back of your hand, and you're blinking blood and can't see out of one eye for an hour.[elif war.result_key == tunnel || war.path == tunnel]Underground, listening. They blow first. The blast comes down the gallery like a train through a cutting and throws you against the timbers, and you lie in the dark with two ribs cracked and clay in your mouth, till the others find you by your coughing.[elif war.result_key == carrying]Up the communication trench in the dark, under a box of bombs, when the machine gun that sweeps the crossroads every night sweeps it. Something nips your calf like a dog at a gate. You don't drop the box.[elif war.result_key == raid || war.result_key == patrol || war.result_key == wiring || war.result_key == listening || war.result_key == bomb || war.result_key == lewis]Out in front, in the dark. A flare goes up, and you freeze the way you've been taught, and a machine gun on their side traverses along the wire. Something nips your hip like a dog at a gate. You lie still till the flare's out.[else]Something nips your hip like a dog at a gate, and you're sat down before you know why. You never see where it came from.[/if][elif war.wound_cause == assign]Behind the line, where you'd stopped thinking about it. A shell on the road, or a stray from nowhere: you never find out which. A burn along your ribs like a poker laid on you.[elif war.wound_cause == underground]It comes in behind you. They dig you out by the boots, coughing, with a timber across your legs and the skin off both shins.[else]A stray one, from nowhere anybody saw. A burn along your arm like a poker laid on it.[/if]

"You lucky sod," somebody says, crouching over you. "That's not even a Blighty one."

You get your field dressing out of your tunic and he ties it on for you, too tight. The stretcher-bearers have worse to carry. You walk, down the communication trench, careful, the way you'd carry a jug of milk, to the aid post in a cellar. It smells of iodine and paraffin and blood gone cold. The doctor looks for four seconds. Iodine that makes you shout, a needle against lockjaw, a dressing, a label tied to your tunic button with your name on it and what's the matter with you, in indelible pencil.

Then the back of a motor ambulance, eight of you sat up on the benches, bumping, and a fortnight at the rest station in a school with the desks stacked out in the yard. Bread and jam. A bath, and a clean shirt somebody else wore first. Sleep, more than you've had since you came out. On the fifteenth morning the sergeant reads your name off a list, and you go back up the road the way you came, with a new field dressing in your tunic.[/if]

Your name will be in the casualty lists in the paper, sooner or later, and your mother reads the lists. There's a letter to write before the post goes.

choices.text: Tell her straight where it is, and that it isn't bad.
choices.text_after:
You put where it went in, and the aid post, and the label, and that it's not even a Blighty
one, so she's not to go looking for you in the hospital lists. You read it over. It sounds
like somebody else.

choices.text: Make a joke of it. A scratch, and a fortnight's holiday.
choices.text_after:
You put that you've had a scratch and the army's giving you a fortnight's holiday for it,
with jam. You draw the jam tin in the margin. It takes you longer than the truth would have.

choices.text: Say nothing about it. She'd only worry.
choices.text_after:
You write about the weather, and the cat at the rest station, and that you're in the pink.
Not a word about it. You put "hoping this finds you as it leaves me", and it nearly does.

x_wound_severe.title: A Blighty one
x_wound_severe.text:
Hit {wound_where}.

[if war.corps == air][if war.wound_cause == shell]Archie bursts beside you, close, and everything goes white and loud at once.[else]The bullets come up through the floor of the cockpit. You hear them going through the fabric, like somebody tearing calico in the shop.[/if] You remember the gun ring cold against your cheek, and your pilot's face turned round to look at you, his mouth open. Then not much.

He gets her down. You never remember the landing. You remember hands lifting you, and the dope on the wings smelling of pear drops, and the ambulance tender bouncing over the grass.[elif war.corps == tank][if war.wound_cause == shell]A shell in the tank park, at night. You're asleep under the tarpaulin off her side, and then you're not anywhere. The crew dig you out of the mud with their hands and carry you to the aid post at the farm on a sheet of corrugated iron, swearing at you to hang on.[else]Something comes through her plate. A white flash inside her, and a noise you feel in your teeth, and the dark full of fumes. The crew get you out of the door in her side, into the mud, and two of them carry you back along her tracks between them, swearing at you to hang on, till they find the infantry's aid post.[/if][else][if war.wound_cause == battle]You don't remember the first part.[elif war.wound_cause == shell]The shell that does it lands close enough to lift you. You come round with earth in your mouth and somebody's hands on you, and one of your legs not answering.[elif war.wound_cause == sortie][if war.result_key == bearer]You're carrying a man in when it happens. The front of the stretcher goes down, and the other three get him in, and then come back for you.[elif war.result_key == signals]You're running with a message. You remember the message. You keep trying to tell them it, after.[elif war.result_key == snipe]They find your hide. One round, through the loophole. You don't remember the rest of that day.[elif war.result_key == tunnel || war.path == tunnel]Underground, listening. They blow first. You remember the dark coming down the gallery at you, and then the dark staying.[elif war.result_key == carrying]Up the communication trench in the dark, under a box of bombs, at the crossroads the machine gun sweeps every night.[elif war.result_key == raid || war.result_key == patrol || war.result_key == wiring || war.result_key == listening || war.result_key == bomb || war.result_key == lewis]Out in front, in the dark. A flare, and the machine gun that was waiting for it.[else]One you never see coming, and never see where it came from.[/if][elif war.wound_cause == assign]Behind the line, on the job that wasn't meant to be the dangerous one. A shell on the road.[elif war.wound_cause == underground]The timbers go, and the dark comes down. They dig you out, in the end, by the boots.[else]A stray one, from nowhere anybody saw.[/if] You remember a stretcher, the bearers swearing at the mud, the sky going past in strips between the trench walls.[/if]
[break]
Morphia [if war.corps == air]from the medical officer on the aerodrome[else]at the aid post[/if], warm and heavy, like falling asleep in front of the fire. A label on your button that somebody wrote in a hurry. An ambulance that finds every hole in the road. At the casualty clearing station a long tent, a row of you, chloroform and wet canvas, and a nursing sister with a lamp who reads your name off the label as if she knew you.

A train with cots in tiers, swaying, and an orderly coming down the middle with a jug of water. A hospital by the sea, at the place the lads call Eat Apples, where a doctor reads your label, and writes on it, and somebody says the word. Blighty.

A boat. The Channel's rough and the man in the cot above you is sick all the way across, and you don't care, because somebody said Southampton. Then a train through England, green fields going by, and at a station a lady pushes a cup of tea in through the window.

A hospital in England. Clean sheets that crackle. A nurse from Leeds who calls everybody "my lad" and smells of soap. [if war.commissioned]Officers don't get the blue suit: you're in a big house in London that a lady has given over to wounded officers, with flowers in the hall and a gramophone, and on Thursdays she takes three of you out in her motor car.[else]When you can stand they give you hospital blues, a blue flannel suit that fits nobody, a white shirt and a red tie, so anybody in the street can see what you are, and old men stop you to shake your hand.[/if]

Your mother comes on the train with a cake in a tin and sits by the bed for two hours not knowing what to say, and it's the best two hours of the war.[if flag.wd_light_quiet] Before she goes she says she saw your name in the paper the other time, in the wounded, the week you wrote about the weather. She doesn't say anything else about it.[elif flag.wd_light_joke] She's brought your letter about the scratch and the fortnight's holiday. "I'm keeping that," she says, "to show you when you're old."[elif flag.wd_light_truth] "You told me straight, last time," she says. "Tell me straight now." So you do, most of it.[/if]

In a couple of months the wound closes. A convalescent camp of huts, physical jerks in the mornings and route marches that get longer every week. A few days at home. [if war.commissioned]A medical board, three doctors at a table, who pass you fit.[elif war.corps == tank]The depot at Wool, and the smell of petrol again.[elif war.corps == air]A depot, and a long wait for a posting, and your old squadron asking for you back.[else]The depot, and a drill sergeant who's never been out, and the musketry all over again.[/if][if war.stage >= 3] A wound stripe to sew on your left sleeve, a strip of brass no longer than a match.[/if] Then your name on a draft, and Folkestone, and the boat the other way.

There's time in hospital, more than you've had since you joined, and a lady comes round the ward with a trolley of paper and pencils.

choices.text: [if war.corps == tank]Write to the crew. Make them laugh.[elif war.corps == air]Write to the fitters. Make them laugh.[else]Write to the lads in the section. Make them laugh.[/if]
choices.text_after:
You tell them about the sheets, and the nurse from Leeds, and the egg you had for your
breakfast, a whole egg, boiled. You know where it'll be read: by a candle in a dugout, out
loud, with the good bits twice.

choices.text: Write home, and for once put down what it's like.
choices.text_after:
No officer reads this one. The censor's on the other side of the water. You put down what
it's like. Not all of it, but more than you've ever put. It takes four pages and most of a
night, and in the morning you nearly tear it up, and then you post it.

choices.text: Say nothing to anybody. Sleep, eat, get well.
choices.text_after:
You sleep fourteen hours at a stretch and wake up hungry. When your mother asks what it's
like out there you say, "Oh, you know," and she doesn't, and she doesn't ask again.

x_fallen.title: {fallen_name}
x_fallen.text:
{fallen_name} is killed {fallen_where}.

[if war.fallen_present]You're near enough to see it, and far enough that there's nothing to do. Afterwards you can never get the order right in your head: the noise, or him going down, or the noise again.[else][if war.transferred]Word comes over from the battalion, a week late, from a man who says it quickly to get it said.[else]You hear it at the ration dump, in the dark, from a man who says it quickly to get it said.[/if][/if]

You knew him before any of this. You knew his mother's kitchen.

choices.text: Go on.

x_fallen_robson.title: Tommy Robson
x_fallen_robson.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Robson's beside you and then he's on his knees, and then he's sat back on his heels, the way he'd sit at the coal face to eat his bait, looking at his hands.

He doesn't say anything. He never did. He looks at you as if he's going to, and then he puts his head down on his chest as if he's tired, and that's all.

You kneel with him till somebody pulls you up. His hands are black with the earth, the way they always were, and you can't stop looking at them.[else][if war.transferred]Word comes over from the battalion. Robson. Killed {fallen_where}.[/if][if !war.transferred]You hear it at the ration dump, in the dark. Robson. Killed {fallen_where}.[/if]

You were marras at the face two years. You knew where he'd be in the dark by the sound of his pick. [if !war.transferred]You stand there with the bread under your arm and listen for it.[/if][if war.corps == tunnel]You'll listen for it underground tonight, and every night.[/if][if war.transferred && war.corps != tunnel]You'll listen for it in the dark tonight, and every night, and not hear it.[/if][/if]

At the end of the rows his da will be out at the cree in the morning, letting the birds go.

choices.text: Write to his da yourself, tonight.
choices.text_after:
You put that he didn't suffer, which you don't know. You put what he said about the army's
pigeons, that they were nowt special, because his da will know it's true.

choices.text: Leave it to the officer's letter. You can't.

x_fallen_bell.title: Jim Bell
x_fallen_bell.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Bell's talking, he's always talking, telling you what the owners will be making out of this one, and then he stops in the middle of a word, and sits down hard, surprised, with his mouth open on the rest of it.

"Hang on," he says. "Hang on, man." And that's the last thing Jim Bell ever says, and he'd have hated it, that it was nothing.[else][if war.transferred]A battalion runner tells you, not stopping. Jim Bell. Killed {fallen_where}.[/if][if !war.transferred]Somebody tells you at the water cart. Jim Bell. Killed {fallen_where}.[/if]

[if !war.transferred]It's quiet in the bay without him. You never knew how much of the noise was his.[/if][if war.corps == tunnel]You'd gone under. You weren't there to hear the last of what he had to say.[/if][if war.transferred && war.corps != tunnel]You'd gone to the [if war.corps == tank]tanks[else]Flying Corps[/if]. You weren't there to hear the last of what he had to say.[/if][if war.corps == tunnel && flag.p16_told_evans] Evans says he'll still buy him that pint, wherever he's gone. He says it in Welsh first, and then in English.[/if][/if][if flag.told_bell_shut] You told him not here, not now. He asked you when, and you hadn't an answer.[/if][if flag.stood_with_bell] You think of him in the beer vat with the Herald held up out of the water, grinning.[/if]

choices.text: Write to his father at the lodge.
choices.text_after:
You tell his father that Jim argued with everybody, sergeants and officers and the Germans
across the wire, and that he was right more often than they liked. His father will read
that out at the Miners' Hall. You know he will.

choices.text: Leave it. You'd never get it right.

x_fallen_charlton.title: George Charlton
x_fallen_charlton.text:
[if war.fallen_present]It happens {fallen_where}. Charlton goes down and curls up small on his side, and calls out, not for his mam, for the pony, for Captain, the way he'd call him in the dark of the stables to come up.

You hold on to him. He's not frightened, that's the strange thing. He's talking to the pony, low, steady, the way he talked to the mules, and he's still doing it when he goes.[/if][if !war.fallen_present && flag.pit_helped_charlton && !war.transferred]The transport sergeant comes up himself to tell you, which nobody expected. George Charlton, killed {fallen_where}. The sergeant stands there turning his cap in his hands. "Best lad with a horse I ever had," he says. "Best I ever had."[/if][if !war.fallen_present && war.transferred && war.corps != tunnel]It comes in a letter from home, a fortnight late. George Charlton, killed {fallen_where}. You read it twice, and sit thinking of the pony stables.[/if][if !war.fallen_present && war.corps == tunnel]Evans finds you with a face on him. A battalion runner told him. George Charlton, killed {fallen_where}. You stand there thinking of the pony stables.[/if][if !war.fallen_present && !flag.pit_helped_charlton && !war.transferred]You hear it at the ration dump, in the dark. George Charlton, killed {fallen_where}. The man who tells you says it quickly, to get it said, and goes, and you stand there thinking of the pony stables.[/if]

He was the gentlest of all of you. He used to carry his pony's bait down the shaft in his own pocket.

choices.text: Write to Mrs Charlton. Tell her about the mules.
choices.text_after:
You tell her about the mule that leaned on him in the dark like Captain used to, and how he
saved his crusts. You tell her he wasn't frightened, which is the only thing you know for
certain.

choices.text: Leave it. She'll have the official letter.

ro_mill_nellie_1.title: Nellie
ro_mill_nellie_1.text:
The post corporal comes along the bay with the bag over his shoulder like a coalman, calling
names. Yours, and then yours again. The second is a square envelope, the hand round and careful
and leaning backwards, and you know whose it is before you've got it open.

Nellie Whittaker. She has the four looms under the window, two alleys down from yours. The last
summer before you went you walked her home from chapel on Sunday nights, up the moor road as far
as the tower and back by the reservoir, and never once held her hand, because her brothers were
twenty yards behind the whole way, whistling.

"I hope you dont mind me writing, your mother gave me the number. The shed is not the same. They
have put a girl on your looms who is fifteen and cries when a shuttle flies out. I mee-maw to her
across the alley like I did to you and she cant read it yet. Is it bad out there. Our Fred says
you will not tell me if it is, so I am not to ask. I am asking. Yours sincerely, Nellie
Whittaker."

Under it, smaller, squeezed in: I still go up to the tower of a Sunday.

The paper smells of the shed, of warp size and warm oil, and you hold it under your nose on the firestep
like a lad with a bag of chips.

choices.text: Write back and tell her the truth, as much as the officer will pass.
choices.text_after:
You tell her about the rats, as big as the shed cats and worse mannered, and the cold at
stand-to, and the mud that pulls your boots off. The platoon officer reads every letter
before it goes, and you write it knowing he will, so it comes out stiff as a notice on the
mill gate. At the end you put: I am asking too. Are you well. She'll know what you mean.

choices.text: Write her a cheerful one: football, French eggs, nothing to worry her.
choices.text_after:
Two sides. The football behind the lines, the French eggs, the farm dog that follows the
company about. You make the sergeant into a comic turn at the Hippodrome. Reading it over by
the candle, you can't find yourself anywhere in it, and you post it anyway.

choices.text: Send her a field postcard. You don't know what to say.
choices.text_after:
I am quite well. Letter follows at first opportunity. You strike out the rest and sign it.
It's the card every man sends his mother, and you know it, and so will she.

ro_pit_lizzie_1.title: Lizzie
ro_pit_lizzie_1.text:
A letter comes up with the rations in a hand you don't know, small and upright, the way they
teach it at the board school. You turn it over three times before you open it.

Lizzie Milburn. She's in service at the manager's house at the top of the rows, and you used to
see her on her afternoon off, walking out along the waggonway towards the sea with her sister.
Twice you walked with them. Once, the last Sunday before you went, her sister went on ahead and
didn't look back.

"I hope you will not think me forward. I had your number off your Mary. The mistress says I am
not to have followers but she never said anything about writing. The master has been round the
rows again saying coal is war work and the lads should stop at home, and your father told him
where he could put it, in front of the whole row. Are you warm. Are they feeding you. Mary says
you will tell me nowt, so tell me something. Yours, Lizzie Milburn."

The paper smells of the manager's kitchen, blacklead and baking, and there's a smear of flour
on the back where she leaned on it to write.

choices.text: Tell her how it is, as near as the officer will pass.
choices.text_after:
You tell her it's like the coal face with the roof off: wet, dark at the wrong times, every man
listening. You tell her about the rats. The platoon officer reads every letter before it
goes, so you write it for him as well, and it comes out like a report to the deputy. At the
bottom, small, the way she did, you put that you think about the waggonway.

choices.text: Tell her it's grand: football, eggs, French beer like dishwater.
choices.text_after:
You make it a trip to Whitley Bay. Football behind the lines, the French beer like
dishwater, a farm dog that follows the company about. Two sides, and none of it's what you'd
tell a marra, and you feel better for writing it, and then you don't.

choices.text: Send a field postcard. You can't think what to put.
choices.text_after:
I am quite well. You strike out the rest. You hold it a minute before it goes in the bag, the
card every man sends his mother, and then you let it go.

ro_farm_rose_1.title: Rose
ro_farm_rose_1.text:
In with your mother's letter is a second one, folded small with no envelope, as if it was put
in at the last minute on the kitchen table. You know the hand from the hymn numbers at church.

Rose Huxtable. Her father has the mill at the bottom of the village, and she's been flour to the
elbows since she could walk. The last harvest before you went she brought the cider out to the
Long Field and stopped to talk, and came again the next day, and the next, and your father
pretended not to see.

"Your mother said I might put in a line. Father has had to take on a boy for the sacks since our
Jim went, and the boy is no good, so it is me on the hoist. I am stronger than you would think.
The wheel is going as I write this, I can feel it through the table. They read out the Roll of
Honour in church, the ones serving, and your name was on it, and I went hot and cold as if it was
the other sort. Write and tell me it isn't. Rose."

There's flour in the fold of the paper. It comes off on your fingers, soft as chalk dust and
smelling of the mill.

choices.text: Tell her straight how it is. The wet, the rats, the noise.
choices.text_after:
You tell her the trench is like a ditch in a wet February with the hedge grubbed out, and the
rats are the size of her father's cats, and the noise never stops long enough to be missed.
The platoon officer reads every letter before it goes, so it comes out like a parish
notice. At the end you put that you can hear the mill wheel if you think about it. You can.

choices.text: Tell her it's not so bad. French farms, French cider, nothing to fret on.
choices.text_after:
French farms, and how badly they plough. French cider, which is thin. A dog that follows the
company about. You make it sound like a long harvest with some noise in it. You read it over,
and it's a cheerful man's letter, a man you don't know, and you post it.

choices.text: Send a field postcard. You've no words for it.
choices.text_after:
I am quite well. You strike out the rest. She'll read it on the mill steps, the card every
man sends his mother, and turn it over to see if there's more.

ro_city_ivy_1.title: Ivy
ro_city_ivy_1.text:
A letter in a lilac envelope, which the post corporal holds up by one corner for the whole bay
to see. It smells, faintly, of the violet cachous she buys at the station kiosk.

Ivy Lambert. She's a telephonist at the exchange in the High Road and sings alto at St Mary's.
Last summer you took her on the tram to the Forest, twice, and once to the Hollow Ponds, where
you rowed her round the island and caught a crab and soaked her shoes, and she laughed till the
boatman came out of his hut to see.

"I hope you do not mind me writing, I had your number from your mother after church. At the
exchange we say Number please four hundred times a day in a voice like the Queen's, and my sister
says I have started saying it in my sleep. The Zeppelins came again. Everybody went out in the
street to look, and so did I, and I was ashamed after. Are you warm enough. Do they let you
sleep. Please write properly and not only that you are well. Your friend, Ivy Lambert."

choices.text: Write properly, the way she asked. Rats, mud, the noise.
choices.text_after:
You tell her the mud, and the rats, and that you sleep standing up and sitting down and
hardly ever lying. The platoon officer reads every letter before it goes and signs the
envelope, so it comes out like a memorandum to the chief clerk. At the end you put: Number
please. She'll laugh. You can hear her.

choices.text: Write her a cheerful one. Football, French bread, nothing to frighten her.
choices.text_after:
The football behind the lines. The French bread, as long as your arm. The sergeant, made into
a comic at the music hall. Two sides in your best office hand, and you're not in it anywhere.
You post it.

choices.text: Send a field postcard. Strike out what doesn't apply.
choices.text_after:
I am quite well. You strike out the rest, neatly, with a ruler made of your pay book. It's the
card every man sends his mother, and you know it, and so will she.

ro_mill_nellie_2.title: Nellie
ro_mill_nellie_2.text:
[if flag.ro_sw_truth]Nellie writes every Sunday now, after chapel, and you can tell from the blots which bits she wrote fast.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_cheer]Nellie's letter is shorter than the last. "I read the lists in the Evening News," it starts, "every name, every night. You need not write me about football. I would rather know."[/if][if flag.ro_sw_little]It's a while since Nellie wrote. This one is a single side. "I had your card. It is on the mantelpiece with our Fred's, the silk ones with the flowers. I don't know what I am to you. I would like to know."[/if]

"The shed is on short time for want of cotton, and half the girls have gone to the munitions,
where the money is. Two from our alley were wed on their lads' leave at Whitsun, by licence, all
done in a week, and everybody said it was daft, and everybody went. I am not asking you
anything. I am only telling you what other girls have done."

You read it in the YMCA hut, on a bench, with a mug of cocoa going cold, and the man next to you
is playing the piano with one finger, the same four notes of a hymn, over and over.

choices.text: Write and ask her to marry you, on your next leave.
choices.text_after:
You write it four times on the hut's paper, with the red triangle at the top, and tear up
three. The fourth goes in a green envelope, so the officer won't read it, and you sign the
line on the flap that says it holds nothing but private and family matters. Her answer comes
in nine days. One word and her name, and the ink's run where something fell on it.

choices.text: Ask her to wait for you, till it's over.
choices.text_after:
You put it carefully. That you'll not have her a wife for ten days and then a widow on a
buff form. That you'd like to come home to her, after, if she'll have you then. She writes back that
she will, and that she'll hold you to it, and you're to bring the ring yourself at Christmas
and not send one in a parcel like a pair of socks.

choices.text: Tell her not to wait. You can't promise her anything.
choices.text_after:
You write that she's to please herself, and not wait on a man who can't say where he'll be in
a month, or whether. You mean it kindly. In pencil it looks hard. She writes back once, short,
to say she understands, and she'll pray for you, and the letters stop.

choices.text: Send another field postcard. You'll write properly after this tour.
choices.text_after:
I am quite well. You strike out the rest. You mean to write properly after this tour, and
then after the next.

ro_pit_lizzie_2.title: Lizzie
ro_pit_lizzie_2.text:
[if flag.ro_sw_truth]Lizzie's letters come every week now, and they've a tram ticket in them for a bookmark, punched.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_cheer]Lizzie's letter is short. "Your Mary reads me the casualty lists out of the Journal," it starts. "I know what it's like. You needn't write me about football, hinny. I'd rather have the truth off you than off the paper."[/if][if flag.ro_sw_little]It's a long while since Lizzie wrote. One side. "I had your card. I don't know what I am to you. I'd like to know, that's all."[/if]

"I have left the manager's house. I am on the trams in Newcastle now, a conductress, with a
peaked cap and a leather bag of pennies, and the men on the Scotswood Road route are worse than
any mistress. Two lasses from the rows were wed at chapel on their lads' leave, by licence, in a
week. Everybody said it was daft and the whole row went. I am not asking you owt. I am only
telling you."

[if war.transferred]You read it at the head of the shaft, waiting for the shift, with the chalk drying white on your hands and the pump thudding below like a heart.[else]You read it in the YMCA hut with a mug of cocoa going cold, and somebody at the piano picking out a hymn with one finger.[/if]

choices.text: Write and ask her to marry you, on your next leave.
choices.text_after:
You write it four times and tear up three. The fourth goes in a green envelope, so no officer
reads it first, and you sign the flap to say it's private and family matters, and it is.
Her answer comes in nine days, on the back of a tram timetable. One word, and her name, and
three crosses, and then, squeezed in: You took your time.

choices.text: Ask her to wait for you, till it's over.
choices.text_after:
You put it carefully. That you'll not have her wed for ten days and widowed by a buff form.
That you'd like to come home to her, after. She writes back that she'll wait, and she'll hold
you to it, and you can bring the ring yourself at Christmas and not post it like a pit check.

choices.text: Tell her not to wait. You can't promise her anything.
choices.text_after:
You tell her to please herself, and not to wait on a man who can't say where he'll be in a
month. You mean it kindly. She writes once more, to say she understands, and that she'll look
in on your mother, and she does, every Sunday. The letters to you stop.

choices.text: Send another field postcard. You'll write properly after this.
choices.text_after: I am quite well. You strike out the rest. You'll write properly when you've something to say.

ro_farm_rose_2.title: Rose
ro_farm_rose_2.text:
[if flag.ro_sw_truth]Rose writes every week now, and there's always flour in the fold.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_cheer]Rose's letter is short. "Father takes the Western Times for the lists," it starts. "I read every name. You needn't write me about French cider. I would sooner know."[/if][if flag.ro_sw_little]It's a long time since Rose wrote. Half a side. "I had your card. I don't know what I am to you. I should like to know."[/if]

"The mill is grinding for the army now and Father has had the tribunal say the boy can stay.
Dolly Thorne from Brendon was married on her young man's leave, banns read while he was still
in France, and the ringers rang what bells they could, and everybody said she was a fool and
everybody went. I am not asking anything. I am only telling you what's done."

You read it in a barn behind the line, on the straw, by the light coming through the slats. The
barn smells of cows and wet oats, so like home you have to put the letter down.

choices.text: Write and ask her to marry you, on your next leave.
choices.text_after:
You write it four times and tear up three. The fourth goes in a green envelope, so no officer
reads it before she does, and you sign the flap: private and family matters. Her answer comes
in nine days, and it says Yes, you great fool, and that she'll speak to the vicar about the
banns on Sunday.

choices.text: Ask her to wait for you, till it's over.
choices.text_after:
You put it carefully. That you'll not have her married for ten days and then a widow. That
you'd like to come home to her, after, if she'll have you. She writes back that she will, and
she'll hold you to it, and you're to bring the ring yourself at Christmas and not send it by
the carrier.

choices.text: Tell her not to wait. You can't promise her anything.
choices.text_after:
You tell her to please herself, and not wait on a man who can't say where he'll be by the
spring. You mean it kindly. She writes once more, to say she understands, and she'll put
flowers by your mother's door on a Sunday, and the letters to you stop.

choices.text: Send another field postcard. You'll write properly after this.
choices.text_after: I am quite well. You strike out the rest. You'll write properly at rest, when there's time.

ro_city_ivy_2.title: Ivy
ro_city_ivy_2.text:
[if flag.ro_sw_truth]Ivy writes every week now, on the exchange's pink message slips when she runs out of paper.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_cheer]Ivy's letter is short. "Father reads the lists in the Daily Telegraph at breakfast," it starts, "and I read them after him. You needn't write me about football. I'd rather know."[/if][if flag.ro_sw_little]It's a while since Ivy wrote. One side. "I had your card. I don't know what I am to you. I should like to know."[/if]

"They have taken on twenty more girls at the exchange, the men are all going. Two of our girls
were married on their boys' leave, by licence, in the same week, and the supervisor said it was
most irregular and gave them each a cruet. I am not asking you anything. I am only saying what
other girls have done."

You read it in the YMCA hut, on a bench, under a gas lamp that hisses, with a mug of cocoa going
cold beside you.

choices.text: Write and ask her to marry you, on your next leave.
choices.text_after:
You write it four times on the hut's paper and tear up three. The fourth goes in a green
envelope, so the officer won't read it first, and you sign the flap: private and family
matters. Her answer comes in nine days. Yes, and that you're to tell your mother yourself,
and that she's already chosen the hymn.

choices.text: Ask her to wait for you, till it's over.
choices.text_after:
You put it carefully, the way you'd draft a letter to a client. That you'll not have her a
widow at twenty. That you'd like to come home to her, after. She writes back that she will,
and she'll hold you to it, and you're to bring the ring yourself at Christmas.

choices.text: Tell her not to wait. You can't promise her anything.
choices.text_after:
You tell her to please herself, and not wait on a man who can't say where he'll be in a
month. You mean it kindly. She writes once more, to say she understands, and she'll sing for
you on Sundays, and the letters stop.

choices.text: Send another field postcard. You'll write properly after this.
choices.text_after: I am quite well. You strike out the rest. You'll write properly when there's something to say.

ro_city_ivy_florence.title: Ivy
ro_city_ivy_florence.text:
A lilac envelope. You'd half forgotten the colour.

"Your mother tells me there is a young lady at your office who writes to you, a Miss Holland,
who has your desk. I am glad you have somebody to write to who knows your work. I think perhaps
that is more use to you out there than a girl who says Number please. I am not cross. I was, on
the Sunday, but the choir had the Nunc Dimittis and you cannot stay cross through that. I shan't
write again unless you want me to. Ivy."

The violet cachous again, faint, on the paper. You fold it along its creases and it goes in your
pocket with Florence's, and the two of them sit there against your chest all through stand-to.

choices.text: Write and tell her the truth about Florence. She's owed that.
choices.text_after:
It takes the evening. You tell her that it's true, and that you didn't mean it to be, and
that she's worth more than a letter like this one. She writes back a postcard of the Hollow
Ponds, with the boats, and on the back: Mind you don't catch a crab. Ivy.

choices.text: Let it be. Don't answer.
choices.text_after:
You don't answer. It sits in your pocket a week and then goes in the brazier, and the lilac
curls up and goes black, and the smell of violets for a second over the coke.

ro_17_letter_mill.title: A letter from home
ro_17_letter_mill.text:
[if flag.ro_sw_married]A letter from your wife. You still have to say it to yourself, your wife, and the word sits oddly, like a new cap. [if start == mill]Nellie[/if][if start == pit]Lizzie[/if][if start == farm]Rose[/if][if start == city]Ivy[/if] writes on Sundays, the way she always did, but she signs it different now, and puts a line under it.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married][if start == mill]Nellie's[/if][if start == pit]Lizzie's[/if][if start == farm]Rose's[/if][if start == city]Ivy's[/if] letter has a ring drawn at the bottom of it in pencil, round and round, till the paper's nearly through.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_little && !flag.ro_sw_married && !flag.ro_sw_after][if start == mill]Nellie's[/if][if start == pit]Lizzie's[/if][if start == farm]Rose's[/if][if start == city]Ivy's[/if] letter is written straight across the page, as if she ruled the lines first, and you know before you've read a word of it.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_married && war.month <= 8]"I have been to the doctor and he says the autumn.
