Your mother is knitting as if it was piecework.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && war.month >= 9]"She came on a Tuesday, a girl, seven pounds, with your mother's chin and a voice on her you could hear in the next street. Your mother is knitting as if it was piecework.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && start == mill] I am still at the looms but the overlooker has put me by the door, for the air.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && start == pit] I have left the trams and come home to your mother's. She would not hear of anything else.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && start == farm] Father says I am not to go up the hoist and I go up when he is at market.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && start == city] I have given in my notice at the exchange. They don't keep married girls in my way, and the supervisor gave me a cruet, the same as the others.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married] The separation allowance comes on a Monday at the post office, and your allotment with it, and I put by what I can. I keep thinking of you not knowing what is happening to me, and me not knowing what is happening to you, and the letters going backwards and forwards in between, crossing."[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married]"I have not changed my mind and I shan't. But they are being married every leave now, by licence, and I stand at the back of church and cry like a fool at every one of them, and I am tired of being the one at the back. If you asked me again I would say the other thing this time. I am only saying."[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_little && !flag.ro_sw_married && !flag.ro_sw_after]"I waited to hear from you properly, and I have had cards. I don't blame you. I expect you can't, out there, and it's not for me to know why. But I have to tell you I have been walking out with[if start == mill] Jack Kenyon from the dye works, who came home from Gallipoli with his arm stiff and wears the silver badge so nobody gives him a white feather[/if][if start == pit] Ned Forster, the deputy's lad, that the pit would not let go for a soldier[/if][if start == farm] Harry Moule, the carrier's son, that the doctors turned down for his chest[/if][if start == city] a Mr Pratt, a telephone engineer at the exchange, who was turned down three times for his eyes and tried a fourth[/if], and he has asked me, and I have said yes. He is kind, and he is here. I hope you won't think too hard of me. I shall pray for you every night. I always have."[/if]

[if flag.ro_fr_spoke && war.transferred]In with it, sent on by somebody in the battalion, there's a picture postcard of the church at Ternecourt, with its crooked weathercock. On the back, in pencil: Un bon souvenir de Ternecourt. Under it, in careful English: For the soldier who said erfs. We are all well. Lucien is home on permission and eats everything. Marthe. You read it twice, and put it in your pay book, and feel like a thief.[/if]

choices.text: Write back the truth. You're frightened, for her and for you.
choices.text_after:
You write it in a green envelope, so it goes past the officer, and you tell her: that you're
frightened, and that you'd not say it to anyone else living. Her answer is two lines. So am
I. Come home. You keep it in your pay book, where the last letter used to be.

choices.text: Write about the baby, and nothing else. Pages of it.
choices.text_after:
Four sides. Names, and which you like, and why. What you'll do with a girl, and with a boy,
and the cradle your father can make out of the old chest. You don't mention the war at all,
and for a whole evening there isn't one.

choices.text: Ask her again, properly. Christmas leave, by licence.
choices.text_after:
You write it in a green envelope, and you don't tear any up this time. Her answer comes in a
week: Yes, and about time, and she's put her name down for the licence, and you're to get your
hair cut.

choices.text: Ask her to hold on till it's over. You meant after.
choices.text_after:
You tell her you meant after, and you still do, and that you'd not have her stood at the back
of church in black. She writes that she'll hold on, then. The ring at the bottom of the next
letter is drawn smaller.

choices.text: Write back and wish her happy. Mean it.
choices.text_after:
It's the best letter you've written her, and the last. You tell her he sounds a decent man,
and that she's to be happy, and that the cards were your fault and nobody else's. You don't
put a field postcard in with it.

choices.text: Don't answer. There's nothing to say.
choices.text_after:
You read it once more, and fold it, and put it in the brazier at stand-down. The paper goes
brown at the edges first, and then all at once.

choices.text: Put it in your pay book. Not tonight.
choices.text_after:
You fold it along its creases and put it in your pay book with the others. You read it again
at stand-to, and again in the dark with your thumb over the words you know, and you don't
write anything back. Not tonight.

ro_17_letter_air.title: A letter from home
ro_17_letter_air.text:
[if flag.ro_sw_married]A letter from your wife. You still have to say it to yourself, your wife, and the word sits oddly, like a new cap. [if start == mill]Nellie[/if][if start == pit]Lizzie[/if][if start == farm]Rose[/if][if start == city]Ivy[/if] writes on Sundays, the way she always did, but she signs it different now, and puts a line under it.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married][if start == mill]Nellie's[/if][if start == pit]Lizzie's[/if][if start == farm]Rose's[/if][if start == city]Ivy's[/if] letter has a ring drawn at the bottom of it in pencil, round and round, till the paper's nearly through.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_little && !flag.ro_sw_married && !flag.ro_sw_after][if start == mill]Nellie's[/if][if start == pit]Lizzie's[/if][if start == farm]Rose's[/if][if start == city]Ivy's[/if] letter is written straight across the page, as if she ruled the lines first, and you know before you've read a word of it.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_married && war.month <= 8]"I have been to the doctor and he says the autumn. Your mother is knitting as if it was piecework.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && war.month >= 9]"She came on a Tuesday, a girl, seven pounds, with your mother's chin and a voice on her you could hear in the next street. Your mother is knitting as if it was piecework.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && start == mill] I am still at the looms but the overlooker has put me by the door, for the air.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && start == pit] I have left the trams and come home to your mother's. She would not hear of anything else.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && start == farm] Father says I am not to go up the hoist and I go up when he is at market.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && start == city] I have given in my notice at the exchange. They don't keep married girls in my way, and the supervisor gave me a cruet, the same as the others.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married] The separation allowance comes on a Monday at the post office, and your allotment with it, and I put by what I can. I keep thinking of you not knowing what is happening to me, and me not knowing what is happening to you, and the letters going backwards and forwards in between, crossing."[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married]"I have not changed my mind and I shan't. But they are being married every leave now, by licence, and I stand at the back of church and cry like a fool at every one of them, and I am tired of being the one at the back. If you asked me again I would say the other thing this time. I am only saying."[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_little && !flag.ro_sw_married && !flag.ro_sw_after]"I waited to hear from you properly, and I have had cards. I don't blame you. I expect you can't, out there, and it's not for me to know why. But I have to tell you I have been walking out with[if start == mill] Jack Kenyon from the dye works, who came home from Gallipoli with his arm stiff and wears the silver badge so nobody gives him a white feather[/if][if start == pit] Ned Forster, the deputy's lad, that the pit would not let go for a soldier[/if][if start == farm] Harry Moule, the carrier's son, that the doctors turned down for his chest[/if][if start == city] a Mr Pratt, a telephone engineer at the exchange, who was turned down three times for his eyes and tried a fourth[/if], and he has asked me, and I have said yes. He is kind, and he is here. I hope you won't think too hard of me. I shall pray for you every night. I always have."[/if]

[if flag.ro_fr_spoke && war.transferred]In with it, sent on by somebody in the battalion, there's a picture postcard of the church at Ternecourt, with its crooked weathercock. On the back, in pencil: Un bon souvenir de Ternecourt. Under it, in careful English: For the soldier who said erfs. We are all well. Lucien is home on permission and eats everything. Marthe. ro_18_letter_mill.title: A letter from home
ro_18_letter_mill.text:
[if flag.ro_sw_married]Your wife's letter is three weeks old and has been to two other units first; the envelope is covered in crossings-out, like a ledger.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married][if start == mill]Nellie's[/if][if start == pit]Lizzie's[/if][if start == farm]Rose's[/if][if start == city]Ivy's[/if] letter has been three weeks finding you. The envelope's soft from somebody's pocket.[/if]

"The papers have maps in them this spring, with arrows, and the arrows are going the wrong way.[if start == mill] Everybody in the shed reads them at dinner time and nobody says anything.[/if][if start == pit] Your mother reads them out at the Store and then goes home and sits.[/if][if start == farm] Father spreads them on the kitchen table and puts his finger on the places.[/if][if start == city] At the exchange the calls never stop, and every one is somebody asking for news.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_wed16] The baby has two teeth and bites with them. She knows your photograph. I hold it up and say Dad, and she shouts at it.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_wed17] I think I may be expecting. I am not to say till I'm sure, your mother says, so I haven't said.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married] Write if it is only a card. I don't mind a card now. I mind nothing."[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married && !flag.ro_sw_cheer] I don't care what the papers say. I have read every one of your letters four times and I know you from them, and you are coming home. I've decided."[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_cheer]"[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_cheer]Then a gap, and the ink's different, as if she put it down and came back to it days after. "Your letters are all football and French eggs, and they have been for three years, and I don't know you from them any more. I have met somebody who tells me things.[if start == mill] He was a weaver at Cobden Street till he lost his hand at Thiepval, and he is learning the books at the Co-op.[/if][if start == pit] He is a putter from the Duke pit, sent home with his lungs.[/if][if start == farm] He came back from Salonika with the fever and is lodging at the mill to help Father.[/if][if start == city] He was at the exchange before the war and came home from Mesopotamia with a limp.[/if] I am going to marry him. I wanted you to hear it from me. I am sorry. I am. I hope you come home safe and find somebody who reads you better than I could."[/if]

choices.text: Tell her the truth about this spring. She asked.
choices.text_after:
You tell her some of it, in a green envelope: the running, the bridges, the days without
sleep. Then you tell her it's over now, the worst, which you think is true. You end with the
baby, or the hope of one, because you can't end with the bridges.

choices.text: Tell her it's quiet where you are. She has enough.
choices.text_after:
It's quiet where you are, you write. Lovely weather. You've seen a hare. All of it's true
this week and none of it was last.

choices.text: Write and tell her: after, as soon as they let you go.
choices.text_after:
Two sides, and on both of them the same thing in different words. As soon as they let you go.
She writes back one line: I've heard. And a ring at the bottom, drawn big.

choices.text: Write her the truth about the spring, all of it.
choices.text_after:
You tell her: the running, and the bridges, and the men left behind. She doesn't answer for a
fortnight, and then she does, and it's four sides, and she's kept all of it, and gives it back
to you in her own words, so you can carry it easier.

choices.text: Write and wish her happy. She's owed that.
choices.text_after:
You write it straight, the first straight letter you've sent her. That she's right, and you
lied to her about the football to spare her, and to spare yourself. That he sounds a good man.
That you'll stand her a drink at the wedding, if you're home, and mean it.

choices.text: Put it in the brazier. You've nothing to say back.
choices.text_after:
It burns slowly, being folded. You poke it open with your bayonet so it'll catch, and stand
there till it has.

choices.text: Keep it till you can think what to say.
choices.text_after:
It goes in your breast pocket, and stays there through the next tour, getting softer. You
take it out at every halt and don't open it, and put it back.

ro_18_letter_tank.title: A letter from home
ro_18_letter_tank.text:
[if flag.ro_sw_married]Your wife's letter is three weeks old and has been to two other units first; the envelope is covered in crossings-out, like a ledger.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married][if start == mill]Nellie's[/if][if start == pit]Lizzie's[/if][if start == farm]Rose's[/if][if start == city]Ivy's[/if] letter has been three weeks finding you. The envelope's soft from somebody's pocket.[/if]

"The papers have maps in them this spring, with arrows, and the arrows are going the wrong way.[if start == mill] Everybody in the shed reads them at dinner time and nobody says anything.[/if][if start == pit] Your mother reads them out at the Store and then goes home and sits.[/if][if start == farm] Father spreads them on the kitchen table and puts his finger on the places.[/if][if start == city] At the exchange the calls never stop, and every one is somebody asking for news.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_wed16] The baby has two teeth and bites with them. She knows your photograph. I hold it up and say Dad, and she shouts at it.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_wed17] I think I may be expecting. I am not to say till I'm sure, your mother says, so I haven't said.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married] Write if it is only a card. I don't mind a card now. I mind nothing."[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married && !flag.ro_sw_cheer] I don't care what the papers say. I have read every one of your letters four times and I know you from them, and you are coming home. I've decided."[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_cheer]"[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_after && !flag.ro_sw_married && flag.ro_sw_cheer]Then a gap, and the ink's different, as if she put it down and came back to it days after. "Your letters are all football and French eggs, and they have been for three years, and I don't know you from them any more. I have met somebody who tells me things.[if start == mill] He was a weaver at Cobden Street till he lost his hand at Thiepval, and he is learning the books at the Co-op.[/if][if start == pit] He is a putter from the Duke pit, sent home with his lungs.[/if][if start == farm] He came back from Salonika with the fever and is lodging at the mill to help Father.[/if][if start == city] He was at the exchange before the war and came home from Mesopotamia with a limp.[/if] I am going to marry him. I wanted you to hear it from me. I am sorry. I am. I hope you come home safe and find somebody who reads you better than I could."[/if]

choices.text: Tell her the truth about this spring. She asked.
choices.text_after:
You tell her some of it, in a green envelope: the running, the bridges, the days without
sleep. Then you tell her it's over now, the worst, which you think is true. You end with the
baby, or the hope of one, because you can't end with the bridges.

choices.text: Tell her it's quiet where you are. She has enough.
choices.text_after:
It's quiet where you are, you write. Lovely weather. You've seen a hare. All of it's true
this week and none of it was last.

choices.text: Write and tell her: after, as soon as they let you go.
choices.text_after:
Two sides, and on both of them the same thing in different words. As soon as they let you go.
She writes back one line: I've heard. And a ring at the bottom, drawn big.

choices.text: Write her the truth about the spring, all of it.
choices.text_after:
You tell her: the running, and the bridges, and the men left behind. She doesn't answer for a
fortnight, and then she does, and it's four sides, and she's kept all of it, and gives it back
to you in her own words, so you can carry it easier.

choices.text: Write and wish her happy. She's owed that.
choices.text_after:
You write it straight, the first straight letter you've sent her. That she's right, and you
lied to her about the football to spare her, and to spare yourself. That he sounds a good man.
That you'll stand her a drink at the wedding, if you're home, and mean it.

choices.text: Put it in the brazier. You've nothing to say back.
choices.text_after:
It burns slowly, being folded. You poke it open with your bayonet so it'll catch, and stand
there till it has.

choices.text: Keep it till you can think what to say.
choices.text_after:
It goes in your breast pocket, and stays there through the next tour, getting softer. You
take it out at every halt and don't open it, and put it back.

ro_fr_16_mill.title: Ternecourt
ro_fr_16_mill.text:
The battalion comes down south in the thaw and goes into billets at Ternecourt, a long street
of brick and whitewash behind Albert, with a pond at one end, a mairie no bigger than a cottage, and a church whose
weathercock has been shot crooked. You're in a barn with forty others and a hen who lays in somebody's helmet.

The estaminet is the front room of the house by the pond: Estaminet du Bon Coin over the door in
faded paint, and chalked on the shutter, Oeufs et frites, Vin blanc, Bière. A stove going,
oilcloth on the tables, a crucifix, a picture of the President cut out of a paper. The mother does the frying in the back
in a pan the size of a cartwheel, and the smell of hot fat and onions comes through the door and
down the street and fetches men out of the barns like a dinner bell.

The daughter carries the plates. She's twenty, perhaps, with her sleeves pushed up and a burn on
one wrist from the pan, and she has the English the Tommies have taught her, some of it not fit,
which she doesn't know. "Bonsoir, Tommy," she says to every man through the door; you're all
Tommy to her. "Egg-chip." She puts it down in front of you. "Two egg. La bière, no good, the
English say. Drink the wine."

[if flag.ro_sw_first && !flag.ro_sw_ended]There's a letter from home in your breast pocket, half answered.[/if]

choices.text: Try your French on her. Merci boko, mamzelle, and whatever else you've got.
choices.text_after:
You've got about six words and you use them all on the eggs. "Tray bon, mamzelle.
Merci boko." She laughs, not quite at you, and puts you right: "Très bon. Merci beaucoup."
Then oeufs, not erfs, with her lips pushed out, and she makes you say it till you do. Her name's
Marthe. The lads have been calling her Martha for a month and she lets them. When you go she
says "Bonne nuit, Tommy," and then, carefully, in English, "Mind the step," and you go out
and miss it.

choices.text: Eat up, pay, and get back to the barn.
choices.text_after:
You eat it fast, with the yolk on your chin, and leave your coppers on the oilcloth. Behind
you the lads are trying their French on her all at once, "Parley-voo, mamzelle?" and worse,
and she's laughing at them, and the
stove's roaring, and you go out into the dark street and your blanket.

ro_fr_16b_mill.title: Marthe
ro_fr_16b_mill.text:
Out at rest at Ternecourt again, what's left of the battalion, after the summer. The street's
the same. The weathercock's the same. The old woman at the pump says "Bonjour, monsieur" to
every one of you, as she did in the spring. The barn has new straw, and nobody says who slept
where last time.

Marthe knows you. She puts the plate down and stands there with the cloth over her arm and says,
"Tiens! Monsieur Erfs," and you both laugh, and it's the first time you have since July.

She has a letter from her brother, Lucien, a poilu since the first week. He's at Verdun. It's six weeks old and the French
censor has been at it with scissors, so it's more holes than letter, and she reads you what's
left in French, slowly, and you understand one word in four. Il tient. He holds. She says it
twice, so you'll know it.

Her father is too old for the army and the farm behind the house wants the beet lifting before
the frost, and there's nobody to lift it; les Boches have seen to that. "C'est la guerre," she
says, as they all do, with the shoulders. On Sunday, she says, if the English have nothing for
you to do. She doesn't look at you when she says it.

[if flag.ro_sw_wed16]In your pocket is the letter that says yes. You're to be married at Christmas. You haven't said.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_after]In your pocket is the letter about the ring. You haven't said.[/if]

choices.text: Go on Sunday. Lift the beet, and walk back with her by the stream.
choices.text_after:
Beet all morning, in clay that holds on to your boots like a hand, the old man working beside
you without a word. After, she walks you back along the stream at the bottom of the village,
and shows you where Lucien used to catch eels, and talks, in French, and you say "Compree" where
it seems to be wanted and don't follow half of it, and it doesn't matter. She doesn't take
your arm. At the barn she says "À dimanche," and then, to be sure of you, in English, "Next
Sunday," the way you'd say the day the post goes.

choices.text: Lift the beet with her father, and leave it at that.
choices.text_after:
Beet all day with the old man, who says nothing at all, and at the end of it gives you a
glass of something clear out of an unlabelled bottle that takes the skin off your throat.
"Eau-de-vie," he says, his one word of the day, and shakes your hand. Marthe gives you a
dozen eggs in your cap to take back to the barn. "Merci bien," she says, and it's enough.

you without a word. After, she walks you back along the stream at the bottom of the village,
and shows you where Lucien used to catch eels, and talks, in French, and you say "Compree" where
it seems to be wanted and don't follow half of it, and it doesn't matter. She doesn't take
your arm. At the barn she says "À dimanche," and then, to be sure of you, in English, "Next
Sunday," the way you'd say the day the post goes.

choices.text: Lift the beet with her father, and leave it at that.
choices.text_after:
Beet all day with the old man, who says nothing at all, and at the end of it gives you a
glass of something clear out of an unlabelled bottle that takes the skin off your throat.
"Eau-de-vie," he says, his one word of the day, and shakes your hand. Marthe gives you a
dozen eggs in your cap to take back to the barn. "Merci bien," she says, and it's enough.

ro_fr_17_mill.title: Moving north
ro_fr_17_mill.text:
The battalion has come back to Ternecourt for the worst of the winter, and now there are orders:
north on Thursday. Nobody says where; everybody says Arras. It's snowing, the soft wet kind,
and the estaminet windows are steamed so thick you can't see in, only the shapes of men and the
red of the stove.

Marthe has your plate ready before you've sat down. "Bière, napoo," she says, which she had from
the Tommies, and brings the wine. When she comes back for the plate she has a bit of
paper folded small, and puts it under the salt. Delattre, Estaminet du Bon Coin, Ternecourt,
Somme, in a hand like a schoolmistress's.

[if flag.ro_fr_walked]Five Sundays you walked by the stream. Once, in the rain, under the willows, she took your arm, and then let go of it when her mother came to the door.[/if][if flag.ro_fr_friend]You lifted the beet, and the potatoes after, and the old man gave you the clear stuff every time, and called you mon gendre, which the lads say means son-in-law, and laughed.[/if][if flag.ro_sw_married] She knows about your wife. She asked to see the photograph, and held it near the lamp, and gave it back and said "Elle est jolie," which she is.[/if]

"Vous m'écrirez," she says, and then in English, "You write." It isn't quite a question.

You write the first one on the march, at a halt, on your knee, in English, with three words of
French at the end from the phrase book in the YMCA hut. The officer who censors it raises an
eyebrow at the French and passes it. Her answer finds you in a fortnight: two sides in French.

rest: all well, more snow, the hens not laying. Then one line in English, her own. The eggs
are not so good with no you.

choices.text: Say goodbye properly, and leave it there.
choices.text_after:
You shake her hand, and her father's, and her mother's, who kisses you on both cheeks and
says "Bonne chance, mon petit," and smells of onions and lavender. Marthe stands in the door with the light behind her while the
company forms up in the snow. You don't look back till the bend in the road, and when you do
the door's shut.

ro_fr_18_mill.title: The road west
ro_fr_18_mill.text:
The road west is full: guns going back, lorries, walking wounded, a battalion of somebody else's
going the wrong way, and in among them the farm carts. The villages behind the old Somme line
are emptying ahead of the Germans, the way they emptied in 1914, and the people are going the
way they came, with everything they can lift.

The column halts. Beside the cart in front, piled with mattresses and a crate of hens, a girl in
clogs is walking with a bundle and a basket, and she has a burn on her wrist, and you know the
wrist before the face.

It's the Delattres. The old man at the horse's head. Madame up on the cart with the clock from
the estaminet in her lap, holding it like a baby. Marthe sees you, and stops in the road so the
cart behind has to pull up.

"Ternecourt," she says. "C'est fini. Les Boches arrivent." You don't need French for that, with
the guns behind you going on and on. "The English will hold?"
[if flag.ro_fr_writes]Her last letter came a fortnight ago, about the hens.[/if]

choices.text: Give her your address at home, in case.
choices.text_after:
You write it on the back of a field postcard against the cart wheel, with a stub of pencil,
your mother's street and the town. "Angleterre," she says, reading it, as if it were the moon,
and puts it inside her coat. The column moves. The
last you see is the clock on the cart, swaying, and her hand up.

choices.text: Give them your bread, and see them over the bridge.
choices.text_after:
You put your shoulder to the tailboard with two others, and the cart goes over the bridge
with the hens complaining, and you give the old man your bread and half your bully. Marthe
says "Tenez bon," and sees you haven't got it, and says it in English, "You hold," and
goes.

ro_fr_18b_mill.title: Ternecourt again
ro_fr_18b_mill.text:
The advance goes back over the ground, and one morning the road the battalion's marching on runs
into Ternecourt. You'd not have known it but for the pond. The church has no tower. The barn
you slept in is a heap of brick with a beam standing up out of it like a finger.

The estaminet has three walls and no roof, and Estaminet du Bon Coin still over the door. There's
a man up on the rafters, nailing a tarpaulin, one-handed, a poilu with his left sleeve pinned up; and below him, handing up the
nails, is Marthe.

[if flag.ro_fr_cart]They went as far as Amiens on the cart, she says, and came back on foot with a pass from the mairie, the day after the English came through.[else]They went west in March, she says, and came back on foot with a pass from the mairie, the day after the English came through.[/if] Lucien is in hospital at Lyon with his lungs, but alive. The man on the roof is Gaston, from the next farm, who was with Lucien at Verdun and came home without his hand. He looks down at you once, and goes on nailing.

You've ten minutes while the company falls out. She brings you a cup of something hot that might
be coffee, and stands with her arms folded, and asks you straight, the way she says everything
in English, because she hasn't the words to go round. "Après la guerre. After. You come back? Or you do not?"

choices.text: Tell her you'll come back for her, after.
choices.text_after:
You tell her, and get the French right for once: après la guerre. She nods, once, as if you'd told her the price of something, and then she turns
round and goes into the roofless room and stands there with her back to you, and Gaston on
the rafters stops nailing. The whistle goes. When you look back from the road she's in the
doorway with her hand flat on the door frame, the way your mother stands.

choices.text: Tell her to marry Gaston. He's here, and he'll stay.
choices.text_after:
You say it badly, in English, and she understands every word. She looks up at the roof, and
back at you, and says "Oui. Il reste. He stays," and takes the cup out of your hands though you've not
finished it. Gaston climbs down to shake your hand, left-handed. "Bonne chance, Tommy," he says, and you
go back to the road.

w_servant.title: A servant
w_servant.text:
[if start == mill]The platoon officer is Mr Ainsworth, the master's younger son. You've known his face since you were a half-timer. On a Friday he'd come through the weaving shed behind his father in a straw boater, with his fingers in his ears against the looms, and the weavers would mee-maw about him over the frames. He's twenty-two now. He still can't abide a loud noise, and he hides it better than you'd think.

He stops you in the support line, by the sump where the water seeps in brown. He wants a servant, he says, and he wants a man from the shed. "Weavers are quick with their hands. And they don't talk. My father always says so." He goes pink, as if he's said something about wages.[/if][if start == pit]The platoon officer is Mr Straker, the manager's son, from the house at the top of the rows. He did his year at the face before he went to the college in Newcastle, the way the managers' sons do, in pit clothes that were too clean, with the deputy at his elbow, and he was a month on your father's shift. You showed him how to hold a pick so it didn't jar his wrists.[if war.mate2] Jim Bell showed him the union rule book, page by page, at bait time, till the deputy moved Bell to another flat.[/if]

He finds you on the firestep at stand-down, with the mist coming off the wire and the smell of the cookers frying. He remembers the pick. "You'll keep your head down, and you'll keep a dugout dry," he says. "A pitman would." He wants a servant.[/if][if start == city]The platoon officer is Mr Pryor, whose uncle sits on the board of the Gresham and Lombard. He spent a summer in the Fire department two desks from yours, learning the business before he went up to Oxford, and he never learned it. You did his totals for him in the afternoons, and on Fridays he bought you a bath bun at the ABC in Cornhill and ate two himself.

He finds you in the bay at stand-down, with the tea coming round in a dixie that tastes of the petrol can it came up in. He wants a servant. "You've a good hand," he says. "And you always knew where everything was. I never did." He asks it the way he used to ask for the totals, as if you could say no.[/if]

Somebody to keep his kit and fetch his water, cook his bit of supper, carry his messages, wake him for stand-to. A soldier-servant: a batman. You'd be let off most fatigues and duties. You'd sleep near the officers' dugout, out of the wet, and eat what comes back from their table, and he'd give you threepence a day on top of your shilling. In the line you'd be with him always. When the company goes over, you go where he goes, and an officer goes in front.

And a servant stays a private. Nobody puts up a stripe on his officer's batman.

choices.text: Say yes, sir. (Excused most fatigues and duties, better rest, a few pence from him; you go where he goes in an attack; a servant stays a private.)
choices.text_after: [if start == mill]You learn him in a week: two sugars, a collar stud that's always lost, his mother's photograph up on the shelf in every dugout before anything else. At night he talks to you about the mill as if you both still worked there, the new looms his father won't buy, the girls they've took on in the card room.[if war.mate2] Duckworth bows to you in the trench and calls you his lordship's man, and pinches your sugar.[/if][/if][if start == pit]His valise smells of camphor and his mother's lavender bags. You dry his socks on a string over the brazier and black his boots with spit, and in the evenings he asks you about seams and props as if the pit was still there under the dugout floor.[if war.mate2] Bell says you're the manager's man now, and spits in the brazier, and helps you carry the valise up the trench anyway.[/if][/if][if start == city]His kit is every item on the outfitter's list, some of them twice. You keep his mess book the way you kept the Fire ledgers, in ink, ruled off on Saturdays, and he signs it without reading it, the way he used to sign them.[if war.mate1] Webb writes in his notebook that you've gone into service.[/if][/if]

choices.text: Say no, sir. You'd sooner stop with the section.
choices.text_after: [if start == mill]"Quite right," he says, the way his father says it at the mill gate to a man who's asked for a rise. He takes a lad from the card room instead, who was a footman once at a big house in Southport and knows what a fish knife's for.[if war.mate1] Shaw says you're soft in the head. Later, on sentry, he says he's glad.[/if][/if][if start == pit]Mr Straker goes red to the ears. "Of course," he says. "Quite right." He takes a groom from Alnwick who's never been down a pit and keeps boots like glass.[if war.mate2] Bell shakes your hand in front of the whole bay.[/if][/if][if start == city]Mr Pryor says of course, he quite understands, and goes off along the duckboards whistling something from a show, out of tune. He takes a man from the transport lines. Some evenings you see him writing his own letters by a candle in a tin, slowly, and crossing out.[/if]

w_servant_next.title: The new officer
w_servant_next.text:
[if start == mill]Since Loos the platoon's had Mr Kershaw. He was a colour sergeant in the regulars twenty years, India and South Africa, and they gave him a commission after the first winter because there was nobody else left to give it to. He's from Bolton. His mother was a weaver, and he says so in the officers' mess, on purpose, to watch their faces. He has a voice you could hear over a shed of four hundred looms, and he smells of carbolic and Nosegay twist.

He knows you were Mr Ainsworth's man. "I've blacked my own boots since eighteen ninety-four," he says. "I'm not stopping now. But I want a man who knows where the tea is, and I'm told you do." He doesn't say he's sorry about Mr Ainsworth. He looks at you a bit longer than he needs to.[/if][if start == pit]Since Loos the platoon's had Mr Hindmarsh, a schoolmaster from Morpeth who taught Standard Four in a pit village up the coast. He knows what a marra is, and a deputy, and a putter, and he asks the men the names of their bairns and writes them down in a little book. He smells of chalk and pipe tobacco, and his spectacles are held on with a bit of string round the back of his head.

He knows you were Mr Straker's man. He asks you the way he'd ask a big lad to stop behind after school and see to the stove. "You needn't," he says. "Mind, I'd be glad of you."[/if][if start == farm]Since Loos the platoon's had Mr Rudd, from Birmingham, who came up with the draft in a new tunic with the shop creases still in it. He's got Mr Venn's dugout, and Mr Venn's candle-box for a table, and the smell of Mr Venn's pipe still in the blanket over the door, and he doesn't know what to do with any of it. He sits on the end of the bunk as if he's waiting to be asked in.

The sergeant has told him you were Mr Venn's man. He asks you himself, standing up too quick and hitting his head on the roof: "Only if you'd want to. I don't know how it's done."[/if][if start == city]Since Loos the platoon's had Mr Carew, who is nineteen and came out from a school in Surrey with a cadet corps, a pocket Horace, and a new revolver he's never fired at anything but a tin. His mother writes to him every day, and so do two aunts. He says "I say" about everything, the gas, the rats, the cold, in the same voice.

He knows you were Mr Pryor's man. He asks you politely, the way he'd ask his housemaster's leave, and he goes pink, the way Mr Pryor used to.[/if]

You know the work now, and you know how it can end: you've packed one officer's valise already, and sent it home. Back with the section you'd do your share of the fatigues with the men from home, and stand where they stand, and go over beside them.

choices.text: Say yes, sir. (Excused most fatigues and duties, better rest, a few pence from him; you go where he goes in an attack; a servant stays a private.)
choices.text_after: [if start == mill]He's no trouble. He shaves in cold water and eats what the men eat, and talks to you about the Wanderers and his wife's mother, and never once about Mr Ainsworth. The first night he hands you his boots, and then takes them back, and blacks them himself on the firestep while you hold the candle.[/if][if start == pit]He's as untidy as a lad. You find his spectacles for him twice a day and his pipe three times, and in the evenings he reads to you out of a little book of poems, the way he read to Standard Four, and stops when the shelling starts, and goes on from the same line when it stops.[/if][if start == farm]You show him how Mr Venn had his tea, and then you learn how he has his, which is stewed black, three sugars, in a pint mug. He writes to his mother most nights.[if war.mate1] Cottle calls him the brass button behind his back.[/if][/if][if start == city]His kit's all new, and he's frightened of the lot of it. You sew his name tapes in and take the school buttons off his greatcoat, and at night he asks you what Loos was like, and you tell him some of it.[/if]

choices.text: Say no, sir. Go back to the section and the men from home.
choices.text_after: [if start == mill]Mr Kershaw nods once, the way a colour sergeant nods at a rifle that'll do. You go back to the section and straight into a wiring party, and your first night is the old firestep, wet to the knees.[if war.mate1] Shaw makes room for you on the step and gives you half his bread without a word.[/if][/if][if start == pit]Mr Hindmarsh says he'd have done the same, and writes something in his little book. You carry your kit back to the section's dugout on your shoulder.[if war.mate1] Tommy Robson shifts up on the floor to make room.[/if][/if][if start == farm]"No," Mr Rudd says. "Of course." He stands there, and you watch him decide not to ask the sergeant for anybody else.[if war.mate2] Pearce has kept your old place on the firestep, and there's a rabbit in a sandbag under it.[/if][/if][if start == city]"Oh," Mr Carew says. "Right-oh." He colours up, and goes off to ask the sergeant. You go back to the section, and the fatigues, and the bay you stood in before.[if war.mate2] Fenton's waiting with a mug of tea and the football results out of a week-old paper.[/if][/if]

x_officer_killed.title: Your officer
x_officer_killed.text:
[if war.officer_killed == 1][if start == farm]The word gets to you about Mr Venn the way it gets to everybody: a name said low by somebody going past, and then said again.

You know what's in his valise, because you packed it. The camp bed, the canvas bucket, a photograph of the spaniels in a leather frame, the socks his mother knitted with a V worked into the tops. It'll go home to the big house by way of the army, and somebody at the big house will undo the straps. You keep hoping it's the housekeeper.[/if][if start == mill]The word gets to you about Mr Ainsworth the way it gets to everybody: a name said low by somebody going past, and then said again. He was in front. He was always going to be in front.

You know what's in his valise, because you packed it. His mother's photograph. A shaving brush with a silver back, and a tin of Gold Flake with three left in it. His letters from home in a bundle, tied with a length of red weft you found in your own pocket, from the shed. It'll go home to the house on the hill by way of the army, and his mother will open it.

You write to her, a page in pencil: that he was well looked after, that he never went short of his tea, that he talked about the mill. You put Dear Mrs Ainsworth at the top and Yours respectfully at the bottom, and your number, and then you sit with it a good while, because you don't know if a weaver's lad is let write to the house on the hill.[/if][if start == pit]The word gets to you about Mr Straker the way it gets to everybody: a name said low by somebody going past, and then said again.

You know what's in his valise, because you packed it. The pit boots he brought out for the mud, that you laughed at and then wished you'd brought. A slide rule in a leather case. Letters from his mother, and a few in another hand, from Jesmond, that he kept apart. It'll go home to the house at the top of the rows by way of the army, and his mother will open it.

You write to Mrs Straker, in pencil, slow. You tell her about the pit boots, because she'll find them and wonder, and that he could hold a pick right by the end, and that he was in front. You don't know how to finish it, so you put your lamp number from the pit under your army one.[/if][if start == city]The word gets to you about Mr Pryor the way it gets to everybody: a name said low by somebody going past, and then said again.

You know what's in his valise, because you packed it. An Oxford scarf. A Baedeker for northern France with the corners gone soft. A box of Turkish cigarettes, half full, that the dugout smelled of for weeks. His uncle's letters on the firm's paper, and his mother's on her own. It'll go home to Surrey by way of the army, and his mother will open it.

You write to her in your best office hand, the hand he said was good: that he was cheerful, that the men liked him, that he spoke of her. You read it over three times for blots, as if the chief clerk was going to see it.[/if][else][if start == mill]The word gets to you about Mr Kershaw the way it got to you about Mr Ainsworth: a name said low, and then said again.

You know what's in his valise, because you packed it, and it isn't much. A razor and a strop. His South Africa medal with two clasps, in a matchbox. A photograph of a woman and four children on a back step in Bolton, all in clogs, all scrubbed. A few letters in a hand that pressed hard through the paper. It fills half the valise. You stuff the rest with straw so it won't rattle on the way home.

You write to Mrs Kershaw. You tell her he blacked his own boots to the end.[/if][if start == pit]The word gets to you about Mr Hindmarsh the way it got to you about Mr Straker: a name said low, and then said again.

You know what's in his valise, because you packed it. The spare spectacles, with the string still on. The book of poems with the corners turned down. And the little book with the bairns' names in it, every man in the platoon, written small, with their birthdays. You keep that back one night, and copy your own page out into your pay book, and then you put it in with the rest for Mrs Hindmarsh in Morpeth.[/if][if start == farm]The word gets to you about Mr Rudd the way it got to you about Mr Venn: a name said low, and then said again.

You know what's in his valise, because you packed it. A shorthand primer. A tin of Birmingham toffee nobody would eat. His mother's letters from Small Heath, forty or fifty, one for every one of his, done up with pink tape from the foundry office.

[if flag.f16_helped_rudd]You write to his mother that the Dunsworthy men came round to him, which is true, and that he always said please, which she'll know.[else]You write to his mother that he was a good officer. You don't know if it's true. You think it might have been, given time.[/if][/if][if start == city]The word gets to you about Mr Carew the way it got to you about Mr Pryor: a name said low, and then said again.

You know what's in his valise, because you packed it. His mother's letters, one for every day, in a pile you kept squared. The pocket Horace. A cake tin with a quarter of a seed cake left in it, from one of the aunts. And right at the bottom, folded flat, his school cap, that he never told you he'd brought.

You write to his mother in the office hand, and you don't know what to put about a boy of nineteen, so you tell her about the cap.[/if]

Nobody asks you to be anybody's man again. The company sergeant major puts you back in the section, and on the fatigue roster, with the men from home.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.officer_killed == 1 && start == farm]Think of the big house.[elif war.officer_killed == 1]Post the letter.[else]Post the letter, and go back to the section.[/if]

s_raid_1.title: The raid
s_raid_1.text:
[if war.stake == 0][if war.vol]You put your name down.[else]The sergeant picked you.[/if] Burnt cork on your face and hands, cap badge off, pay
book left with the quarter bloke. A cosh made of an entrenching-tool handle with a nut bolted on
the end. The officer goes through it again in a whisper in the sap: out through our wire, across,
in where the Boche parapet's been knocked about, a prisoner if we can, back in twenty
minutes.

Out in front the grass is wet and it's dark as a coal hole, and the dark smells of turned earth and cordite.
Behind you is {mate}. You can hear him breathing.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Raid night. The burnt cork, the cosh, and an officer younger than you who keeps
looking at his wristwatch as if it might tell him something. There's a thin moon. He says it'll be
behind cloud by midnight. He's wrong.

The sap smells of wet sandbags and of the cork, which smells like a blown-out candle. Behind you is
{mate}, chewing on nothing.[/if]

choices.text: Go fast and upright to the gap. Time matters more than cover. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You run bent double across the grass, every step loud as a door slamming, and nobody fires.

choices.text: Crawl it the way you practised, one arm at a time. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Elbows and knees, face in the wet grass, a yard at a time. It takes an age.

choices.text: Go wide round the shell holes, slow, freezing at every flare. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You lose the others twice in the dark and find them again by the smell of the cork.

choices.text: Tell the officer your rifle's jammed, and go back in. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: He looks at you in the dark for a moment and says nothing at all.

s_raid_2.title: The raid
s_raid_2.text:
[if war.stake == 0]Their wire. Close up it's not a fence, it's a thicket, rusty, taller than you, with tins hung in
it to rattle. The gap the guns made is narrower than the officer said. Somebody's cutting with
the long-handled cutters, each snip like a gunshot in your head.

Ten yards beyond it, their parapet. You can hear a man coughing on the other side, and smell
pipe tobacco, and something frying.[/if][if war.stake == 1]The wire again, and this time the guns have done their job: it lies in heaps and tangles, with
gaps you could drive a cart through, which means they'll know exactly where you're coming. A last
few strands are left across the gap, and the cutters are at them. A flare goes up to the left and
the whole party lies still in the long grass with the wire an arm's length off.

You can smell their trench from here: wet sandbags, cabbage, the latrine. Somebody beyond the
parapet is whistling a tune you nearly know.[/if]

choices.text: Through the gap and straight over their parapet. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: The wire takes a strip out of your sleeve and your arm with it, and then you're over, and dropping.

choices.text: Wait for the cutters, then go through in turn. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Snip. Snip. Your turn. You go through on your belly with the barbs catching your back.

choices.text: Hold back at the wire and cover the others in. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You lie at the wire with your rifle on their parapet, and the others go in without you.

s_raid_3.title: The raid
s_raid_3.text:
[if war.stake == 0]In their trench. It's cleaner than ours, and deeper, and for one second it's empty. Then a man
comes round the traverse with a mess tin in each hand and stops dead, and looks at you, and
opens his mouth.

There's a dugout entrance two yards on, steps going down, a blanket over the door, light under it.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Down into their trench, and you land on duckboards that rock under you like a punt. A dugout
entrance, a blanket hung across it, and down below a gramophone going, a waltz, tinny and slow.

And coming up the steps, bent under the curtain, a man with two mess tins of coffee, steaming. He
straightens up and sees you, and doesn't drop them.[/if]

choices.text: Grab the man with the mess tins. He's your prisoner. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: He doesn't fight. "Kamerad," he says, and drops the tins and puts his hands up, and what was in them goes all over your boots, still hot.

choices.text: Bomb the dugout and get out the way you came. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Pin, throw, down. The blanket blows out flat. You don't wait to see.

choices.text: Shout the others back now, before their trench wakes up. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You're back over their parapet before the first flare goes up.

x_raid_done.title: After the raid

choices.text: Get your head down.

s_patrol_1.title: Patrol
s_patrol_1.text:
[if war.stake == 0]Three of you, a corporal and {mate} and you, out through the gap in our wire at eleven. The job is
to find out whether they've put new wire out by the old sunken road, and come back and say.

No man's land at night isn't empty and isn't quiet. Rats. A tin rolling in the wind. Somewhere
out to the left a wounded man from last week, or a cat, or the wind in the wire.[/if][if war.stake == 1]The sunken road again, a corporal and {mate} and you, to see what they've done to their wire since.
Fog tonight, [if start == mill]thick as the shed on a damp morning[/if][if start == pit]thick as the reek off the pit heap on a wet night[/if][if start == city || start == farm]thick as wet wool[/if], so you can't see the man in front,
only hear the creak of his webbing and his breath going in and out.

The fog tastes of coal smoke from somewhere far off, which makes no sense out here.[/if]

choices.text: Go straight for the sunken road. Get there and get back. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You go quickly, crouched, and get there in ten minutes, with your heart going like a shuttle.

choices.text: Bound from shell hole to shell hole, the way you were taught. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Hole to hole. Down, listen, count twenty, up. The mud gets into everything.

choices.text: Lie still a while first and listen to their trench. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You lie with your face in the wet and listen to them talking, and someone over there laughs, and it's like a knife.

choices.text: Tell the corporal you've heard something, and you should go back. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: He knows you've heard nothing. He takes you back anyway.

s_patrol_2.title: Patrol
s_patrol_2.text:
[if war.stake == 0]The sunken road. And there's somebody in it.

A German patrol, six or seven, lying up along the bank thirty yards from you, the same as you, in
the dark, listening. You can see a helmet against the sky. You can hear one of them breathing
through his mouth. A hand closes on your arm: {mate}.[/if][if war.stake == 1]The sunken road, and at the far end of it there are men. Not ours. A working party, five or six,
putting out wire of their own, and one standing over them with his rifle slung, smoking, the
cigarette cupped in his hand so it shows only when he draws on it.

Thirty yards. {mate} has seen them too. You can feel him not breathing beside you.[/if]

choices.text: Bomb them, now, while they don't know you're there. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: Two bombs, and the dark goes white and loud, and somebody over there screams in German, and you're running.

choices.text: Lie flat and count them. That's what you're out here for. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Seven. One has a long pistol. One is smoking under his coat, the fool. You count them twice.

choices.text: Ease back out of the road, an inch at a time. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: It takes you twenty minutes to go thirty yards backwards on your belly.

choices.text: Get out of there and go back in, quick and low. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: You go back too fast and a sentry nearly shoots you at our wire.

s_patrol_3.title: Patrol
s_patrol_3.text:
[if war.stake == 0]Coming back is the dangerous bit, everybody says, and everybody's right. Our own sentries have
the wind up. The password this week is Blackpool. The gap in our wire is somewhere ahead, and in the
dark one stretch of wire looks like every other.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Coming in, and the fog has come up off the low ground while you were out, white and thick, and
now there's no parapet anywhere, ours or theirs. You've lost the line of the road. Somewhere ahead
is our wire and the gap in it, and somewhere behind is theirs, and in this they're the same.

A sentry coughs, close. You don't know whose. The password this week is Blackpool.[/if]

choices.text: Stand up at the wire and call the password. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: "Blackpool!" A rifle bolt, a pause, and a voice from home: "Come on then, you daft beggar."

choices.text: Feel along the wire for the gap with your hands. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You find the gap by the strip of white tape somebody tied to the picket. You could kiss him.

choices.text: Wait in a shell hole till the flares die, then crawl in. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You get in just before stand-to with the cold right through you.

x_patrol_done.title: After the patrol

choices.text: Get your head down.

s_wiring_1.title: Wiring
s_wiring_1.text:
[if war.stake == 0]Out in front with a coil of barbed wire on a stick across two men's shoulders, and screw pickets,
and mallets with sacking tied round the heads. The barbs catch your gloves, your puttees, your
face. Every few minutes a flare goes up from their side, and the whole party freezes where it
stands like children playing statues.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Pickets and a coil tonight, and two knife rests, wooden frames already strung with wire, carried out
between two men to drop across the worst gaps. They catch on everything. The wire sings
when it brushes against itself, a thin high note, and you'd swear the whole German army can hear it.[/if]

choices.text: Work fast. Get the pickets in before the moon's up. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You get six pickets screwed in, your hands raw, before the corporal tells you to slow down.

choices.text: Work with the others, a picket at a time. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Screw, turn, turn, turn. The picket bites into the clay and holds.

choices.text: Do the work close to our own wire, where there's cover. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You do the cushy end. Nobody says anything. Somebody has to do the far end.

s_wiring_2.title: Wiring
s_wiring_2.text:
[if war.stake == 0]A flare goes up right over you. It hangs, and hangs, and you're stood in the open with a coil of
wire in your arms and every bit of you lit up white, and you can see your own shadow on the
ground going round slowly as the flare swings.[/if][if war.stake == 1]A machine gun starts up from their side, traversing, low, the rounds cracking past just over the
grass in a long sweep from left to right, like a man watering a garden. It isn't aimed at you. It
isn't aimed at anything. It's coming your way, and you're stood up with a coil of wire in your arms.[/if]

choices.text: Keep working. Moving men are harder to see than you'd think. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You keep unrolling the wire, slowly, steadily, and the flare dies, and nobody fires.

choices.text: Freeze. Don't move a finger till it dies. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You don't breathe. The flare comes down somewhere behind you, fizzing in the grass.

choices.text: Drop flat into the nearest shell hole. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You're down in the water before you know you've moved, and the wire's somewhere on top of you.

s_wiring_3.title: Wiring
s_wiring_3.text:
[if war.stake == 0]One more length and it's done, the corporal says. It's nearly light. You can see the shape of
their parapet now, which means they can see the shape of you.[/if][if war.stake == 1]The rain's come on, and the wire's slick in your hands, and the pickets won't go in: the mallet
skids off the wet heads with a noise you'd swear they can hear in Berlin. One more length, the
corporal says. There's a grey line in the east. The rain's no cover once it's light.[/if]

choices.text: Finish the length. Whatever it takes. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You run the last coil out and stamp it down and you're in through our wire as the light comes up grey.

choices.text: Finish what you can and come in with the party. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You get most of it in, and come back in with the others, and the corporal says it'll do.

choices.text: Come in now and leave the last of it. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You leave the last coil lying in no man's land. Someone will have to go out for it.

choices.text: Tell the corporal you're done in, and go back first. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: You go back in on your own, and leave them to it.

x_wiring_done.title: After wiring

choices.text: Get your head down.

s_listening_1.title: Listening post
s_listening_1.text:
[if war.stake == 0]A hole in the ground out past our wire, two men in it, a string running back to the trench. One
tug for all right, two for something moving, three for them coming. You've a rifle, four Mills bombs
and a flask of cold tea, and three hours to lie here.

In the hole with you is {mate}. His knee is pressed against yours. You can feel it trembling, or
it's yours.[/if][if war.stake == 1]The Coffin, they call this post, because of its shape and for the other reason. Two hours in it with
rain on your back the whole time, running down your neck, filling your boots. The string runs back
into the dark and you keep your hand on it like a rosary.

In the post with you is {mate}, so close you can smell the tea on his breath.[/if]

choices.text: Crawl out ahead of the post to see better. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You lie out in front of the post in the grass, ten yards nearer them, with your ear on the ground.

choices.text: Settle in the hole and listen, the way you were told. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You settle in, and the cold comes up out of the ground into you, and you listen.

choices.text: Keep down below the lip of the hole. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You keep your head down below the lip, and the night goes on over you.

s_listening_2.title: Listening post
s_listening_2.text:
[if war.stake == 0]A sound. Out in front, to the right, the wire rattling, or a rat at it. Then nothing. Then again:
a click, metal on metal, and a whisper you can't make out. It might be a German patrol. It might
be a loose picket in the wind. It's two in the morning and every sound is a man.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Voices. Close. Two men talking low in German, out in front, and the smell of their tobacco
comes to you on the wind. One of them laughs, quietly, the way men laugh on sentry at three in the
morning. A match flares and goes out. They're in a shell hole twenty yards off, doing what you're
doing.[/if]

choices.text: Throw a bomb at the sound. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: The bomb goes off in the wire, and somebody over there yells, and their whole trench opens up on the dark.

choices.text: Two tugs on the string. Let the trench know. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Two tugs. The string comes back once. They've got it.

choices.text: Lie still. Wait to be sure. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You wait. The sound doesn't come again. You'll never know.

s_listening_3.title: Listening post
s_listening_3.text:
[if war.stake == 0]The relief's late. The sky's going grey in the east. If they don't come soon you'll have to get
back across in daylight, and their snipers will be up.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Your relief comes crawling out on time, for once, and then a flare goes up and catches him
halfway, and he lies flat in the open twenty yards off with the light hanging over him. He can't
come on and you can't go back past him till it dies, and the sky behind their line is going grey.[/if]

choices.text: Go back now, before it's any lighter. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You run for our wire in the grey, and dive through the gap, and land on somebody's breakfast.

choices.text: Wait for the relief. That's the order. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: They come at last, swearing about the communication trench, and you crawl back in.

choices.text: Stay in the hole all day if you have to. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You lie in the hole all day with the flies, and come in after dark, stiff as a board.

x_listening_done.title: After the listening post

choices.text: Get your head down.

s_carrying_1.title: Carrying party
s_carrying_1.text:
[if war.stake == 0]The ration dump at the end of the communication trench: boxes of small-arms ammunition, coils of
wire, duckboards, sandbags of bread, a dixie of tea for the front line with the lid tied on with
string. You're to take it all up. Two miles of trench, in the dark, in the wet, under a
battery of five-nines that knows the route as well as you do.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Rations and ammunition as usual from the dump, and on top of them tonight trench mortar bombs, the
ones the lads call toffee apples, a ball on a stick, slung on poles between pairs of men. If one goes off, the carrying party goes with it. Nobody
smokes. Nobody even talks about smoking.[/if]

choices.text: Take two loads at once and save a journey. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You set off with an ammunition box on each shoulder, and your shoulders tell you about it every yard.

choices.text: Take your load and go with the party. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You get the dixie of tea, which is the worst job, because if you spill it the front line will kill you.

choices.text: Take the light load: the bread. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You take the bread. It's the lightest load and everybody knows it.

s_carrying_2.title: Carrying party
s_carrying_2.text:
[if war.stake == 0]Halfway up, the battery starts. Whizz-bangs, you hear them after they arrive: a crack and a
flash and earth coming down on your load like rain on a slate roof. The trench is knee-deep in
places and the duckboards float. Somebody ahead is shouting to keep moving.[/if][if war.stake == 1 && war.stage <= 2]Gas. Somebody's banging a shell case up ahead, and the shout comes back down the line, and you're
getting your gas helmet on with a box of bombs on your shoulder, one-handed: the flannel bag over
your head, wet and stinking of chemicals, the tail tucked into your collar, the eyepieces steaming up
so the trench goes to fog. Then the shells start, behind the gas. You can't see the duckboards and
you can't see the man in front.[/if][if war.stake == 1 && war.stage >= 3]Gas. Somebody's banging a shell case up ahead, and the shout comes back down the line, and you're
getting your mask on with a box of bombs on your shoulder, one-handed, the rubber stinking, the
eyepieces steaming up so the trench goes to fog. Then the shells start, behind the gas. You can't
see the duckboards and you can't see the man in front.[/if]

choices.text: Keep moving. Get through the shelled stretch fast. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You run, bent double, slopping through the water, with the load banging your back.

choices.text: Get down between shells, then move. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Down, count, up, move. Down. You've got the rhythm of it now. That frightens you.

choices.text: Shelter in a dugout entrance till it stops. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You squeeze into a dugout entrance with three others and the load, and wait it out.

s_carrying_3.title: Carrying party
s_carrying_3.text:
[if war.stake == 0]The last stretch. There's a man down in the trench in front of you, one of the party, sitting in
the water holding his leg and swearing, quietly, in a steady stream, like a man reading a list.[/if][if war.stake == 1]The last stretch, and a man of the party is down in front of you. He hasn't stopped one: he's just down, sat in the
water with his back to the trench wall and his load beside him, saying he can't, he can't do another
yard, he's not hurt, he just can't. His eyes are fixed on nothing at all.[/if]

choices.text: Take his load too, and leave him for the bearers. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You get both loads up to the front line, staggering, and fall asleep on the firestep the minute you put them down.

choices.text: Get him up and walk him in with you. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You get his arm over your shoulder and walk him in, and he swears at you all the way, and thanks you at the end.

choices.text: Stay with him and wait for the stretcher-bearers. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You wait with him in the water. The bearers come an hour later. The load doesn't get up till morning.

x_carrying_done.title: After the carrying party

choices.text: Get your head down.

s_bomb_1.title: Bombing raid
s_bomb_1.text:
Eight bombers and a sergeant, a sandbag of Mills bombs each, in the sap at one in the morning. The
pins are bent back ready so you won't fumble them. The bombs are cold and heavy and fit your hand
the way a cricket ball does.

choices.text: Lead the way out to their wire. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You go first, and the others follow your shape in the dark.

choices.text: Go out in your place in the party. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You go out fourth, behind the sergeant's boots.

choices.text: Go out last and keep the line back to the sap. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You go last, the safest place, and the job nobody wants to be seen wanting.

choices.text: Tell the sergeant you can't go tonight. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: The sergeant looks at you a long moment and takes your bombs off you himself.

s_bomb_2.title: Bombing raid
s_bomb_2.text:
[if war.stake == 0]In their trench. This is the work: along it a bay at a time. Pin, throw over the traverse, count,
down, the bang, then round the corner fast before they can throw back. Their bombs come over
too, the potato mashers, a tin on a stick, turning end over end in the light of the last explosion.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Their trench, and it's a maze: a turn every few yards, a sap going off, a dugout, another turn,
and you can't tell which way their bombers are coming from. A stick bomb comes over the traverse
turning end over end and somebody kicks it on into the next bay, where it goes off. Your ears have
gone. You're working by the light of the bangs.[/if]

choices.text: Lead round each traverse. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: Three bays. Four. You stop counting. Your arm aches from throwing.

choices.text: Throw for the man in front. Keep him supplied. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You throw, and pass up bombs, and throw, and the trench fills with smoke you can taste.

choices.text: Hold the bay you're in. Block it with sandbags. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You build a block out of their own sandbags, and hold it, and the others go on without you.

s_bomb_3.title: Bombing raid
s_bomb_3.text:
[if war.stake == 0]The sergeant blows his whistle. Out. Their machine gun has started from somewhere further along
and the gap in the wire is behind you and getting further away.[/if][if war.stake == 1]The whistle. Out. Their bombers are coming down the trench at you from both ends now, and their
machine gun has opened up on the wire behind, sweeping the gap you came in by. There's a wounded man
of yours at the foot of the parapet, and the gap is fifty yards off.[/if]

choices.text: Bomb the machine gun before you go. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: Your bomb goes over the sandbags at the muzzle flash, and the flash stops.

choices.text: Go back with the party, carrying the wounded. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You go back with a man over your shoulder who keeps apologising.

choices.text: Run for the gap. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You run, and dive, and you're through.

x_bomb_done.title: After the bombing raid

choices.text: Get your head down.

s_lewis_1.title: The gun
s_lewis_1.text:
[if war.stake == 0]Getting the gun into position: twenty-eight pounds of it, the drums in their canvas panniers, your
No. 2 behind you with the spares, out along a sap to a shell hole with a view. You've cleaned it
twice since dark. You can feel every grain of grit in it.[/if][if war.stake == 1]The two-seater is still there, slow and grey against the cloud, turning over the support line the
way a kestrel turns over a field. Each time it comes round, a gun behind their line fires, and the
shell lands a little nearer the cookhouse. He's ranging their battery on you. The gun has to go up
on the post at the end of the bay, on its swivel, pointing at the sky, with you standing under it in
the open.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.stake == 0]Set up in the forward hole with the best field of fire.[else]Get the gun up on the post now, while he's low.[/if] ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: [if war.stake == 0]The forward hole. You can see the whole of their parapet from here, which means it can see you.[else]You get it up on the swivel and the butt into your shoulder, standing on the firestep in full view of both armies.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.stake == 0]Set up where you were told.[else]Wait for him to come round again, then get it up.[/if] ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: [if war.stake == 0]The bipod legs bed into the sandbags. The butt goes into your shoulder like it lives there.[else]He comes round. You have the gun up and a drum on before he's straightened out.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.stake == 0]Set up back in the sap, under cover.[else]Fire from the bay, with the gun propped on the parados.[/if] ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: [if war.stake == 0]You set up in the sap. You can see half as much from here. You're twice as safe.[else]Propped on the back wall of the trench the gun can't swing far, and you can only fire at him when he's nearly overhead.[/if]

s_lewis_2.title: The gun
s_lewis_2.text:
[if war.stake == 0]You open up. The gun shakes against your shoulder and the cooling fins go hot and the empty cases
spill out of the side and ring off the sandbags. Forty-seven rounds, and you're changing the drum
by feel. Then it stops. A stoppage. The cocking handle's forward. You know what that is. Your
hands know before you do.[/if][if war.stake == 1]You've never fired at anything that moves this fast. You were told to aim in front of him, the length
of his machine, and then some, and you can't tell where the bullets go once they leave the muzzle.
He sees you. The machine tilts and the observer in the back swings his gun round and fires down at
the trench, and you hear his bullets go into the sandbags beside your feet.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.stake == 0]Clear it fast and keep firing.[else]Stand and keep firing at him, whatever he fires back.[/if] ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: [if war.stake == 0]Pull, pull, a new drum, and it's going again, and the muzzle flash lights up the whole hole.[else]You stand there and fire up at him, a whole drum, with his bullets kicking the earth off the parados behind you.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.stake == 0]Clear it properly, by the drill.[else]Short bursts, the way you were taught, and lead him.[/if] ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: [if war.stake == 0]Handle back, look, clear it, by the numbers. Your No. 2 hands you the drum without being asked.[else]Short bursts. Lead him. Short bursts. Your No. 2 has a drum ready before you call for it.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.stake == 0]Get the gun down out of sight while you clear it.[else]Duck under the parapet while he passes, and fire when he's going away.[/if] ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: [if war.stake == 0]You get it down into the bottom of the hole and work on it blind, and the firing stops for a minute too long.[else]You crouch while he passes, then come up and fire at his tail as he goes. A going-away shot. You'll never know.[/if]

s_lewis_3.title: The gun
s_lewis_3.text:
[if war.stake == 0]It's done. Now the gun has to come back in, and their machine gunners know exactly where it's
been. The first shells are already coming down behind you.[/if][if war.stake == 1]He's turned away east, low, and you can't tell if it's because of you. But their battery has stopped
ranging on the cookhouse. Now it's ranging on the post, on the place it saw the gun fire from, and the
first shell lands thirty yards short.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.stake == 0]Carry the gun back yourself, fast.[else]Fire one more drum after him before you take it down.[/if] ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: [if war.stake == 0]You run with the gun across your shoulders, and it gets heavier with every yard.[else]One more drum at a dot over their lines. Then the next shell lands twenty yards short, and you get it down.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.stake == 0]Take it back in turns with your No. 2.[else]Get the gun off the post and move it along the trench.[/if] ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: [if war.stake == 0]Gun, then drums, then gun. The sap's longer than it was.[else]Off the swivel, along three bays, and down. The next shell lands on the empty post.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.stake == 0]Wait in the hole for the shelling to ease.[else]Leave the gun on the post and get into the dugout.[/if] ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: [if war.stake == 0]You wait with the gun in your lap like a sleeping child, until it eases.[else]You sit in the dugout and listen to them shell the post, and wonder what will be left of the gun.[/if]

x_lewis_done.title: After the gun

choices.text: Clean the gun.

s_signals_1.title: The line
s_signals_1.text:
The pliers in your pocket, the reel of cable on your back, the buzzer in its leather case banging
on your hip. Somewhere between here and battalion the line is cut, and battalion is shouting into
a dead telephone.

choices.text: Run along the top of the trench where it's quickest. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You run along the top in the dark with the wire running through your fingers.

choices.text: Follow the wire along the trench floor. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You follow it bay by bay, the wire cold and wet in your hand.

choices.text: Wait for the shelling to slacken first. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You wait. Battalion waits. The colonel's voice, they'll tell you later, went quiet.

s_signals_2.title: The line
s_signals_2.text:
[if war.stake == 0]The break, at last, in the worst place: where the communication trench has been blown in, and
the two ends of the wire are fifteen yards apart across open ground that's under fire.[/if][if war.stake == 1]The break is out on top, where the line crosses a strip of the old no man's land between two
trenches. A shell has gone clean through it, and the two ends are lying in the mud twenty yards
apart, and their machine gun sweeps that stretch every few minutes, as regular as a clock.[/if]

choices.text: Run the new wire across the open in one go. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You run, paying out cable, and fall flat at the far end with your heart hammering, and the cable's across.

choices.text: Crawl the wire across. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You crawl it across with the reel on your back and the bullets cracking overhead.

choices.text: Take the long way round, through the next trench. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: It takes three times as much cable and three times as long, and you nearly run out.

s_signals_3.title: The line
s_signals_3.text:
[if war.stake == 0]You splice it, fingers numb, by feel, the rubber tape in your teeth. Now to test it.[/if][if war.stake == 1]You make the joint by feel in the dark, the copper twisted and the tape held in your teeth,
lying in a puddle, the cold coming up through your tunic. The buzzer's on your hip. Battalion will
want to know it's through.[/if]

choices.text: Test it there, in the open. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You clip on the buzzer. Dot dash. Battalion answers.

choices.text: Get back into cover, then test it. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: In the trench, the buzzer. It answers.

choices.text: Leave it for the next man to test. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You get back in and tell them it's done, and hope it is.

x_signals_done.title: After the line

choices.text: Get your head down.

s_snipe_1.title: The hide
s_snipe_1.text:
Before dawn you crawl into the hide: a hollow in the parapet behind a steel plate with a slit in
it, a sack over the slit, your observer beside you with the telescope and the notebook. You stay
till dark. Fourteen hours. You've a bottle to piss in and a tin of bully.

choices.text: Take the forward hide, the one with the better view. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: The forward hide. You can see their trench from here, and the ruined house behind it, and everything in between.

choices.text: Take your usual hide. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Your hide. You know every lump in its sandbags.

choices.text: Take the deep hide, with the narrow slit. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: The deep hide. You can see a slice of their parapet the width of your hand.

s_snipe_2.title: The hide
s_snipe_2.text:
[if war.stake == 0]Mid-morning. Your observer touches your arm. At a loophole in their parapet, a piece of mirror,
and behind it a man shaving, his braces down, the lather white on his face. He puts you in mind
of your father at the scullery sink. He has no idea.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Mid-morning, the sun on their parapet. At a loophole someone's left the steel plate open, and
behind it a man has propped a bit of mirror on a sandbag and is shaving with a cut-throat razor,
taking his time over his chin. A boy, by the look of him. You'd swear he was whistling, though
you can't hear it from here.[/if]

choices.text: Take the shot. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: The rifle kicks. The mirror's gone. Your observer writes something in the notebook and doesn't look at you.

choices.text: Watch the loophole and wait for a better target. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You wait. He finishes shaving. At noon a man with an officer's cap comes to the same loophole.

choices.text: Let him shave. Mark the loophole and keep still. ({risk_careful})
