choices.text_after: You watch him rinse his razor, and wipe his face, and go.

choices.text: Pack it in for the day. Something's wrong out there. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: You've a feeling a plate's been moved over there. You trust it, and get out.

s_snipe_3.title: The hide
s_snipe_3.text:
[if war.stake == 0]Afternoon. A rifle bullet hits your steel plate with a sound like a bell, and the whole hide
rings. They've found you. Their sniper is out there somewhere, and he's looking at your slit.[/if][if war.stake == 1]A puff of earth jumps off the sandbag an inch from your slit, and the crack comes after it, flat
and close. Then another, the other side. He's bracketing you, the way a gunner would. He knows where
you are to a yard.[/if]

choices.text: Find him. He fired; he's shown himself. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You find the flash, a dark place in a heap of bricks. You wait. You fire.

choices.text: Close the slit and wait for dark. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You close the slit and lie in the dark with the plate between you and him, and the hours go slow.

choices.text: Crawl out the back of the hide, now. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You go out the back on your belly, and leave the hide to him.

x_snipe_done.title: After the hide

choices.text: Clean the rifle.

s_tunnel_1.title: The gallery
s_tunnel_1.text:
Down the shaft on the ladder, sixty feet, the air getting thicker and warmer. Along the gallery on
your back on the trolley, to the face. The candle goes small and blue. Clay, wet, the smell of it
and of men's sweat and of the bags of spoil going back hand to hand.

choices.text: Work the face, kicking the clay out fast. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You lie back on the plank cross and kick the spade into the clay with both feet, and the spoil goes back down the line.

choices.text: Work it quietly, the way you were taught. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Quiet as you can, the clay coming away in lumps, each one handed back without a word.

choices.text: Shore it up first, frame by frame. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You get the timbers in before you dig another foot. The roof creaks, and holds.

s_tunnel_2.title: The gallery
s_tunnel_2.text:
[if war.stake == 0]You put your ear to the listening stick against the clay. You can hear them. The Germans, digging
their own gallery, close: the scrape, the thud, a voice. Then the digging stops. They're
listening too.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Through the listening stick, nothing. Then, so faint you might be imagining it, a ticking. Not
digging. Something steady, like a clock in an empty house. You've heard the old hands talk about it.
It might be their pump. It might be something else.[/if]

choices.text: Keep digging, quietly. Get to them first. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You keep digging, slow, silent, and your own heartbeat is the loudest thing in the gallery.

choices.text: Stop and listen. Count how long they're quiet. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You lie still with your ear to the clay for an hour. They start again. You breathe.

choices.text: Pull back down the gallery and report it. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You crawl back down the gallery on your belly and tell the officer, in a whisper, though you're a hundred yards off.

choices.text: Get everybody out of the gallery. Now. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: You get everyone out, and up the shaft, and nothing happens, and then you have to go back down.

s_tunnel_3.title: The gallery
s_tunnel_3.text:
[if war.stake == 0]The officer decides: a camouflet, a small charge, to blow in their gallery before they blow in
yours. The ammonal comes down the line in bags. Somebody has to tamp it and lay the leads.[/if][if war.stake == 1]The order comes down: blow them, now, before they blow you. The charge comes along the gallery in
sandbags passed hand to hand, and the leads after it, and nobody talks above a breath. The candle
flame has gone small and blue at the tip. The air's going bad.[/if]

choices.text: Lay the charge yourself. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You lay it with your hands steady, which surprises you, and you're up the shaft when it goes. The ground jumps.

choices.text: Tamp and pass up the bags, with the others. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: You tamp the charge with sandbags, bag after bag, till the gallery's sealed.

choices.text: Work the windlass at the top of the shaft. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You wind, and wind, and the men come up out of the dark one by one, grey with clay.

x_tunnel_done.title: After the gallery

choices.text: Wash the clay off, if you can.

s_bearer_1.title: The wounded
s_bearer_1.text:
[if war.stake == 0]Over the parapet with the stretcher, four of you, into the dark. The man you're going for is
calling, somewhere ahead and to the left, and every time he calls, their sentry sends a flare up
towards the sound. The grass is wet and smells of cordite and something else.[/if][if war.stake == 1]The wounded man is in a shell hole thirty yards out, and it's daylight, and the Germans can see
the hole. Their sniper has already hit the first man who tried for him. You can hear him in there,
talking to himself, saying the same thing over and over.[/if]

choices.text: Go straight out to him, upright, the red cross showing. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You walk out as if you were crossing a street. Nobody fires. Then somebody does.

choices.text: Crawl out to him by the shell holes. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Hole to hole, on your elbows, dragging the stretcher, the canvas catching on everything.

choices.text: Wait for the flares to die, then go in the dark. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You wait, flat, while he calls. It's the longest ten minutes of the war.

s_bearer_2.title: The wounded
s_bearer_2.text:
[if war.stake == 0]You've got him. A big man, a sergeant, hit in the thigh, the blood black on the grass. When you
lift him onto the stretcher he screams, and the whole German line must hear it.[/if][if war.stake == 1]He's hit in the belly, and he begs you not to move him. He holds your wrist and won't let go.
If you don't move him, he'll die where he is. If you do, he may die on the way.[/if]

choices.text: Lift him and go, now, whatever the noise. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: Four of you lift together and run, bent double, the stretcher bucking.

choices.text: Dress the wound first, then lift him. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: A field dressing, then another, tied tight, your hands steady because they have to be.

choices.text: Drag him into the shell hole and wait. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You get him down into the hole and lie across him while the machine gun goes over.

choices.text: Leave him for the next party. Get yourself back. ({risk_back})
choices.text_after: You tell him somebody's coming. You go. You hear him behind you, the whole way.

s_bearer_3.title: The wounded
s_bearer_3.text:
[if war.stake == 0]The last thirty yards with the stretcher, towards our wire. The gap is narrow, one of the four of
you is stumbling, and a machine gun has started from their side, low, feeling for you.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Back at our parapet, and he has to go over it: a man on a stretcher, lifted up and over a wall of
sandbags under fire, with hands reaching up out of the trench to take him.[/if]

choices.text: Run for it with him. ({risk_bold})
choices.text_after: You run, and the stretcher runs with you, and then you're over and down.

choices.text: Keep the pace even. Don't jolt him. ({risk_steady})
choices.text_after: Even, even, the way you'd carry a full bucket, all the way in.

choices.text: Lie up in front of our wire till it's quiet. ({risk_careful})
choices.text_after: You lie out in front of our own wire with him for an hour, talking to him so he stays awake.

x_bearer_done.title: After

choices.text: Wash your hands.

w_step.title: Out there
w_step.text: [if war.step == 1]You go out.[/if][if war.step == 2]Halfway. The worst of it is now.[/if][if war.step == 3]Nearly done. Getting back is its own job.[/if]

choices.text: Push it. Get it done fast. ({risk_bold})
Steady. Do it the way you were taught. ({risk_steady})
Careful. Keep low and take your time. ({risk_careful})
Turn back. ({risk_back})

x_sortie.title: Back in
x_sortie.text:
[if war.result == ok]It went the way it was meant to. The sergeant nods at you, which from him is a speech.[/if][if war.result == failed]It went wrong, the way these things do, and nobody can say quite where.[/if][if war.result == turned]You came back without doing it. Nobody says anything. Everybody knows.[/if]

{result_note}

choices.text: Get your head down while you can.

c_enlist_mill.title: The drill hall
c_enlist_mill.text:
The queue starts at the drill hall door and goes back past the Co-op and round into Bury Road.
Somebody has chalked GOD SAVE THE KING on the wall, and under it somebody else has put AND OUR
ALBERT, and Albert Shaw is stood right in front of it pretending he can't read.

It's warm for September. The street smells of the mill on a hundred men at once: machine oil,
cotton fluff in their hair, the sour sweat of the weaving shed. Without the looms going your
ears feel hollow, the way they do on a Sunday.

The recruiting sergeant doesn't shout. He's like a good tackler: he doesn't need to.

"Age?"

"Just turned {age_words}, sir."

Behind you Walter Pilling is going to say nineteen. Walter Pilling was born the same winter as
your sister, and everybody in the queue knows it, and nobody says a word.
[break]
What you take with you from the shed is what you'll have out there.

choices.text: The knack you have with a loom, and legs for a ten-hour day.
The knack you have with a loom, and the voice that leads the chapel choir.
Legs for a ten-hour day, and the voice that leads the chapel choir.

c_enlist_pit.title: The Miners' Hall
c_enlist_pit.text:
The queue comes out of the Miners' Hall door and goes down past the Store and the Primitive
Methodist chapel nearly to the pit gates, and behind it the winding wheel's still turning,
because the fore shift isn't up yet. When they do come up they come straight over, black to the
eyes, bait tins under their arms, and join the end of it, and nobody tells them to go home and
wash first.

The colliery band played the first lot to the station in August. They're not playing today.
They're in the queue.

The street smells of the pit on a hundred men: coal dust and wet pit clothes and sweat, and
over it all the sulphur off the heap that's been burning since before you were born. There's a
blue mark on every forehead and every set of knuckles, where the coal got into a cut and healed
in.

The manager came down this morning in his good coat and said coal was war work too. Jim Bell
asked him if coal would pay the widows, and the manager went red and went home.

"Age?"

"Just gone {age_words}, sir."

Tommy Robson's in front of you, your marra at the face these two years, saying nothing, which
is how Tommy says most things. George Charlton's behind you, still smelling of the stables,
because he went down the pit last night to tell his pony he was going.
[break]
What you bring from underground is what you'll have out there.

choices.text: Digging and timbering, and a back for a long shift.
Digging and timbering, and a hand with the engines and the pumps.
A back for a long shift, and a hand with the engines and the pumps.

c_enlist_city.title: Guildhall
c_enlist_city.text:
The queue goes out of the Guildhall yard and down Gresham Street and round into Basinghall
Street, four deep, and every man in it is wearing a bowler hat. Clerks. From the insurance
offices and the banks and the shipping firms, from every desk in the City, come out at dinner
time with their sandwiches in their pockets and stood in the queue instead.

It's warm for September. The street smells of horse dung and hot stone and the river, and of
the City on a hundred men: ink, brilliantine, the starch in a hundred stiff collars. A man in
front of you is still holding a ledger.

The manager came round the office at eleven and shook every man's hand and said the Gresham
and Lombard would make up their salaries for as long as it lasted. Arthur Webb, from the next
desk, wrote it down. Percy Fenton was out of the door before the manager finished. Leonard Marsh
sat up half the night with a card from the optician's, learning the letters.

The sergeant writes your name. "Age?"

"Just turned {age_words}, sir."
[break]
What you bring from the office is what you'll have out there.

choices.text: A clerk's head for reading and figures, and a bowler's arm from Saturday cricket.
A clerk's head for reading and figures, and the St John Ambulance certificate.
A bowler's arm from Saturday cricket, and the St John Ambulance certificate.

c_enlist_farm.title: Harvest home
c_enlist_farm.text:
The harvest's in, and the harvest supper's in the big barn at Court Farm, the way it is every
year: trestle tables, a ham, cider from the squire's own press, the fiddler from Brendon, and
the barn still smelling of the corn it held all summer. Only this year the squire stands up at
the end with a paper in his hand, and there's a recruiting sergeant beside him in a red sash,
and nobody's dancing.

The squire's son, young Mr Venn, is taking a commission. He'll have a platoon, the squire says,
and he'd like it to be Dunsworthy men.

Will Cottle puts his tankard down and stands up first, because his father's looking at him and
he can't bear it. Dan Pearce stands up because Will has, and because it's further from the
keeper. Bert Yeo, who rang the bells for the harvest thanksgiving that morning, stands up
because everybody else is.

The sergeant writes your name. "Age?"

"Just gone {age_words}, sir."
[break]
What you bring from the land is what you'll have out there.

choices.text: A shotgun and a poacher's eye, and the legs to walk the moor all day.
A shotgun and a poacher's eye, and a hand with the threshing engine.
The legs to walk the moor all day, and a hand with the threshing engine.

c_general.title: The last night
c_general.text:
Your mother has sewn your name into everything you own. The kitchen smells of hot iron and the
starch she's put in your collars, which the army will take off you in a week. She's not
talking much. She keeps finding things to fold.

There's one more thing you've got that the army didn't give you.

choices.text: First aid. The ambulance class at the works, certificate in a frame.
A throwing arm. Second eleven, and you can hit a stump from the boundary.
A voice. When you start a hymn, men join in.

c_training.title: Training
c_training.text:
Eight months of it. Huts with floors that never dry. Drill in your own clothes till Christmas,
then in blue serge, then at last in khaki that smells of the store and makes your neck raw.
Route marches in the rain until your feet are one blister and then they harden and you stop
noticing. Digging practice trenches in a field and filling them in again. Bayonet drill on
sacks of straw, the corporal yelling at you to scream, and you feel daft screaming, and then
one day you don't.

You learn to sleep anywhere. You learn to eat anything. You learn the men from home all over
again, the way you never knew them [if start == mill]in the shed[/if][if start == pit]at the face[/if][if start == city]across the office[/if][if start == farm]in the fields[/if]: who snores, who cries, who shares.

In May the orders come. France.

{section_line}

choices.text: Go aboard.

w_tour.title: In the line
w_tour.text: [if war.back_from_leave && war.corps != tank]Back from leave. You remember the railhead, the smell of horse dung and wet canvas and coal smoke, and the day and a half it took to come back, and home already doesn't seem real. [/if][if war.back_from_leave && war.corps == tank && war.stage == 4]Back from leave. You remember the railhead, the smell of horse dung and wet canvas and coal smoke, and the day and a half it took to come back, and home already doesn't seem real. [/if][if war.corps != tank && war.corps != air][if war.month == 1 && war.take == 0]January. The ground's iron and the bully beef comes up frozen in the tin. You rub whale oil into your feet every morning, under the eye of a corporal, because trench foot is a crime now, and the oil stinks of fish and the cold gets in anyway.[/if][if war.month == 1 && war.take == 1]January. Frost on the wire in the morning, every barb furred white. The braziers fill the dugouts with coke fumes that give you a headache like a hammer, and you sit in them anyway, because outside your breath freezes on your scarf.[/if][if war.month == 2 && war.take == 0]February, and the thaw. The trench walls go soft and slide in, a bay at a time, and you dig them out and they slide in again. The rats are fat from the winter. One runs over your face in the night and you've stopped waking up for it.[/if][if war.month == 2 && war.take == 1]February. Wet, and then wetter. The duckboards float. Everything you own is damp, your blanket, your socks, your bread, and the whole line smells of wet wool and wet earth and the latrine.[/if][if war.month == 3 && war.take == 0]March. Rain on the wind, and the wind straight off Fritz's line, so it smells of him: his cooking, his tobacco, his latrines. The pumps go all night and the water comes back in all day.[/if][if war.month == 3 && war.take == 1]March. A raw grey month. The sky sits on the trench like a lid. You don't feel your feet from one end of the tour to the other.[/if][if war.month == 4 && war.take == 0]April. Green coming through the churned ground in no man's land, thin and bright, as if nobody had told the grass. At night the frogs croak in the shell holes, a whole chapel choir of them.[/if][if war.month == 4 && war.take == 1]April. Showers and sun, both in an hour. Behind the lines there's blossom on the orchard trees by the billets, and you stand under it with your mess tin and can't take it in.[/if][if war.month == 5 && war.take == 0]May. Warm enough to take your tunic off in the support line and go down its seams for chats. The flies are starting, and the smell from no man's land is starting with them.[/if][if war.month == 5 && war.take == 1]May. The hawthorn's out along the roads behind the lines, white as washing, and the smell of it comes up the communication trench at dusk, sweet, and then the other smell, underneath.[/if][if war.month == 6 && war.take == 0]June. The nights are so short that stand-to is at three in the morning, and the sky's going grey before you've got your boots dry. The water comes up in petrol tins and tastes of petrol and chloride.[/if][if war.month == 6 && war.take == 1]June. Dust, and flies, and the long light evenings. You can read a letter on the firestep at ten at night, and you do, over and over.[/if][if war.month == 7 && war.take == 0]July. Heat. The flies are on everything: the pozzy, the bread, your mouth if you leave it open. Thirst all day. The sandbags are hot to the touch at noon.[/if][if war.month == 7 && war.take == 1]July. The trench bakes. Once the morning hate is over, men sleep through the afternoon in whatever shade the parapet gives, faces covered with their caps against the flies.[/if][if war.month == 8 && war.take == 0]August. Thunderstorms in the night that you mistake for guns, and guns you mistake for thunder. Behind the lines the French women are getting the harvest in by hand, and they don't look up at the columns going past.[/if][if war.month == 8 && war.take == 1]August. Wasps at the jam tins and the heavy smell of hay from the fields behind the lines, and a storm every few nights that fills the trench to your knees.[/if][if war.month == 9 && war.take == 0]September. Mist in the mornings, low on the ground, so that at stand-to the German line isn't there and then is. Blackberries in the hedges behind the billets; you eat them till your fingers are purple.[/if][if war.month == 9 && war.take == 1]September. The nights drawing in. The air smells of turned earth and the first fires of the year in the farmhouses behind the lines.[/if][if war.month == 10 && war.take == 0]October. Rain, and the mud comes back like an old enemy. Greatcoats again. The leaves are coming down off the last trees in the wood behind the support line, what's left of the trees.[/if][if war.month == 10 && war.take == 1]October. A wet, rotten month. Your puttees never dry. The rum ration starts again and you've never been so glad of anything.[/if][if war.month == 11 && war.take == 0]November. Fog. Dark by half past four. You stand on the firestep in a world the width of your own arm, and every sound in it is close.[/if][if war.month == 11 && war.take == 1]November. Cold rain that turns to sleet at night. The rum comes round at stand-to in the morning and you hold it in your mouth as long as you can, for the warmth.[/if][if war.month == 12 && war.take == 0]December. Frost again, and the parcels start coming up from home: plum puddings in tins, mufflers, socks, a cake from the Co-op in greaseproof paper. The post corporal is the most popular man in the battalion.[/if][if war.month == 12 && war.take == 1]December. The short days. You're in the dark at both ends of every working party. Somebody in the next bay is singing a carol under his breath, badly, and nobody stops him.[/if][/if][if war.corps == tank][if war.month == 1 && war.take == 0][if war.stage == 3]January, at Wool, in Dorset. Huts on a heath, a wind straight off the sea, and sentries round a shed you aren't allowed near yet. You learn the engine off a blackboard in a hut that smells of wet greatcoats and paraffin, and every night you start a letter home and can't think what you're allowed to put.[else]January at the tankodrome. Frost on the tracks in the morning, and the tanks stood in rows under their nets like cattle in a frozen field. The fitters work with their gloves off and blow on their fingers between every nut.[/if][/if][if war.month == 1 && war.take == 1][if war.stage == 3]January. The ranges at Lulworth, on the cliffs, firing out over a grey sea. The wind takes your breath and the gun jumps in the cold, and between shoots you stand behind a hut stamping your feet and watching the gulls hang in the air over the targets.[else]January. The tank park is mud frozen into ruts the shape of the tracks, so every tank that moves lurches like a drunk. The crews sleep in a hut with a stove that glows red and warms a yard of air round it.[/if][/if][if war.month == 2 && war.take == 0][if war.stage == 3]February, and France: Bermicourt, a village with a chateau full of red tabs, and the workshops at Erin down the road. You learn her on the drill ground, round and round in the frozen mud, the gearsmen at the back working the levers when the hammer knocks on the engine cover.[else]February. The camouflage nets are stiff with frost and tear when you pull them. You spend the short days patching and painting her for the spring, and the paint won't dry in the cold.[/if][/if][if war.month == 2 && war.take == 1][if war.stage == 3]February at Erin. A town of sheds going up in a field, aeroplane hangars, the first engines hung up on chains, and fitters in overalls who've never seen the line and talk about it as if they had. Murray walks along the rows of plates rapping the rivets with his knuckle and shaking his head.[else]February. Every week the word comes that they're coming, and every week they don't. You kick a tin about the tank park and listen to the guns on the horizon, east, steady as a pump.[/if][/if][if war.month == 3 && war.take == 0]March. A cold wind across the tank park that gets in at the rivets and whistles. The nets flap on their poles all night like washing that won't dry.[/if][if war.month == 3 && war.take == 1]March. Mud again. A tank going out to the practice ground throws it off her tracks in clots the size of loaves, and the crew come back caked to the eyes.[/if][if war.month == 4 && war.take == 0]April. Rain and sun by turns, and the sheds steaming when the sun comes out. There are fitters everywhere with spanners, because there's a show coming, and everybody knows it, and nobody says where.[/if][if war.month == 4 && war.take == 1]April. Lying up in a wood with the tanks under nets, the trees just coming into leaf over them. A blackbird sings on her roof. In the evening the crews sit on the tracks and smoke, and the steel's still warm from the day.[/if][if war.month == 5 && war.take == 0]May. Warm at last. You take the guns out of her and strip them on a groundsheet in the sun, every part laid out in a row like knives in a drawer, and the oil smells sweet in the heat.[/if][if war.month == 5 && war.take == 1]May. Hawthorn along the lanes behind the tank park. Inside her in the afternoon the steel's too hot to lean on, and you work in your vest, and the sweat runs into your eyes.[/if][if war.month == 6 && war.take == 0]June. Inside her it's an oven before nine in the morning. The heat comes off the engine in waves and the fumes with it, and when you climb out the fresh air goes to your head like beer.[/if][if war.month == 6 && war.take == 1]June. Long light evenings. The crews dig the tanks in and string the nets over them, and lie on the grass underneath reading old papers, with the smell of hot oil and cut grass mixed.[/if][if war.month == 7 && war.take == 0]July. The tank park is dust. It gets in the bearings, in the tea, in the bread, in your ears, and the fitters curse it all day. The water's rationed, and you shave in the dregs of your tea.[/if][if war.month == 7 && war.take == 1]July. Thunder at night, and you lie awake in the hut counting, and it isn't guns, and then it is. In the morning the nets are full of rainwater, and somebody always forgets and pulls one.[/if][if war.month == 8 && war.take == 0]August. Heat, and wasps at the jam, and the harvest coming in round the tank park, French women with sickles who don't look up when a tank goes by.[/if][if war.month == 8 && war.take == 1]August. A smell of hot metal and hay. You grease the tracks link by link in the sun, and the grease runs, and the flies come to it in clouds.[/if][if war.month == 9 && war.take == 0]September. Mist in the mornings over the tank park, so the tanks come out of it one at a time like cows out of a field. The nights in the huts are getting cold again.[/if][if war.month == 9 && war.take == 1]September. Blackberries in the hedge behind the workshops. The fitters pick them in their breaks with black oily fingers, and the berries taste of petrol.[/if][if war.month == 10 && war.take == 0]October. Rain. The tank park goes back to mud, and she sinks into it a little more every night where she stands, as if she were tired.[/if][if war.month == 10 && war.take == 1]October. The leaves coming down on the nets. Greatcoats again, and the stove lit in the hut, and the smell of wet wool drying.[/if][if war.month == 11 && war.take == 0]November. Fog over the tank park, thick and yellow. You find her by the smell of oil and walk round her twice before you're sure she's yours.[/if][if war.month == 11 && war.take == 1]November. Short days. You work on her by a hurricane lamp in the afternoons, and your fingers go dead on the cold steel.[/if][if war.month == 12 && war.take == 0]December. Frost, and parcels from home. You eat your Christmas cake sitting on a track, out of the wind, in your greatcoat.[/if][if war.month == 12 && war.take == 1]December. The short days, and the nets white with frost every morning. Somebody has tied a sprig of holly to a gun mounting.[/if][/if][if war.corps == air][if war.month == 1 && war.take == 0]January. Snow on the field, and the machines stand in the hangars with their engines wrapped in sacking. The oil's like treacle in the mornings; Sallis warms it on a primus before he'll start one. In the hut the stove's red, and your bed's an arm's length from it.[/if][if war.month == 1 && war.take == 1]January. Too cold for flying most days, and nobody's sorry. When you do go up, the cold at height gets into your teeth till the fillings ache, and the gun oil thickens so the Lewis fires slow, like a man stammering.[/if][if war.month == 2 && war.take == 0]February. Low cloud and rain, and the field's a bog. The wheels throw mud up over the lower wings on take-off, and the riggers scrape it off with their hands. Days in the hut, playing nap for matches.[/if][if war.month == 2 && war.take == 1]February. A hard frost and a clear blue sky, which means flying, all day. You come down with your face stiff under the whale oil, and for ten minutes your mouth won't make words.[/if][if war.month == 3 && war.take == 0]March. The wind's gone round to the east. Every dawn the mechanics are out on the field in the dark, running the engines up, and the noise goes round the aerodrome like a threshing day.[/if][if war.month == 3 && war.take == 1]March. Rain, and the machines grounded, and the cards out in the hut. The east wind brings the guns with it at night.[/if][if war.month == 4 && war.take == 0]April. Larks over the aerodrome from first light, going up and up, singing, as if nobody had told them about any of it.[/if][if war.month == 4 && war.take == 1]April. Showers and sun, both in an hour, and rainbows over the field. You fly through a shower at three thousand feet and come out of it soaked through and freezing, with the sun in your eyes.[/if][if war.month == 5 && war.take == 0]May. Long light evenings. The machines go up after tea and come down in the dusk, and the field smells of cut grass and petrol and the stew from the cookhouse.[/if][if war.month == 5 && war.take == 1]May. From two thousand feet the hawthorn shows white in every hedge, and the whole country's drawn out under you in chalk lines, like a map on a schoolroom wall.[/if][if war.month == 6 && war.take == 0]June. Haymaking in the fields round the aerodrome. The French women used to look up from their rakes when the machines came in low over them. They don't any more.[/if][if war.month == 6 && war.take == 1]June. Thunderheads building up in the afternoons, white and tall, and no pilot will go near one. At night you sleep between sheets with the hut door open, and hear the guns like a cart on cobbles, a long way off.[/if][if war.month == 7 && war.take == 0]July. Heat on the field, and the dope on the wings smells stronger in the sun, sweet and sickly. On the ground you sweat in your shirt. Two miles up your feet are still cold.[/if][if war.month == 7 && war.take == 1]July. You fly in the morning, before the haze comes up. In the afternoon you lie on the grass in the shade of a hangar with your cap over your face and listen to the riggers singing.[/if][if war.month == 8 && war.take == 0]August. Rain on the hangar roofs at night like gravel thrown on a drum, and the cloud down on the poplars in the morning, and no flying, and nobody minds.[/if][if war.month == 8 && war.take == 1]August. Harvest in the fields round the aerodrome, the stooks standing in rows. From the air they look like stitches in a sack.[/if][if war.month == 9 && war.take == 0]September. Mist on the field at dawn so thick the machines wait in the hangar mouths with their engines ticking over, and the mechanics stand about with their hands in their pockets, waiting for the sun.[/if][if war.month == 9 && war.take == 1]September. The swallows sit along the wires by the hangars in rows, getting ready to go. Sallis says they go to Africa. He says it as if he'd like to go with them.[/if][if war.month == 10 && war.take == 0]October. Rain, and more rain. Days without flying, the cloud down on the poplars, the wind slapping the hangar canvas, and a fug of wet wool and pipe smoke in the hut.[/if][if war.month == 10 && war.take == 1]October. The first frost on the wings in the mornings. Sallis scrapes it off with the edge of his hand before anybody's let climb in.[/if][if war.month == 11 && war.take == 0]November. Fog on the field till noon, and dark by half past four. The machines hardly go up.[/if][if war.month == 11 && war.take == 1]November. Cold rain blowing across the field, and the windsock hanging heavy and wet on its pole.[/if][if war.month == 12 && war.take == 0]December. Frost, and the parcels coming up from home. Sallis gets a cake from Coventry and cuts it into sixteen with a hacksaw blade.[/if][if war.month == 12 && war.take == 1]December. The short days. Somebody's put a tree in a petrol tin in the hut, with spent cartridge cases hung on it for baubles.[/if][/if][if war.back_from_wound && !war.transferred] You're back with the battalion, the wound pulling every time you lift your arm, and the lads look at you as if you'd been somewhere they'd rather be.[/if][if war.back_from_wound && war.transferred] You're back with the [if war.corps == air]squadron[else]company[/if], the wound pulling every time you lift your arm, and the crew make you a brew without being asked.[/if][if war.lost_last == 1 && !war.transferred] {lost_last_name}'s place on the firestep has somebody from the draft in it, a lad who doesn't know where to put his feet.[/if][if war.lost_last >= 2 && !war.transferred] There are gaps in the section now. You keep looking for faces that aren't there.[/if][if war.lost_last >= 1 && war.transferred && war.take == 0] Word comes over from the battalion of men from home gone since. You hear it, and [if war.corps == tunnel]go down the shaft[else]go back to the work[/if].[/if][if war.lost_last >= 1 && war.transferred && war.take == 1 && war.corps != tank] A battalion man at the water point tells you who from home has gone west since. You don't ask him to say it twice.[/if][if war.lost_last >= 1 && war.corps == tank && war.take == 1 && war.tour >= 22] A battalion man at the water point tells you who from home has gone west since. You don't ask him to say it twice.[/if][if war.promoted_last && war.rank <= 4] The new stripe is sewn on crooked. Men who were your mates last week say '[if war.rank <= 2]Corporal[/if][if war.rank >= 3]Sarge[/if]' in a voice that isn't quite their own.[/if][if war.promoted_last && war.rank >= 6] Another pip on your cuff, sewn on by your servant by candlelight.[if war.rank == 7] You have the company now, what's left of it, and a captain's worries with a lieutenant's pay until the paper comes through.[/if][/if][if war.award_last] The {award_last_name} is in battalion orders. Nobody says a word about it to your face, and everybody talks about it behind your back.[/if][if war.detailed_last == wiring] Last tour the sergeant put you on a wiring party.[/if][if war.detailed_last == patrol] Last tour you were sent out on a patrol.[/if][if war.detailed_last == raid] Last tour they put you on a raid, whether you liked it or not.[/if][if war.detailed_last == listening] Last tour you did a stint in a listening post.[/if][if war.detailed_last == carrying] Last tour you were on a carrying party, two miles of trench each way.[/if][if war.detailed_last == bomb || war.detailed_last == lewis || war.detailed_last == snipe || war.detailed_last == signals || war.detailed_last == tunnel || war.detailed_last == bearer || war.detailed_last == tank || war.detailed_last == air] Last tour they sent you out on your own work, though you'd said you weren't fit.[/if][if war.detailed_last != none && war.detailed_ok] It went all right.[/if][if war.detailed_last != none && !war.detailed_ok] It went wrong, the way these things do.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.take == 0]Go on.[/if][if war.take == 1]Another tour.[/if]

w_duty.title: A front-line tour
w_duty.text:
[if war.duty == raid][if war.stage == 1][if war.month <= 9]Summer in the Loos country, among the slag heaps and the pithead towers, in trenches cut white into the chalk. Brigade wants to know who's holding the line opposite before the push that everybody whispers about and nobody's been told of.[else]Autumn in the old Loos line. Since the battle there are craters where the redoubt was, the rain has turned the chalk to a grey paste that gets under your nails, and brigade wants a prisoner to say who's come in opposite.[/if][elif war.stage == 2][if war.month <= 6]The Somme, the downland behind the line still green, larks over it, and the villages still with their roofs on. Before the big attack the brass hats want a prisoner every week to say what's opposite, and tonight it's the battalion's turn.[elif war.month <= 9]The Somme, after the first of July. Their new line is on the far side of a wood smashed to stumps, and on a warm night you can smell the wood from here, split green timber and gas and the dead.[else]The Somme in the autumn rain, the chalk gone to a grey glue that sucks at your boots. Their line's a row of flooded shell holes, and the raid's to find out which of them are held.[/if][elif war.stage == 3][if war.month <= 5]Arras[if war.month <= 4], after the hardest winter anybody can remember, with the frost still splitting the chalk of the parapet[else] in May, the chalk trenches east of the town white in the sun, and the dead of April not all buried[/if]. The staff want prisoners from every yard of the line opposite, and they want them now.[elif war.month <= 7]Flanders: flat wet fields round Wipers, ditches running between them, and every bit of rising ground is theirs. Something big is coming, and before it the staff want a man from every regiment opposite.[else]The salient in the autumn, the mud past anything you've known: shell holes lip to lip, full of green water, and their line a string of concrete pillboxes. Getting to one means an hour in that mud before you start.[/if][else][if war.month <= 3]Winter in the salient, in the line the battalion took last autumn: frozen shell holes, duckboard tracks, a German pillbox for company headquarters with its door facing the wrong way. Their raiders have been over twice this month, and the Old Man wants one of theirs back.[elif war.month <= 7]Since the retreat the line's new, scraped across farmland, with green corn coming up in no man's land and a farmhouse standing in their wire. Nobody's sure who's opposite now, or quite where.[else]Open country, and Jerry going back: hedges, orchards, villages with people still living in the cellars. Their line's a chain of posts along the hedgerows, and the raid's to take one before they move again.[/if][/if][/if][if war.duty == patrol][if war.stage == 1][if war.month <= 9]Summer in the Loos country. No man's land here is an old beet field gone to thistles, with the slag heaps black against the sky behind their line, and nobody's sure what they've done to their wire this week.[else]Autumn in the old Loos line. The men from the September attack are still lying out in front of their wire, in the long grass, and the patrol goes out among them.[/if][elif war.stage == 2][if war.month <= 6]The Somme, and the downland quiet, larks over no man's land all day and the wind smelling of turned earth. Somebody at brigade wants to know about every yard of their wire.[elif war.month <= 9]The Somme, after the first of July. Nobody's sure where their new line runs through the smashed woods, and the patrol's to go and find it.[else]The Somme in the autumn rain. The patrol's to find whether a line of shell holes out in front is theirs or empty, and in this weather it could be either.[/if][elif war.stage == 3][if war.month <= 5]Arras[if war.month <= 4], and the cold[/if]. No man's land in front of the town is chalk[if war.month <= 4] under old snow[else] scabbed with new grass, white under the flares[/if], and a man crawling on it shows like a fly on a tablecloth.[elif war.month <= 7]Flanders in the summer, flat as a board, the ditches still running and the frogs going in them all night. The patrol's to look at their wire before the big show everybody can feel coming.[else]The salient after the rains. There's no proper no man's land out here, only mud and water and pillboxes, and the patrol's to find which of them are held.[/if][else][if war.month <= 3]Winter in the salient. Out in front the shell holes are frozen over, and the ice cracks under a man's knee like a pistol shot.[elif war.month <= 7]Since the retreat the line's new, through fields and hedges nobody's fought over before. The patrol's to find where their posts are in the young corn.[else]Open country, and they're going back. The patrol's to find out whether the village in front is still held, and the lane into it smells of their horses.[/if][/if][/if][if war.duty == wiring][if war.stage == 1][if war.month <= 9]Summer in the Loos country, the nights short, and the chalk out in front throws back every flare like snow. The new belt has to be in before the push.[else]Autumn in the old Loos line, after the battle. The wire in front went in the bombardment, nearly all of it, and the line's been naked since.[/if][elif war.stage == 2][if war.month <= 6]The Somme, before the push. The wire in front of the battalion has to be thick enough to stop the Germans, with lanes left in it for our own men to go out by in the summer.[elif war.month <= 9]The Somme in the summer. The new line's only days old, a chain of shell holes joined up with a spade, and it has no wire at all.[else]The Somme in the autumn rain. The pickets won't hold in this mud: you screw them in and they lean over like drunks on a Saturday night.[/if][elif war.stage == 3][if war.month <= 5][if war.month <= 4]Arras, in a frost that's gone a foot down into the ground. The pickets have to be screwed into earth as hard as a flagstone.[else]Arras in May, and the chalk's dry and hard. The pickets squeal going in, and the noise carries.[/if][elif war.month <= 7]Flanders, the short summer nights. Under the grass the ground's wet a spade deep, and the pickets go in easy and come out easier.[else]The salient in the autumn. Wire's no use in this mud, everybody says, and you're to put it out anyway, round a pillbox that used to be theirs.[/if][else][if war.month <= 3]Winter in the salient, and word that they'll attack in the spring. Every battalion's wiring every night, belt behind belt.[elif war.month <= 7]Since the retreat the line's new and there's hardly any wire in front of it: a few strands across a field of young corn, and a farm gate.[else]Open country, going forward, and not much wiring to do. Tonight it's a few strands across a road at the edge of a village, in case they come back.[/if][/if][/if][if war.duty == listening][if war.stage == 1][if war.month <= 9]Summer in the Loos country, and the miners on both sides are busy under the chalk. Some nights in the post you can feel their picks through the ground, under your belly.[else]Autumn in the old Loos line, the nights getting longer. The post's in the lip of a crater from the battle, with the chalk raw and white in it and cold as a cellar step.[/if][elif war.stage == 2][if war.month <= 6]The Somme, before the push. Behind you the guns are coming up all night, wheels and harness and horses blowing, and out in the post you can hear the Alleyman listening to it.[elif war.month <= 9]The Somme in the summer, in a line nobody's had time to make. The post's a shell hole with a groundsheet over it, and the smell from no man's land comes in under the sheet.[else]The Somme in the autumn, and the post half full of water. You lie in it with the cold coming up through your greatcoat.[/if][elif war.stage == 3][if war.month <= 5]Arras[if war.month <= 4], a hard frost. Sound carries on frozen ground[else] in May, a still night. Sound carries over the chalk[/if]: a cough in their trench comes across as clear as a cough in chapel.[elif war.month <= 7]Flanders in the summer, the frogs going in the ditches all night, so loud you have to listen under them.[else]The salient in the autumn. The post's a shell hole with a duckboard laid across the water in it, and every sound out here is the mud sucking at somebody's boots.[/if][else][if war.month <= 3]Winter in the salient, and everybody waiting for their big attack. The colonel wants ears out in front every night, in case it's tonight.[elif war.month <= 7]Since the retreat the line's new, through farmland. The post's in a ditch under a hawthorn hedge, and the hedge drips on you all night.[else]Open country, and the line moving. The post's in a sunken lane outside a village, and you can hear their transport going away on the cobbles, east.[/if][/if][/if][if war.duty == carrying][if war.stage == 1][if war.month <= 9]Summer in the Loos country. The communication trench runs a mile and more through chalk, past the pithead towers, and the white dust of it gets in your teeth.[else]Autumn in the old Loos line, and rain. The trenches are chalk slurry to the knee, and everything the line needs comes up it on men's backs.[/if][elif war.stage == 2][if war.month <= 6]The Somme, before the push. Everything for the big attack goes up on men's backs at night: shells, wire, gas cylinders, water in petrol tins, more than anybody's ever seen.[elif war.month <= 9]The Somme in the summer, across the old front line and on over ground that was theirs, where nobody's had time to dig a trench to carry anything along.[else]The Somme in the autumn. The communication trenches have gone to soup, and the carrying parties go up over the top instead, on duckboards, in the open.[/if][elif war.stage == 3][if war.month <= 5]Arras: the carrying party goes up from the town through the caves and tunnels under it, by electric light, and comes out into the [if war.month <= 4]frost[else]night air[/if] at the far end.[elif war.month <= 7]Flanders in the summer, everything going up for the big show. The roads round Ypres are shelled every night, and the party goes up past the dead horses at Hell Fire Corner.[else]The salient in the autumn. There's no trench to carry along: a duckboard track over the mud a plank wide, and a man who steps off it can go in to his waist.[/if][else][if war.month <= 3]Winter in the salient, along duckboard tracks frozen slippery as glass. The party falls, and gets up, and falls.[elif war.month <= 7]Since the retreat, across new country: a line of posts in farmland, and the party goes up through an orchard and along a hedge.[else]Open country, going forward, and the carrying's mile on mile now, along roads that were theirs last week, with their signboards still up.[/if][/if][/if]

[if war.duty_nco]The platoon sergeant wants men for {duty_name} tonight, and it's your section's turn. You're to find the men, and he doesn't care how. The men from home know the work. The new men from the draft don't, and they know it too.[else]The sergeant wants men for {duty_name} tonight. {friend_line}[/if]

[if war.duty == raid]A raid: blackened faces, cap badges off, no pay books, coshes and Mills bombs, and a run across in the dark to drag a prisoner back. The ones who come back from raids don't sleep for a day after.[/if][if war.duty == patrol]A patrol means lying in no man's land for hours, cold right through, listening to Fritz talk in his trench and trying not to breathe.[/if][if war.duty == wiring]Wiring means out in front with mallets wrapped in sacking and coils of wire that bite through your gloves, freezing every time a flare goes up.[/if][if war.duty == listening]A listening post is a hole in the ground out past the wire, two men and a string back to the trench, and every sound in the dark is somebody coming.[/if][if war.duty == carrying]A carrying party: up the communication trench and back with ammunition boxes and duckboards and coils of wire, all night, in the wet, shelled by guns that know the route as well as you do.[/if]

choices.text: [if war.duty_nco]Take it out yourself.[else]Volunteer.[/if] ({duty_risk}, {duty_cost})
Send one of the men from home. He knows the work. (For him: {duty_risk})
Send one of the new men from the draft. The section will know you did. (For him: {duty_risk_draft})
Keep your head down and let him choose.

w_mission.title: Your own work
w_mission.text:
[if war.path == bomb][if war.stage == 1][if war.month <= 9]Summer in the Loos country, among the slag heaps. Bombing's the new trade this year, and the colonel wants his bombers to try the chalk trench opposite.[else]Autumn in the old Loos line. Since the battle the two lines are a bomb's throw apart among the craters where the redoubt was, and under the minnies the bombers fight over a few yards of wet chalk every night.[/if][elif war.stage == 2][if war.month <= 6]The Somme, before the push. The staff want to know what's in the deep dugouts under the trench opposite, and the bombers are to go and look.[elif war.month <= 9]The Somme in the summer, among the smashed woods, where the two lines run into each other and the bombing never stops, a bay won and a bay lost.[else]The Somme in the autumn rain. The bombs come out of the sandbag wet and gritty, and their trench is a ditch of mud.[/if][elif war.stage == 3][if war.month <= 5]Arras[if war.month <= 4], in the frost[/if]. Their trench is chalk, deep and well made, and the bombers have practised on a copy of it behind the line, dug out from the aeroplane photographs.[elif war.month <= 7]Flanders in the summer, before the big show. Their front line's a string of fortified farms and concrete blockhouses, and the bombers are to try one.[else]The salient in the autumn. Their posts are shell holes and pillboxes in the mud, and the bombers have fifty yards of it to cross before they can throw.[/if][else][if war.month <= 3]Winter in the salient, and the colonel wants a prisoner before their spring attack. The ground's frozen, and it rings under your boots like a yard.[elif war.month <= 7]Since the retreat the line's new, cut shallow through farmland, and their trench opposite runs along the edge of a field of young corn.[elif war.month <= 8]Open country, and the Germans going back. Their trench tonight is an old one of ours from 1916, and the old hands know every turn of it.[else]The old Hindenburg Line, the deepest trench you've ever seen, concrete steps going down into the dugouts and the wire in front like a gentleman's hedge.[/if][/if][/if][if war.path == lewis][if war.stage == 1][if war.month <= 9]Summer in the Loos country. The Lewis gun's new this year, the battalion has only a few, and the Germans have heard about them.[else]Autumn in the old Loos line, on the chalk among the craters, where the two lines are close enough to hear each other cough.[/if][elif war.stage == 2][if war.month <= 6]The Somme, before the push. The gun teams have been told the guns go over with the first wave, and they've practised it on a field of beet behind the line.[elif war.month <= 9]The Somme in the summer, in a line that was theirs a week ago, with the flies everywhere and the smell of lime.[else]The Somme in the autumn. The mud gets into everything, and a Lewis gun hates mud more than anything.[/if][elif war.stage == 3][if war.month <= 5][if war.month <= 4]Arras, a cold spring. The oil thickens in the gun overnight, and you keep the drums inside your greatcoat against your chest.[else]Arras in May, warm at last, and the chalk dust gets into the gun the way the frost did in April.[/if][elif war.month <= 7]Flanders in the summer, flat ground, and Jerry's aeroplanes overhead all day, looking.[else]The salient in the autumn. The gun has to be kept off the mud on a sheet of corrugated iron, and you sleep with the breech cover inside your shirt.[/if][else][if war.month <= 3]Winter in the salient, waiting for their big attack. The Lewis guns are the line now: posts spread out across the mud, a gun in each, and gaps between.[elif war.month <= 7]Since the retreat, in a new line through farmland, the gun in a hedge bottom with a field of young corn in front and the larks going up out of it all day.[else]Open country, going forward. The gun goes with the leading platoon, and you carry it across stubble and through gaps in hedges.[/if][/if][/if][if war.path == signals][if war.stage == 1][if war.month <= 9]Summer in the Loos country, chalk underfoot, and the cable's pinned along the trench wall with bent nails. A shell anywhere near brings it down.[else]Autumn in the old Loos line. Since the battle the lines are cut a dozen times a night, and the chalk's so wet the wire shorts out in it.[/if][elif war.stage == 2][if war.month <= 6]The Somme, before the push. The cable's being buried six feet down for the big attack, and until it's done the old lines run along the trench walls the way they always have.[elif war.month <= 9]The Somme in the summer, in ground that was theirs, where the only cable is what somebody ran out across the open.[else]The Somme in the autumn. The mud takes the cable down into it, and you find it by pulling it up out of the slime a yard at a time.[/if][elif war.stage == 3][if war.month <= 5]Arras: the signal office is a cellar under the town, warm and stale with the smell of paraffin, and the lines run out of it through the [if war.month <= 4]frost[else]chalk[/if] to every company.[elif war.month <= 7]Flanders in the summer. The ground's too wet to bury a cable deep, their guns are on the ridges, and every line along the canal bank is cut by noon.[else]The salient in the autumn. Lines don't last an hour in this mud, and half the messages go back by pigeon and runner anyway.[/if][else][if war.month <= 3]Winter in the salient. The wires run along the duckboard tracks, frozen stiff, and snap when they're bent.[elif war.month <= 7]Since the retreat, in a new line through farmland. The wire runs along hedges and over field gates, and last week the cows got at it.[else]Open country, going forward. The lines run out behind the advance across the fields, and a lorry or a gun team drives over them every hour.[/if][/if][/if][if war.path == snipe][if war.stage == 1][if war.month <= 9]Summer in the Loos country. There's a slag heap behind their line, and a German sniper on it somewhere, because men keep being hit in the same bay.[else]Autumn in the old Loos line, the craters full of rain. Their snipers are up in the ruins of the pit buildings; ours are down in the chalk.[/if][elif war.stage == 2][if war.month <= 6]The Somme, before the push, in a quiet sector the staff want kept quiet. The sniping officer wants their snipers kept down.[elif war.month <= 9]The Somme in the summer, among the smashed woods. Every stump could hold a sniper, and some of them do.[else]The Somme in the autumn. The light's poor and goes early, and there's no more than eight hours of it to see anything in.[/if][elif war.stage == 3][if war.month <= 5]Arras: the plate's set in a parapet of [if war.month <= 4]frozen [/if]chalk, and you go out to it in the dark[if war.month <= 4] over crusted snow[else], with the hawthorn behind the line sweet on the air[/if].[elif war.month <= 7]Flanders in the summer, flat land, their line on the low ridge. They look down on you all day, and you look up at them.[else]The salient in the autumn. The hide's in a smashed pillbox, the concrete cold and sweating, looking out over the mud to their line.[/if][else][if war.month <= 3]Winter in the salient, a few posts spread across the mud, and sniping's the one thing that goes on every day.[elif war.month <= 7]Since the retreat, in a new line through farmland. The hide's in a hedge, and their line runs along the edge of a wood across a field of young corn.[else]Open country, going forward, and their snipers are in the church towers and the attics of every village.[/if][/if][/if][if war.path == tunnel][if war.stage == 1][if war.month <= 9]Summer in the Loos country, under the chalk, where both sides have been mining since the spring. Chalk cuts clean, and it carries sound like a bell.[else]Autumn in the old Loos line, under the craters where the redoubt was. Their miners are working below you, and yours below them.[/if][elif war.stage == 2][if war.month <= 6]The Somme, before the push. There are mines going in under their line for the summer, big ones, and nobody's to talk about them. This gallery's one of the small ones.[elif war.month <= 9]The Somme in the summer. The big mines went up on the first of July, and the galleries that are left are for listening, and for small charges.[else]The Somme in the autumn. Water comes into the gallery faster than the pump can take it out.[/if][elif war.stage == 3][if war.month <= 5]Arras: the tunnellers have been digging all winter, under the town and out under the line, and you can walk a mile underground by electric light.[elif war.month <= 7]Flanders in the summer. The mines under the ridge went up in June and shook the billets twenty miles off, and now the galleries go down through wet sand into the blue clay.[else]The salient in the autumn. Up top it's mud; down here in the blue clay it's dry, and warm, and quiet.[/if][else][if war.month <= 3]Winter in the salient. There's hardly any mining left in the war, and most of the company's digging dugouts, but here both sides are still under the ground, listening.[elif war.month <= 7]Since the retreat the company's mostly digging deep dugouts for the new line, but under one old trench there's a gallery of theirs, and somebody's heard digging.[else]Open country, going forward, and the company's work is bridges and booby traps now. But the old line here has galleries under it, theirs and ours, and somebody's heard digging.[/if][/if][/if][if war.path == bearer][if war.stage == 1][if war.month <= 9]Summer in the Loos country. The aid post's in a miner's cottage in the village behind the line, and the carry back to it is a mile of chalk trench.[else]Autumn in the old Loos line. The men from September are still lying out in the beet in front of their wire, and nobody goes for them now. The bearers are for the living.[/if][elif war.stage == 2][if war.month <= 6]The Somme, before the push. The aid posts are being dug deeper and wider for the summer, and the bearers are learning the way to them in the dark.[elif war.month <= 9]The Somme, after the first of July. The carry back is a mile over ground that was theirs, and the trench you need is always the one that's been blown in.[else]The Somme in the autumn. It takes six men to carry one through this mud, and the carry back to the aid post can take four hours.[/if][elif war.stage == 3][if war.month <= 5]Arras: the dressing station's in the caves under the town, lit by electric bulbs, and the carry back to it is over [if war.month <= 4]frozen [/if]chalk.[elif war.month <= 7]Flanders in the summer, the ditches still running between the fields. The aid post's a concrete shelter on the canal bank.[else]The salient in the autumn. Six to a stretcher in this mud, and the carry back along the duckboards can take all night.[/if][else][if war.month <= 3]Winter in the salient, along the frozen duckboard tracks, the stretcher slipping every few yards.[elif war.month <= 7]Since the retreat, in a new line through farmland. The aid post's in a farmhouse kitchen, with the plates still on the dresser.[else]Open country, going forward, and the aid post moves every day. The carry back's longer every night.[/if][/if][/if][if war.path == tank][if war.stage == 3][if war.month <= 5]Arras country: chalk, and [if war.month <= 4]sleet[else]dust[/if], and the smashed suburbs of the town, and the roads choked with guns going up.[elif war.month <= 8]Flanders, flat and wet under the grass, and every road in the salient watched from their ridge.[else]Autumn, and the company's out of the salient, on chalk downland further south where the ground still drains, and nobody will say why.[/if][else][if war.month <= 3]Winter, the ruts frozen in the tank park, and talk all along the line of a German attack in the spring.[elif war.month <= 7][if flag.tk18_whippet]Since the retreat the Whippets have been kept back behind the new line, to go wherever a hole opens.[else]Since the retreat the line's new, scraped across farmland in front of Amiens, and nobody knows the ground.[/if][else]Open country now: stubble, hedges, villages with their roofs on, and the Germans going back.[/if][/if][/if][if war.path == air][if war.stage == 3][if war.month <= 7]Summer over Flanders. From up there the salient's a brown smear across the green, with the ruins of Ypres in the middle of it, white as bone.[else]The salient from the air in the autumn: shell holes lip to lip, and every one full of water, flashing up at you like broken glass.[/if][else][if war.month <= 3]Winter over the old salient, the ground white, their lines drawn on it in black like a pen drawing.[elif war.month <= 7]Since the retreat the squadron's on a new field further back, and the line below is new: farmland, hedges, villages that still have their roofs.[else]Open country under you now, and the line moving east every day, so the maps are out of date by the time they're printed.[/if][/if][/if]

[if war.path == lewis && war.stake == 0]A raid is going over at two in the morning and the gun's to cover it. You set up at the head of a sap out past the wire with your No. 2 and four drums of rounds. The gun's casing is so cold it burns your fingers through the mittens. When the raiders go, you fire short bursts over their heads at the German parapet, and every burst lights you up like a lamp in a window, and every German on that stretch can see exactly where you are.[/if][if war.path == lewis && war.stake == 1]A German two-seater comes over low in the evening, slow and fat and close enough to see the observer's goggles. The officer wants the gun up on its post for it. You'll be standing in the open with the gun pointing at the sky and your back to their line, firing up at it while it fires down at you.[/if][if war.path == signals && war.stake == 0]The line to battalion's gone again. Somewhere in the half mile of communication trench behind you a shell has cut it, and the colonel wants the company commander and can't have him. You take the pliers, a reel of cable and the buzzer, and go along it in the dark, running the wire through your fingers, feeling for the break.[/if][if war.path == signals && war.stake == 1]The line to battalion's gone again, and this time it isn't in the trench. Between the front line and the support line the wire crosses a strip of the old no man's land, out on top, and something has cut it out there. Battalion is shouting into a dead telephone. Somebody has to go out and find the break.[/if][if war.path == bomb]A bombing raid tonight: eight of you, faces blacked with burnt cork, no cap badges, no pay books, a sandbag each of Mills bombs. Into their trench, along it a bay at a time, a prisoner if you can get one, and back before their machine guns wake up.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Before dawn you crawl into the hide in the parapet, a steel plate with a slit, a sack over the slit, your observer beside you with the telescope and the notebook. You stay till dark. They have snipers looking for this plate. Some mornings you see a man over there shaving in a bit of mirror, his braces down, and he puts you in mind of your father at the scullery sink.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]Down the shaft, along the gallery on your back on the trolley, to the face. Candle, the smell of wet clay and your own sweat. You lie with the listening stick against the clay and listen for them. If you can hear them digging, they're far enough off. If they stop, they're listening for you. If it goes quiet for a day, they've laid a charge.[/if][if war.path == bearer && war.stake == 0]A man of the night patrol is down out on the wire in front of the next company, and he's calling. The bearers are wanted. Four of you, a stretcher, the red cross on your arm, which is no use at all in the dark, and the flares going up over the place where the calling is.[/if][if war.path == tank][if war.stake == 0]The order comes at dusk: take her up to the line tonight, to a lying-up place behind the support trench, ready for a show in the morning. Four miles across country in the dark, at a walk, behind a guide with a lamp, along a white tape somebody has laid on the ground. Every yard of it, they'll hear you coming.[/if][if war.stake == 1]A tape's been laid from the tank park to the start line, and the guide is to meet you at the crossroads at ten. The nets come off, the engine has to be started, and then it's the whole night at a man's pace, with the shells feeling for the roads and the enemy listening for engines.[/if][/if][if war.path == air][if war.stake == 0]Your name's on the board in the flight office for the morning: a shoot with one of the heavy batteries, on a German battery in a wood that's been shelling the road. Up and down the same beat for an hour and more, straight and level, while the battery fires and the Archie gunners over the line get your height and keep it.[/if][if war.stake == 1]Your name's on the board for photographs tomorrow: the line opposite the corps, all of it, in strips, from five thousand feet, dead straight and dead level so the plates join up. Dead straight and dead level is what the German scouts like best, coming out of the sun.[/if][/if][if war.path == bearer && war.stake == 1]A man of the wiring party was hit at dusk and is lying in a shell hole thirty yards out. It's light enough now for their sniper to see the hole, and he has already hit the first man who went for him. The bearers are wanted.[/if]

The work's yours now. You can say you're not fit for it. You'll usually be sent anyway.

choices.text: [if war.path == lewis]Take the gun up.[/if][if war.path == signals]Go.[/if][if war.path == bomb]Black your face and go.[/if][if war.path == snipe]Go out to the hide.[/if][if war.path == tunnel]Go down.[/if][if war.path == bearer]Take the stretcher and go.[/if][if war.path == tank]Take her up.[/if][if war.path == air]Get your coat and go out to the machine.[/if] ({mission_risk})
Say you're not fit for it tonight.

w_sick.title: Rest
w_sick.text:
[if war.take == 0]Out at rest, in a barn behind the lines. Somebody's got a mouth organ going and somebody else is
frying bread in a mess tin, and the smell of it should make you hungry. You hold your mug of
tea in both hands so the others won't see it shake. It shakes anyway. The tea goes cold and you
don't drink it.[else]Out at rest. You've slept twelve hours and you're more tired than when you lay down. Every time a door
bangs in the farmyard you're flat on the straw before you know you've moved, and the others
pretend they haven't noticed, which is kind of them, and you hate it.[/if]

The medical officer holds a sick parade every morning at seven. He's a busy man, and a tired
one, and he's seen every way there is of swinging the lead.

choices.text: Report sick. The MO may give you a tour out of the line.
Say nothing and carry on.

w_course.title: A course
w_course.text:
The company sergeant major stops you at the water cart. There's a place going on a course,
two weeks behind the lines, and he's put your name down unless you'd rather he didn't.

[if war.course == lewis]The Lewis gun: twenty-eight pounds of it, a drum of forty-seven rounds on top like a gramophone record, and a temper. When it jams it jams in the worst place. The gun team are out of the attacks till they're needed and then they're needed more than anybody, and every German gunner looks for them first.[/if][if war.course == signals]Signals: flags, lamps, the buzzer, the field telephone and its miles of wire. When the wire's cut, and it's always cut, the signaller runs the message himself, across whatever's between him and battalion.[/if][if war.course == bomb]Bombing: the Mills bomb, pin and lever, four seconds. The bombers go first along an enemy trench, a bay at a time, and the men who come back from a bombing course don't joke about it.[/if][if war.course == snipe]Sniping: a rifle with a telescopic sight, a hide in the parapet, a partner with a periscope and a notebook. Hours of nothing. Then a second.[/if][if war.course == bearer]Stretcher-bearing: field dressings, splints, the tourniquet and when not to use it, and how four men carry a fifth through a trench built for one. The bearers carry no rifle. They go out to where the fire is because that's where the wounded are, and more of them are decorated than anybody, and more of them are killed.[/if][if war.course == lead]An NCO course: map reading, fire orders, how to keep a section together when the corporal's gone. They want men who can take charge.[/if]
[if start == mill && war.course == lewis && war.mate2] Duckworth says his dad could strip one blindfold. "It's only a loom that shoots," he says.[/if]

choices.text: Take it. Two weeks out of the line, and a trade after.
Stay with the section.

w_tunnel.title: The tunnellers
w_tunnel.text:
The Royal Engineers want miners. Six shillings a day against your one, out of the attacks, and
work you know. The tunnellers do not go over the top. They go under it.

choices.text: Go to the tunnellers. You will leave the section.
Stay with the men from home.
Push on. ({risk_push})
Help the man beside you. ({risk_help})
Go to ground. ({risk_ground})

[if war.stalled]Get up and [if war.battle == somme_autumn || war.battle == passchendaele]drag the section on through the mud.[else]get the section moving, wire or no wire.[/if][else][if war.battle == spring_offensive]Go along the bay and hold the section together.[else]Get them across: go out in front and take the section with you.[/if][/if] ({risk_lead})

w_leave.title: Home on leave

choices.text: Go back. A stripe is waiting: [if war.corps == air]the squadron[else][if war.transferred]your company[else]the battalion[/if][/if] promotes the men who return.
Go before the board for a commission.
Take it: {offer0}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer1}. Your war ends here.
Take it: {offer2}. Your war ends here.

e_armistice.title: The Armistice
e_armistice.text:
{ending_line}

Nobody cheers, where you are. The guns stop, and the silence comes down so hard that men look
up at the sky as if something's wrong with it. Somebody starts to laugh and can't stop. A
corporal sits down on an ammunition box and takes his boots off, both of them, right there in
the open, and nobody tells him not to.

You are {age} years old and {rank_a}, and you have been in France since you were a boy. You
can smell the wet and the cordite and the horse lines, and under all of it, for the first time
in years, nothing burning.

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_posting.title: Home
e_posting.text:
{ending_line}

The war goes on without you. You read it in the paper over breakfast, like everybody else,
the long columns in small print, and you read every name, every day, and you know some of them.

Some nights you're glad. Some nights you lie awake in a proper bed with clean sheets, listening
to the rain on the slates, and you'd give anything to be in a wet bay with the lads, and you
couldn't say to anybody why.

[if flag.ro_sw_first][if flag.ro_sw_ended || flag.ro_sw_jilted]{sweetheart} is married to somebody else. You see her in the street with a pram, and she smiles, and you lift your cap.[else][if flag.ro_sw_married]You're home with {sweetheart}, in a house of your own, with the war in the paper on the table between you every morning.[else][if flag.ro_sw_wed16 || flag.ro_sw_wed17]You marry {sweetheart} that spring, in your uniform because it's the best thing you have.[else][if flag.ro_sw_after || flag.ro_sw_wait2]{sweetheart} didn't have to wait till it was over after all. You're married that spring.[else]You walk out with {sweetheart} on Sundays, the way you did before.[/if][/if][/if][/if][/if][if flag.ro_fr_promise || flag.ro_fr_address] Now and then a letter comes from France, from Marthe. You answer every one.[/if]

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_captured.title: Taken
e_captured.text:
{ending_line}

A boy in grey with a rifle bigger than he is takes your water bottle and your cigarettes and,
after a moment, gives you one of the cigarettes back. You walk east all day with your hands on
your head, then without, past their guns and their horses and their wounded, who look exactly
like yours.

The rest of your war is behind wire: black bread, turnip soup, work in a salt mine or on a
farm, letters that take months. Your mother gets a card in your handwriting from a camp with a
name she can't say, and she takes it round to every house in the street.

[if flag.ro_sw_first][if flag.ro_sw_ended || flag.ro_sw_jilted]{sweetheart} hears from your mother that you are missing, and then that you are a prisoner, and says she's glad you're out of it.[else][if flag.ro_sw_married]{sweetheart} is told you are missing, and for weeks she doesn't know if she's a wife or a widow. Then the card in your hand comes through the Red Cross. She sends a parcel every week after that, and half of them never reach you.[else][if flag.ro_sw_wed16 || flag.ro_sw_wed17]{sweetheart} waits for the card through the Red Cross like everyone else, and then writes to the camp every week. One letter in three reaches you. You keep them all, in your cap.[else][if flag.ro_sw_after || flag.ro_sw_wait2]{sweetheart} writes to the camp every week. One letter in three reaches you. She is still waiting, she says. Now it's a different kind of waiting.[else]{sweetheart} writes to the camp now and then, through the Red Cross.[/if][/if][/if][/if][/if][if flag.ro_fr_writes || flag.ro_fr_promise] Somewhere a letter from Marthe is lying in a sorting office, addressed to a man who isn't there.[/if]

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_invalided.title: Wounded out
e_invalided.text:
{ending_line}

[if war.end_cause == battle && war.corps != tank && war.corps != air]You lie where you fell till the light goes, and the stretcher-bearers find you by your calling. You don't remember calling.[/if][if war.end_cause == shell && war.corps != air]The shell comes down in the bay and the next thing you know you're on the duckboards with a man you don't know kneeling on your arm to stop the bleeding.[/if][if war.end_cause == sortie]Out in front, in the dark. The others drag you back through the wire on a groundsheet, and every yard of it you feel.[/if][if war.end_cause == assign || war.end_cause == other || war.end_cause == underground]It happens fast, the way it always does, and then for a long while nothing happens at all.[/if][if war.corps == tank && war.end_cause != sortie]Splinters and the heat inside her, and then you're on the ground beside her tracks, and somebody is cutting your sleeve off.[/if][if war.corps == air && war.end_cause != sortie]The pilot gets the machine down on our side of the line, and men run out to you from a battery, and you don't remember the landing.[/if]

Morphia at the dressing station, a label tied to your tunic button, the clearing station, the ambulance train. The hospital ship smells of carbolic and vomit and the sea. In England a woman gives you tea with sugar in it, and you cry like a child and can't stop, and she just holds the cup for you till you can.

Weeks in a hospital bed. Then a medical board: three officers at a table, your papers, a doctor's hand on the wound. No longer physically fit for war service. They give you a paper to say so, and a pension of a few shillings a week, by the size of the wound.

You go home in hospital blue, then in your own clothes that don't fit. [if war.stage >= 3 || war.stage == 2 && war.month >= 9]A silver badge on your lapel, so that nobody in the street hands you a white feather.[else]In the street a girl you've never seen pushes a white feather into your buttonhole, because you're young and out of uniform, and you let her.[/if] The wound aches when it rains.

[if start == mill]The mill takes you back on lighter work, sweeping and carrying for the tacklers, and the women in the weaving shed stop the looms for a minute when you come in, and then start them again.[/if][if start == pit]You can't go back down. They find you a job on the screens at the pit head, picking stone out of the coal with the old men and the boys, and every morning you watch the cage go down without you.[/if][if start == farm]Your father puts you on the light work, and doesn't say anything about it, and gets up an hour earlier himself so there's less for you to do.[/if][if start == city]The firm keeps your desk, as it promised. The other desks fill with women and old men, and the casualty lists go up in the front hall, and you read them every morning before you take your coat off.[/if][if war.mate1 || war.mate2 || war.mate3] Letters come from the section. You read the names in them, and the names that aren't in them.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_first][if flag.ro_sw_ended || flag.ro_sw_jilted]{sweetheart} is walking out with somebody else now. She crosses the road to say she's glad you're home, and she means it.[else][if flag.ro_sw_married]{sweetheart} meets every train for a week till yours comes. She doesn't look at the wound first. She looks at your face.[else][if flag.ro_sw_wed16 || flag.ro_sw_wed17]You marry {sweetheart} in the spring, by licence, in your hospital blue because your suit won't go over the bandages, and the ringers ring what bells they can.[else][if flag.ro_sw_after || flag.ro_sw_wait2]{sweetheart} said she would wait till it was over, and it's over for you sooner than either of you thought, and not whole. You're married in the spring.[else]{sweetheart} comes to see you the first Sunday. You walk, slowly, and she doesn't hurry you.[/if][/if][/if][/if][/if][if flag.ro_fr_promise || flag.ro_fr_address] You write to Ternecourt. A letter comes back after a long while: Marthe is glad you are alive, and she does not say what else.[/if]

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_broken.title: Shell shock
e_broken.text:
{ending_line}

It's your hands first. You look down and they won't stop, and then it's your legs, and then
you're lying in the bottom of the trench and you can hear somebody making a noise like a
kicked dog and it's you. They carry you down the line on a stretcher, though there's not a
mark on you, and you're ashamed of that the whole way.

[if war.stage >= 4 || war.stage == 3 && war.month >= 6]At the clearing station they tie a label to your tunic with four letters on it, NYDN: Not Yet Diagnosed, Nervous. It means they don't know what's wrong with you either.[else]At the clearing station they tie a label to your tunic that says shell shock, and the orderly who reads it looks at you a long moment, as if you might be shamming.[/if] A train, a ship, a train. Nobody on them talks much.

[if war.commissioned]A hospital for officers in a big house in the country: lawns, a lake, men in good suits who scream in the night, and a doctor who asks you, every morning, what you dreamed.[else]A hospital for nerve cases, a long ward of men like you. Some shake. Some don't speak at all. One stammers so badly he writes everything down, and his writing is beautiful. A doctor asks you, every morning, what you dreamed, and you lie to him.[/if] They try rest, and milk puddings, and weaving baskets, and in time you sleep three hours a night, then four.

A medical board, and a paper: no longer fit for war service. [if war.stage >= 3 || war.stage == 2 && war.month >= 9]A silver badge for your lapel, so that nobody hands you a white feather.[/if] The doctors call it neurasthenia. At home a door banging sends you under the table. Your mother learns to close them quietly. Your father doesn't talk about it, which is how he talks about it.

[if start == mill]The noise of the weaving shed is too much. You do the books for the Co-op instead, in a back room with the door shut, and the women bring you tea and don't say anything.[/if][if start == pit]You can't go down.
