The cage, the dark, the roof talking: you stand at the pit head with your snap tin and can't step in. The manager finds you a job at the lamp cabin, counting the lamps out and in.[/if][if start == farm]The farm is quiet, which helps. You go out with the dog before it's light, every day, and walk the hedges till your hands stop.[/if][if start == city]The firm keeps your desk. The trams are the worst, the bang of the points. You walk to the office instead, an hour each way, and your mother puts dinner by.[/if]

[if flag.ro_sw_first][if flag.ro_sw_ended || flag.ro_sw_jilted]{sweetheart} hears you're home, and ill, and sends a card with violets on it, and doesn't come.[else][if flag.ro_sw_married]{sweetheart} sits with you in the evenings when your hands won't stop. She doesn't ask. When a door bangs she's between you and it before you know.[else][if flag.ro_sw_wed16 || flag.ro_sw_wed17]{sweetheart} comes to the hospital. The first time you can't speak to her. The second time you can. The wedding waits a year, and then it doesn't.[else][if flag.ro_sw_after || flag.ro_sw_wait2]{sweetheart} comes to the hospital, and comes again, and says she'll wait, and does.[else]{sweetheart} writes to the hospital, short letters about the weather and home, which are the only kind you can read.[/if][/if][/if][/if][/if][if flag.ro_fr_promise || flag.ro_fr_address] A letter from Marthe comes to the house. It's a year before you can answer it, and by then there's nobody left at that address.[/if]

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_court.title: Court-martial
e_court.text:
{ending_line}

The court sits in a schoolroom behind the lines, three officers at a table with the children's
sums still on the blackboard behind them. Nobody asks how long you'd been in the line. You
don't know how to tell them about the noise. It takes twenty minutes.

Most sentences are commuted. Most men go to prison, or back to the line under a cloud that
follows them into every bay. Your name goes in the paper at home, or it doesn't, and either way
your mother stops going to chapel.

[if flag.ro_sw_first][if flag.ro_sw_ended || flag.ro_sw_jilted]{sweetheart} reads your name in the paper, or hears it, and doesn't say anything to anybody.[else][if flag.ro_sw_married]{sweetheart} goes on going to chapel, and sits where everyone can see her, every Sunday.[else][if flag.ro_sw_wed16 || flag.ro_sw_wed17]{sweetheart}'s father forbids her to write to you. She writes anyway, once, and it's the only letter you get.[else][if flag.ro_sw_after || flag.ro_sw_wait2]{sweetheart}'s father forbids her to write to you. She writes anyway, once, and it's the only letter you get.[else]You don't write to {sweetheart}. You can't think what to say.[/if][/if][/if][/if][/if]

Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

e_error.title: Lost track
e_error.text:
The war asked a question no scene answers. This is a content bug: Menu, Save code, and send it with a note.
Of the section from home, {friends_home} came home. Awards: {awards_line}. The record: {grade}.

y_1915.title: France
y_1915.text:
You come off the boat at Boulogne into rain, and march up a cobbled hill past a shuttered boulangerie and French women who
don't look at you, to a camp of wet tents on a cliff. The sea's grey and the sky's grey and
somewhere inland, so faint you think it's thunder, you can hear the guns.

Nine of you from home in the same section. {section_line}

choices.text: Go up the line.

y_1916.title: The second year
y_1916.text:
A year in France. You know now what you didn't know last spring: which noise to duck for and
which to ignore, how to sleep in four inches of water, how to eat with a dead man in the
parapet a yard from your mess tin.

You're {rank_a} now. {section_line} Everybody says this is the year. The big push. The
end of it by the autumn.

choices.text: Go back up the line.

y_1917.title: The third year
y_1917.text:
Nobody says it'll be over by the autumn any more. Nobody says anything about when.

You're {rank_a} now, and you've been out long enough that the new lads call you an old
sweat and mean it. {section_line} [if war.section <= 5]You don't make friends with the new men the way you did. You learn their names when you have to.[/if]

choices.text: Go back up the line.

y_1918.title: The fourth year
y_1918.text:
The Russians are out of it. The Americans are coming, they say, millions of them, and nobody
has seen one. Everybody knows the Germans have men to spare now, and that they'll come in the
spring.

You're {rank_a}. {section_line} [if start == mill]You can't remember the shed, some days. You can remember the noise of it.[/if][if start == pit]You can't remember the pit, some days. You can remember the dark of it, and the smell of the lamp.[/if][if start == city]You can't remember the office, some days. You can remember the scratch of the pens.[/if][if start == farm]You can't remember the farm, some days. You can remember the smell of the byre on a winter morning.[/if] You can't remember your mother's face without the photograph.

choices.text: Go back up the line.

mill.label: The mill town
mill.summary: Cotton and weaving sheds, the mill whistle at six. Half the men in your street joined the same week.

pit.label: The pit village
pit.summary: The colliery, the chapel and the club. You have worked underground since you were fourteen.

city.label: The city office
city.summary: A clerk's stool in a shipping office, a season ticket on the tram, and a rifle club on Saturdays.

farm.label: The farm village
farm.summary: Horses, hedges and a shotgun for the rooks. The harvest was in when the recruiting sergeant came.

glossary.means: A small French café-bar behind the line that sold soldiers egg and chips, beer and wine.
The raised step in a trench that a man stood on to see and fire over the top.
The bank of earth and sandbags along the front of a trench, facing the enemy.
The bank of earth along the back of a trench.
Soldiers' word for Britain, home. A 'Blighty one' was a wound bad enough to get you sent there.
A street in the City, London's square mile of banks and insurance offices, where the clerks worked.
The old word for insurance, above all life insurance; many firms had it in their name.
A big bound book in which an office wrote every sum owed and paid, by hand, in ink.
The department of an insurance office that insured ships and their cargoes.
The small sum an office kept in a tin for stamps and cab fares, every penny written down.
The neat, even handwriting a clerk was trained in for keeping ledgers.
In book-keeping, a page's total copied to the top of the next page, so the count never stops.
A pad of soft paper on a desk, for drying wet ink.
Lettering in thin gold leaf; the gilder was the craftsman who laid it.
A board in an office, church or school listing its men who had gone to the war, and those killed.
The largest insurance company in London, with thousands of clerks; 'the Pru' for short.
The great London market where ships and cargoes were insured.
The street of banks in the City of London.
The big railway station on the edge of the City, where the trains from east London came in.
The firm's own football team of eleven men, which played other offices on Saturday afternoons.
Look after her properly; here, that the firm will go on paying her money.
A suburb of small terraced houses in east London, a short train ride from the City.
The London railway station where the leave trains from the Channel boats came in.
London's electric railway, running in tunnels under the streets.
The small gauze hood on a gas lamp that glowed white when lit; houses were lit by gas.
The small back room of a house with the sink and the wash boiler, where washing was done.
The little book the landlord's collector signed each week when the rent was paid.
The best room, facing the street, kept for visitors and Sundays; its curtains drawn by day meant a death.
A tin for keeping tea in; many families kept their important papers in it too.
A famous make of English biscuits, sold in decorated tins.
A well-known English soap, clear and amber-coloured; a small comfort from home.
A huge German airship; from 1915 they crossed the sea at night to bomb London and other towns.
A long gas-filled craft driven by engines, such as the German Zeppelins that bombed London by night.
Midday; working people called the midday meal dinner.
A pound: about three weeks of a private soldier's pay.
A halfpenny, the small copper coin a child might be given for running an errand.
Bets written on scraps of paper and run to a street bookmaker; against the law, and everybody did it.
A big, cheap department store in Holborn, London, famous for sports goods and toys.
A J. Lyons teashop, one of a chain all over London: cheap, clean, with waitresses in black and white.
A big London variety theatre, with songs, comic sketches and turns.
A theatre of comic songs and turns; its songs were what everybody knew and sang.
A public holiday, when all London crowded on to trains and trams for a day out.
The Pickwick Papers, Charles Dickens's comic novel of 1837, loved and often read aloud.
The Londoner's seaside town on the Thames estuary, with a pier more than a mile long.
A boating lake on the edge of Epping Forest, 'the Forest', where east London couples walked on Saturdays.
In rowing, to miss the stroke or dig the oar too deep, and be knocked off the seat.
A tube of fur or cloth a woman carried in winter to keep both hands warm.
A woman's matching jacket and skirt, her best outdoor clothes.
The meal given after a wedding, whatever the time of day.
Married quickly on a bought licence, without the three weeks of notice read out in church.
Courting; a couple seen out walking together were understood to be serious.
The telephone exchange, where rows of young women at switchboards connected every call by hand.
What the telephone operator said when a caller lifted the receiver, before she connected the call.
A baby's cloth napkins, washed every day and hung up indoors to dry.
The casualty lists: columns of the killed, wounded and missing, printed in the newspapers.
Loans from the public to pay for the war; a touring tank sold them in town squares.
A free school run by the local council, where working people's children went.
A card game for four, played in pairs.
A Scottish dance for couples, marched and turned to a brisk tune.
Writing paper with a black border, used by a family in mourning.
A Methodist or Baptist church; chapel people were strict and close-knit, and everybody knew everybody's business.
Bible classes for children at church or chapel on Sundays, taught by members of the congregation.
The Sunday school's yearly outing for the children, with tea and buns.
The evening service in the Church of England.
The stone vault under a church, where the old tombs are.
The football player in the middle of the front line, whose job is to score.
The three players behind the forwards in the football of the day; the right half played on the right.
The rubber bag inside a leather football that holds the air.
The short cut stalks left standing in a field after the harvest.
Coal miners; here the men of the battalion's company from a northern pit town.
A small iron truck that carried coal along the rails of a mine.
'Come on', as they say it in the north-east of England.
About a thousand infantrymen under a lieutenant-colonel; the unit a soldier belonged to.
One of a battalion's four companies of about two hundred men, lettered A to D.
About twelve battalions with their own guns, some eighteen thousand men, under a general.
The general commanding a brigade, which was three or four battalions.
The officer who ran a battalion's office and paperwork for its commander.
The battalion's office, where its records and orders were kept.
Written orders for stores; nothing was issued in the army without one.
The medical officer: the battalion's doctor.
The officer who read the men's letters and cut out anything of use to the enemy.
Formally accused of breaking army rules, and brought before an officer for punishment.
The small brown book every soldier carried: his record, his pay, and a page for his will.
A printed army card with set phrases; the soldier crossed out the ones that did not apply.
A spell of some days in the trenches before the battalion was relieved.
Out of the trenches for some days, lodged in a village behind the line.
A trench running back from the front line, so men could come and go under cover.
One straight stretch of a trench between two corners, held by a few men.
A shelter dug into the side or floor of a trench, roofed with timber and earth.
The order for every man to man the firestep, armed; given at dawn, at dusk and when attacked.
The strip of open ground between the two front lines, belonging to neither side.
Up out of the trench and over its front bank, to attack across open ground.
With the rifle held slanting across the chest, as men were ordered to advance.
Men sent up the line at night loaded with rations, water, wire or ammunition.
The place behind the line where each night's food and stores were left to be carried up.
The soldier's two-part metal tin, to cook in and eat and drink from.
A small measure of rum, given out before an attack or after a cold night.
The soldier's heavy woollen overcoat, reaching below the knee.
A needle from his 'housewife', the soldier's small roll of needles, thread and buttons.
The small spade and pick every infantryman carried to dig himself cover.
Iron bottles of poison gas dug in under the front bank; opened, the wind carried the cloud across.
A flannel bag soaked in chemicals, worn over the whole head, with a small window; the 1915 gas mask.
A harsh-smelling white powder scattered in trenches and latrines against disease.
Men trained to throw hand grenades, then called bombs; they cleared trenches and cellars.
The British hand grenade from 1915: a ribbed iron egg with a pin and a lever.
The second man of a machine-gun team, who carried the ammunition and changed the drums.
Tins that burned to pour out thick white smoke, lit to hide an attack.
A sham attack, made to draw the enemy's guns and reserves away from the real one.
The main attack; 'the push' was the soldiers' word for a great offensive.
An iron basket or pierced bucket of burning coke, for warmth.
A signaller's small set for sending Morse code down a telephone wire.
A code of short and long signals for each letter, sent by buzzer, lamp or flag.
The soldiers who dug and limed the latrines and kept the camp clean.
A strongpoint built to hold out even when surrounded.
To the depth and pattern the army manual laid down, and no further.
Guns firing single ranging shots to fix their aim on a target before a bombardment.
The army's great camps and offices on the French coast, far behind the fighting.
Back from the front, towards the hospitals and the coast.
Women of the Women's Army Auxiliary Corps: clerks, cooks and drivers in khaki, in France from 1917.
A one-piece dress cut like a coat and buttoned down the front; the WAAC uniform.
Demobilised: released from the army after the war ended.
The German airman in the red aeroplane, who shot down more machines than any other.
The soldiers' name for the twin iron pit towers at Loos, after the bridge in London.
A long double slag heap south of Loos; crassier is the French for a slag heap.
A fortified village and wood north of the Somme front, attacked on 1 July 1916 as a diversion.
The soldiers' name for Foncquevillers, the ruined village behind the British line at Gommecourt.
The Queen Victoria's Rifles, one of the London battalions that attacked at Gommecourt.
The flat, wet country of Belgium around Ypres.
The soldiers' name for Ypres, the Belgian town the British held all through the war.
A ridge and village near Ypres; the battle for it in 1917 was fought in rain and deep mud.
The battle of November 1917, where massed tanks broke the German line; the ground was lost again within a fortnight.
French for 'wines and beers': the sign on a café-bar.
French for 'no good'.
French for 'the war is over'.
Soldiers' French for 'merci beaucoup': thank you very much.
Soldiers' French for 'oeufs', eggs; egg and chips was what every estaminet sold.
Soldiers' French, from 'il n'y en a plus': finished, none left, gone, dead.
Soldiers' French for 'ça ne fait rien': it doesn't matter.
Soldiers' French for 'vin blanc', the cheap white wine sold behind the line.
The soldiers' name for a German, or the Germans.
An early soldiers' name for the Germans, from the French 'Allemand'.
The soldiers' name for Scottish troops.
The ordinary British soldier, from 'Tommy Atkins', the name on the army's sample forms.
The soldiers' name for staff officers and generals, from the gold braid on their caps.
Soldiers' name for men with safe jobs at the base, far behind the line.
German trench-mortar bombs, from 'Minenwerfer': big, slow, and seen coming down.
Soldiers' word for tea, picked up by the old army in India.
Soldiers' word for easy, comfortable or safe.
Soldiers' words for killed.
The first name of the Tank Corps, a branch of the Machine Gun Corps until July 1917.
The steel box built out from each side of a heavy tank, which held her guns and gunners.
One of two men at the back of a heavy tank who worked each track's gears on the driver's signal.
A heavy baulk of timber chained to a stuck tank's tracks, which dragged it under her to give grip.
A great bundle of brushwood bound with chains, dropped into a wide trench so a tank could cross.
Hot flecks of lead and steel thrown about inside a tank when bullets struck her plates outside.
A light, fast tank with a crew of three and four machine guns, first in action in March 1918.
A machine gun of French design, fed by strips or belts of cartridges; the Whippet carried four.
The Tank Corps' own word for a camp where tanks were kept and mended, copied from aerodrome.
A newer heavy tank that one man could drive without gearsmen; it reached France in May 1918.
Soldiers' short word for the heavy guns; in the Tank Corps, the big tanks as against the Whippets.
A mechanic who kept engines running; in the Flying Corps, the man answerable for one aeroplane's engine.
The line an attack sets off from at the fixed minute, often marked on the ground with tape.
The place where the railway stopped behind the front; men, stores and tanks were unloaded there.
A district of Glasgow on the Clyde, full of shipyards.
A town of foundries and chain-makers in the Black Country, west of Birmingham.
Black Country speech for 'you'll'.
Glasgow speech for 'I'd'.
A motor bus of the London General Omnibus Company, the red buses of the London streets.
The steam engines at a pit head that wound the cage of men and coal up and down the shaft.
A steam engine that drove the machine that beat the grain out of the corn at harvest.
The factories filling shells; the explosive turned the women workers' skin yellow and made many ill.
The cinema: silent films, shown with a piano playing.
A flying field with its sheds and huts; what was later called an airfield.
A slow, steady British two-seater aeroplane, used to direct the guns and photograph the German line.
The airmen's rhyming name for the RE8, after a music-hall comedian of the day.
A fast aeroplane with one seat, built to fight other aeroplanes; later called a fighter.
A ring-shaped mounting round the back cockpit that let the gunner swing his gun to any side.
The airmen's name for anti-aircraft guns and their shell bursts, from a music-hall song.
A flight to watch a battery's shells fall and signal each miss until the guns are on the target.
A low flight over an attack to find how far the infantry have got, by their flares.
A flight up and down our own side of the front, watching for German machines.
A loud electric horn; an aeroplane sounded it to ask the infantry below to light their flares.
A coloured flare fired into the air from a brass pistol, used as a signal.
Signalling without wires, by Morse. A machine like the RE8 could send to the guns but not hear them.
A Flying Corps rank for a tradesman in the ranks, about equal to a private.
The varnish painted on an aeroplane's linen skin to tighten and weatherproof it; it smelt of pear drops.
The oil burnt in the spinning rotary engines of many scouts; its smell hung about them.
A small screw fitting that tightens one of the bracing wires of an aeroplane.
The body of an aeroplane.
The metal cover round an aeroplane's engine.
Sheets of glass coated to take a photograph; the air cameras of the time used them, not film.
The light open motor lorry of the Flying Corps, used to carry men and stores.
The captain in charge of a flight, one of the three groups of about six machines in a squadron.
The Flying Corps in Britain; a worn-out airman was posted there to rest and to teach.
Not Yet Diagnosed: what the doctors wrote on the label of a man whose nerves had given way.
The papers' and officers' name for the Germans; to an airman, any enemy machine or the man in it.
A soldier in the ranks, not an officer.
A district of East London. German aeroplanes bombed a school there in June 1917 and killed eighteen children.
A jam: a machine gun stops firing until the gunner finds the fault and clears it.
The handle on the side of a machine gun, pulled back to load it or to clear a jam.
A bullet that burns as it flies, so the gunner can see where his fire is going.
A light machine gun one man could carry, fed from a flat round drum of cartridges on top.
A canvas carrier for the Lewis gun's spare drums of cartridges.
A wall of bursting shells laid down by the guns, often moving forward just ahead of the infantry.
The minute fixed for an attack to begin.
A bend or buttress of earth built into a trench, so no shell or gun could sweep its length.
A small, low fort of thick concrete with slits for machine guns.
A bulge in the front line, open to fire from three sides; here the one round Ypres.
A belt of deep trenches, concrete and wire the Germans built and fell back to early in 1917.
A light gun pulled by horses, firing a shell of about eighteen pounds.
A group of four or six guns and the men who serve them.
Aimed straight at a target the gunners can see, at close range.
Hooking the guns to their horse teams, ready to move off.
A lane worn down below the level of the fields, with a bank on each side.
A soldier of the Royal Engineers: digging, bridges, mines and explosives.
A short trench dug forward from the front line towards the enemy.
A small opening to watch or fire through; a sniper kept his rifle on the enemy's.
The first place behind the line where the wounded were bandaged and sorted.
The army's name for a chaplain.
The star on an officer's cuff or shoulder that shows his rank; a second lieutenant wore one.
The hut where a unit's sergeants ate and spent their evenings, apart from the men and the officers.
The brass letters on a soldier's shoulder strap that named his regiment.
The army's word for any note or written report.
Tinned corned beef, the soldier's standing ration.
The explosive that fired British cartridges and shells; its smoke had a sharp, sweetish smell.
Having lice. In the trenches nearly every man had them.
A weaving-shed overlooker, who kept the looms running and the weavers at their work.
Northern speech for 'nothing'.
Northern speech for 'stop it'.
The early morning shift at a pit.
An oil lamp with a glass chimney, which the wind cannot blow out.
The soldiers' name for the Germans, or a German, from 1917.
German for 'comrade'; what a German soldier called out when he gave himself up.
French for 'no fighting'.
A military policeman, from the red cover on his cap.
The Australians, a name they gave themselves in 1917.
A German shell 5.9 inches across, and the gun that fired it; heavy enough to wreck a trench.
A wound bad enough to get a man sent home to Britain, and not bad enough to kill him.
Lost his nerve; was frightened.
Soldiers' and airmen's word for an attack or a battle.
The sheath a man's bayonet hung in at his belt.
The second line of trenches, a short way behind the front line.
Work parties: the digging, carrying and cleaning that filled a soldier's days out of battle.
A soldier's lodging behind the line: a barn, a loft or a room in a village house.
The two-wheeled cart a gun or wagon was hooked to, for hauling by horses.
Calls every man's name from the list; no answer means killed, wounded or missing.
About fifty men under a junior officer, in four sections.
The smallest body of infantry: about ten men under a corporal.
The lowest rank of officer; he commanded a platoon.
The government department in London that ran the army and sent out the news of casualties.
The soldier's khaki uniform jacket.
The Devonshire Regiment, the county's own infantry.
A local panel that heard men's claims to be let off conscription, for their work, health or conscience.
The regular officers' sneer at wartime officers from clerks' and tradesmen's families.
A private soldier of the cavalry.
The headquarters next above the battalion; a brigade was four battalions, three from 1918.
The regiment's base at home, where recruits were trained and sent out to fill the gaps.
The soldiers' name for heavy German shells that burst in a cloud of black smoke.
The military police, from the red covers on their caps.
The soldiers' name for a second lieutenant, who wore a single star, or pip, as his badge.
The soldiers' and newspapers' word for a conscientious objector, a man who refused to fight.
Soldiers' slang: was killed, or badly hit.
French for eggs, said something like 'uh'; the soldiers said 'oofs'.
French for 'thief'.
French: 'my brave lads'; what French country people called the soldiers.
French: 'It is straight.'
Devon speech: 'you'm' is 'you are', 'she'm' is 'she is'.
A female sheep.
A male sheep that has been castrated.
Young cows that have not yet had a calf.
A wire noose set on an animal's path to catch it: the poacher's tool.
A pair; said of game birds or animals that have been shot or caught.
The gamekeeper: the man a landowner paid to rear his game birds and catch poachers.
The chief landowner of a country parish, who owned most of its farms and cottages.
A village and the country round it that share one church.
The room in a big country house where the sporting guns were kept and cleaned.
A small flat bottle of spirits, carried in the pocket out hunting.
The servant who looked after the horses at a big house.
The gates at the foot of a big house's drive, with the gatekeeper's cottage beside them.
The rough string used to tie sheaves of corn; a farm used it for everything.
A horse-drawn machine that cut the corn and tied it in sheaves, dropping them in rows.
In England, any grain crop: wheat, barley or oats.
Short hooked blades, held in one hand, for cutting corn.
Cut sheaves of corn stood on end together in the field to dry; to stook is to set them up.
The feast a farmer gave his workers when the last of the harvest was in.
The big boxed machine, driven by a steam engine, that beat the grain out of the corn.
A steam engine on wheels that hauled loads along the road and drove farm machines.
The two poles a horse stands between to pull a cart.
The long cut a plough opens and turns over in the soil.
The strap round a horse's belly that holds its saddle or pack on.
A brown horse with a black mane and tail, bred for riding after hounds.
Makes the soft low neigh a horse gives in greeting.
A heap of potatoes or roots kept in the field through winter under straw and earth.
Black birds of the crow kind that nest together in treetops; their colony is a rookery.
A young cock, the male farmyard fowl.
A small wood.
A tall coarse fern that covers moors and hillsides.
A woman of the Women's Land Army, sent to do farm work in place of the men at war.
Trousers ending at the knee, worn with leggings; a startling thing on a woman in 1917.
A man who drove and looked after a farm's cart horses.
The horse and cart that took goods, post and passengers between a village and its market town.
A yellow West Country fruit loaf, coloured and flavoured with saffron.
A West Country pastry case baked with meat and potato inside, made to be carried to work.
A little tea, sugar or tobacco wrapped in a twisted scrap of paper.
A thin cotton cloth, used in the kitchen to cover and strain food.
A small silver coin, six pennies; a private soldier's pay was two of them a day.

glossary.term: finds you as it leaves us
glossary.means: A stock opening for letters of the time: I hope you are as well as we are.
A man's first name; an officer called his men by their surnames only.
An outhouse with a boiler for hot water, where clothes, and muddy men, were washed.
A kitchen sideboard with open shelves above for the plates.
A lidded brass pan of hot coals on a long handle, slid between the sheets to warm a bed.
The neat, sloping handwriting taught in schools.
Two weeks.
A house drew its window blinds in daylight to show there was a death in the family.
The roofed gate into a churchyard.
The notice of a coming marriage, read out in church on three Sundays beforehand.
Courting: seen about together as a couple.
29 September, a quarter day, when rents fell due and farm workers were hired.
25 March, a quarter day, when farm rents fell due and tenancies changed hands.
2 November, the church's day of prayer for the dead.
The main body of a church, where the people sit.
The largest, deepest bell in a church tower; it rings last in each round.
The smallest, highest bell in a tower; it rings first.
The thick woolly grip woven into a bell rope, where the ringer's hands take hold.
A long set piece of ringing, with every bell in the tower rung in changing order.
About three-quarters of an hour of unbroken ringing, 1,260 changes, rung to mark an occasion.
The tower's record of the ringing done there, and who rang.
A set pattern for ringing five bells in changing order, with the tenor keeping time behind.
The orders the bells are rung in, one after another, no order repeated; ringers learn them by heart.
The leader of a church's band of bell-ringers.
Rung with a leather pad on one side of the clapper, so alternate strokes sound dull; rung for the dead.
The long, low, deafening room of a cotton mill where hundreds of looms ran side by side.
The machine that weaves cloth; a weaver minded several at once, on her feet all day.
The pointed wooden holder that carries the thread to and fro across a loom, very fast.
A pick is one thread laid across the cloth; weavers were paid by the number woven.
The narrow gangway between rows of looms; the weavers who shared one were close friends.
The part of a cotton mill where raw cotton was combed out; dusty work, done mostly by women.
Talking with big, silent mouth shapes and reading lips, as weavers did in the noise of the looms.
A man paid a few pence a week to wake mill workers by rattling their windows with a pole.
The small white hoods on gas lamps that glowed when lit; mills and houses were lit by gas.
The mill's steam hooter, which called the workers in each morning and sent them home.
Plain, cheap cotton cloth, the kind the Lancashire mills wove by the mile.
The Co-operative Society shop, owned by its customers; most mill families bought their groceries there.
A small plot of rented ground, away from the house, where a working man grew vegetables.
A big metal tub built over a small fire, for boiling the family's washing.
Strong-smelling red soap that killed germs; every kitchen and washhouse smelt of it.
The cheapest and most popular cigarettes of the time, sold five to a paper packet.
A cigarette.
Boiled sweets with a sharp chemical smell of pears.
The church holiday seven weeks after Easter; in Lancashire the great holiday of early summer.
Lancashire for a member of your own family: 'our Jack' is your brother Jack.
Mother, in Lancashire speech.
Lancashire for 'anything'.
Lucky, and not deserving it.
The brown official envelope in which the army told a family their man was dead or missing.
A job judged too useful at home, such as gas or munitions work, for the man to be called up.
Been sent his call-up notice; from 1916 men were ordered into the army at eighteen.
Men who signed on under Lord Derby's scheme in late 1915, to be called up later when wanted.
Slatted wooden boards laid along the bottom of a trench or across mud, to walk on.
A pit dug under the trench floor for water to drain into.
Extra trenches dug close behind the front line to hold the men waiting to attack.
In 1918, the thinly held front strip of posts, meant to slow an attack, not stop it.
The battalion doctor's dugout just behind the line, where the wounded were first bandaged.
A batch of new men sent out from home to fill a battalion's losses.
The company's field kitchens on wheels, with a fire and boilers for stew and tea.
A large iron cooking pot with a lid; the company's stew and tea came up the line in them.
Tinned corned beef, the soldier's everyday meat.
Soldiers' word for jam; the army's was nearly always plum and apple.
The army doctor's laxative pill, handed out for almost every complaint.
The form a recruit signed and swore to on joining, giving his age.
The two tags on a cord round a soldier's neck, stamped with his name, number and religion.
The packet of bandage every soldier carried sewn inside his tunic.
Long strips of cloth wound round the leg from ankle to knee.
The soldier's harness of woven belts and straps that carried his pouches, pack and water bottle.
A waterproof sheet to lie on, also worn as a cape in rain.
The steel helmet, first issued to British soldiers early in 1916.
The official code word for the poison gas cylinders at Loos; 'gas' was not to be said.
A mining town in northern France; the British attacked there on 25 September 1915, using gas.
Stay level with the men on either side of you, in a straight line.
At zero hour, the exact minute fixed for an attack to begin.
Shells that fail to go off.
Men sent out into no man's land at night to put up or mend the barbed wire.
Men who carried messages on foot when the telephone wire was cut.
Soldiers of the Royal Engineers, who built the bridges, roads and defences.
No falling back. In army speech, to retire was to retreat.
The British name for the deep German steel helmet, which came down over the ears and neck.
The Royal Flying Corps, the army's aeroplanes and airmen.
The stout old general who commanded the French army from 1914 to 1916.
The King's paper that made a man an officer.
The officer in charge of a battalion's food, clothing and stores.
Wheat or oats still uncut in the field. In England 'corn' meant any grain.
A sweepstake: each man pays to pick a date, and the right guess takes all the money.
French for 'eggs and chips': the sign outside every café that fed British soldiers.
French soldiers. The word means 'hairy ones', and they called themselves by it.
The town hall of a French village.
German for the local commander's office in a town the German army occupied.
French for 'the English'. To the French every British soldier was one.
Australian soldiers.
Long-serving soldiers who had been in the army since before the war.
The soldiers' name for Étaples, the great British base camp on the French coast.
A light, fast German shell that arrived before you heard it coming.
The shelling each side gave the other at about the same hour every morning.
Pretending to be ill to get out of duty.
Picking the lice, called chats, out of the seams of your shirt.
The wall of coal at the far end of the workings, where the men cut it.
Pit word for the food a man takes to work, eaten where he stands.
A fathom is six feet; pit depths were measured in them. Two hundred fathoms is 1,200 feet.
The lift in a pit shaft that carries men and coal tubs up and down.
The tall frames over a pit shaft, with wheels that wind the cage up and down.
The pitman who sets and fires the explosive charges that bring down coal or stone.
In a pit, the roof coming down, often burying the men under it.
The hill of waste stone tipped beside a pit; they often smouldered inside for years.
The hut at the pit top where each man collected his safety lamp before going down.
The engine and ropes that drag the coal tubs along the roadways of a pit.
A part of a pit no longer worked, where bad air and gas collect.
The tunnels and cut-out places of a mine.
The pit's steam hooter, sounded for the change of shift, and for an accident.
Coal miners; a pit is a colliery.
At the surface of a pit, as against underground.
Moving belts at the pit top where stone was picked out of the coal by hand.
Pit talk: the rock overhead creaking and shifting, as it does before it comes down.
The pitman who cuts the coal at the face: the hardest and best-paid work underground.
Setting wooden props and frames to hold up the roof and sides of a tunnel or dugout.
Upright timbers set to hold up the roof of a mine or dugout.
A machine with a toothed wheel that cuts under the coal; it makes a great clatter.
A pit entered by a sloping tunnel from the hillside, with no shaft.
A seam is a layer of coal in the rock, from a foot to six feet thick.
The gas left in a pit after an explosion: mostly carbon monoxide, deadly, with no smell.
The coal owners: the companies and families who owned the pits and set the men's pay.
The lodge was the pit's branch of the miners' union; its committee were the men elected to run it.
The union lodge's great painted silk banner, carried at galas and at a member's funeral.
The union's hall in a pit village, for meetings, the reading room and the lodge's business.
The colliery office's slips showing what a pitman earned in the fortnight, and what was stopped.
Men in work marked as too needed at home for the army to take them.
A north-east word for a pigeon loft: a shed where a man keeps his racing birds.
North-east word for father.
North-east and Scots word for a child.
Tyneside speech for going.
A man from Tyneside; in the army, any north-east pitman.
North-country and Scots word for a stream.
The rows: the terraces of pit cottages owned by the colliery, where the pitmen's families live.
The Co-operative shop, owned by its members; a pit village bought nearly everything there.
Dark peppermint boiled sweets, a Tyneside favourite.
Timing racing pigeons home: each bird's leg ring goes into a sealed clock as it lands.
A pigeon's colouring: blue-grey, with dark chequered markings on the wings.
Men who keep and race homing pigeons.
A game of throwing iron rings at a pin set in clay, played for money in pit villages.
North-east word for the outdoor lavatories at the bottom of the yards.
Small outbuildings in the yards, each with a boiler, where the family's washing was done.
A house drew its blinds when one of the family had died.
A boiler built into the brickwork beside the kitchen fire, for heating water.
A machine with two rollers and a handle for wringing the water out of washing.
The working men's club: the village's own bar, run by its members.
Everyday word for tobacco.
Coal washed up on the beach, gathered free for the fire.
The Newcastle Daily Journal, a north-east newspaper that printed the casualty lists.
The Daily Herald, a labour newspaper that took the working man's side.
The House of Commons, in Parliament.
Split peas boiled to a soft paste, eaten cold with ham in the north-east.
A seaside town on the Northumberland coast, a short train ride from Newcastle.
The collector who called at the door each week for the pennies of burial insurance.
A small plot of land, enough for hens, a pig and vegetables.
An open motor coach with rows of seats, hired for day trips.
A wind-up machine with a horn, for playing records.
Hard white beef fat, used for puddings.
Twenty shillings made a pound. An infantry private was paid one shilling a day.
The Military Service Act of 1916, which made single men of 18 to 41 liable for the army.
Labourers who dug canals, railways and tunnels with pick and shovel.
London's deep underground railway, bored through clay.
A coal-mining valley in South Wales.
A Cornishman's friendly name for another man.
A Welshman's friendly name for another man.
The Welsh name for Wales.
A short straight stretch of fire trench between two bends, held by a few men.
The army's corps of builders, miners and signallers; its privates were called sappers.
A steam or sulphur chamber for killing the lice in uniforms.
A trench where men are gathered just before they attack.
The senior sergeant of a company; he kept its roll and its discipline.
A section was about ten men under a corporal, who lived and fought together.
Four battalions together, about four thousand men.
The lowest rank above private, with one stripe on the sleeve.
A canvas bag slung from the shoulder, for rations and small kit.
A soldier's waterproof sheet, to lie on or to wear as a cape.
The early gas mask: a chemical-soaked flannel bag over the whole head, with a small window.
A message written on a slip of thin paper.
Soldiers' name for a great attack; in 1916, the one coming on the Somme.
Over the sandbags of the parapet and out to attack: the same as over the top.
The army's horse-shoer, who also put down horses too badly hurt to save.
A horse's or mule's right front leg.
A hot, wet dressing bound on to draw out a swelling or infection.
The room at a barracks where men under arrest were held.
A small charge fired underground to wreck an enemy tunnel without breaking the surface.
The electric wires run from a charge back to the man who fires it.
A listening instrument: two discs pressed to the ground, with earpieces, to hear digging.
The box with a plunger handle that sends the electric current to fire a mine.
Soldiers' name for a heavy German shell that burst in a cloud of black smoke.
Soldiers' name for a general or senior staff officer, from the gold braid on his cap.
Soldiers' name for a lance-corporal.
French for a brewery.
French for a coal pit; the pits round Loos went by number, as Fosse 8.
French for a pit's slag heap; the word was on the army's maps at Loos.
French for a grocer's shop.
The sign over the door: the Estaminet of the Good Corner, a common name for a French village bar.

glossary.term: Oeufs et frites, Vin blanc, Bière
glossary.means: Eggs and chips, white wine, beer: all a village estaminet sold, and all a soldier wanted.
French for good evening.
French for good night.
French for good day, sir; said to any stranger in a village street.
Proper French for very good, and thank you very much.
French for well, look: said on seeing somebody you did not expect.
The French name for the Germans, and not a kind one; British officers and newspapers took it up.
French for it's the war: said with a shrug of every shortage, loss and hardship.
French for till Sunday: a goodbye that fixes the next meeting.
French for water of life: a strong clear spirit a farmer made from his own fruit.
French for thank you kindly.
French for you will write to me.
French for she is pretty.

glossary.term: Ici tout va bien. Il neige encore
glossary.means: French for all is well here, it is still snowing.
French for good luck.
French for my little one: what an older woman calls a young man she is fond of.
French for it is finished. The soldiers' napoo meant much the same.
French for England.
French for hold fast.
French for after the war: what every plan and promise in France waited on.
